title: PM Shehbaz arrives in Peshawar for apex committee meeting, security briefing
description: Prime minister is also expected to address a grand jirga during his visit
content: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif arrived in Peshawar on Thursday to attend an apex committee meeting on the law and order situation in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), with a major development package for the province also expected to be announced during his visit, sources said. According to sources, the prime minister was scheduled to receive a briefing on the security situation in the province and participate in the apex committee meeting, which will discuss peace and stability in K-P. Members of the provincial advisory council arrived at Governor House to meet PM Shehbaz, while relevant officials of the Regional Development Secretariat were also present there, sources added. The prime minister is also expected to address a grand jirga during his visit. The visit marked Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s first trip to Peshawar since the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11, which resulted in the suspension of the provincial government led by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). The federal government imposed the measures under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, citing a deterioration in the security situation, an increase in terrorist attacks, and what it described as the provincial administration’s failure to cooperate effectively in counter-terrorism efforts. Under the new arrangement, executive powers were transferred to Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, assisted by an advisory council, while emergency measures were imposed in 12 districts. The PTI rejected the federal government’s position and opposed the move. The decision followed weeks of tensions between the Centre and the PTI-led provincial administration, alongside negotiations aimed at securing agreement on a joint strategy against terrorism. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said the federal government had made repeated attempts to obtain the provincial government’s cooperation before resorting to the constitutional measures. Prime Minister Shehbaz also said the government had been left with no alternative after negotiations failed to produce an agreement. The first provincial Apex Committee meeting following the imposition of governor’s rule was held at Governor House on October 12, co-chaired by Governor Kundi and Interior Minister Naqvi. The meeting reviewed the security situation and counter-terrorism measures, with participants agreeing to strengthen the police and Counter-Terrorism Department through additional equipment, vehicles, weapons and manpower. The forum also called for coordinated action by relevant institutions to restore peace and improve law and order.

title: Iran's IRGC Navy says seven vessels hit, warns US of wider response
description: Trump says US ‘not negotiating’ with Iran, something will happen ‘fairly soon’
content: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said on Thursday that four vessels involved in illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were simultaneously hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday. The IRGC added that three more vessels collided with mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned the US military that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. Trump says US ‘not negotiating’ with Iran, something will happen ‘fairly soon’ US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that Washington is not negotiating with Iran, adding that “something one way or the other” will happen “fairly soon.” “No, I think we’re not negotiating,” Trump told reporters upon returning from a rally in South Carolina. “We are going to have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon.” “Most people seem to think it’s after the election, and we’re going to see what happens,” he added. Earlier, during his remarks at the rally, Trump said the US could end its war with Iran now but wants to ensure that the outcome is lasting. “It’ll end very soon. We could leave now, but we want to make sure it lasts for a long time,” he said. He claimed the US had defeated Iran militarily and financially, adding that Tehran would “never have a nuclear weapon.” Read: CDF Munir meets senior Iranian officials as Pakistan continues diplomatic push to end conflict His remarks came as The New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries have developed plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, citing US officials and others briefed on the deliberations. The report said it is far from certain that Trump will approve the strikes, noting that he has repeatedly vetoed plans to return to major combat this year. A White House official told the Times that the administration does not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist.” US, Israel develop plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections: report The US and Israeli militaries have developed plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections, with preparations advancing for a potential short but intensive campaign, The New York Times reported on Wednesday. Citing US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations, the newspaper reported that the two militaries have stepped up exercises, including flights over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers. Potential targets could include Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile and drone arsenal, and energy infrastructure, according to the report. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss possible new strikes, the newspaper reported. Plans to target Iran’s nuclear program could include a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried site, according to the Times. The report said it is far from certain that Trump will approve the strikes, noting that he has repeatedly vetoed plans to return to major combat this year. Iran threatens to target US political assets, infrastructure if new war erupts Iran would consider US political assets and infrastructure belonging to countries participating in a new war against it as “legitimate targets” if Iranian officials were assassinated or civilians killed, a senior Iranian security official warned on Wednesday, according to the Fars News Agency. The Tehran-based official said Iran assumes that the US and Israel will launch another attack and considers Washington’s diplomatic gestures “unreliable.” The official said this perception had intensified following remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens, which Tehran interpreted as giving a historical and civilisational justification for Washington’s war against Iran. According to the official, Iranian political and intellectual leaders have increasingly concluded that US Middle East policy is directed by Israel, which they believe is preventing Washington from pursuing a diplomatic solution. The official claimed that Israel takes priority in US President Donald Trump’s regional policies. Read more: US-Iran talks continue through Pakistan, Qatar: Iranian FM Iran already considers itself at war with the US and views Washington’s economic and naval blockade, along with restrictions on Iranian airspace, as a continuation of the military aggression that began on February 28, the official said. He added that growing pressure from different segments of Iranian society was pushing authorities toward “decisive action” to break the blockade under what Tehran considers its right to self-defence. According to the official, Iran has instructed various operational units that, in the event of another large-scale conflict involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, it would consider US political assets and the infrastructure of countries participating in the war as “legitimate targets.” The warning comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over the US naval blockade and restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Two killed, eight injured in attack on airport in Saudi oil city Dammam
description: US orders some diplomats, family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes
content: Two people were killed, and eight were injured in an attack on Wednesday evening on King Fahd International Airport in Saudi Arabia's eastern oil city of Dammam, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Thursday. Those killed were a Saudi citizen and an Indian national, the authority said. The injuries ranged from minor to serious. Damage was being assessed, it added. Airport operations had resumed, and air traffic had returned to normal, the authority said. Meanwhile, The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia and plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters. The order came amid attacks in Saudi Arabia that killed at least one person and injured eight others at a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people were killed in a drone attack on an oil field. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a post on X that the department ordered the departure of "non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only" amid attacks by the Houthis in Yemen on civilian targets in the country. Washington had returned some diplomatic personnel to the region in recent months after many were pulled out when Tehran launched attacks on US facilities after the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February. Read: 2 killed after Saudi air defenses intercept drone targeting Aramco oil field "Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott said. Four US officials told Reuters that US missions in other Gulf states would also be ordering family members to leave. Pigott did not address changes to other missions outside Saudi Arabia. The latest withdrawals follow an escalation of the fighting in Yemen, opening another front ​in the regional conflict triggered by the US-Israeli ⁠war on Iran. The wider conflict has snarled global energy trade and hurt Gulf economies. Houthis strike Yemen’s Al-Rayyan airport for fourth time in hours: Army Yemen’s army said on early Thursday that the Houthi group targeted Al-Rayyan International Airport in the city of Mukalla, the capital of Hadramout province, for the fourth time within hours. The army’s official spokesman, Maj. Gen. Majed al-Nuzaili, said the “Houthi terrorist militia targeted Al-Rayyan International Airport in Mukalla for the fourth time,” according to September Net, a website affiliated with Yemen’s Defence Ministry. In a statement, Nuzaili said that “targeting airports aims to impose a blockade on the Yemeni people,” the website reported. Al-Rayyan is one of Yemen’s most important civilian airports, serving millions of people in Hadramout and other provinces. The Houthis had not immediately commented on the attack. Two killed after Saudi air defenses intercept drone targeting Aramco oil field Two foreign nationals were killed and two others injured Wednesday after Saudi air defenses intercepted a drone attempting to target a facility at Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oil field in the country’s Eastern Province, the Energy Ministry said. A ministry official said Saudi air defenses intercepted the drone as it attempted to strike one of the facilities at the oil field, according to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA). Debris from the interception sparked a fire in a vehicle belonging to a contractor working at the field, outside the facility’s perimeter, the official said. Read more: Oil rises as US orders diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating tensions The incident did not affect operations at the oil field, the ministry added. The official identified the two fatalities as Philippine and Nepalese nationals, while the injured were Pakistani and Indian nationals. Relevant authorities responded to the incident and took the necessary measures, according to the statement.

title: PTI lawmakers back talks to restore K-P govt
description: Internal rifts spill into public amid calls for negotiations
content: The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) parliamentary party in the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Assembly has backed talks with the government and the establishment to restore the provincial government and secure the release of detained Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, non-functional Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and other cabinet members and lawmakers. The lawmakers urged the party's central leadership to ensure the parliamentary party was represented in any negotiations. The PTI parliamentary party held an online meeting on Wednesday to discuss the situation following the imposition of governor's rule and emergency measures. Participants expressed concern that the party leadership had not consulted them on its future strategy, sources said. They agreed on the need for a joint approach to address the political situation. Meanwhile, differences within the party have surfaced over the K-P chief ministership, party leadership and fears of a possible forward bloc, prompting party chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan to ask leaders to stop publicly criticising one another. PTI Chief Whip Amir Dogar, meanwhile, signalled the possible resumption of talks with the government, while dismissing the reports of any divisions within the parliamentary party and insisting that opposition leaders Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas enjoyed its full confidence. Speaking to The Express Tribune, Dogar said party's founder Imran Khan had entrusted responsibilities of the opposition leaders in the National Assembly and the Senate to Achakzai and Abbas, respectively, therefore, no change in the opposition leadership could be made without Khan's consent. Dogar also maintained that Sohail Afridi was the party's constitutional and lawful chief minister in K-P and enjoyed Khan's confidence. "Any attempt to replace him without approval would amount to stabbing the party in the back," he said. There were reports of internal tensions in the PTI following the imposition of an emergency and governor's rule in K-P after the opposition's talks with the government collapsed earlier this month. Dogar, however, expressed the hope that negotiations with the government would resume in the coming days. Dogar spoke against the backdrop of a purported audio recording of former K-P chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur criticising the party's Secretary General Salman Akram Raja over his mishandling of the party's affairs that contributed to the K-P governor's rule as well as the party's present predicament. Gandapur reportedly demanded that Raja delete his recent social media post, apologise and substantiate his allegations. He also questioned Raja's claims about lawmakers allegedly planning to announce a provincial president and a new candidate for chief ministership without Khan's approval. In his post, Raja had warned that the party's unity was under attack by "undemocratic decision-makers". He alleged that a group had severed contact with Afridi and his team, paving the way for an emergency and governor's rule. He urged party members not to heed to conspiracy claims before an investigation. Raja also maintained that Junaid Akbar remained the PTI provincial president, while Ali Asghar Khan was serving as acting president in Akbar's absence. He said Afridi continued to hold the chief minister's office under the Constitution and the law. Gandapur objected to Raja's remarks, including his reference to "snakes and snails", saying such language insulted lawmakers who had stood by Khan for decades. Former minister Aftab Alam and other lawmakers also urged Raja to consult the provincial parliamentary party before commenting on sensitive matters. Speaking by telephone to The Express Tribune, Gohar said he had spoken to Gandapur, Sheikh Waqas Akram, Ali Asghar Khan and Raja, and asked them to refrain from issuing statements against one another. He insisted that the party's provincial lawmakers had neither violated party policy nor intended to do so. Gohar reiterated that Afridi was, and would remain, the PTI's chief minister in K-P. Dogar, meanwhile, said the party remained committed to negotiations despite "unprecedented oppression", adding that more than 10 PTI members of the National Assembly were in jail.

title: Balochistan division imperative: Bugti
description: Seeks stronger local govts, increased resource allocations
content: Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti has called for a review of the country's administrative structure, citing the province's vast geographical expanse and governance challenges. He said additional administrative units, stronger local governments and a revised resource-sharing framework were needed to improve public service delivery in the province. Speaking at a national dialogue on administrative reorganisation and the creation of new provinces in the country, the chief minister said governing a vast province like Balochistan solely from Quetta posed significant administrative challenges. He called for a review of the country's administrative structure, governance models and the question of establishing new provinces. Bugti welcomed the ongoing national debate on governance reforms, describing it as a positive development. However, he said discussions on such important issues should not remain confined to seminars and hotels but should be taken to parliament, where broader political consensus could be developed. The chief minister said it was necessary to assess whether the Westminster-style democratic system was delivering the desired results to citizens and whether existing administrative and territorial arrangements were creating obstacles to efficient governance and service delivery. He noted that some of the challenges attributed to governance systems may stem from the current administrative divisions themselves. Highlighting the unique geographical realities of Balochistan, Bugti compared the province's vastness with other parts of the country. He said a journey across Punjab from the Wagah border to the southern district of Rajanpur takes six to seven hours, whereas travelling from one point to another within a single district of Balochistan can take up to ten hours. This, he said, illustrated the scale of the province's administrative challenges and underscored the need for reforms tailored to local realities. Emphasising the importance of political unity, the chief minister said meaningful administrative reforms could only be implemented through broad-based consensus among political stakeholders. While seminars and public discussions played an important role in generating awareness, he maintained that practical solutions would emerge only when political parties engaged in serious deliberations within parliament. Bugti argued that Balochistan required not only additional provinces or administrative units but also a more efficient provincial administrative structure capable of addressing public needs effectively. Referring to an incident during his tenure as interior minister, he recalled a suicide attack near a shrine in the remote Sarona area of Khuzdar district that claimed multiple lives. He said criticism had arisen over the delayed arrival of the deputy commissioner at the site, but the official had needed nearly nine hours to travel from the district headquarters to the scene. According to Bugti, the incident highlighted the challenges posed by vast distances and the limitations of the existing administrative framework. The chief minister also called for a broader approach to resource allocation under the National Finance Commission (NFC) Award.

title: Supreme Court rules on repeated service litigation
description: Justice Ayesha faults railways over promotion disputes
content: The Supreme Court has ruled that government departments must avoid unnecessary litigation in service matters, stressing that public authorities should resolve employees' grievances internally in accordance with settled law instead of allowing disputes to repeatedly return to the courts. "A government department must not function as a compulsive litigant, allowing institutional passivity to repeatedly drag settled controversies back into the courts, leaving civil servants in prolonged uncertainty while wasting public funds and consuming precious judicial time over issues already resolved," says a seven-page judgment authored by Justice Ayesha Malik. The Supreme Court division bench, led by Justice Ayesha Malik, set aside a Federal Service Tribunal decision concerning the promotion of Pakistan Railways employees. The judgment observed that, as a public authority and state institution, the Railways department was expected to act as a model employer toward its officers. Service jurisprudence required public employers to conduct their internal affairs with probity and administrative responsibility, ensuring that settled service conditions remained stable and were not undermined by administrative indecision. The court said that a corresponding responsibility rested on civil servants themselves. As state officers entrusted with public responsibilities, they were expected to demonstrate selflessness, administrative restraint and institutional loyalty, giving priority to the public interest rather than exploiting administrative uncertainty for personal gain. It observed that employees who entered service, completed probation and advanced through regular promotions under an established departmental practice could not seek to overturn that framework at a later stage merely because a different interpretation of the rules offered them a personal advantage. "The pursuit of personal ambition must always remain subordinate to the overarching duty owed to the State," the judgment stated, adding that civil servants had a responsibility to preserve the stability, predictability and operational harmony of state institutions. The court noted that the prolonged dispute between administrative practice and statutory probation rules originated from the Railways department's longstanding reliance on merit in the Central Superior Services (CSS) examination at the time of initial induction. That approach developed into an established departmental practice governing seniority over several decades and was also recognised by the Supreme Court, according to the judgment. The court said the history of the dispute highlighted a fundamental requirement of good governance: public institutions must learn from recurring litigation and develop a culture of administrative finality. Where an administrative practice had repeatedly been tested and upheld by the courts, a responsible public authority was required to apply the settled legal position internally rather than treating every representation as a fresh controversy. The judgment observed that the railways had been fully aware that its longstanding practice, based on CSS examination merit, had received judicial affirmation. It was therefore under a positive administrative obligation to decide the employees' representations in accordance with the law. "Instead, it sat in silence and failed to decide the representations," the court said. By failing to resolve the departmental appeal on established legal principles, the department encouraged avoidable litigation and forced the courts to reconsider a controversy that should have been laid to rest, it added. The judgment emphasised that timely internal resolution of service grievances was essential not only to protect employees from prolonged uncertainty but also to prevent the waste of public funds and judicial resources. Public authorities, it said, should exercise proactive leadership and settle disputes administratively when the applicable legal position was already clear. The court underscored that both government departments and civil servants had institutional responsibilities: departments must act consistently with settled law, while employees must respect established service frameworks and place public interest above individual advantage.

title: Courts paralysed after judge assault
description: Lawyers, clerks and judicial staff staged separate protests
content: Judicial proceedings at Rawalpindi's Judicial Complex and district courts were disrupted on Tuesday as lawyers, their clerks and judicial staff staged separate protests following an alleged attack on Civil Judge Malik Ali Miran inside his chamber. On the appeal of the District Bar Association, lawyers observed a complete strike and boycotted court proceedings, while judicial staff also stopped work in protest over the incident. The protests prompted heightened security at the Judicial Complex and the old district courts. Additional police personnel were deployed to deal with any possible confrontation between the two sides. Visitors were allowed into the Judicial Complex only after strict checking at the main entrances. Judicial staff and lawyers' clerks and assistants held separate rallies inside the Judicial Complex. Judicial staff chanted slogans against terrorism and hooliganism, while lawyers' clerks protested against what they described as intimidation and the registration of a false case. The Bar Clerks Association expressed full support for the lawyers and the District Bar Association, condemning the terrorism-related case as retaliatory and fabricated. It demanded the withdrawal of the FIR and warned that daily protests would continue if the case was not withdrawn. An FIR was registered against seven lawyers, including Aslam Khan Niazi, on the complaint of the judge's reader, Tahir Abbas Shah. The case includes charges relating to terrorism, assault and attempted murder. No lawyer had been arrested, and the FIR was sealed. District Bar Association President Malik Sajid Mahmood and Secretary Qamarul Haq Niazi said the arrest of any lawyer would have serious consequences, declaring that the arrest of a lawyer was a red line for the bar. They said the lawyers were willing to negotiate and resolve the matter through dialogue but would not be blackmailed. They also called on judges to correct their conduct. Judges remained silent publicly but reportedly observed an unofficial strike, remaining in their chambers instead of hearing cases. On their instructions, court staff wore black armbands and held a protest rally inside the Judicial Complex, raising slogans over the incident. Court staff returned to their duties in courtrooms after 1pm, before the end of the court day, and the process for filing new cases was reopened. However, hearings in cases scheduled for the morning had largely been adjourned, with fresh dates given to litigants. The courts had become largely empty of visitors after 9.30am. The authorised authority of the Lahore High Court also took notice of the incident. During high-level consultations between the bar and the bench, it was decided that the matter would be resolved through dialogue. Details of FIR According to the complainant, during court hours, Aslam Niazi and Muhammad Farooq Aslam attempted to enter the judge's chamber along with other lawyers. When they were stopped, they allegedly used abusive language, engaged in physical altercations and forced their way inside. Court staff subsequently entered the chamber as well. The FIR alleges that Aslam Niazi verbally abused the civil judge and loudly questioned why an application against him had been accepted. The judge reportedly replied that he had decided the application in accordance with the law and that an appeal could be filed against the decision. The complainant alleged that Aslam Niazi then threatened the judge with serious consequences and struck him on the head with a glass, hitting him above the left eye.

title: Governor halts supply of hazardous wheat
description: Inquiry finds flood-damaged grain at Azakhel godown unfit for human consumption
content: A high-level meeting chaired by Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Wednesday reviewed an inquiry into the supply of substandard and potentially hazardous wheat from the Azakhel wheat godown to flour mills across the province. The Governor Inspection Team presented its detailed findings during the session. Team Chairman Mukhtiar Ahmad informed the governor that the team had thoroughly inspected the sprawling 150-kanal facility at Azakhel. Six godowns located in two blocks of the complex were found to have been inundated by floodwater. Samples of the damaged wheat were dispatched to the Pakistan Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (PCSIR) laboratory for analysis. The laboratory report declared the flood-affected grain harmful to human health and unfit for human consumption. According to the inquiry, critical protective measures to shield the godown from floodwater had never been implemented. Despite repeated flood alerts issued by the Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA), authorities failed to adopt even basic precautionary steps. After the flooding occurred, the Food Department neglected to constitute a technical assessment committee to evaluate the quality and safety of the stored wheat. The report explicitly recommended disciplinary action against the officers found responsible for this negligence. Governor Kundi questioned why, despite the site's history of repeated flooding, a proper protective wall had never been constructed around the godown. Officials briefed him that existing gaps and holes in the incomplete barrier allowed rainwater and floodwater to pour directly into the storage blocks, spoiling large quantities of wheat. Further discrepancies came to light: the Food Department's official stock records contained no entry acknowledging the flood-damaged wheat, and no scientific testing of the affected stocks had been carried out by the department itself prior to the Governor Inspection Team's intervention. In clear and firm directions, Governor Faisal Karim Kundi ordered an immediate halt to the supply of any wheat deemed hazardous to health from the Azakhel facility to flour mills. He emphasized the urgent need to safeguard remaining wheat reserves, enforce strict quality controls on food commodities, and fix individual responsibility for lapses that placed public health at risk. The governor stressed that protecting essential food stocks is a fundamental responsibility of the provincial administration. He directed relevant departments to ensure that all future storage facilities are adequately protected against natural disasters and that transparent record-keeping and independent quality assessments become standard practice. Officials were instructed to submit a follow-up compliance report detailing the steps taken to implement the recommendations of the inquiry.

title: Islamabad LG polls set for Dec 20
description: Nomination papers to be filed from Nov 2-6; final candidate list due on Nov 25
content: Local government elections in the federal capital will be held on December 20, the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) announced on Tuesday, issuing the election schedule along with strict instructions to ensure a transparent and impartial electoral process. According to the schedule, nomination papers will be available from October 30 and may be filed from November 2 to 6. The list of candidates will be published on November 7, while scrutiny of nomination papers will take place from November 9 to 13. Appeals against decisions on nomination papers may be filed from November 14 to 18, with decisions to be announced from November 19 to 23. The final list of candidates will be displayed on November 25, followed by the allotment of election symbols on November 26. Polling will take place from 8am to 4pm on December 20, and the ECP said it will announce election results between December 21 and 24. The commission has prohibited the use of government resources for election campaigning. The ECP will also bar transfers and postings of government officers after the schedule is announced, and public servants will not be permitted to take leave without the ECP's approval. The President, Prime Minister, federal ministers and governors will not be allowed to campaign in the local government elections. However, members of Parliament, senators and local government representatives may participate in campaigning. The ECP warned that legal action would be taken against government officers found influencing election results and public office-holders violating electoral laws. It also directed that election offices remain open during public holidays and that election-related activities be conducted during official working hours, with strict compliance with the code of conduct. The commission said all relevant institutions and officials must follow its instructions to ensure that the electoral process is completed transparently, fairly and in accordance with the law. Earlier, the ECP had decided to hold the Islamabad local government elections under the 2015 local government law and ordered the immediate issuance of the schedule. Chief Election Commissioner Sikandar Sultan Raja observed that holding local government elections was a constitutional obligation, but the federal government had failed to provide the new local government law and relevant rules. The ECP said delimitation had been carried out six times and election schedules issued four times in Islamabad. It maintained that holding the elections under the 2015 law would not affect the existing delimitation.

title: City fish harbour gets security overhaul
description: CM orders dedicated police station, RFID tracking, crackdown on export irregularities
content: With a deadly shooting exposing the fault lines at Karachi Fish Harbour, the Sindh government has ordered a sweeping security overhaul at the province's key seafood hub, where 20,000 people enter daily and unchecked commercial activity, congestion and weak access controls have raised serious law-and-order concerns. Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah on Wednesday directed Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar to strengthen security and pursue the establishment of a dedicated police station at the harbour in consultation with the Fisheries Department. Chairing a meeting at his office, CM Shah also ordered mandatory registration of all harbour users, the introduction of RFID-based identification cards and an upgrade of the existing database to improve access control and monitoring. The meeting reviewed law and order, infrastructure deficiencies, utility connections, fish auction arrangements, the management of the Fishermen Cooperative Society and the regulation of seafood exports. Officials informed the meeting that the harbour operates round the clock, accommodating fishermen, auction agents, vendors, labourers, transporters, seafood processors, ice dealers and foreign nationals. The large volume of activity, coupled with inadequate security personnel, has placed pressure on the facility's security and infrastructure. The briefing cited a firing incident on September 8, reportedly triggered by a dispute over placing fish on a road, in which one person was killed and six others injured. CM Shah directed officials to ensure that fish unloading, auctions and related commercial activities take place only in designated areas, keeping roads and access routes clear. The chief minister ordered the completion of registration records and the integration of the harbour's management information system with the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) verification system, a mobile application and the Crime Record Management System. The meeting was informed that the Karachi Fisheries Harbour Authority (KFHA) had registered 5,196 boats and issued 170,000 computerised cards to harbour users since 2001, including 155,000 crew cards. Officials were also directed to obtain missing registration details of people associated with the Fishermen Cooperative Society. Established by the federal government in 1959 over 84 acres, the harbour was transferred to Sindh in 1974 after fisheries came under provincial jurisdiction. The KFHA was established in 1984 to oversee its management and rehabilitation. The meeting also examined a Rs5.7 million electricity bill disputed by the Fishermen Cooperative Society following the removal of a meter. CM Shah directed the fisheries minister to resolve the matter and arrange a separate electricity connection. A separate water connection was also ordered to meet operational needs and support compliance with European Union requirements for seafood exports. Officials were asked to examine the restoration of the harbour's cold storage facility, while illegal encroachments in designated areas used by ice dealers were ordered to be removed. The society proposed establishing a new auction hall at K-6, removing hotels and allocating dedicated spaces for fish vendors. The fisheries minister was directed to examine the proposals to reduce congestion and prevent disputes over the use of roads and common areas. CM Shah also called for tighter monitoring of seafood exporters operating outside the harbour, citing concerns over alleged illegal fish warehouses, revenue losses and discrepancies between recorded weights and export declarations. Officials were directed to improve documentation and traceability and take action under applicable laws. The meeting reviewed progress on a Rs2.779 billion rehabilitation scheme for the harbour's external services. Of the total cost, Rs1.426 billion has been spent, while Rs311 million has been allocated for the current fiscal year, of which Rs46.65 million has been released. While road works are 90% complete, the CCTV system is only 5% complete. Several other components, including the fixed jetty and floating pontoons, have yet to record physical progress. CM Shah directed the fisheries department to remove bottlenecks and accelerate pending works, particularly CCTV surveillance, street lighting and the security control room.

title: Lahore Gymkhana concedes inadequate rent payment
description: Lawmakers question successive govts over unvalued deal
content: The Lahore Gymkhana Club's chairman has acknowledged that the Rs5,000 annual rent for more than 100 acres of prime state land is inadequate, suggesting it should be raised to at least Rs10 million, prompting a Punjab Assembly committee to question how successive governments had allowed the arrangement to continue for decades without proper valuation or oversight. The special committee questioned the failure of governments to secure appropriate return from over 100 acres of prime state land leased to the club for the nominal annual rent of Rs5,000. The Punjab Assembly Special Committee No. 6, chaired by MPA Samiullah Khan, on Wednesday sought to establish how such a concession had continued for decades without proper valuation, government oversight or scrutiny of the lease terms. The committee was informed that the land's estimated value ranged from Rs76 billion to Rs218 billion. Committee members questioned the government's failure to ensure an appropriate public return from an asset of such magnitude, stressing that institutional autonomy could not exempt the club from accountability for its occupation and use of state land. Appearing before the committee alongside members of the club's management, Chairman Salman Siddique acknowledged the concerns raised by the lawmakers and expressed willingness to provide the relevant record and cooperate in the inquiry. He said he was himself surprised by the nominal annual rent, particularly in view of the extent of the land occupied by the club and its improved financial position. Comparing the club's present circumstances with the financial constraints it had faced during the 1990s, he said the annual rent should be at least Rs10 million. The members said the acknowledgment had reinforced the need to determine why successive government authorities had allowed the arrangement to continue without scrutiny. They stressed that the responsibility for protecting public assets rested with the relevant government institutions, which were required to enforce lease conditions and ensure accountability.

title: Women filmmakers capture Pakistan's untold stories
description: Eight of them showcase documentaries exploring gender barriers, climate change, child marriage
content: Five years after its launch, Patakha Pictures is continuing its efforts to support emerging documentary filmmakers in Pakistan, providing women with funding, mentorship and a platform to tell stories rooted in their communities. The initiative, founded by two-time Academy Award-winning filmmaker Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy through SOC Films, marked the milestone at a special event in Karachi on October 19, which also showcased the work of eight women filmmakers selected for the 2026 edition of its filmmaking mentorship and funding programme, Claim the Frame. Presented in partnership with the British Council Pakistan and the Scottish Documentary Institute, the programme brought together eight filmmakers from Punjab, Sindh and Gilgit-Baltistan, working in four pairs to produce documentaries exploring subjects ranging from women challenging gender barriers to climate change, child marriage and healthcare in remote areas. Speaking to The Express Tribune, Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy said the celebration marked five years of the initiative's funding and mentorship programme for female filmmakers in Pakistan. "We have funded over 75 filmmakers. Their films have played in over 100 festivals around the world and have won over 22 awards," she said. Reflecting on the diversity of stories presented at the event, Obaid-Chinoy said eight filmmakers had travelled from different parts of the country, including Shimshal in Gilgit-Baltistan, to showcase their work. "Their films have been about monsoon brides, they've been about midwives, they've been about tent pegging, they've been about camel racing very diverse films," she said. For Obaid-Chinoy, the programme addresses a significant gap in Pakistan's filmmaking landscape: the lack of access to funding, mentorship and opportunities for aspiring filmmakers. "Pakistan has so much talent. What we don't have is access and opportunity, which is what Patakha Pictures provides," she said. She added that the initiative emerged from the recognition that filmmakers with strong ideas often struggle to find the resources and guidance required to bring their stories to the screen. "If you have an excellent idea, if you have access to make a film, where would you go in Pakistan to get funding and mentorship? We saw a void over there. That's where we stepped in," she said. Obaid-Chinoy said the filmmakers participating in the programme demonstrated what could be achieved when emerging talent was given the right platform. She also described the programme as a way of creating a wider network of women storytellers who could take their experience back to their communities and support others interested in filmmaking. "When we fund and mentor them and they come to Karachi and spend time with us, what they say is that they are all ambassadors of their communities, because they have been given funding and mentorship to create films, that they will in turn go off and mentor other people," she said. "So we've started a pay-it-forward process." The 2026 edition of Claim the Frame brought together four creative pairs, each exploring a different subject through documentary filmmaking. Filmmakers Ishma Areeb and Javaria Waseem, from Lahore, tell the story of Anum Shakoor, a woman who found strength and healing through horses before entering the predominantly male world of tent pegging. The second pair, Karachi-based Aleezeh Fatima and Aisha Manzoor, explore the relationship between climate change, poverty and child marriage in rural Sindh. Their film examines how environmental and economic pressures intersect with the lives of vulnerable communities. Kinza Waqar and Jazaba, working between Bahawalpur and Lahore, turn their attention to the Cholistan Desert. Their documentary follows Bakht Ali, using his life, artistic practice and relationship with the desert to portray resilience and the traditions rooted in the region. Kinza waqar said "Naturally, I had to face several challenges as a woman behind the camera. At one point, there was no way to cross over except on foot. So, we carried the camera and tripod on our shoulders and walked until we reached the location. When we got there, we realised that the island had its own set of challenges. There were insects biting our feet and getting stuck to our skin, and we had to squeeze them out and remove them. All this was happening while the camera was rolling, and I had to keep filming despite the difficulties." Laila Jamil, Arts Director at the British Council Pakistan, said the value of Claim the Frame extended beyond the films themselves to questions of representation and whose perspectives were given space. "Pakistan has no shortage of talent or stories worth sharing; what matters is creating the space, support and opportunities for more voices to be heard," she said. Jamil added that the partnership between Patakha Pictures, the Scottish Documentary Institute and the British Council was helping women filmmakers shape narratives that reflected the diversity of their experiences and the world around them.

title: Pakistani celebrities react as death of 15-year-old Waseem Abbas in Multan sparks calls for justice
description: The death of orphaned teenager Waseem Abbas sparked outrage' actors like Yumna Zaidi, Mishi Khan demand justice
content: The death of 15-year-old Muhammad Waseem Abbas in Multan prompted an outpouring of grief and anger on social media, with Pakistani celebrities and public figures calling for justice and questioning the failure to protect a vulnerable child. Actors Yumna Zaidi, Mishi Khan, Ahsan Khan, Sehar Khan and Faizan Sheikh and more were among those reported to have reacted to the tragedy, which has also drawn attention to the safety of children sent away from institutional care to learn vocational skills. The incident has renewed concerns about the treatment of vulnerable children, the responsibilities of those entrusted with their care and the need for accountability when allegations of violence emerge. According to police, Waseem was an orphan living at an orphanage run by a non-governmental organisation. He had reportedly been sent to learn electrical work under contractor Tauqeer Nazir, who was carrying out work at a private housing society in Multan. Police said Waseem had been working with the contractor for approximately a week before the incident. On October 17, following an argument related to work, the teenager allegedly attempted to leave. Investigators said the contractor pursued him in a car and struck him, causing fatal injuries. CCTV footage reportedly showed the boy running away before being hit by the vehicle. Waseem sustained a severe head injury and died at the scene, according to rescue officials cited in news reports. Police arrested Nazir and registered a murder case against him and another suspect, identified as Amjad Ali. Investigators also questioned members of the orphanage administration as they examined the circumstances in which Waseem had been sent to work. The case remains subject to investigation, and the allegations against the suspects must be determined through the legal process. Among the celebrities reacting to Waseem's death was actor Yumna Zaidi, who shared a response on her Instagram stories as news of the incident spread. "Fear of Allah? The consequences will be harsh. So do not oppress the orphan. Ad. Duhaa verse. 9", she wrote. Veteran actor and television host Mishi Khan also expressed anger over the alleged circumstances surrounding the teenager's death. In an Instagram post, she wrote, “Why didn’t he stop the monster who was driving?? And what was the reason that the kid ran from their workplace ?? Our investigation standard needs reforms as there are many glitches". Her reaction reflected the anger felt by many social media users, who have called for accountability and questioned how a child entrusted to adults for vocational training could find himself in such circumstances. Actor Ahsan Khan also stressed justice on the matter, taking to his story to add: "True justice demands that the legal system reject all excuses and hold the killer fully acountable under the law to signal that the lives of the weak cannot be discarded by the powerful". Actor Faizan Sheikh also commented on the state of law and order in the country, writing to his story: "A new low everyday!" Seher Khan continued, "Honestly, I can't wrap my head around the kind of cruelty people are capable of. This world is becoming so difficult to process". Actor Faiza Khan further expressed his sentiments to add, "This is what happens in a country where there is no rule of law". The reactions have added to a broader conversation about the responsibilities of adults and institutions that take on the care of children, particularly those who may lack the financial security or family support needed to protect their interests. The circumstances of Waseem's case have also prompted questions about how children are selected for placements, whether their working conditions are monitored and what procedures exist for responding when a child reports mistreatment or attempts to leave a workplace. Police have said they are investigating the case, including the roles of the suspects and the circumstances surrounding Waseem's placement. These questions will need to be addressed through the investigation and any subsequent legal proceedings. As the investigation continues, the calls for justice are accompanied by a greater demand: that children entrusted to the care of adults must never be left without protection, oversight or a means of seeking help.

title: Sarmad Khoosat calls for royalties as ‘Humsafar’ prepares for Spanish-language release
description: The producer questioned the absence of royalties as Humsafar heads to Spanish-speaking audiences
content: Filmmaker Sarmad Khoosat drew attention to the lack of royalty payments for Pakistani television artists after the hit drama Humsafar was announced for a Spanish-language release, highlighting concerns over how creative professionals benefit from the continued success of their work. Khoosat, who directed the popular drama, shared an announcement by HUM TV on his Instagram story on Tuesday, revealing plans to dub the series into Spanish. Reacting to the news, he wrote, “If only there were royalties,” accompanied by a blank-faced emoji. PHOTO: sarmadkhoosat/Instagram The remark has renewed discussion about compensation for artists when their work reaches new audiences through international distribution, repeat broadcasts and re-releases. Royalties allow performers, directors, producers and other creative contributors to receive payments when a production is reused or redistributed. Depending on the agreement, these payments may continue over multiple broadcasts, although the amounts can decrease with successive screenings. Pakistan's television industry, however, has long struggled with the absence of a consistent royalty system. The practice was discontinued in the 1990s, when several prominent actors reportedly agreed to give up royalty rights in exchange for higher payments from the state-run Pakistan Television (PTV). In interviews in 2021, veteran performers expressed regret over the decision, saying it had deprived artists of a potential source of continuing income. The arrangement also helped establish a precedent that private television channels have largely continued to follow. Khoosat is not the first prominent name associated with Humsafar to raise concerns about the issue. Actor Mahira Khan, who starred in the drama alongside Fawad Khan, spoke about royalties in March while promoting her film Aag Lagay Basti Main. Khan pointed out that established stars such as herself and actor Fahad Mustafa might be better positioned to manage without royalty income. Junior performers, technicians and other crew members, however, often face greater financial uncertainty and have fewer opportunities to secure long-term earnings from their work. The debate also gained wider public attention in 2021 when actor Naila Jaffery spoke about the financial difficulties she experienced while battling cancer. She argued that royalty payments could have helped cover medical costs and provided greater financial security during a particularly challenging period. Her appeal brought renewed focus to the vulnerability of artists who may contribute to successful productions but receive little or no additional compensation when those projects continue generating commercial value. The planned Spanish release of Humsafar has once again raised a central question for Pakistan's entertainment industry: should the people responsible for creating enduring television hits continue to benefit financially as their work finds new audiences years after its original broadcast? For Khoosat, the international expansion of a drama remains a milestone, but the absence of royalties highlights a longstanding gap between the global reach of Pakistani entertainment and the financial protections available to the people behind it.

title: Authors urge UK to halt 'draconian' Palestine Action ban as Rooney sales end
description: Over 150 writers and artists urge the UK to amend its Palestine Action ban, defending Sally Rooney’s book sales
content: More than 150 writers and personalities signed an open letter Wednesday urging the UK government to amend its "draconian" ban on Palestine Action after Irish author Sally Rooney said she was halting book sales in Britain as a result. The Labour government has been heavily criticised by some for proscribing Palestine Action as a "terrorist" group in July 2025, with thousands of people arrested since for protesting against the move. "Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist. Her books must be available to the public," said the letter signed by such notable figures as Nobel laureates Annie Ernaux and Anne Carson. Rooney and her publisher Faber last week announced they had to end the sale of her books in the UK because of her support for the pro-Palestinian group. The proscription, which the organisation is appealing, puts Palestine Action on the same blacklist as Hamas and Hezbollah, making it illegal in the UK to be part of, support or finance it. Rooney has repeatedly expressed her support for Palestine Action and said she intends to fund the group, which is not proscribed by Ireland, where the author lives and works. Faber said the ban meant it could not legally pass on royalties earned in the UK to Rooney, whose best-sellers, including Normal People and Intermezzo, have earned her praise as the "voice of a generation". "Their withdrawal from sale, on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation, is an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country," the open letter, also signed by actors Paul Mescal and Tilda Swinton, adds. "We categorically reject censorship - whether direct or indirect - and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity." Other signatories include authors Colm Toibin, Arundhati Roy, Jhumpa Lahiri, Zadie Smith and Julian Barnes. Last week, police said they were looking into a social media post by Sarah Helm, the wife of the UK's national security advisor, for supporting the group -- although they later said it did not merit a criminal investigation. Palestine Action's stated goal on its website is to end "global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime". Its proscription came after a series of high-profile stunts protesting the war in Gaza, including targeting weapons factories, especially those belonging to Israeli arms group Elbit. Britain's Supreme Court is set to hear an appeal against the ban from the group's cofounder Huda Ammori next month.

title: End of an era? How the Hermes Birkin bag is losing its scarcity appeal
description: Birkin bags used to sell at more than double their retail price tags on resale platforms, pre-pandemic era
content: London-based Cai Baochun used to make a hefty profit reselling Hermes' famed Birkin bags for more than double their $10,000 retail price. Now he has stopped stockpiling them as second-hand prices fall. “I don’t want to lose money,” said Cai, who started selling the bags on online platforms such as Vestiaire Collective and ‌on social media in 2020 and rode a pandemic-era luxury spending boom. The resale value of unworn Birkins sold as second-hand online has dropped by more than $6,000 from its 2022 peak, he said. The decline reflects a broader shift in the market for one of luxury's most exclusive products whose appeal and success have been driven by scarcity. Increasing supply of Birkin bags in the second-hand market is depressing resale premiums, according to resellers, industry consultants and analysts interviewed by Reuters, raising questions about a strategy that helped propel Hermes to become one of the world's most profitable luxury companies. Named after the late British-French actor Jane Birkin, the handbag has been central to Hermes' performance. Between 2015 and 2025, group annual sales tripled to €16 billion ($18 billion) while its market value surged. Last year, Hermes posted an operating margin of 41%, above that of rivals including Chanel, Kering-owned Gucci and LVMH's leather and fashion division, which includes Louis Vuitton and Dior. Resale market under pressure Managing Director of Lilac Blue Antoinette Hunter unboxes a 2025 Birkin bag in the shade of peppermint at the Knightsbridge private Hermes resale boutique in London, Britain, October 19, 2026. PHOTO: Reuters All of that was underpinned by an aura of exclusivity. Six resellers ⁠who source bags directly from Hermes shoppers said access to a Birkin is generally linked to spending on Hermes scarves, clothes and shoes, although the exact policy differs between regions and stores. Two estimated customers typically spend $10,000 to $20,000 before being offered the Birkin or the Kelly, the brand's other popular bag. Hermes, which says a Birkin takes 15 hours to craft, does not disclose its selling policies or how many bags it makes. It declined to comment for this story. Of the nine Birkin resellers Reuters interviewed in the US, Europe and Asia, six said resale prices had fallen over the past year as more handbags became available, while five reported softer demand. Antoinette Hunter, who founded luxury handbag reseller Lilac Blue in 2007, said when she got the first request for a Birkin, few people knew the bag. She eventually sourced one from a member of Japan’s royal family. Acquiring Birkins is no longer a challenge, Hunter said, but it's harder to make money from resales. She said the price for an unworn black Birkin 25 bag, one of the most sought-after models, has fallen by around £4,000 ($5,336) since 2022, to around £24,000. Cai, who sells via Vestiaire Collective and Instagram, says his price for the bag is around £20,000. Hermes sells the same model for £9,390 in Britain, a Hermes sales assistant in London said. Although Hunter still sees plenty of demand for Hermès bags, particularly the most high-end ones, she said the decline in resale prices might dissuade some from buying directly from Hermes. "If Hermes continues to raise the prices, and the prices on the resale market continue to drop, that margin gets squeezed, and ‌perhaps it will ⁠become less appealing," she said. Brokerage Bernstein, which tracks individual auction results, said in a September note the resale price on Birkin 25 bags averaged about 1.7 times the retail tag in the third quarter, down from about 2.6 times at their 2022 peak. Business model under scrutinty Hermes Birkin bags are displayed at London Bear, an exclusive boutique for authenticated pre-owned luxury fashion, in London, Britain, October 19, 2026. PHOTO: Reuters Hermes' leather goods division, which includes other handbag models, generates 44% of annual group revenue. For more than a decade, limited supply and strong demand allowed Birkins to command hefty resale premiums, benefiting both Hermes and resellers as the prospects of making a profit via the secondary market encouraged Hermes clients to buy more from the brand. "It was a win-win," said Sarah Davis, founder of California-based Fashionphile. The company said its Birkin listings have grown 32-fold in 15 years. The company's website currently lists 212 Birkins on sale. Hermes has gradually expanded the production of its handcrafted items, opening one workshop per year on average. Meanwhile, the ⁠rise of resale platforms such as Vestiaire Collective and The RealReal, alongside vintage boutiques with online shops and social media channels, has made it easier than ever to resell. The bags and other Hermes items remain highly sought after, resellers said, but the brand is showing some strain. Hermes’ shares have lost nearly 40% of their market value this year, making the brand one of the worst performers among listed luxury companies. Earlier this month, UBS analysts downgraded Hermes shares to "sell", saying that growing secondary-market supply of Birkins and Kellys could weaken the brand's scarcity-driven business model. "We believe the nature of ⁠the business is changing," they said in a note, estimating that the number of the handbags listed for sale worldwide is now six to seven times higher than before the pandemic. The company is expected to report quarterly sales growth of 5.2% on Thursday, which would mark its weakest quarterly growth in six years, according to Visible Alpha estimates. While leather goods revenue is still expected to grow by 10%, demand for clothing, silk scarves and perfumes is cooling, a sign fewer customers are making the purchases traditionally required to buy ⁠a Birkin at a later stage, two equities analysts and two industry consultants said. Asked in July whether Hermes should slow production to protect the brand, Hermes CEO Axel Dumas told reporters that some people feared making too many bags would hurt its exclusivity, while others questioned why it was not making more. He added that output depended largely on the number of fully trained artisans and available high-quality leather. Not all resellers see weakness. Davis said prices for the bag on the Fashionphile platform have remained firm and even risen slightly this year, pointing to renewed attention generated by Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland's handbag collection.

title: Oil rises as US orders diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating tensions
description: Brent crude futures rise $1.29, or 1.2%, to $110.11 a barrel
content: Oil prices rose on Thursday as more attacks by the Houthis in Saudi ‌Arabia prompted the United States to order some diplomats and family members to leave its missions in the Kingdom. Brent crude futures rose $1.29, or 1.2%, to $110.11 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude gained 97 cents, or 1%, to $98.12. Brent had settled largely ​unchanged on Wednesday, while WTI had eased 67 cents. The US State Department plans to withdraw family members ​from a number of other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters. Yemen's Houthis struck several targets on Wednesday, with at least one person killed and eight more wounded at a ​civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oil field. Explosions were ​also heard in Sirik in southern Iran, Iranian media reported on Wednesday, saying the nature and origin of the explosions were unknown. On Wednesday, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the Financial Times that Iran was fully prepared to defend itself, and President ​Masoud Pezeshkian told state media the US could not expect dialogue while blockading and threatening Iran. There were at ​least 18 attacks on shipping over the past two weeks, Kpler data showed, while LSEG analysts warned that Iran was targeting ‌tankers ⁠well beyond the Strait of Hormuz, reaching into the Gulf of Oman and jeopardising Gulf crude loadings and ship-to-ship transfers supporting regional loadings. Read: Oil rises on Middle East supply fears, US inventory drawdowns Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for talks on ending the war in Ukraine amid Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two. The ​Kremlin said Putin had agreed ​to resume US-mediated peace talks ⁠with Ukraine as soon as next month. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he supported the talks and hoped they would start as soon as possible. US crude stocks fell by ​3.06 million barrels to 412.5 million barrels last week, the US Energy Information ​Administration said on ⁠Wednesday, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for an 820,000-barrel draw. Distillate stockpiles, which include diesel and heating oil, rose 1.68 million barrels in the week to 104.3 million barrels, versus expectations for a 1.16 million-barrel drop, ⁠EIA data ​showed. The Trump administration is offering to loan up to nearly ​a third of the 1-million-barrel US emergency heating oil reserve, the Department of Energy said on Wednesday, seeking to contain prices that have ​surged on diesel shortages due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

title: Govt mulls $2b LNG import decision
description: Ministry warns of supply cuts, unrest; CCOE yet to take up 22-cargo summary
content: The government is sitting on a decision to import an estimated $2 billion worth of gas to cope with winter demand, despite the Petroleum Division's advice to begin the import process from the first week of October to avoid any disruption of supplies and social unrest. The Petroleum Division had cautioned that due to any further delay in importing the gas, the government may have to resort to disconnecting supplies to the industry, power, fertiliser, compressed natural gas (CNG) and cement sectors to make sure residential consumers keep getting rationalised supplies and unrest is avoided. But the Cabinet Committee on Energy (CCOE) has not yet taken up the gas load management summary of the Petroleum Division, which had sought authorisation for import of 22 cargoes of liquefied natural gas (LNG), some of those to be sourced from the United States and Azerbaijan, according to government officials. The division had sent a summary to the CCOE last month after finalising the demand for the import of 22 LNG cargoes in consultation with the Task Force on Power Sector Reforms and the National Coordination and Management Council (NCMC). The summary sought authorisation of the cabinet body to start the import process by different companies from October 7 to October 10 for the import of 12 out of 22 cargoes, according to these details. But so far no formal decision has been taken, although Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif chaired a couple of meetings to finalise the exact quantity of cargoes. The cabinet secretary did not respond to a request for comments. Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz said the matter was pending a decision with the CCOE. The government had hoped to receive at least 11 cargoes from Qatar under a long-term deal, but due to the uncertain situation in the region, Doha has already extended the force majeure till November, according to the officials. Despite reaching a consensus on the need for the import of 22 cargoes, there was a view that only 15 cargoes should be imported. But this could heighten shortages during the peak winter season, the sources added. On Sunday, Pervaiz said in Lahore that the prime minister had already held a few meetings to address "the bigger problem we will face as we move into winter, the gas and LPG". The minister had said that after reviewing the situation with the prime minister, whatever difficult decisions were needed would be taken and fuel arrangements would be made from wherever required. A senior government functionary said one of the major reasons for the delay was the cost of LNG import. At an average price of $87 million per cargo, the government needs nearly $2 billion for importing gas from November to February. The gross official foreign exchange reserves remained at a little over $21 billion even after borrowing $3 billion through Eurobonds ahead of making a major debt payment of the same amount. The Ministry of Economic Affairs published the external borrowing report on Wednesday. It showed that Pakistan received $5.4 billion in external loans during the July-September period. This is inclusive of the Eurobonds, as other financing sources are drying up. The government had initially estimated the cost of import at $1.5 billion, including supplies from Qatar at roughly $12 per million British thermal units (MMBTU). But due to the extension in force majeure, there were high chances that spot purchase may be the main bet to meet demand, according to the sources. The CCOE had been requested to keep domestic consumers as top priority for sustained supply of gas during 5am to 10pm with optimum pressure during cooking hours to avoid any social distress and unrest. According to the proposal, industry, power and fertiliser will get gas supplies as per their demand on an as-and-when-available basis, whereas supplies to CNG would be curtailed, especially in December 2026 and January 2027. In extreme winter situations, and in case of unavailability of required LNG cargoes or disruption in indigenous gas supply at sources in the north, gas supply to CNG, cement and industry would be curtailed for diversion to the domestic sector. The Petroleum Division had requested the CCOE that Pakistan LNG Limited should be allowed to arrange four cargoes from Azerbaijan under a bilateral deal, and that such an arrangement should be put in place by October 10, a deadline that has already lapsed and could now carry political and financial costs. The plan also included imports by Pakistan State Oil in collaboration with other players for four cargoes, but such arrangements were to be made by October 7, according to the sources. The proposal also required Pakistan LNG Limited to explore three cargoes from a United States government-nominated firm by October 7, with the deal to be finalised by the end of this month. However, this too has not materialised, said the sources. The government was looking for nine cargoes to meet power sector demand and another 13 for the requirement of the residential sector. The Petroleum Division was of the view that due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, the likelihood of delivery of the contracted cargoes by Qatar was uncertain. During the winters, demand is projected to almost double from 850 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) to 1,600, with a major increase in demand on the Sui Northern Gas Pipeline Limited (SNGPL). SNGPL demand is projected to grow from 550 mmcfd to 1,100. The government officials said at least two fertiliser plants on SNGPL will face suspension of gas supplies. According to the food ministry, closure of Fauji Fertiliser Bin Qasim, FatimaFert and Agritech may cause a shortfall of 109,000 metric tonnes of urea per month. The Petroleum Division has tentatively worked out the impact on foreign exchange reserves of importing urea versus importing LNG and subsidy. It was of the opinion that import of LNG and its supply will have higher financial implications for one month only compared with import of urea.

title: Closer ties with foreign firms to expand industries
description: Pakistan needs to attract investment into industries capable of selling globally, developing local suppliers
content: A foreign investor builds a factory in Pakistan, employs local workers and sells its products in the domestic market. Production rises, jobs are created and business activity expands. Yet if the factory depends heavily on imported machinery and materials, earns its revenue in rupees and sends part of its profits overseas, its contribution to the country's foreign exchange position may remain limited. Now consider a different arrangement. A Pakistani manufacturer joins hands with an overseas company, adopts its technology, improves production standards and begins supplying customers in international markets. The partnership creates jobs at home while bringing in export earnings. Local suppliers may also benefit as the business expands. For Pakistan, where the demand for dollars regularly outpaces the economy's ability to earn them through merchandise exports, the difference between these two investment models deserves greater attention. Economic analyst Shahid Anwar believes closer partnerships between domestic manufacturers and foreign companies could help Pakistan make better use of its existing industrial base. "Pakistan needs to look beyond the headline figure for foreign investment and examine the economic activity it creates over time," said Anwar, a former secretary-general of the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI). According to the State Bank of Pakistan data, net foreign direct investment (FDI) reached around $495 million in July and August 2026, compared with $399 million in the same period a year earlier. The improvement followed a weaker full year, when net FDI fell to $1.67 billion in FY26 from $2.48 billion in FY25. World Bank data shows that FDI has remained below 1% of gross domestic product since 2010. Investment has also remained concentrated in a narrow range of activities. Pakistan Economic Survey for FY26 shows that the power sector attracted 52.7% of net FDI in the first nine months of the fiscal year, while financial businesses accounted for 43.5%. Telecommunications recorded a net outflow of $465.5 million, which the survey attributed to a one-time divestment. Anwar argues that Pakistan needs to attract more investment into industries capable of selling internationally, developing local suppliers and reducing dependence on imported goods. The need is underscored by the country's trade performance. Goods exports declined 5.93% to $30.1 billion in FY26, while imports rose 8.14% to $69.8 billion, according to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics. September brought some improvement in exports, which increased 17.6% year-on-year to $2.94 billion. But imports also climbed by more than 11% to approximately $6.49 billion. The trade deficit for July-September reached $10.79 billion, about 15% higher than a year earlier. The World Bank estimates that Pakistan has nearly $60 billion in untapped export potential. Yet exports have fallen from 16% of GDP in the 1990s to around 10%, leaving considerable room for improvement. "Many Pakistani manufacturers can produce at scale, but entering overseas markets requires consistent quality, modern processes and reliable buyers. A foreign partner who brings those capabilities can help a local business move beyond the domestic market and compete internationally," said Arshad Zia, a mid-scale businessman. Joint ventures could help achieve these objectives by combining established Pakistani factories and workforces with overseas technology, technical expertise and access to customers. The approach will not replace investment in new factories where additional capacity or new units are required. Instead, it will provide another route for expanding businesses that already have productive facilities. Zia added that though this transition for Pakistani industries was not that easy, already some joint ventures were underway and were providing good results. "Such JVs, however, are largely for high-end industries, where money is not an issue, but for an average businessman, JVs are still not accessible." Anwar, on the other hand, proposes assessing major investment projects through what he calls a "dollar test". Under this approach, authorities will examine projected export earnings, purchases from local suppliers and expected foreign exchange payments for imported inputs, profits and dividends over a 10-year period. The results will be reviewed annually. He called on the Board of Investment to work with chambers of commerce and industrial associations to match Pakistani manufacturers with suitable foreign partners. He also recommended linking tax and tariff incentives to verified exports, domestic sourcing, technology adoption and workforce training, while publishing an annual breakdown of investment by sector. "Attracting capital remains important, but the greater prize is investment that strengthens local production, connects Pakistani businesses with global markets and continues earning dollars long after the initial funds have arrived," Anwar added.

title: Karachi's heat bill lands on the poor
description: Baba Bhit Island sees outages of up to 18 hours; built-up area up 32% since 2010
content: Karachi's built-up area has expanded by about 32% between 2010 and 2025, exceeding 1,400 square kilometres, as agricultural land, rangeland and open spaces have increasingly given way to urban development, raising concerns over the economic costs of heat stress, water scarcity and inadequate infrastructure. According to an official note by the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), satellite-based land-use and land-cover (LULC) analysis shows that the expansion of the country's largest city has significantly altered its surrounding landscape over the past 15 years. The trend is increasing pressure on the city's natural environment and infrastructure, with potential implications for labour productivity, public health, agricultural activity and the cost of providing essential services. SUPARCO warned that the spread of built-up surfaces intensifies the urban heat island effect, in which densely developed areas retain more heat than surrounding rural areas. Urbanisation also reduces natural water infiltration and drainage capacity, potentially increasing flood risks during intense monsoon rainfall. The findings point to a growing economic challenge for Karachi, where expanding settlements and commercial activity are placing greater demands on electricity, water supply, transport and drainage systems. Concrete expansion raises heat risks Urban planner M Toheed, associated with the Institute of Business Administration (IBA), said Karachi's green cover had declined by around 40% while built-up areas had increased in the last one and a half decades. The estimate requires further verification through comparable land-cover measurements, but the broader concern is that the city's expanding concrete footprint is reducing its capacity to moderate temperatures. "The concrete base is building up, and this has serious repercussions on every kind of life here," Toheed said. The conversion of open and vegetated land into buildings, roads and other paved surfaces can reduce shade and evapotranspiration, increasing heat exposure in densely populated neighbourhoods. The consequences are particularly severe when high temperatures coincide with Karachi's humidity, which limits the body's ability to cool itself through sweating.
