title: IMF flags unfair tax system
description: IMF flags unfair tax system
content:
Salaried contribution rises to Rs629b as realty, agriculture and retail stay untaxed
As Pakistan's tax system becomes more unfair during the first two years of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme, the Fund's Regional Director, Jihad Azour, on Tuesday emphasised a fairer and more neutral tax system for improving compliance and business expansion.
The opening speech by Azour during the first day of a two-day conference on the tax system appeared divorced from ground realities, where the salaried class has been squeezed but the retailers, agriculture and real estate sectors largely remained untaxed.
"A fairer tax system can encourage compliance, better services can strengthen trust, and a more neutral tax structure can allow productive firms to expand rather than remain small or informal," Azour said while delivering the opening speech.
He further said that broadening the tax base, strengthening revenue administration, reducing tax expenditures, protecting priority spending and improving public service provision are Pakistan's priorities.
However, during the first two years of the IMF programme, tax contributions by influential sectors such as retailers, agriculture and real estate remained negligible, and IMF management agreed to reduce withholding tax rates for the real estate sector this June. The IMF also endorsed a tax scheme for traders that allowed them to deal in cash and would promote informality in the economy.
Yet retailers remained outside the tax net, and as of October 15 only 137 new retailers joined the scheme against the annual target of one million. According to the Federal Board of Revenue's (FBR) data, income tax collection from the real estate sector dived 38% to a mere Rs35.2 billion in the first three months of the current fiscal year. It was Rs22 billion less than the comparative period of the last fiscal year after the government cut income tax for the realty sector by 50%, which the IMF also endorsed.
In fiscal year 2024, the realty sector had paid Rs200 billion in income taxes, which hardly increased to Rs236 billion in the last fiscal year, but it may now dip even below Rs150 billion after rate cuts.
Punjab and Sindh cumulatively collected Rs5.1 billion in agriculture income tax as of June this year under the new regime introduced as part of the IMF programme. According to details shared with the IMF, in the last fiscal year, the agriculture income tax target was Rs2 billion but the Sindh government collected only Rs1.1 billion. The Punjab government's budget books showed that against the last fiscal year's target of Rs10.5 billion, the collection was only Rs4 billion.
Compared with this, before the start of the IMF programme, the annual contribution of the salaried class was Rs391 billion, which within two fiscal years of the IMF programme increased to Rs629 billion as of June 2026.
In his speech, Azour stated that the tax workshop comes at a critical moment in Pakistan's reform journey. Despite an era of shocks and uncertainty, Pakistan has made important progress toward restoring macroeconomic stability, rebuilding confidence, strengthening external buffers and supporting gradual recovery, he added. The workshop was taking place in the middle of a discussion at the highest level of government on whether the current FBR can deliver. The prime minister has shelved a plan to abolish the FBR, but the discussion reinforced the failure to bring tax broadening reforms.
The regional director stated that the next milestone is to turn this stabilisation into stronger and more durable growth.
"Moving beyond the cycles of adjustment toward a more competitive, investment-friendly and inclusive economy is the ambitious set of reforms that was set clearly by the government and supported by the IMF through the Extended Fund Facility (EFF)," he added.
Azour said Pakistan's exposure to higher energy and food prices, disruption to trade and supply chains, weaker external demand and an abrupt tightening in global financing conditions heightens the premium on preserving stability while supporting the recovery.
In this context, he added, fiscal policy must do more than achieving the primary balance targets and protecting that sustainability.
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has recently questioned Pakistan's economic stabilisation, terming it "stunted and borrowed". In his letter to the prime minister, Iqbal stated that the focus of the economic stabilisation was on fiscal numbers. Azour said Pakistan must reinforce policy credibility, foster the recovery and create space for the public investment and social spending needed to support stronger long-term growth and the well-being of the Pakistani people.
He said tax reform was critical to Pakistan's economic growth agenda and was at the centre of the EFF objectives. A stronger, broader, fairer and more predictable tax system can support fiscal sustainability while reducing distortions that hold back investment, productivity growth and formal job creation, said the regional director. The director said Pakistan's stabilisation gains have been hard won. Credibility now depends on continuing to meet fiscal and external objectives and enhancing resilience, while demonstrating that reforms are sustained and institutionally anchored, he added.
A medium-term tax strategy can serve this purpose if it sets clear objectives, well-designed policies, ambitious sequencing and transparent implementation responsibilities, according to the regional director.
The EFF-supported programme recognises that stabilisation is necessary, but not sufficient. Pakistan needs reforms that raise productivity, improve competitiveness and unlock private investment, he added.
"When the tax system is simpler, more neutral and predictable, it lowers the cost of formality, improves resource allocations and gives businesses greater confidence to invest and grow," according to Azour.
He emphasised that fairness is central to reform's success. Taxpayers are more likely to comply when rules are transparent and when the system does not reward informality or provide preferential treatment, according to the regional director.
But contrary to this concept, Pakistan's tax system has become more unfair, and the government launched an easy tax scheme for traders that promotes informality by allowing them to deal in cash. The scheme has also been endorsed by the IMF.
Azour said many countries have strong reform ideas, but fewer translate them into durable results. Implementation requires ownership, coordination, engagement and communication. Ownership across institutions, coordination between the federal government and provinces, engagement with the private sector and civil society, and a careful communication strategy so that citizens and businesses can understand and trust, he added.

content:
'American Horror Story' returns for season 14 at FX after season 13 sets streaming records for the franchise in 2026
American Horror Story has been renewed for season 14 at FX, with the announcement arriving ahead of the season 13 finale scheduled for October 29.
Created by Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk, the horror anthology series continues its run as FX’s longest-running hour-long series. The renewal follows a strong streaming debut for its latest instalment, which attracted four million views in its first four days, marking the best streaming performance for a premiere in the franchise’s history.
Season 13 also marked the series’ return after a three-year gap following the 2023 premiere of season 12, titled Delicate . title: Elizabeth Holmes mania fuels 186  viewership surge for Amanda Seyfried   s  The Dropout
description: Amanda Seyfried   s  The Dropout  saw viewership rise 186  as Elizabeth Holmes    documentary renewed interest in Theranos
content:
Amanda Seyfried’s 'The Dropout' saw viewership rise 186% as Elizabeth Holmes’ documentary renewed interest in Theranos
Amanda Seyfried’s The Dropout has recorded a significant viewership surge following renewed interest in Elizabeth Holmes sparked by A24’s documentary You Can See Everything .
The Hulu limited series, which premiered in 2022, saw viewing hours increase by 186% in September compared with August, according to Variety . The rise followed the September 6 announcement that the documentary had been produced in secret and continued as its wide theatrical release on October 16 approached.
In August, The Dropout accumulated 420,000 hours of viewing time, equivalent to approximately 62,000 estimated views. The figure climbed to 1.2 million hours in September, representing around 176,000 estimated views.
The series recorded another increase during the week of October 12, when viewing hours reached 422,000, marking a 92% rise from the previous week. By the time of Variety’s report, the show had accumulated 997,000 viewing hours during October, bringing its combined total since September to 2.2 million hours and approximately 296,000 estimated views.
Streaming search platform JustWatch also reported growing interest in the Hulu series. Searches for The Dropout increased by 200% week over week following the documentary’s release, placing it at No. 10 in the platform’s streaming search rankings.
The renewed attention has extended beyond television. John Carreyrou, the journalist who exposed the fraudulent practices at Holmes’ blood-testing company Theranos, returned to the New York Times bestseller list with his 2018 book, Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup .
Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything premiered as a surprise screening at the Telluride Film Festival.
Created by Elizabeth Meriwether, The Dropout earned critical acclaim, with Seyfried winning an Emmy for her portrayal of Holmes. The actress recently said she was unsure whether she would want to meet Holmes but had followed her story on and off since making the series.

title: Ban on PTI may no longer be needed after governor   s rule in K P  Tarar
description: Says government may no longer need to pursue ban on PTI  accuses PTI of facilitating terrorism in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
content:
Says government may no longer need to pursue ban on PTI, accuses it of facilitating terrorism in K-P
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said on Tuesday that a ban on the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) might no longer be necessary following the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, adding that the party had already lost its government in the province due to its alleged support for terrorism.
The emergency and governor’s rule were declared on October 11 after negotiations between the government and opposition failed , culminating in a PTI long march towards Islamabad that began on October 4. Last week, a joint session of parliament adopted two separate resolutions ratifying the presidential proclamations imposing a state of emergency and governor’s rule in K-P for two months, amid protests from the opposition. Before that, both houses of parliament had separately approved the emergency in the province by majority vote under Clause 1 of Article 232 of the Constitution, despite objections from opposition lawmakers.
Speaking on a private television programme, Capital Talk , the minister said non-functional K-P Chief Minister Sohail Afridi was in protective custody. He added that an advisory council would decide whether Afridi should be arrested or whether a case should be registered against him.
Defending the decision to place Afridi in protective custody, Tarar said it was a natural step after the imposition of an emergency to take key figures into protective custody to prevent potential sabotage or threats to law and order.
Read : PHC seeks Centre’s response over imposition of emergency, governor’s rule in K-P
Criticising the PTI government’s performance in the province, he alleged that it had failed to deliver development projects and improve infrastructure.
“There is no infrastructure in Kohat. The Kohat Tunnel and motorway were built during the PML-N government, and no work has been done there since,” he said, adding that no development had taken place across the province.
“Peace is the fundamental requirement for all these things to happen. They have not even taken a stand for peace. In their view, the TTP are very good people, whom they do not want to condemn,” Tarar said.
Talking about the negotiations with the opposition, the minister said members of the PTI delegation involved in negotiations had been disappointed after Afridi rejected the terms of an agreement reached with the government while blaming the former chief minister and his associates for the collapse of the talks.
Reiterating his earlier position on banning the PTI, Tarar said a principled decision had already been taken, while a final decision would follow the completion of legal preparations. However, he said a ban might no longer be required.
“I believe there may no longer be a need for it because the PTI, as a party, is already absent from parliament. As a result of violations, it did not have an electoral symbol, and its members are not present in the House,” he said.
Lashing out at the PTI over what he described as its alleged support for the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other militant groups, Tarar said the party had governed the province for more than 13 years.
The minister said that terrorism had been brought under control after 2017 through the complete implementation of the National Action Plan, but alleged that the PTI government had subsequently facilitated the return of militants.
Also Read : Tariq Fazal rubbishes linking governor's rule in K-P to mineral extraction
He said the party had lost its provincial government as a consequence of its alleged facilitation of terrorism, adding that there was little point in pursuing a ban under the circumstances.
The minister also praised Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman for his role in the negotiations but urged him not to politicise the issue of terrorism.
“Maulana Sahib is an experienced and astute politician. I believe it does not suit him to bring politics into the security of the province,” Tarar said, adding that the elimination of terrorism was an unequivocal objective that had to be achieved at all costs.
Acknowledging JUI-F’s sacrifices and efforts in the fight against terrorism, the minister said all political parties should unite against the menace.
“This is the time for everyone to stand together against terrorism, but terrorism and politics must be kept separate because this is a matter of the safety and security of the people,” he said.

title: Brent falls as Iran s president discusses mediation with CDF Munir
description: Brent crude futures settle down at  108 79 after reaching a five month high of   111 99 earlier in the session
content:
Brent crude futures settle down at $108.79 after reaching a five-month high of $111.99 earlier in the session
Oil prices settled down ​after touching a five-month high on Tuesday as traders weighed a meeting between the Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, a key US-Iran mediator, against continued Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.
Brent crude futures settled down 76 cents, or 0.69%, at $108.79. Earlier in the session, the front-month contract reached $111.99, a five-month high.
The November contract for US West Texas Intermediate crude, which expired on Tuesday, settled ​down $1.87, or 1.8%, at $101.79. That was down from the session high of $110.48, the highest since April for a nearby contract. ​The more active December contract settled down 72 cents at $97.82 a barrel.
Iran's President Pezeshkian discussed mediation efforts ⁠and regional developments during a meeting with Field Marshal Munir in Tehran, Iran's Nournews reported on Tuesday.
Read : CDF Munir meets senior Iranian officials as Pakistan continues diplomatic push to end conflict
Pakistan's mediation efforts ​resulted in an interim peace agreement signed in June. But that deal quickly faltered amid new fighting between Iran and the US weeks ​later.
The talks in Tehran are against the backdrop of continued attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, who said on Monday they launched several attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military targets, such as an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and Abha airport.
Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the ​Houthi claims, and Reuters could not independently verify them.
"Oil prices remain well-supported... This suggests the market is pricing in a significant risk ​premium, given the situation's volatility," ING analysts said in a note on Tuesday.
At least 18 vessels were reportedly attacked over two weeks, which keeps the risk ‌premium ⁠intact, shiptracker Kpler said in a note on Monday.
Also on Monday, a Houthi attack on a training camp for government security forces in Yemen's Shabwa province killed 58 people and injured more than 200.
Read More : Death toll from Houthi attack on Yemen training camp rises to 73
The renewed attacks heightened fears about regional stability and underscored continuing risks to energy supply from the region, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement he is "committed to completing the elimination of ​the Iranian regime," and spoke with ​US President Donald Trump about it ⁠on Sunday.
Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their traditional destinations after the US suspended sanctions and secured the lifting of an export ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil ​in recent days, according to shipping data from Kpler and LSEG.
The US is working with domestic refiners to ​squeeze more crude ⁠through its refining complex, US Energy Under Secretary Kyle Haustveit said on Tuesday at the Drake Forum in Titusville, Pennsylvania, a sentiment echoed by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright later on Tuesday in Houston.
The US is also pushing shuttered domestic refineries to reopen, Wright added.
US crude oil stockpiles ⁠were expected ​to have fallen last week along with product inventories, an extended Reuters poll showed ​on Tuesday. Eight analysts polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that crude inventories fell by about 800,000 barrels in the week ended October 16.

title: Taliban s unfinished victory
description: Afghanistan s opposition landscape is becoming more varied
content:
Afghanistan's opposition landscape is becoming more varied
The Taliban won Afghanistan's war for power. They have yet to secure a peace that includes their opponents, protects former soldiers and reassures their neighbours. The persistence of armed resistance exposes that unfinished task. For Pakistan, whose security is threatened by militants operating from Afghan territory, the distinction between controlling a country and governing it responsibly carries deadly consequences.
Afghanistan's opposition landscape is becoming more varied. A compilation published by South Asia Times attributes 119 claimed attacks across 26 provinces to resistance organisations during August and September 2026. These claims require independent verification. The UN Secretary-General's September assessment, as summarised by Security Council Report, found that fragmented opposition had not significantly challenged Taliban control during its reporting period.
These accounts describe different dimensions of the conflict. Dispersed attacks can coexist with government military superiority. The question is whether the Taliban are eliminating the causes of resistance or merely containing their armed expression.
The National Resistance Front under Ahmad Massoud and the Afghanistan Freedom Front remain established resistance organisations. The Afghan United Front, led by former army commander Sami Sadat, announced armed operations in August, claiming attacks in Kandahar and Helmand. Southern activity complicates the portrayal of opposition as an exclusively northern phenomenon.
That geographical diversification matters politically. It challenges the equation of Taliban authority with Pashtun consent. Pashtuns are a diverse community whose interests cannot be reduced to those of one armed movement. Opposition involving southern networks also demands analysis beyond the contrast between a Pashtun government and disaffected northern minorities.
At the centre of the problem lies exclusion. A narrow governing circle cannot build lasting national consent while denying meaningful participation to communities beyond its own networks. Tajiks, Hazaras, Uzbeks and other Afghans need credible avenues to influence decisions. Pashtuns outside the ruling establishment have an equal stake in that principle.
Exclusion alone does not explain every attack, and resistance leaders must answer for their own conduct. Nevertheless, a political order that offers opponents no peaceful route to influence leaves fewer incentives for accommodation. Inclusivity is therefore a security requirement, especially where experienced commanders and surviving military networks remain available.
The Taliban's broken amnesty illustrates the danger. UN reporting documented 218 extrajudicial killings, 424 arbitrary arrests and detentions, more than 144 instances of torture and ill-treatment, and 14 enforced disappearances involving former officials and security personnel between August 2021 and June 2023. These historical findings establish a grave failure of promised protection.
An amnesty asks defeated personnel to place their survival in the hands of yesterday's enemies. When that bargain fails, trained men may turn towards clandestine networks for protection. Their experience, local knowledge and relationships can strengthen resistance organisations. The scale of recruitment remains uncertain, but the incentive created by fear is clear.
Militarily, scattered operations do not establish an insurgency's ability to hold territory, sustain supplies or coordinate a national campaign. If persistent, however, attacks across multiple provinces can increase the burden of protecting officials, installations and transport routes.
The strategic risk is a cycle in which attacks provoke wider repression, repression deepens grievances, and grievances preserve recruitment opportunities. Breaking that cycle requires protection, accountability and political access. Another series of arrests cannot supply the trust that an honoured amnesty and meaningful participation might have built.
For Pakistan, Kabul's domestic failures intersect with a separate, documented security threat. The UN Monitoring Team's August 2026 report states that Taliban support for the TTP continued as it escalated attacks against Pakistan. The report also records Kabul's denial of harbouring terrorist groups.
The same report describes attempts to restrain the TTP, including relocating approximately 2,000 fighters and family members farther from the border and a reported warning against continued attacks. These measures deserve scrutiny. Their significance depends on whether they disrupt recruitment, financing and attack planning.
Here lies Kabul's central contradiction: it claims authority sufficient to demand respect for Afghan sovereignty, yet its conduct falls short of the responsibilities accompanying that authority. Governing Afghanistan entails preventing its territory from enabling attacks against neighbouring countries.
Pakistan should seek a negotiated verification framework: designated liaison officers, documented responses to specific threat notifications, verified action against identified facilities and facilitators, and coordinated investigation of financing channels. Regular reviews should track unresolved cases. Regional participation could support verification where agreed, with safeguards for sensitive information and clear responsibilities.
Pakistan must continue strengthening its own intelligence, policing and prosecution. Those obligations do not absolve Kabul. Nor should Islamabad confuse Afghan resistance organisations with ISKP. The UN report records serious setbacks to ISKP alongside its continuing threat. Different actors require distinct assessments; opposition to the Taliban alone establishes no common political project.
Another Afghan civil war would threaten Pakistan through displacement, disrupted commerce and opportunities for terrorist networks. Islamabad's interest lies in a functioning neighbour.
The Taliban's unfinished victory is ultimately a test of government. Can they protect former adversaries, accommodate excluded communities and act against networks threatening their neighbours? The resistance landscape makes those questions harder to evade. Pakistan cannot be asked to absorb the consequences while Kabul offers assurances unsupported by action.
Afghanistan needs a peace its people can trust. Pakistan needs a neighbour whose commitments it can verify. Kabul must deliver both.

title: The anatomy of a hard state
description: Thomas Hobbes imagined a different world
content:
Thomas Hobbes imagined a different world
More than half a century ago, Swedish economist Gunnar Myrdal introduced the concept of the soft state in his monumental Asian Drama. Studying the stubborn persistence of poverty across South Asia, he identified a phenomenon conventional economic theory struggled to explain. Countries possessed constitutions, laws, development plans and elaborate administrative structures, yet remained trapped in poverty, inequality and institutional dysfunction.
The problem concerned the relationship between power and obligation. The governing classes refused to impose discipline upon themselves and their influential allies. Laws were selectively implemented. Corruption flourished through collusion between public officials and private interests. Institutions became instruments of accommodation.
Myrdal's soft state could legislate without governing, command without transforming, and accumulate authority without exercising it consistently. One wonders whether Myrdal would find contemporary Pakistan particularly unfamiliar.
A hard state, the antithesis of Myrdal's soft state, would rest upon institutional integrity. The law would acquire meaning because it applied to everyone. Public office would become an obligation. Hardness, in this conception, would lie in the states' ability to hold the powerful to the same laws it imposes upon the powerless.
Thomas Hobbes imagined a different world. Writing amid the bloodshed of seventeenth-century England, he conceived the Leviathan, a sovereign formidable enough to rescue society from chaos. There is something distinctly Hobbesian about Pakistan's contemporary rhetoric. Security becomes the organising principle of political life, stability the supreme virtue, and obedience an essential condition of collective survival.
Yet Hobbes wrote in the shadow of civil war. Pakistan's crisis is more intricate. Its institutions have exercised tremendous coercive power for decades, while the underlying structures of economic privilege, political patronage and administrative decay have endured. The difficulty lies in the uneven distribution of that power's consequences. The state can mobilise considerable resources to contain a demonstration, yet struggle to provide drinking water to a village. It can impose restrictions overnight, while judicial decrees gather dust for years. It can scrutinise the finances of ordinary citizens, while fortunes built through proximity to power remain difficult to penetrate.
The machinery is formidable. Its application is selective.
Consider the economy, that elaborate theatre in which Pakistan's inequalities are endlessly reproduced. The small manufacturer negotiates expensive electricity, unpredictable taxation and bureaucratic obstacles. The salaried employee watches each adjustment disappear into deductions. The farmer struggles against costs he cannot control and markets he cannot influence. Elsewhere, privileged interests negotiate exemptions, subsidies and regulatory advantages. Economic opportunity becomes intertwined with political access. Influence acquires a market value greater than innovation.
A genuinely hard state could dismantle this arrangement. It could confront cartels, recover public wealth, enforce contracts and make powerful interests answer for their obligations. But imagine a harder state that leaves the underlying distribution of privilege untouched. The shopkeeper faces another inspection. The manufacturer receives another demand. The taxpayer carries another burden. Meanwhile, the familiar beneficiaries of patronage remain comfortably insulated from the discipline demanded of everyone else.
Enterprise becomes defensive. Investment retreats. Young people regard emigration as their most promising economic strategy. The country grows increasingly efficient at extracting obedience while remaining incapable of creating opportunity.
A nation cannot police its way into prosperity.
The political consequences are darker still. Pakistan is a federation of complicated histories, wounded memories and competing aspirations. In Balochistan, grievances concerning political exclusion, disappearances and resource distribution coexist with deadly militant violence. In Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, communities have lived for decades beneath the shadow of terrorism and successive security operations.
The state must confront armed violence. But a bullet cannot settle every political grievance, and a checkpoint cannot manufacture belonging. When every expression of discontent becomes a security question, the distance between dissent and disloyalty begins to shrink. The citizen who demands accountability becomes an inconvenience to be managed.
Every republic possesses safety valves. Parliament absorbs political anger. Courts restrain arbitrary authority. Elections offer peaceful change. A free press exposes failures before they metastasise. Federalism allows diverse communities to negotiate their place within a shared national destiny. Seal these openings, and the pressure gathers silently, like floodwater against a dam whose foundations have already begun to crack.
The streets may grow quieter. Newspapers may become cautious. Those exercising authority may interpret the silence as stability, perhaps even contentment. But silence is a treacherous measure of national health. People can stop speaking long before they stop feeling.
Max Weber understood that the state claims a monopoly over the legitimate use of force. That single word separates public authority from mere domination. Legitimacy emerges when laws bind the powerful, when institutions restrain those entrusted with them, and when citizens possess remedies against injustice. Without such restraints, the social contract begins to resemble a bargain written by one party alone. Taxes are compulsory, services uncertain. Obedience is demanded, accountability negotiated. Patriotism becomes a test administered from above. Eventually, those temporarily entrusted with state power begin to imagine themselves indistinguishable from the state itself.
Yet the republic belongs to its citizens. Governments, commanders and officeholders are merely its custodians, entrusted with powers that derive their legitimacy from the constitutional order.
A genuinely hard state must therefore possess the courage to discipline itself. It must enforce judicial decisions that inconvenience the influential, investigate wrongdoing within its own institutions, tolerate uncomfortable criticism and protect the constitutional rights of those who disagree with its rulers. Restraint is perhaps the most demanding expression of strength. Any authority can impose its will upon the powerless. Far fewer possess the integrity to limit themselves.
For nearly eight decades, ordinary Pakistanis have asked their republic for remarkably little. A decent education for their children. A livelihood that preserves their dignity. A court that delivers justice. A government that treats them as citizens rather than subjects. The tragedy is that these modest expectations have become revolutionary demands.
When the dust finally settles, we may discover that we have built a state powerful enough to silence its people, but too feeble to confront its own reflection.

title: Empowering women through academic leadership
description: Securing the delegation s participation  however  was not straightforward
content:
Securing the delegation's participation, however, was not straightforward
Universities are often judged by buildings, budgets, rankings and distinguished faculty. Yet their true character sometimes emerges through a decision that opens doors. I witnessed one such decision during the Frontiers of Physics National Symposium, jointly organised by the Karachi Physics Society and Pakistan Physical Society at the University of Karachi on October 67, 2026.
Among the participants was a delegation of 25 students and faculty members from Begum Nusrat Bhutto Women University, Sukkur. The young women, accompanied by four faculty members - two women and two men - had undertaken an arduous bus journey of nearly twelve hours each way to attend the symposium. Their presence represented far more than participation in an academic event; it reflected determination, enthusiasm and a remarkable willingness to travel long distances in pursuit of knowledge. Above all, it demonstrated that women's empowerment becomes truly meaningful when institutional encouragement translates into genuine opportunities for academic exposure, intellectual growth and the freedom to explore horizons beyond geographical and social boundaries.
The symposium brought together researchers working in high-energy physics, quantum technologies, condensed matter, biomedical physics and sustainable energy. For established scientists, conferences offer opportunities to exchange findings. For students, particularly those with limited academic exposure, they can change the direction of an entire career.
Securing the delegation's participation, however, was not straightforward. Pakistani universities operate under persistent financial constraints, and arranging a visit for roughly 25 participants required institutional support. We therefore approached its Vice Chancellor, Prof Dr Tehmina Mangan, explaining why their presence mattered. Despite austerity pressures, she gave the request special attention and helped make their participation possible. I appreciated not only the decision but the educational vision behind it: a restricted budget should not automatically mean restricted horizons.
This gesture carries particular significance for women's higher education. Pakistan has no shortage of talented, ambitious young women, but their opportunities can be narrowed by geography, limited resources, social expectations and insufficient exposure to professional networks. A student from Sukkur should have the same freedom to imagine herself in a research laboratory, at an international conference or leading a scientific team as a student from any major city. Empowerment is not achieved by repeating inspirational slogans. It is achieved by creating circumstances in which women can travel, participate, question, collaborate and be taken seriously as emerging scholars.
The composition of the delegation itself offered a hopeful lesson. Women students participated with the guidance of both female and male faculty members, illustrating that advancing women's education need not be framed as a contest between genders. It is a shared academic responsibility. Institutions flourish when women are encouraged to lead and when colleagues, irrespective of gender, help remove unnecessary barriers from their path.
After decades in academia, I have come to value these opportunities deeply. Education cannot be confined to prescribed syllabi and examination halls. Scientific confidence develops through exposure, mentorship and the discovery that the world of research is open to those willing to enter it.
The occasion was particularly meaningful as it coincided with my retirement from the University of Karachi, reminding me that a university's greatest responsibility is to create opportunities for future generations. I sincerely commend Dr Tehmina Mangan, my colleagues and friends in the university administration who supported her efforts in facilitating this academic visit, the accompanying faculty members, and the enthusiastic students. Their collective efforts demonstrated how visionary leadership, institutional cooperation and academic commitment can overcome financial constraints. True women's empowerment lies not merely in encouraging dreams, but in opening doors to their fulfilment. After all, a university's greatness is measured not by what it possesses, but by the futures it makes possible.

title: Karachi s waste problem
description: Karachi s sanitation crisis begins well before waste arrives at a disposal site
content:
Karachi's sanitation crisis begins well before waste arrives at a disposal site
The inauguration of Sindh's first engineered sanitary landfill at Jam Chakro is a welcome and long-overdue step towards addressing Karachi's worsening waste disposal problem. The development, alongside four planned garbage transfer stations, deserves recognition. However, it also raises a fundamental question. What good is a modern landfill if much of the city's garbage never reaches it?
Karachi's sanitation crisis begins well before waste arrives at a disposal site. There was a time when municipal workers routinely swept streets and garbage was collected from neighbourhoods. Over the years, this basic service has steadily deteriorated, leaving residents in many localities dependent on private collectors or forced to tolerate heaps of refuse accumulating along roadsides. The disappearance of regular collection has allowed illegal dumping grounds to proliferate, with waste frequently finding its way into stormwater drains and vacant plots. The problem is compounded by weak oversight and fragmented responsibility. Only days before the inauguration, the Sindh Assembly's Public Accounts Committee raised concerns about uncollected garbage across Karachi and questioned the functioning of the Sindh Solid Waste Management Board. Substantial public expenditure on waste management must translate into cleaner neighbourhoods rather than merely larger contracts and new infrastructure.
A lasting solution requires an integrated system that begins at the household and extends to final disposal. Regular street sweeping and scheduled garbage collection must be restored across all neighbourhoods, supported by adequate collection points and enforceable performance standards for contractors. Greater attention must also be paid to waste segregation and recycling so that landfills do not become overwhelmed by material that could otherwise be recovered. Above all, municipal authorities must establish clear lines of accountability, allowing residents to report failures and expect timely action. The Jam Chakro project represents an important investment, but it cannot substitute for the everyday functioning of municipal services.

title: Another polio reminder
description: Another polio reminder
content:
Country has conducted four large-scale vaccination campaigns in 2026
The confirmation of a polio case in Karachi is a reminder that no part of the country can be considered safe from the crippling disease. The city had been polio-free for nearly two years before the case of the current victim, a baby boy from Jamali Colony in Karachi East. The boy was reportedly malnourished, which makes people more susceptible to diseases, but reports did not confirm whether or not the boy had been vaccinated.
The latest victim is the seventh person to get polio in the current year, and some critics have been quick to blame external factors, but the fact is that eradicating a disease such as polio should not be this hard - vaccines are donated by other countries and NGOs, while several local and international NGOs also pitch in to support your study abroad effort. Despite all the foreign support, environmental surveillance has consistently revealed polio traces around Karachi, so even if people are not getting sick, we continue to detect the virus in water throughout the year, meaning that it was only a matter of time before something went wrong.
The country has conducted four large-scale vaccination campaigns in 2026, reaching over 45 million children, and has reduced cases from 74 in 2024 to 31 in 2025 and now seven this year. Such gains are real and deserve recognition, but the ultimate goal - zero cases - remains elusive, and each new infection pushes it further out of reach. It does not help that insecurity and access constraints abound in southern Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, while pockets of vaccine refusal and misinformation also contribute to the virus threat.
There is still an optimistic take on the situation, as one single case should not be cause for knee-jerk reactions. Pakistan has made significant progress in reducing annual cases, and with the right social conditions, we could significantly boost vaccine coverage and access to reliable information. Polio will almost certainly hit a few more kids in the coming years, but we hope this next batch will be the last.

title: Pushing for de dollarisation
description: Pakistan s stated intention to promote  protect WTO s multilateral trading system to ensure inclusive global growth
content:
Pakistan's stated intention to promote, protect WTO's multilateral trading system to ensure inclusive global growth
Pakistan put forward a pertinent proposal concerning developing economies by calling for the use of national currencies in mutual settlements. It also voiced the need to establish mechanisms, such as development banks, to offset global financial shocks. Speaking at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Dushanbe yesterday, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar pushed the envelope further on a resolve previously attained by the 10-member bloc in Islamabad in 2024. He stressed the need for a roadmap to gradually increase the share of national currencies in trade, moving away from the monopoly of the US dollar. The proposed establishment of an SCO Fund and new investment avenues are direct extensions of this strategy.
Establishing a parallel global economy has been a longstanding goal for developing nations, particularly those facing US sanctions. As targets of Western restrictions that stifle growth and block international market access, Russia and Iran are leading this push. To reduce reliance on the greenback and alleviate debt burdens, these nations have proposed trading through a basket of mutually acceptable local currencies. While BRICS remains central to this effort, its recent New Delhi summit stopped short of proposing a common currency, focusing instead on interoperable payment systems and national-currency trade.
Pakistan's stated intention is to promote and protect the WTO's multilateral trading system to ensure inclusive global growth. The Global South has long criticised the protectionist policies and unilateral coercive measures of Western nations which have left the world with a deeply lopsided developmental landscape. These nations argue with good reason that the US dollar's monopoly, established primarily after the 1973 Middle East oil crisis, violates the spirit of international law by exacerbating inequality and suppressing growth. Incorporating currencies like the yuan, ruble, yen and rupee into international trade settlements is indispensable to erecting a new financial architecture built for equitable global development.

title: Learning poverty
description: We often cite that 28 2 million school age children are out of school
content:
We often cite that 28.2 million school-age children are out of school
Once a student asked me a question that was far more serious than anything I would normally expect to hear in the classroom. "Sir, how are we supposed to continue our education when we cannot afford it?" I had no easy answer.
Being a teacher, we tell children that education is their ticket to a better life. We tell parents that education is the best investment they can make. We tell the country that its future depends on an educated generation.
A report revealed that Pakistani households spent Rs2.8 trillion on education, compared with Rs2.23 trillion spent by the public sector. In other words, families financed 56% of the country's total education expenditure.
Stop there for a moment. If families are paying more for education than the state, how much of an educational right is actually being exercised? And the poorest families are not the ones with spare money. They are the ones forced to choose. School fee or electricity bill? Books or groceries? Transport fare or medicine?
When education becomes a competition against basic necessities, dropping out is no longer necessarily a matter of losing interest. Sometimes it is simply mathematics. And Pakistan's mathematics is worrying.
We often cite that 28.2 million school-age children are out of school. But what about those who are actually inside schools? An education survey 2026 found that 77% of 10-year-olds could not read and understand a simple text. Do you call that literacy?
We often talk about merit as if every child begins from the same starting line. They do not. One student attend a well-resourced private school, have qualified teachers, private tuition, a computer, internet access and a quiet room in which to study. Another sits in an overcrowded classroom, share textbooks with siblings, travel long distances to school and study at night when electricity is available.
Then we put both students in the same examination hall and call the result pure merit. Is it?
I am not arguing against merit. Quite the opposite. Merit matters. But opportunity comes before merit can be fairly measured. The question should not only be, "Who scored the highest?" It should also be, "Who achieved this despite having the least?"
The Constitution already recognises the importance of education. Article 25-A guarantees free and compulsory education for children between 5 and 16 years of age. But what happens after 16? Does the need for education suddenly disappear? Does poverty stop mattering when a student enters university?
Of course not. In fact, the financial burden often becomes greater.
Pakistan needs doctors, engineers, scientists, teachers, technicians, researchers, IT professionals and skilled workers. We speak of our young population as a demographic opportunity, but a young population without affordable, quality education can become an opportunity lost.
And this is happening at precisely the wrong time. Education spending is only 0.8% of GDP this year, down from previous years.
We cannot want a knowledge economy while treating education as an expense to be postponed. We cannot talk about competing with the world while telling poor families to somehow find the money.
The answer is not simply to abolish every fee, nor is it realistic to expect the state to finance every educational expense without limits. What we need is stronger public education, better teachers, transparent financial assistance, affordable higher and technical education, and greater investment in digital access and skills.
Above all, education must be treated as a national investment rather than a private burden.
Because when a talented student drops out, Pakistan does not save the cost of educating that student. It loses the doctor, engineer, teacher, scientist or skilled professional that student might have become.
Perhaps we should stop asking poor families why they cannot afford to educate their children.
Education is supposed to be the ladder out of poverty. We should not make the ladder so expensive that the poor cannot reach it.

title: Princess Diaries    actor Erik von Detten faces lawsuit over  2 1 million gold deal
description: Princess Diaries    actor Erik von Detten faces lawsuit over  2 1 million gold deal
content:
Erik von Detten faces an elder abuse and fraud lawsuit over alleged gold coin sales worth millions of dollars
The Princess Diaries actor Erik von Detten is facing a lawsuit alleging elder abuse and fraud over gold coin purchases worth millions of dollars.
An elderly California couple filed the lawsuit on May 11 in Los Angeles County Superior Court, naming von Detten, 44, and precious metals company Rosland Capital LLC as defendants, according to court documents reviewed by USA TODAY.
The plaintiffs, Sheila Greenberg, 85, and Norman Greenberg, 97, allege they spent approximately $2.1 million on gold coins that were worth only $1.3 million. They are seeking $900,000 in damages, recovery of their alleged losses and additional punitive damages.
According to the complaint, the couple first contacted Rosland Capital in 2020 after seeing a television advertisement. They were subsequently connected with von Detten, who works for the company as a broker.
The Greenbergs claim they disclosed having approximately $2 million in retirement accounts and limited knowledge of gold investments. They initially purchased Lady Liberty gold coins worth roughly $1 million, which were reportedly stored at Delaware Depository rather than delivered to them. The couple also alleges they paid recurring storage and account maintenance fees.
The lawsuit further claims von Detten later purchased approximately $1 million in additional coins on their behalf. The plaintiffs allege they eventually discovered substantial markups that left the coins worth significantly less than they had paid.
The complaint includes five claims against von Detten and Rosland Capital, including violations of California's elder abuse protection law, fraud, breach of fiduciary duty, constructive fraud and conversion. The defendants have not publicly responded to the allegations in the provided report. The case remains pending, and the plaintiffs have requested a jury trial.
Von Detten is best known for playing Josh Bryant opposite Anne Hathaway in the 2001 Disney film The Princess Diaries . His other credits include Brink! , the television series So Weird and voicing Sid in Toy Story .
The actor largely stepped away from Hollywood to pursue a career in finance at the age of 25, explaining in a 2021 interview that he wanted more consistent employment to support his family.

title: North Korean state media releases photos of Kim Jong Un amid death rumors
description: Photos come after earlier rumours circulated online alleging Kim Jong Un died from  severe cerebral haemorrhage
content:
Photos come after earlier rumours circulated online alleging Kim Jong Un died from 'severe cerebral haemorrhage'
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un appeared in photos released by state media on Tuesday after rumours circulated on social media claiming he had died of a brain haemorrhage.
Kim visited a consumer goods exhibition featuring clothing and footwear on Monday, according to the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The report was accompanied by photos showing Kim touring the exhibition alongside his daughter, Ju Ae, and party and government officials.
Earlier on Sunday, Xie Wanjun, who identifies himself as chairman of the China Democracy Party, a group banned by China, claimed in a social media post that Kim had suffered a "severe cerebral haemorrhage and fallen into a coma" before being transferred to Peking Union Medical College Hospital for emergency treatment due to "the poor medical conditions in North Korea."
Read : What would happen to North Korea if Kim Jong Un died
Xie, who lives in the US, further claimed that Kim had died from the severity of his condition and a delay in receiving optimal treatment, adding that his body had been secretly transported back to North Korea and that authorities were concealing news of his death.
North Korean state media regularly publishes photos of Kim and reports on his activities.
Rumours about Kim's death have circulated before, as North Korea's limited access to information makes it difficult to independently verify reports about the country's leadership.
The North Korean leader, who is believed to be 42, is also believed to have health problems, although his medical condition has not been publicly confirmed.

title: DWTS    suspension  What really led to Val Chmerkovskiy   s absence
description: Val Chmerkovskiy   s    DWTS    suspension followed an inappropriate post  not an HR complaint by Carrie Ann Inaba
content:
Val Chmerkovskiy’s ‘DWTS’ suspension followed an inappropriate post, not an HR complaint by Carrie Ann Inaba
Val Chmerkovskiy’s suspension from Dancing with the Stars was not the result of a human resources complaint filed by judge Carrie Ann Inaba, according to a report by PEOPLE .
The professional dancer, 40, confirmed on October 17 that he would miss the October 20 episode following an “inappropriate” social media post referencing Inaba’s criticism of his wife, Jenna Johnson.
The controversy began after Inaba, 58, commented on Johnson’s performance during the October 13 episode. Chmerkovskiy subsequently shared a TikTok status that has since been deleted, alluding to Will Smith slapping Chris Rock at the 2022 Academy Awards in defence of his wife, Jada Pinkett Smith.
In the post, Chmerkovskiy wrote that viewers “almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom”, referencing Smith’s role in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air .
PEOPLE reported that the suspension followed an investigation by BBC Studios, the production company behind Dancing with the Stars , after Chmerkovskiy publicly apologised for his remarks. The action was taken under the studio’s protocols rather than in response to an HR complaint from Inaba.
On October 17, Chmerkovskiy explained that his initial intention had been to defend his wife but acknowledged that his choice of reference was inappropriate.
“Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was,” he said in his statement.
BBC Studios also addressed the incident, describing the post as inappropriate and stating that it did not reflect the standards expected of people associated with the show. The company added that the well-being of everyone working on the programme was a priority.
Chmerkovskiy’s absence from the October 20 episode means former professional dancer Alan Bersten will partner Johnson for a Viennese waltz during Dedication Night.
Dancing with the Stars airs Tuesdays at 8pm ET on ABC and Disney+, with episodes available to stream on Hulu the following day.

title: Primary suspect in Laiba Ejaz suicide case dies after being shot by accomplices  police
description: Muhammad Nauman succumbed to his injuries after his accomplices opened fire on police team in Islamabad  says police
content:
Muhammad Nauman succumbed to his injuries after his accomplices opened fire on police team in Islamabad
The primary suspect in the case involving the suicide of former International Islamic University Islamabad (IIUI) student Laiba Ejaz died after being wounded by gunfire from his own accomplices during an exchange of fire with police in Islamabad.
According to a police spokesperson, the suspect, identified as Muhammad Nauman, was in custody and was being taken to a location for recovery on the basis of information provided by him when the incident occurred.
The spokesperson said four of Nauman’s accomplices, travelling on two motorcycles, had been lying in wait along the route. They opened indiscriminate fire on the police team in an attempt to secure his release.
Read : Islamabad student found dead after allegedly losing Rs7m in education scam
Nauman was wounded by gunfire from his own accomplices, the spokesperson said, adding that police personnel remained unharmed due to their bulletproof jackets and other precautionary measures.
The injured suspect was taken to a hospital for medical treatment but later succumbed to his injuries, the spokesperson confirmed.
Search operations were under way to arrest the remaining suspects, according to the police.
Laiba, who had aspired to study at a top US university, was found hanging from a tree near a road in Islamabad on October 9, after her family allegedly lost around Rs7 million to a consultant who had promised to secure her admission and a scholarship.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also took notice of the incident and directed the inspector general of Islamabad police and the chief commissioner to take immediate action against the suspect. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also vowed to look into the case personally.
The FIA’s Anti-Human Trafficking Circle in Islamabad registered a case against Nauman and Fatima Sarwar under Sections 419 (cheating), 420 (cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property) and 109 (abetment) of the Pakistan Penal Code, read with Sections 18 and 22 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1979.
Preliminary investigations revealed that the suspects allegedly acted in connivance to deceive Laiba with promises of a US visa and scholarship. They allegedly received a total of Rs9.3 million from the family.
The FIA said the suspects allegedly prepared fake scholarship award letters, university admission offer letters and fee payment receipts to keep the family under the impression that the process was genuine. Of the total amount, Rs2.9m was transferred through Laiba’s personal bank account, while the remaining sum was received in cash, according to the agency.
Also Read : Islamabad court grants five-day remand of suspect in Laiba suicide case
Laiba's family stated that she had aspired to enrol at Harvard University for further studies and that they had made significant financial sacrifices to secure Laiba’s academic future and fulfil her dream. Laiba’s father sold his plot and pitched in Rs2.1 million from the sale’s proceeds, while her mother sold her gold jewellery.
According to the family, the suspect who reportedly defrauded them claimed to be an accounts officer at the Islamabad High Court and at other times presented himself as an employee of the superior judiciary or an officer of a sensitive institution. The family claimed that despite the substantial payment, the promises regarding admission and the scholarship given to Laiba were never fulfilled.
Laiba’s maternal uncle, Rana Amjad, stated that the Harvard University admission letter, scholarship letter and other documents provided by the suspect turned out to be fake upon verification.
He said that Laiba suffered severe distress and mental anguish after the alleged fraud came to light. Her family demanded a thorough investigation into the matter, the arrest of all individuals involved in the alleged fraud, and the recovery of the money.

title: NCCIA arrests Khanewal man indicted in  126m US postal fraud case
description: NCCIA registers case against Faheem Akram  indicted in US over alleged  126m counterfeit postage scheme
content:
Registers case against Faheem Akram over alleged sale of 5.1m counterfeit US postage labels
The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) Lahore Zone on Tuesday arrested Faheem Akram, a Pakistani national indicted by United States authorities over an alleged online scheme involving the sale of more than 5.1 million counterfeit US postage labels, causing losses exceeding $126 million to the country’s postal service.
According to the NCCIA, Akram allegedly operated the scheme from August 2023 till last month, selling counterfeit shipping labels for around $2 each. The agency cited transactions worth approximately Rs35 billion, while clarifying that the $126 million figure represented alleged losses to the US Postal Service.
A case has been registered and the investigation is under way.
Read : Pakistani national indicted in US over alleged $126m postage fraud
The US Department of Justice had announced on September 28 that a federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida had indicted Akram, 33, a resident of Khanewal, on charges including conspiracy to defraud the US government, counterfeit postage and wire fraud.
According to US prosecutors, a website, LabelsBank.com was not authorised to sell US Postal Service products and services. It allegedly offered counterfeit postage at a fixed price, irrespective of a parcel’s weight, size or destination, allowing customers to ship packages at rates substantially below legitimate postal charges.
US court records showed that more than 5,200 people had used the website to purchase over 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels. A court order authorised the seizure and shutdown of the website.
The investigation identified 16 bank accounts allegedly linked to the case, of which seven belong to the suspect, five to his brother, two to his wife, and one each to a sister and maternal aunt.

title: Balochistan govt rejects comparison with K P  says cooperating with Centre on combatting terrorism
description: Balochistan   s security forces  carried out more than 60 000 IBOs  raids over the past two years  says official
content:
Balochistan’s security forces carried out more than 60,000 IBOs, raids over the past two years, says official
The Balochistan government on Tuesday rejected comparisons with the former provincial government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), stating that, unlike the latter, it was cooperating with the federal government in the fight against terrorism.
Speaking at a press conference in Quetta, Balochistan Home and Tribal Affairs Minister Mir Ziaullah Langau rejected comparisons between the two provinces, saying misleading statements about the province’s security situation were unhelpful at a time when national unity was needed to combat terrorism.
The minister said greater cooperation by the K-P government with federal authorities and security forces in implementing the National Action Plan could have helped avoid the need for emergency measures, further calling on political leaders to support state institutions and work together to address the country’s security challenges.
Read : Govt calls on all political parties to unite, forge consensus against terrorism and set aside differences
Langau also criticised Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman over his remarks concerning Balochistan and security forces, further noting that Rehman and his party had also faced difficult circumstances and suffered from terrorism.
During the press conference, Additional Chief Secretary (Home) Hamza Shafqaat informed that Balochistan’s security forces had carried out more than 60,000 intelligence-based operations and raids over the past two years, killing 1,100 suspected terrorists and arresting 450 others.
Shafqaat said the fight against terrorism had also claimed the lives of more than 300 police officers and other security personnel, while 551 civilians had been killed in terrorist attacks.
He said the provincial government had introduced 18 laws and established 17 departments to strengthen its counterterrorism efforts. A faceless court had also been established, with cases involving 90 individuals registered, he added.
Shafqaat said around 1.1 million Afghan nationals had returned to Afghanistan. He added that the government was taking steps to improve security on national highways and had digitised the Home Department and arms licensing system to improve administrative efficiency.
He said the Balochistan government stood firmly with security forces and stressed that success in the fight against terrorism required cooperation among provincial administrations, the federal government and security institutions.
Read More : Balochistan govt announces ‘all-out war’ against terrorists amid rising unrest
Adviser to the chief minister of Balochistan for Information and Political Affairs Shahid Rind rejected claims that the K-P government had been removed because it failed to approve the Mines and Minerals Act.
He said Balochistan was reviewing its own mining legislation and consulting opposition parties to address their concerns and build consensus, further adding that Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti had taken the opposition into confidence during the legislative process and that the provincial cabinet and assembly had approved laws aimed at combating terrorism.
Referring to political developments in K-P, Rind said the provincial chief minister’s reported attempts to march towards Islamabad were among the factors surrounding the imposition of emergency measures there. He added that the Balochistan chief minister had not announced any similar march towards the federal capital.
The officials reiterated that the provincial government would continue working with security forces to combat terrorism and improve security across Balochistan.

title: New AI tool can predict cancer survival chances from selfie  study
description: Trained on over 40 million facial images  AI tool analyses facial features to estimate biological age  mortality risk
content:
Trained on over 40 million facial images, AI tool analyses facial features to estimate biological age, mortality risk
US researchers have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) tool that can predict cancer patients' survival chances from a single facial photograph, according to a study published on Monday in the journal The Lancet Digital Health.
Developed by researchers at Mass General Brigham in the US state of Massachusetts, the system, called FAHR-Face, analyses facial features to estimate biological age and mortality risk, potentially helping doctors make treatment decisions.
The model was trained on more than 40 million facial photos and adapted into two tools: FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates biological age, and FAHR-FaceSurvival, which predicts cancer patients' survival directly from facial images without relying on age estimates.
Read : Alibaba open-sources AI model detecting cancer, 150 medical conditions
Researchers found that the survival model focused mainly on areas beneath the eyes and around the nose, while the age-estimation model examined facial features around the mouth and temples, suggesting the two systems identify different health-related patterns.
The survival model was trained on images of 34,363 patients and tested on another 3,820, with results independently validated using data from 4,892 cancer patients in the Netherlands.
Researchers found that patients classified in the highest-risk group had more than three times the mortality risk of those in the lowest-risk group, even after accounting for clinical factors.
Read More : Scientists train AI model to predict future illnesses
Patients whose faces appeared at least five years older than their actual age also had a 21% higher mortality risk, while those appearing at least five years younger had a 17% lower risk.
Combining the two models further improved the accuracy of survival predictions, according to the study.
Researchers said the technology could help doctors assess patients' health and guide treatment decisions, although further validation is needed before it can be widely used in clinical practice.

content:
Carrie-Anne Moss praises Hudson Williams and teases their major scene in 'Yaga', premiering October 23 on AMC+
Carrie-Anne Moss has praised Heated Rivalry star Hudson Williams while teasing a significant scene they share in the upcoming supernatural mystery series Yaga .
Speaking during AMC+'s Spotlight Panel at New York Comic Con on October 9, the 59-year-old actress discussed working with Williams, 25, in the eight-episode series created by Kat Sandler.
“I think I just have one scene with him,” Moss said. “It was really great. It’s a big one, though. It’s a big scene. And he’s lovely. And what more can I say? He’s a lovely guy. He’s talented.”
Sandler, who also attended the panel, jokingly reminded Moss that she could not reveal details about the scene, keeping the mystery surrounding Williams’ role intact.
Based on Sandler’s 2019 play of the same name, Yaga reimagines the Slavic folklore figure Baba Yaga, a powerful witch known for her unpredictable nature and complicated morality.
The story follows private investigator Rapp, played by Noah Reid, as he investigates the disappearance of Henry Park, a young fishery heir portrayed by Williams. The actor also plays a second character, Logan, adding another layer to the mystery.
Moss plays Katherine, a university professor whose connection to Henry draws her into the investigation. As the case unfolds in the coastal town of Whittock, secrets, ancient magic and mysterious relationships emerge.
Known for playing Trinity in The Matrix franchise, Moss said she was already intrigued by the Baba Yaga legend before speaking with Sandler about the project. She also praised her character, describing Katherine as a role that suited her acting style.
Yaga will premiere on AMC+ on Friday, October 23, with two episodes released initially. New episodes will follow weekly, leading to a two-episode finale on November 27.

title: Govt increases petrol by 88 paisas  diesel by 53 paisas per litre for Oct 21
description: Petrol price increases to Rs382 02 per litre  while HSD will cost Rs389 80 under daily price mechanism
content:
Petrol price increases to Rs382.02 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs389.80 under daily price mechanism
The federal government on Tuesday increased the price of petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) by 88 paisas and 53 paisas per litre, respectively, for October 21.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs382.02 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs389.80 per litre for Wednesday.
The latest revision comes a day after the government decreased the price of petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs5.16 and Rs7.69 per litre, respectively, for October 20.
Read : Govt cuts petrol by Rs5.16, diesel by Rs7.69 for Oct 20
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Oil prices ​slipped after touching a five-month high on Tuesday as traders weighed a meeting between the Iranian president and ‌Pakistan's army chief, a key US-Iran mediator, against continued Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.
Brent crude futures fell 83 cents, or 0.76%, to $108.72 at 12:31 pm EDT. Earlier in the session, the front-month contract reached $111.99, a five-month high.
"Oil ​prices remain well-supported. This suggests the market is pricing in a significant risk premium, given the situation's volatility," ING analysts said in a note on ‌Tuesday.

title: Andrew Garfield to receive Maltin Modern Master Award at Santa Barbara Film Festival
description: The award celebrates artists whose careers have made a significant impact on the film industry
content:
The award celebrates artists whose careers have made a significant impact on the film industry
Andrew Garfield will receive the Maltin Modern Master Award at the Santa Barbara International Film Festival, recognising his contributions to cinema and his work across a range of acclaimed film projects.
The award is one of the festival’s major tributes, celebrating artists whose careers have made a significant impact on the film industry. Garfield joins a long line of actors and filmmakers recognised by the Santa Barbara International Film Festival for their achievements on screen.
Garfield has built a reputation for taking on diverse roles in independent films and major studio productions. He earned Academy Award nominations for his performances in Hacksaw Ridge and Tick, Tick… Boom! , while his portrayal of Eduardo Saverin in The Social Network helped establish him as a prominent figure in Hollywood. He also gained widespread recognition for playing Peter Parker in The Amazing Spider-Man films and returning to the role in Spider-Man: No Way Home .
More recently, Garfield has continued to pursue varied projects, including We Live in Time and After the Hunt . He also stars as Sam Altman in Luca Guadagnino’s film Artificial , which examines the world of artificial intelligence and the people behind its development.
The Maltin Modern Master Award is named after film critic and historian Leonard Maltin, who has been closely associated with the festival’s tribute programme. The honour recognises individuals whose work has helped shape contemporary cinema.
The Santa Barbara International Film Festival is known for its annual awards-season events, bringing together performers, directors and other film industry figures ahead of the Academy Awards. Garfield’s recognition adds to the festival’s tradition of celebrating influential talent and performances.

title: Pakistan committed to fiscal reforms and sustainability  President Zardari tells IMF delegation
description: Says economy grew to 3 7  in FY25 26  fiscal deficit fell to 2 6  of GDP
content:
Says economy grew to 3.7% in FY25-26, fiscal deficit fell to 2.6% of GDP
President Asif Ali Zardari on Tuesday reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to fiscal sustainability, energy sector reforms, privatisation and social protection, saying the government was pursuing inclusive and green economic growth.
In a meeting with International Monetary Fund (IMF) Middle East and Central Asia Department Director Jihad Azour at Aiwan-e-Sadr in Islamabad, the president said Pakistan had moved from economic stabilisation towards recovery, according to a press release issued by the President’s Secretariat.
The president cited an increase in the size of the economy to $452.1 billion in the fiscal year 2025-26, while real gross domestic product (GDP) growth accelerated to 3.7% from 3.2% in the preceding fiscal year.
He also highlighted improvements in fiscal management, saying the fiscal deficit had declined to 2.6% of GDP in FY2025-26 and the country recorded a primary surplus for the third consecutive year.
Read: KDA's cash crunch fails to stop perks for favoured officials
President Zardari appreciated the IMF’s continued engagement with Pakistan and its support for the country’s reform programme under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and the Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).
Referring to the conclusion of the fourth review of the EFF and the third review of the RSF, along with the staff-level agreement, he expressed confidence in the country’s continued progress towards “economic recovery and stability”.
The president reiterated the government’s commitment to increasing revenue mobilisation, improving tax administration and reforming public sector institutions. He said efforts were underway to expand tax documentation, digitalise revenue collection and curb tax evasion.
He added that the reform programme enjoyed the support of all political stakeholders, with provincial governments also contributing towards meeting the agreed targets.
Read more: Pakistan seeks global finance overhaul
The president also underscored Pakistan’s efforts to promote peace amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
Azour acknowledged Pakistan’s continued engagement with the IMF under the ongoing programme and stressed the need to sustain reforms to strengthen macroeconomic stability, maintain fiscal discipline and support sustainable economic growth.
The IMF delegation included Pakistan mission chief Iva Petrova and resident representative Mahir Binici.
Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb, Senator Sherry Rehman, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla, former finance minister Syed Naveed Qamar and the finance secretary also attended the meeting.
Pakistan remains engaged with the IMF under a $7 billion EFF and a $1.4 billion RSF. Earlier this month, Pakistan and the Fund reached a staff-level agreement following the fourth review under the EFF and the third review under the RSF.
The staff-level agreement is subject to approval by the IMF Executive Board and upon approval, Pakistan will have access to about $1 billion (SDR 760 million) under the EFF and about $210 million (SDR 154 million) under the RSF, bringing total disbursements under the two arrangements to about $5.7 billion.
Pakistan will chair the Boards of Governors of the IMF and the World Bank Group in 2027, marking the country's first return to the leadership of both institutions since 1953.
