Minister says it's unfortunate that attempts being made to link emergency with things other than terrorism
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry on Monday rubbished linking governor's rule and the imposition of an emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) to mineral extraction in the province.
The emergency and governor's rule were declared on October 11 after negotiations between the government and opposition failed, culminating in a PTI long march towards Islamabad that began on October 4.
Last week, a joint session of parliament adopted two separate resolutions ratifying the presidential proclamations imposing a state of emergency and governor's rule in K-P for two months, amid protests from the opposition.
The opposition has decried the move as an attempt to encroach on the province's mineral wealth and vowed to resist what it has said is the forcible occupation of Pakhtun lands and the appropriation of their natural resources.
Speaking on a private television programme, Chaudhry said political parties were trying to link the emergency to the debate over minerals because they thought the emergency was imposed to gain power as part of a "power game".
"It's not a power game but a peace game, because of which an emergency has been imposed".
The minister noted it was unfortunate that attempts were being made to link the emergency in K-P with things other than terrorism, further adding that the emergency had been imposed in extraordinary circumstances and a constitutional option has been used for that purpose.
Chaudhry further said that the "expectations of certain political parties have not been met, including people in my own party who wanted a share of the authority in the new political setup. It was explained to them that the people selected in the advisory council were done so on merit and were experts in their respective fields."
While explaining the reasons for the imposition of an emergency in K-P, the minister underlined that there were differences of opinion between the former provincial government and the federal government on the issue of counterterrorism, further adding that the former chief minister was not even willing to condemn terrorism and the TTP.
On the security situation in K-P, Chaudhry stated that Dera Ismail Khan was among the 12 districts in which operations would be conducted in the first phase. "There is no writ of the government there in DI Khan, and I can provide you the names of parliamentarians who give protection money to safely return to their home."
Talking about US Chargé d'Affaires Natalie Baker's statement in which she claimed that Pakistan possessed seven trillion dollars of mineral wealth, Chaudhry noted that Pakistan's partnership with the US was old, further adding that Natalie took the names of both Balochistan and K-P.
"Mines and minerals that have been buried for the past 80 years, should they not be extracted to pay off Pakistan's loans? The federal government has stressed that people from K-P and Balochistan will have the first right to the mineral wealth of their province, and the money will be spent on provincial development".

title: NAB claims Rs9 17tr recovery in nine months

content:
Says auction of recovered railway land could finance ML-I without foreign loans
National Accountability Bureau (NAB) Chairman Lt Gen (retired) Nazir Ahmed Butt has claimed that the bureau recovered assets worth Rs9,171.92 billion between January and September 2026.
He said the auction of reclaimed Pakistan Railways land could generate more than Rs10 trillion and provide sufficient resources to finance the long-delayed Main Line-1 (ML-I) project without foreign borrowing.
He said NAB expected significantly larger recoveries from the power sector than those secured from the railways, describing practices in the sector as "daylight robbery". The bureau would subsequently examine entities operating under the Ministry of Industries and Production, he added.
Speaking at a briefing for senior journalists in Islamabad, the NAB chairman also claimed that money laundering outflows from Pakistan had stopped, accused some countries that champion democracy of shielding suspected money launderers, and called for a comprehensive overhaul of the Capital Development Authority (CDA), saying its existing system was not functioning properly.
Butt said NAB had recovered cash and assets worth Rs26 trillion between March 2023 and December 2025, while its recoveries between January and September 2026 alone amounted to Rs9,171.92bn.
He said the bureau had recovered billions of rupees' worth of railway land as assets after just two and a half months of work. The land, he added, could provide the financial foundation for ML-I if properly monitored and auctioned.
"The assets and land we have recovered for Pakistan Railways are worth more than Rs6 trillion. If they are properly monitored and auctioned, the amount could exceed Rs10 trillion," he said, arguing that the project could be completed without relying on foreign loans.
According to the chairman, NAB's ongoing scrutiny of the power sector would bring numerous matters into the open during the first half of 2027. Once its work in the sector was completed, the bureau would turn its attention to organisations under the Ministry of Industries and Production. He expressed confidence that recoveries from the power sector would substantially exceed those made from railway assets.

National Assembly Opposition Leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai on Monday questioned the non-issuance of production orders for detained lawmakers and the whereabouts of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi following the imposition of emergency in the province.
"You have removed a provincial government; now tell us where the K-P CM [Sohail Afridi] is and where our members of parliament have disappeared," Achakzai said while speaking on a point of order.

title: Love turns into suspicion  in  Shabnam
description: Love turns into suspicion  in  Shabnam
content:
Inside Coke Studio Nu.WAV's latest release featuring Maanu, Zoha Waseem
Love, doubt and suspicion take centre stage in 'Shabnam', the latest release from Coke Studio Nu.WAV, featuring Maanu and Zoha Waseem and produced by Talal Qureshi. Released on October 18, the track explores how two people can experience the same relationship in entirely different ways, with neither perspective fully resolving the tension between them.
The song began as an unfinished collaboration between Talal Qureshi and Maanu before Zoha joined the project. Named after morning dew, which disappears before it can be held onto, 'Shabnam' reflects the fleeting and uncertain nature of relationships. Maanu approaches the song with suspicion and unanswered questions, while Zoha offers a perspective of her own, creating a musical exchange that remains deliberately unresolved.
The accompanying music video, directed by Fida Moin, extends this uncertainty into a surreal domestic setting. Everyday objects and familiar gestures take on exaggerated meanings through Maanu's perspective, blurring the boundaries between reality and imagination. The unease eventually spills into a birthday gathering that descends into chaos, while Qureshi appears as a DJ who arrives at a party only to find himself in the middle of a household consumed by suspicion.
The visual world draws on Brutalism and German Expressionism, with production design and art direction by Tanya Mirza. Concrete structures, cool grey tones, imposing interiors and carefully arranged objects create a setting that feels recognisable yet uncomfortable.
Speaking about the track, Coke Studio Nu.WAV Executive Producer Kamal Khan said the tension between the characters was present from the beginning. He noted that the collaboration evolved into two people telling different versions of the same story, with Moin's direction balancing humour and strangeness against the underlying paranoia.
The release also brings together artists with distinct musical backgrounds. Maanu has built a presence in Pakistan's indie, pop and hip-hop scene through projects including Melancholic, Khwaab and Thikaana. His appearance alongside Annural Khalid on Coke Studio Season 15's 'Jhol' brought him wider recognition.
Zoha Waseem, meanwhile, combines classical and ghazal influences with contemporary pop. She first attracted attention through performances honouring Madam Noor Jehan at Alhamra in Lahore before reaching wider digital audiences with releases including 'Majboor'.
Qureshi, a prominent figure in Pakistan's electronic music scene, has previously produced Coke Studio's Season 14 track 'Peechay Hutt', alongside projects including 'AAG' and TURBO.
Written by Maanu and Zoha Waseem, 'Shabnam' is co-produced by Maanu, with the arrangement shared by Maanu and Qureshi. The release is the fourth of six songs planned for Coke Studio Nu.WAV, following 'Dil', 'Rangeen' and 'Maheya', with two further releases expected in the coming weeks.

content:
Lack of positive cues, high oil prices, geopolitics keep key sectors under pressure
Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) closed lower on Monday as subdued activity and persistent selling in key sectors kept investors cautious, with the benchmark index failing to sustain its recovery amid a lack of positive triggers.
The KSE-100 index shed 453.63 points, or 0.27%, to settle at 165,966.09 at the end of trading. Earlier, the session began on a weak note, when the index dropped to 166,120.90, down 298.81 points, or 0.18%, at 9:38 am, reflecting early selling pressure.
The market attempted to recover during the day, with the index climbing to the intra-day high of 166,698.46 points. However, the recovery proved short-lived and the index later touched the low of 165,918.35 before ending the session in negative territory.
Selling was observed in major sectors, including automobile assemblers, cement, commercial banks, oil and gas exploration companies and oil marketing companies. The broad-based pressure limited the market's ability to build on its intra-day recovery and left the benchmark below the previous close.
Investor sentiment remained fragile as the market lacked fresh positive cues that could encourage sustained buying. With selling pressure persisting across key sectors, investors remained cautious, keeping the overall tone subdued through the session.
According to KTrade Securities, the KSE-100 index declined 454 points (-0.27%) to close at 165,966 amid cautious investor sentiment and subdued volumes reaching 109 million shares. Trading activity was concentrated in Pakistan Refinery, Cnergyico Pk, TPL Trakker, WorldCall Telecom and Saif Power, while selective buying in MCB Bank, Attock Refinery, Pakistan Oilfields, TRG Pakistan and Bank Alfalah provided partial support.
Sectoral weakness was broad-based, led by commercial banks, cement firms, investment banks and technology companies, where UBL, Systems Ltd, Fauji Fertiliser and Hub Power led the decline. Meanwhile, Brent crude remained elevated above $100/barrel, resulting in macroeconomic uncertainty.
"We expect the market to remain cautious and range bound, with near-term direction contingent on global oil prices, geopolitical developments and corporate earnings. A sustained recovery in trading volumes is critical to underpinning broader market participation and a durable rally," KTraded added.
In his report, Arif Habib Limited (AHL) Deputy Head of Trading Ali Najib mentioned that the market opened on a negative note and touched the intra-day low of 165,918 before staging a recovery to the high of 166,698. However, the recovery proved short-lived as selling pressure intensified in the second half, erasing the gains and dragging the index back towards its intra-day low by the close.
On the corporate front, Engro Fertilisers reported 3QCY26 net profit of Rs9.1 billion (EPS: Rs6.83), up 57% year-on-year (YoY), supported by strong fertiliser offtake. The company announced a cash dividend of Rs5.50/share, compared with Rs4.50/share in the same period of last year, implying an 80% payout ratio. The payout may reflect a cautious capital allocation approach amid potential liabilities.
"Going forward, the market is likely to remain volatile and range bound between 164-168k amid cautious investor sentiment and evolving macroeconomic and geopolitical developments," Najib said.
Overall trading volumes decreased to 370.9 million shares against Friday's total of 396.9 million. The value of traded shares stood at Rs19.6 billion.
Shares of 499 companies were traded in the ready market. Of these, 163 stocks closed higher, 302 fell and 34 remained unchanged.
Pakistan Refinery was the volume leader with trading in 52.9 million shares, gaining Rs1.86 to close at Rs108.81. Foreign investors sold shares worth Rs254.1 million, the National Clearing Company reported.

Ambassador urges businesses to forge partnerships, explore new markets, pursue practical projects
Portugal Ambassador Paulo Domingues has called for a major transformation in Portugal-Pakistan economic relations, stressing that the two countries must move beyond cordial diplomatic ties and translate their longstanding friendship into tangible trade, investment and joint-venture opportunities.
Highlighting the significant untapped potential between the two economies, he urged businesses on both sides to forge direct partnerships, explore new markets and pursue practical projects that could substantially expand bilateral commerce.
Addressing a meeting at the Karachi Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI), the ambassador said that although relations between Portugal and Pakistan were friendly and steadily improving, bilateral trade remained considerably below its potential. He emphasised that the two countries had complementary economic strengths and considerable scope to deepen cooperation across multiple sectors.
"Portugal and Pakistan have much more to offer each other. We must work together to turn our friendly relations into real business opportunities. Our political and economic relations are good and growing steadily, but the trade figures remain relatively low compared with the enormous potential that exists between our two countries. There is significant untapped potential that we must identify and develop through sustained efforts," he said.
Domingues observed that Portuguese businesses had yet to fully explore the Pakistani market, partly because they remained insufficiently aware of the opportunities it offered. In contrast, he noted that Pakistani businesses were increasingly exploring Portugal, with business missions already visiting the country to examine commercial prospects in different sectors. He expressed confidence that trade would increase as these initiatives gained momentum.
"The challenge is to bring our business communities together and encourage more Portuguese entrepreneurs and companies to visit Pakistan. Portugal and Pakistan may be geographically far apart, but geography should never limit our ambitions. We have a strong foundation for cooperation and what we need now is greater engagement between our companies," he remarked.
The ambassador identified several promising areas for cooperation, including trade and industry, renewable energy, technology, agriculture, fruit cultivation and innovation. He said the Portuguese embassy could help Pakistani and Portuguese companies identify buyers, suppliers, distributors and reliable long-term commercial partners.
Highlighting Portugal's experience in clean energy, he pointed out that approximately 70% of Portugal's electricity generation came from renewable sources, offering valuable opportunities for knowledge-sharing, technology cooperation and potential investment partnerships.

description: Rs5 5b airport upgrade underway
content:
Completion targeted for Jan 2028; outages limited to feeders with high losses
Practical work has commenced on the prime minister's announcement to upgrade Dera Ghazi Khan (DG Khan) Airport for international flights, Federal Minister for Energy (Power Division) Sardar Awais Ahmad Khan Leghari said during an inspection visit to the project, according to a statement issued by the Ministry of Energy on Monday.
The expansion project, costing Rs5.5 billion, is slated for completion by January 2028. Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA) teams are actively working on-site, with steady progress underway across multiple fronts, including runway expansion, the minister said.
Speaking during the visit, he reviewed ongoing progress and examined the runway expansion work. He noted that upgrading the airport for international flights will provide superior travel facilities to the local population and unlock new avenues for progress and prosperity across South Punjab.
The minister highlighted that the prime minister had announced four major development projects for DG Khan: airport expansion, the establishment of a cancer hospital, a long-term sewerage project and the widening and rehabilitation of road networks. The sewerage project is being designed to cater to the region's requirements for the next 50 years, while improved, wider roads will ensure smoother commuting. The completion of these initiatives will significantly enhance civic amenities and accelerate regional development.
Addressing nationwide electricity load management, he noted that load-shedding is being conducted strictly according to an established schedule. He pointed out that gas supply and availability constraints stemming from broader geopolitical tensions have driven up power generation costs, compelling reliance on more expensive energy sources.
He reaffirmed that the government is introducing modern technology to combat power theft and curtail line losses. In this regard, Advanced Power Management System (APMS) systems are being deployed on transformers nationwide to detect electricity theft and enable targeted enforcement.
The minister explained that APMS will identify specific transformers in high-theft areas, enabling targeted disconnections so that thousands of paying consumers on an entire feeder are not penalised for the actions of electricity thieves. This modern system will curtail power theft, minimise line losses and optimise the electricity distribution network.
He reiterated that load-shedding will continue on feeders reporting 30% or higher aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses, emphasising that no leniency will be shown towards electricity thieves or chronic defaulters. He underscored that the government remains fully committed to reforming the power distribution network, curbing operational losses and delivering better services to consumers.
The minister expressed confidence that ongoing development initiatives in DG Khan will yield substantial improvements in travel connectivity, public healthcare, sanitation and road infrastructure, while elevating the airport to international standards will create new opportunities for DG Khan and south Punjab.
Earlier, the project director of the PAA briefed the minister on the airport expansion project and presented him with a commemorative shield. The minister also planted a sapling and offered prayers as part of a plantation campaign at the site.
Member of the National Assembly Sardar Ammar Leghari, Member of the Provincial Assembly Ali Yousaf Leghari and former members of the provincial assembly Sardar Yousaf Leghari and Aleem Shah were also present on the occasion.

title: Govt eyes UNIDO help for industrial growth
description: Govt eyes UNIDO help for industrial growth
content:
Believes clean energy-driven development, local manufacturing will curb trade deficit
Adviser to the Prime Minister for Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar Khan held a meeting with a delegation of the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (Unido) to discuss industrial development, international cooperation, climate change, clean energy, competitiveness and productivity enhancement.
He stated that Pakistan was moving towards industrial growth, economic stability and the adoption of modern technologies. He emphasised that the country's large youth population represented a significant national asset, but sustainable economic progress and employment generation could not be achieved without industrialisation.
The adviser noted that Pakistan's first-ever National Industrial Policy had been formulated to provide a strategic direction for industrial growth, enhance productivity and strengthen the country's economic foundations. He underscored that addressing the trade deficit required export-led economic growth alongside the promotion of import substitution and local manufacturing.
Khan said that Pakistan possessed considerable untapped potential in both industry and agriculture. He stressed the need to utilise the country's natural resources more effectively, develop value-added industries and strengthen domestic production to create employment opportunities and improve export competitiveness.
Highlighting the challenges posed by climate change, he said that its adverse effects were significantly impacting Pakistan's agricultural output and industrial production. He underlined the importance of international cooperation, sustainable energy solutions and climate-resilient industrial development.
The adviser highlighted Pakistan's natural resource potential, particularly in gemstones and other valuable minerals. He noted that industrial opportunities were expanding across diverse sectors, ranging from olive oil production to gemstone processing, and called for developing local value chains to maximise economic returns from the country's resources.
Discussing the transition towards cleaner transportation, Haroon Akhtar Khan said that Pakistan was witnessing significant progress in the electric vehicle sector. He pointed out that the New Energy Vehicle (NEV) Policy had already been introduced and efforts were underway to accelerate the adoption of electric vehicles and expand charging infrastructure across the country.
He further stated that the promotion of solar energy had opened new opportunities for rural communities and the agricultural sector. In this regard, he highlighted the proposed Battery Energy Storage System Policy, which would support the development of local manufacturing capabilities for electric vehicle batteries and strengthen Pakistan's domestic industrial base.
Khan emphasised that Unido could play an important role in supporting Pakistan's industrial transformation through technical cooperation, technology transfer, capacity building and investment facilitation. He identified industrial development, renewable energy, climate resilience and local manufacturing as promising areas for enhanced collaboration.
The Unido delegation appreciated the opportunities for cooperation with Pakistan and highlighted the importance of sharing expertise, technical skills and best practices among member countries. The delegation identified renewable energy, particularly solar energy, as a promising area of collaboration.
It also underlined the importance of developing renewable energy infrastructure, strengthening industrial value chains and improving productivity through modern technologies and innovative industrial practices. It noted that enhanced cooperation could help attract investment, facilitate technological advancement and create new employment opportunities.

title: Gold flat as international prices slip
description: Gold flat as international prices slip
content:
Global market moves lower ahead of Fed decision; rupee inches up
Gold prices remained unchanged in Pakistan on Monday, as a stronger US dollar and rising Treasury yields pressured international bullion prices, while investors awaited the US Federal Reserve's policy decision next week.
In the local market, the price of gold stood at Rs439,036 per tola, unchanged from the previous session, according to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association (APGJSA). Similarly, the price of 10-gram gold remained stable at Rs376,402. On Saturday, gold had declined by Rs1,600 per tola.
In the international market, spot gold fell 0.5% to $4,143.91 per ounce by 11:34 am EDT (1534 GMT), while US gold futures for December delivery declined 0.4% to $4,163.30 per ounce, as per Reuters. The US dollar edged higher, making dollar-denominated gold more expensive for holders of other currencies. Meanwhile, yields on 10-year US Treasury notes rose 0.6%, adding further pressure on the non-yielding metal. Adnan Agar, Director at Interactive Commodities, said international gold prices were trading near $4,144 per ounce, with the session's low at $4,140 and high at $4,195. He said the market remained confined to a range of approximately $4,070-$4,080 on the lower side and around $4,200 on the upper side.
According to Agar, the direction of the next significant move will depend on which side of this trading range prices break through. A sustained move beyond either boundary could provide a clearer signal for the market's next direction.
Investors are also monitoring developments in the oil market and upcoming US economic data. Oil prices slipped from a five-month high after US President Donald Trump granted a waiver related to sanctions on Russian oil. Market attention is turning to next week's Federal Reserve policy announcement and the release of personal consumption expenditures (PCE) data, a key measure of US inflation.
Traders see an 83% probability that the Fed will leave rates unchanged this month, reflecting expectations that policymakers will maintain their current stance. "There are concerns that central banks will have to tighten their policies further to control inflation, which is providing yields another boost. And with yields remaining elevated, gold investors are wondering whether it makes more sense to be in the bond market right now," said Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at Forex.com.
Meanwhile, silver prices in Pakistan moved higher, contrary to no movement in gold, rising Rs59 per tola to reach Rs6,234. The Pakistani rupee gained Rs0.01 against the US dollar on Monday, closing at 276.90 in the inter-bank market, compared with the previous close of 276.91.

title: Gas deregulation plan heads to PM
description: Gas deregulation plan heads to PM
content:
Legacy circular debt, cross-subsidies identified as key to viability of restructured entities
The government is weighing a phased deregulation of the gas sector, with a proposed restructuring roadmap to be presented to the prime minister after a high-level review chaired by Federal Minister for Finance and Revenue Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb, according to a statement issued by the Ministry of Finance on Monday.
The framework aims to establish a financially sustainable, efficient and competitive gas market that supports businesses, encourages private investment and protects consumer welfare, the ministry said. It sets out a phased transition towards greater competition supported by effective regulation, improved operational performance and a more sustainable approach to pricing and supply. Participants reviewed sectoral challenges including circular debt, cross-subsidies, unaccounted-for-gas (UFG) losses and supply-demand imbalances. Discussions focused on addressing legacy liabilities and improving the financial viability of gas utilities, and on ensuring existing pressures do not undermine the proposed market structure or burden consumers.
A sustainable resolution of legacy circular debt and an approach to cross-subsidies were identified as important to the viability of restructured entities. The ministry said resolving these liabilities is central to the transition to a competitive gas market, and that legacy liabilities have weighed on the sector's finances and the government's fiscal position.
The meeting reviewed expected outcomes including enhanced energy security, increased private-sector investment, reduced fiscal and sovereign risks, greater business-to-business transactions, more stable gas pricing, improved access to competitively priced gas for exporters, and lower system losses through efficiency benchmarks and performance-based incentives.
The finance minister stressed aligning all stakeholders around a practical and implementable reform architecture. The framework draws on international experience, including gas-sector reforms in Türkiye and the United Kingdom, while accounting for Pakistan's institutional structure, market conditions and consumer interests.
Participants stressed careful sequencing to safeguard security of supply, protect regulated consumers and create a predictable environment for private-sector participation. Officials were told the design must keep supply secure throughout the transition.
The framework will be presented to the prime minister, following which further technical work and stakeholder consultations will refine the reform approach and support an orderly transition, the ministry said. The meeting reaffirmed the government's commitment to advancing reforms in a phased and consultative manner to strengthen financial sustainability, improve operational efficiency, attract investment and develop a more competitive gas market.

title: Fourth quarter growth slows to 2
description: Fourth quarter growth slows to 2
content:
Industry contracts 4.7%, govt approves $14.8b import data revision to fill gap
Pakistan's economic growth rate slowed to 2% during the last quarter of the previous fiscal year due to a contraction in the industrial sector, as the economy struggled to cope with continued fiscal stabilisation coupled with the impact of the Middle East conflict.
A year after The Express Tribune reported the $11 billion trade data discrepancy, the government also on Monday approved a revision of import data for five fiscal years till June 2025, adding cumulatively $14.8 billion to imports.
The National Accounts Committee (NAC) approved the "fresh" economic growth figure for the fourth quarter (April-June) of fiscal year 2025-26 and the revision in import data.
"Due to a high base growth of 6.1% in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2025, the economy has posted a modest growth of 2% during the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026," according to an official statement issued by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) after the NAC meeting.
It added that in the fourth quarter, the agriculture sector grew 3.7% but there was a contraction of 4.7% in the industrial sector, which pulled down the overall growth rate to a mere 2%.
The 118th meeting of the NAC was chaired by the secretary of the Ministry of Planning and Development. It added that the committee approved incorporation of revised imports data in the national accounts estimates from fiscal year 2021 to 2025, quarterly gross domestic product (GDP) growth rates and updated annual growth rates for the last two fiscal years.
Due to a slower growth rate in the last quarter, the government also slightly revised downward the annual growth rate for the last fiscal year to 3.65%.
Due to positive contributions from all constituents, the agriculture sector grew by 3.7% in the fourth quarter of the last fiscal year compared with almost flat growth in the corresponding period. Important crops grew by 2.2%, mainly due to increases in the annual benchmark for wheat, rice and sugarcane.
The PBS reported that industry contracted 4.7% in the fourth quarter compared with 20% value addition in the corresponding period. The government has attributed the massive contraction to the high base impact, but the prolonged period of fiscal stabilisation has hurt the formal sector. Regional tensions and the consequent increase in fuel prices have also dampened demand in the economy.
The PBS said the mining and quarrying industry still grew 8.9% due to higher mineral production, including gas (11.73%), oil (22.20%) and coal (8.17%).
Large-scale manufacturing (LSM) for the April-June quarter grew by a mere 0.41%, compared with 2.97% in the corresponding quarter. Small-scale and slaughtering witnessed normal growth. Because of an extremely high base growth of 123%, lower energy subsidies and a high consumer price index (CPI) deflator, the electricity, gas and water supply industry contracted by 33.2% in the fourth quarter of the last fiscal year, according to the PBS.
The construction industry posted growth of 3.52% due to higher cement production and higher spending on infrastructure in the public sector.
The services industry grew by 3.62% in the last quarter of the previous fiscal year. The PBS stated that despite a contraction in the import component, wholesale and retail trade grew by 0.75% due to growth in agricultural and manufacturing output. The transport and storage industry grew by 3.3% due to increased road transport and railways.
The PBS revised upward the import figures for five fiscal years, 2021 through 2025, due to differences in reporting between the PBS and the Pakistan Single Window (PSW) data, which was more comprehensive. The Express Tribune had reported last year that import figures were underreported by as much as $11 billion for just two fiscal years.
After the news story, the government and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) began scrutinising the data, which culminated on Monday in a revision of trade statistics.
The PBS stated that extraordinary revisions in source data also require subsequent revisions to national accounts estimates. The national statistical system has seen significant revisions in import data from fiscal year 2020-21 to fiscal year 2025 due to a systematic shift in import data compilation from Pakistan Revenue Automation Limited (PRAL) to the PSW, according to the handout.
While differences in data compiled through the two systems were relatively small during the first three years (fiscal years 2021 to 2023), significant variations emerged in fiscal years 2024 and 2025, it added.
The NAC approved that imports in fiscal year 2024-25 were in fact $64.5 billion, $6.1 billion more than earlier officially reported. Imports for fiscal year 2023-24 are now officially $59.9 billion, $5.1 billion higher than earlier reported figures.
Imports for fiscal year 2022-23 are now $56.9 billion, also higher by $1.7 billion. These were $81.1 billion for fiscal year 2021-22, higher by $1.1 billion. For fiscal year 2020-21, the new import figure is $57.3 billion, also up by $919 million.
The PBS said data on imports is used in compiling value added of wholesale and retail trade through the commodity flow approach, subsequently affecting growth rates of services and the overall economy. Further, changes in trade data also affect the economy as a whole, including overall size and per capita income, it added.
As a result of these revisions, Rs227 billion has been added to the size of the economy for fiscal year 2023-24, which then grew to Rs105.5 trillion. Likewise, the economy for fiscal year 2024-25 was increased by Rs137 billion and the total size amounted to Rs114.2 trillion, according to the PBS.
There was also a marginally positive impact of the revision in the size of the economy on per capita income.

Sia has reached a custody agreement with estranged husband Daniel Bernad, retaining primary custody of their son while establishing visitation and holiday arrangements.
Singer Sia has settled her custody dispute with estranged husband Daniel Bernad, reaching an agreement on arrangements for their young son, Somersault Wonder Bernad, affectionately known as Summi.
According to court documents obtained by TMZ , the former couple has agreed on a custody schedule that allows Sia to remain their son's primary custodial parent, while Bernad will receive generous visitation rights.

The settlement follows a prolonged custody dispute that escalated in October 2025, when Bernad sought emergency custody and accused the singer of posing a danger to their child. Sia denied the allegations, and a judge rejected his emergency custody request. The former couple was subsequently ordered to attend mediation to resolve their differences.
In April 2026, Sia and Bernad reached a separate agreement requiring the singer to pay $42,500 per month in child support. They also agreed to share legal custody and divide holiday time with their son.
The custody dispute unfolded alongside disagreements over spousal support. Bernad previously sought more than $250,000 per month in spousal support, according to TMZ.
Sia filed for divorce in March 2025 after approximately two years of marriage. Despite their separation, the former couple has now established arrangements covering their son's care, visitation and education.
The latest agreement marks a significant development in the custody battle, with Sia retaining primary physical custody while both parents have arrangements in place for spending time with their son.

Famed journalist Christiane Amanpour announced on Monday that after 43 years at CNN , she would leave the network next June.

Amanpour covered major global conflicts, including the Gulf War, the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine, and Iran.
“Remember: always be truthful, not neutral,” she said in her statement.
She said she will continue her podcast, The Ex Files, which she co-hosts with her former husband Jamie Rubin. Her program with public broadcaster PBS, Amanpour & Company, is scheduled to end in December.
CNN Chairman Mark Thompson praised Amanpour as “one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere” and thanked her for decades of journalism.
Under a recently finalised merger deal, CNN is moving into new ownership under a media giant called Skydance , which will also include CBS and its news division, and the streamers HBO Max and Paramount.

title: Kala Chapra and Lawrence of Arabia
description: Kala Chapra and Lawrence of Arabia
content:
Colonel TE Lawrence occupies a peculiar place in history
TE Lawrence's autobiographical masterpiece, Seven Pillars of Wisdom, remains one of the most influential accounts of irregular warfare, featuring on the reading lists of military academies and professional military education institutions around the world. Yet, for me, the book holds little attraction. It is the enigmatic, intriguing and self-effacing personality of its author that draws me to this extraordinary figure of history. The celebrated film Lawrence of Arabia, together with my childhood memories of Kala Chapra in Karachi, offers a more compelling reason to revisit his story. Sometimes obscurity offers refuge to greatness. Few figures illustrate this paradox better than Lawrence of Arabia.
As a young child, I remember travelling towards Karachi airport and seeing an enormous airship hangar known as Kala Chapra. The hangar was eventually dismantled in the 1960s, but it survives in the recollections of those who witnessed its imposing presence. What I did not know as a child was that Karachi had another, rather extraordinary association with Lawrence of Arabia. The very city whose skies and landmarks formed part of my childhood had once been home to a man who, having become a legend, was desperately trying to escape his own fame.
Colonel TE Lawrence occupies a peculiar place in history. The world remembers him as the British officer in flowing Arab robes who helped lead the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire during the First World War. The celebrated film Lawrence of Arabia immortalised his desert exploits, with Peter O'Toole's portrayal turning him into an enduring figure of heroic adventure.
Lawrence had encouraged Arab aspirations for independence while serving British imperial interests in the Middle East. The political settlement that followed the war fell far short of Arab expectations of independence. Conflicting wartime promises and the subsequent division of Ottoman territories left him confronting an uncomfortable truth: military success and political betrayal could coexist.
Perhaps this explains his growing determination to escape the public identity imposed upon him. In 1922, he enlisted in the Royal Air Force under the assumed name John Hume Ross, seeking the anonymity of an ordinary serviceman. When his identity was exposed, he was discharged. He subsequently joined the Royal Tank Corps under the name TE Shaw before returning to the RAF in 1925. A man celebrated across the world had abandoned his former military rank and public acclaim for the inconspicuous existence of an ordinary airman.
And this is where my childhood recollection of Kala Chapra acquires a significance I could scarcely have imagined. In January 1927, Lawrence arrived at the RAF depot at Drigh Road, Karachi, serving under the name Aircraftman TE Shaw. Far removed from the Arabian desert where his name had become legendary, he worked as a low-ranking airman in the Engine Repair Section, performing largely clerical duties rather than exercising any command.
There is a particular irony in the thought that Lawrence, whose desert exploits had captivated the world, was living anonymously in the very part of the subcontinent that I would later call home.
Karachi was not the end of Lawrence's Indian adventure. In 1928, he was posted to Miranshah, in the North-West Frontier Province, now called Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, where he served with the RAF. This was another world altogether: a stark, isolated military station in the rugged country bordering Afghanistan. Lawrence's story was not confined to Arabia or England; for a time, it unfolded in Karachi and along the North-West Frontier, places that remain integral to our own history.
There is something deeply human in this attempt to disappear. Most people spend their lives trying to become somebody. Lawrence, having become somebody in the eyes of the world, spent much of his remaining life trying to become nobody.
On 13 May 1935, Lawrence was involved in a motorcycle accident near his home in Dorset, England. He died six days later, aged 46. His death brought a premature end to a life that had already acquired the proportions of a modern myth.
Yet Lawrence's fascination lies not merely in his military achievements or tragic end. It lies in the contradictions that made him so difficult to understand. He was celebrated for his courage but burdened by guilt; admired for his leadership but suspicious of the fame it brought; and remembered as a man of extraordinary action who ultimately sought refuge in obscurity. His life raises an uncomfortable question: what happens when the world's idea of greatness becomes a prison for the person who embodies it?
The old Kala Chapra of Karachi and the elusive Lawrence of Arabia may appear to belong to entirely different worlds. Yet their histories intersect in the colonial aviation world of Karachi, where a man who had helped shape the destiny of Arabia served quietly under an assumed name. Both survive in memory, reminding us that disappearance is not always the same as oblivion. Sometimes what vanishes from sight acquires a more enduring presence in the mind.

title: Democratic values  not technical legalism
description: Peaceful protest is a democratic right  subject to reasonable restrictions prescribed by law
content:
Peaceful protest is a democratic right, subject to reasonable restrictions prescribed by law
On October 11, 2026, the federal government imposed an emergency and governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, bringing the PTI-led administration to an end. The federal government cited the deteriorating security situation to justify its actions. Critics, however, denounce it as a direct assault on provincial autonomy. The situation also raises a question greater than the interpretation of constitutional clauses: can democracy flourish without democratic conventions and restraint?
Driven by PTI's Long March toward Islamabad and deep-seated disagreements over counterterrorism, the confrontation rapidly reached a point of no return. The federal government denounced the protest as a threat to public order, accusing the provincial administration of offering only lukewarm cooperation against regional militancy. Conversely, PTI rejected these allegations, asserting that freedom of movement and peaceful assembly were its fundamental constitutional rights.
Peaceful protest is a democratic right, subject to reasonable restrictions prescribed by law. Similarly, providing security, maintaining peace and acting against violence is an equally vital constitutional duty. Yet, public order must not become a pretext for suppressing political dissent, just as the right to protest cannot justify disregarding public safety.
Although Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution contain exceptional remedies for emergencies and failures of constitutional machinery, the fundamental question remains whether exercising such power aligns with democratic norms and is democratically justified.
Unfortunately, the political history of Pakistan presents a sobering commentary on the country's democratic development.
On August 22, 1947, just eight days after the independence, the elected government of Khan Abdul Jabbar Khan, popularly known as Dr Khan Sahib, in the then North-West Frontier Province was dismissed on the Governor-General's directives. The Governor of the province, Sir George Cunningham, acted under Section 51(5) of the adapted Government of India Act, 1935, and Khan Abdul Qayyum Khan subsequently formed a Muslim League ministry. Dr Khan Sahib's government had enjoyed the support of the majority.
While Partition, the referendum and deep political mistrust created exceptional circumstances that were used to defend the dismissal, the central question remains: should an elected ministry be dismissed by an executive order, rather than being tested on the floor of the legislature?
That event revealed an enduring weakness: constitutional authority could be exercised having no regard for parliamentary conventions. In 1953, Governor-General Ghulam Muhammad dismissed Prime Minister Khawaja Nazimuddin despite the latter enjoying parliamentary support. In 1954, he dissolved the Constituent Assembly. In 1958, the first Constitution was abrogated and a martial law was imposed. Collectively, these dismissals and the abrogation eroded the democratic fabric and undermined the culture of constitutional restraint. As a result, Pakistan's political history became plagued by repeated disruptions, suffering the routine suspension, abeyance and abrogation of its supreme law.
The Constitution of 1973 is not the provisional framework of 1947. Article 232 addresses specified emergencies; Article 234 concerns circumstances in which provincial government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. Each is subject to constitutional conditions and safeguards, including parliamentary scrutiny. Their application must be judged by evidence, necessity and compliance with prescribed procedures.
Exercise of authority under the extraordinary provisions also requires careful separation. A security emergency under Article 232 is not synonymous with a constitutional breakdown under Article 234. Each has its own legal touchstone. Regarding the current steps, it is for the parliament and the courts to examine whether the circumstances genuinely satisfy those touchstones, whether other political alternatives were truly unavailable, and whether the measures remain proportionate and temporary. Otherwise, exceptional authority risks becoming routine. That safeguard protects citizens beyond party affiliations.
The federal government asserts that worsening militancy and lack of cooperation warranted intervention. PTI disputes that assessment and sees the decision as negating its electoral mandate. Both claims require independent examination. Had the provincial constitutional machinery really broken down? Had the situation been worse than from 2005 to 2014 when the merged districts were directly administrated by the federal government? Does a political confrontation alone establish constitutional failure?
Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa has remained in the grip of militancy, displacement and economic devastation for decades. Counterterrorism demands cooperation among institutions, professional policing, public confidence and political legitimacy. The 18th constitutional amendment strengthened provincial autonomy precisely because excessive centralisation had developed a sense of deprivation and alienation. But, now, autonomy is circumvented through other means.
The UK presents a useful democratic norm, wherein "His Majesty's Government" and "His Majesty's Most Loyal Opposition" are recognised as legitimate participants in the same constitutional framework. Formal powers are restrained by conventions; political conflicts are ordinarily resolved through Parliament and elections. Opposition is not disloyalty, and governing authority is not a licence to silence opponents.
Such a culture does not occur merely by legislative measures but evolves through sound political traditions. It requires political actors to respect limits even when they possess legal power, and to defend principles regardless of which party governs. Would today's federal parties accept similar intervention in a province they controlled? Would PTI, if governing federally, afford its opponents the autonomy it demanded?
The solution lies in dialogue and political reconciliation. Federal authorities must respect provincial mandates; provincial leaders must meet legitimate security responsibilities. These obligations reinforce, rather than cancel, one another.
The lesson from 1947 to October 2026 is not that constitutional arrangements are identical, but that repeated reliance on extraordinary powers will erode democratic dispensations. Legality is indispensable. Constitutionalism lives in values, conventions, political attitudes and institutional restraint. Without them, even the most carefully written Constitution remains vulnerable whenever power becomes the ultimate objective.

title: A nuclear order sans guardrails   Islamabad s case for talking
description: Pakistan sits at the centre of that equation
content:
Pakistan sits at the centre of that equation
The global order is running on habit more than rules, and political instability has become its background noise. The war in Ukraine grinds on, the Middle East has just lived through a US-Israeli war with Iran, and governments from Europe to Asia are rewriting their alliances in real time. In February, New START expired, and for the first time in decades no treaty caps the strategic arsenals of the US and Russia. The nuclear equation is no longer bipolar, and it is no longer only about arsenals. It is about thresholds, perceptions and which capitals can still pick up the phone. Deterrence theory was built for two superpowers; it is now being stretched across a crowded field of nuclear states, missile defences and fast-moving technology.
Pakistan sits at the centre of that equation. The four-day military exchange with India in May 2025, marked by missiles, drones and air combat, ended in a ceasefire on 10 May. India's own Chief of Defence Staff later conceded that aircraft were lost on the first night, and the story of effortless superiority did not survive contact with the evidence. Islamabad's reading is that credible deterrence kept a short war short, a reading that deserves a serious hearing.
Alliances and diplomacy have moved accordingly. In September 2025, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, treating aggression against one as aggression against both. Beijing remains its partner of first resort, with CPEC entering its second phase. Then came the Iran war. Pakistan helped broker the 8 April ceasefire, hosted the first direct US-Iran talks in decades on 11-12 April, and signed the Islamabad Memorandum as guarantor in June. Last week the UN Secretary-General came to Islamabad to salute that leadership. Pakistan has become a venue where adversaries meet.
That is the backdrop to INC-2026, the Islamabad Non-Proliferation Conference on 20 and 21 October. Credit belongs to the Strategic Vision Institute for convening it. Bringing scholars from Russia, China, the US and Europe to Islamabad takes institutional confidence and a reputation for honest brokerage. Thirteen international speakers from six countries, nine in person and four online, will take up deterrence after May 2025, the collapse of arms control, missile defence and emerging technology. They include SIPRI's Wilfred Wan, Sir Lawrence Freedman and Rose Gottemoeller, who negotiated New START for Washington. They will sit alongside Pakistani scholars and diplomats, among them Ambassador Kamran Akhtar, Pakistan's envoy in Vienna, and SVI's Dr Naeem Salik.
Given that missile treaties do the real work, academic settings are still considered relevant because ideas precede policy. Peter Haas's work on epistemic communities showed how networks of experts shape what decision-makers consider thinkable. South Asia's nuclear debate has long run on borrowed categories: Waltz's confidence that nuclear weapons induce caution, Sagan's warning about organisational failure, Snyder's stability-instability paradox. May 2025 tested all three, and that evidence belongs to scholars as much as to spokesmen. Universities and think tanks also train the analysts and diplomats who will inherit these questions, and they can disagree in public without starting a crisis. A researcher who has heard Pakistan's reasoning first hand carries something no textbook written elsewhere can supply.
Pakistan arrives with a record worth hearing. Its six nuclear power plants supply 3,530 MW at a capacity factor above 90% and, by Foreign Office figures, 18.3% of the country's electricity. In March the IAEA Board of Governors unanimously approved safeguards for Chashma-5, a 1,200 MW unit under construction. In space, EO-1, EO-2 and EO-3 now form an indigenous Earth-observation series, and SUPARCO named Pakistan's first astronaut in these same weeks. The chosen pilot will spend about a week aboard China's Tiangong station, the first foreign astronaut it has carried.
None of this settles the deeper debate, and the conference should not pretend it does. But credibility in the nuclear order is earned by being safeguarded, being present and being willing to be questioned. Islamabad is offering all three. If INC-2026 leaves behind a record of arguments rather than slogans, it will have done more for stability than another communiqué.

title: Abandoning Gaza
description: WFP will now assist 1 1 million people instead of 1 6 million
content:
WFP will now assist 1.1 million people instead of 1.6 million
For Palestinians who have endured years of relentless bombardment and starvation, the prospect of losing humanitarian assistance is yet another cruel blow. The World Food Programme's decision to discontinue monthly food assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza, owing to a funding shortfall, is an indictment of the international community's diminishing commitment to a population that remains dependent on outside help for survival.
That such a withdrawal is taking place while 1.4 million Palestinians continue to face acute food insecurity speaks volumes about the world's willingness to look away from a humanitarian catastrophe that is far from over. The WFP will now assist 1.1 million people instead of 1.6 million, while those fortunate enough to remain beneficiaries will receive reduced food rations and cash assistance. Whatever limited improvement has occurred is largely attributable to the very humanitarian assistance that is now being withdrawn. Cutting this lifeline risks reversing those gains and condemning already malnourished families to further deprivation. The international community cannot absolve itself of responsibility by citing financial constraints. The WFP requires $450 million over the next six months to sustain its operations in Gaza and the West Bank. That such a sum remains difficult to mobilise, while governments continue to commit enormous resources to military expenditure, exposes a disturbing imbalance in global priorities. The drastic reduction in American contributions to international humanitarian programmes has compounded the crisis.
Wealthy nations, particularly those wielding influence over the conflict, must be held accountable for their failure to ensure that civilians have access to the necessities of life. Israel, meanwhile, must remove restrictions on humanitarian and commercial supplies and facilitate relief operations. Donor governments must immediately restore funding, while global institutions should press for guarantees that humanitarian assistance will reach those who need it without political obstruction.

title: Mental health crisis
description: Mental health crisis
content:
Mental health must no longer be treated as a secondary concern
Pakistan's first nationally representative mental health survey has revealed a quiet but serious crisis gripping the nation. Evaluating nearly 18,000 adults across all four provinces between 2018 and 2022, the landmark study paints a deeply concerni X ng picture of the nation's health landscape. The data shows that 32 per cent of adults - nearly every third - are living with a diagnosable mental or behavioural disorder; and 38 per cent have experienced a psychological disorder at some point during their lifetime. The breakdown of specific conditions highlights a widespread trauma: PTSD i.e. Post Traumatic Stress Disorder affects one in five adults (20%); depression is suffered by more than one in 10 individuals; and suicidal thoughts are experienced by 6 per cent.
That this escalating crisis warrants priority focus goes without saying. Addressing a crisis of this magnitude requires immediate, structural interventions led by the government in partnership with the private sector. The foremost steps that need to be taken are: 1) Psychological services must be integrated into basic rural health centres and basic healthcare infrastructure to work around the severe shortage of specialised psychiatric facilities. 2) Lady health workers, school teachers and community leaders should be educated in basic 'psychological first-aid' to enable early detection and timely support at the grassroots level. 3) Government-backed digital counseling apps should be introduced to provide immediate, cost-effective crisis intervention, particularly for those battling acute depression or suicidal thoughts. And 4) Public education drives should be launched to help dismantle the intense social stigma that prevents individuals from discussing their emotional struggles or seeking professional help.
Mental health must no longer be treated as a secondary concern. A sustained, well-funded national strategy is urgently required to secure a healthier, more resilient future for generations to come.

title: A global troika
description: A global troika
content:
Troika possesses the power and potential to bring sanity to otherwise messy global politics
Diplomacy is the art of navigating a path through adversity. Russian President Vladimir Putin's off-the-cuff proposal for a trilateral summit with his American and Chinese counterparts is an epoch-making initiative. It could go a long way toward not only providing clarity to wayward realpolitik, but also helping formulate a way forward toward a rules-based world order. The Czar was candid; he minced no words when stating that the upcoming APEC summit in China could act as an icebreaker to deliberate on issues confronting evolving multilateralism, especially the conflict in Ukraine.
This troika possesses the power and potential to bring sanity to otherwise messy global politics. It is worrisome that two major wars are underway across two continents, both of which could turn out to be catastrophic. The war in the Middle East has already taken a severe toll, interrupting supply chains and causing soaring oil prices that are pushing the world to the brink of a recession. Likewise, the Russo-Ukrainian war has effectively dismantled the deterrence that existed between Russia and the US since the heyday of the Cold War. Both of these flashpoints can be effectively addressed if Presidents Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping gather for a huddle of statesmanship.
The previous APEC meeting in South Korea served as an opportunity for Xi and Trump to forge a coordinated understanding over North Korean fractures; a similar approach could be adopted for the Middle East. Similarly, a tête-à-tête between Putin and Trump over Ukraine - with Xi playing the role of an honest broker - could be a blessing in disguise. Notwithstanding the Ukrainian Foreign Minister's objections to the proposed trilateral moot, the initiative must go ahead in all sincerity.
World leaders must take a cue from Islamabad, whose solitary initiative to mediate between arch-foes, the US and Iran, led to a landmark memorandum of understanding that paused a dreaded war in the Middle East. The huddles at the Oval Office in September between Trump and Xi, alongside the Alaska understanding between Putin and Trump, should serve as precedents for carving out an unprecedented detente on the global stage.

title: Rebuilding trust in public health
description: Rebuilding trust in public health
content:
Question is relevant for so many places around the world in the era of misinformation and massive funding cuts
A few days ago, at the Boston Book Festival, I was part of a panel on health and disease. I was joined by two other authors who, along with me, shared some ideas from our recent books that came out in the last year. The last question in the session was from a young student, who asked us how we can rebuild trust in public health in the current moment. This question is relevant for so many places around the world in the era of misinformation and massive funding cuts. We were out of time, so all of us on the panel gave very short – and perhaps not very satisfying – answers. But her question made me think of an incident from a few years ago.
During the pandemic, right around the time when the vaccines were first coming to the market, I got a chance to speak (remotely) to students in a biology class in a high school that had majority of its students coming from socio-economically disadvantaged backgrounds. Those were days when we all were trying to figure out zoom and were fidgeting around mute buttons and cameras capturing us in unflattering moments. Towards the end of my talk, a young African American student asked a question. She asked me that while she understood the need for vaccines, how we knew that this was not going to be another Tuskegee. By Tuskegee she meant the four decades long study, from 1932 to 1972, supported and sponsored by the US Federal Government to study untreated syphilis among African American sharecroppers (most of whom were very poor) in Alabama. The participants in the study were denied treatment, despite potent drugs becoming widely available by 1940s, in order for the researchers to 'understand the disease and its natural progression'. There was no informed consent. During the course of the study, dozens of participants died, many suffered immensely and all were misled and deceived.
The Tuskegee study that ended only after a journalist broke the story is now considered a major topic in bioethics, consent, racism, and injustice against the weak. The student who asked me this question knew both the history of public health in America and the suffering of poor communities. Her question was polite and simple, but it asked something quite fundamental. Why should she, a young African American woman coming from a poor background, trust the government? I was not prepared for this, and I do not think I had a good answer. I told her what I thought was true then, and I still believe it today. Trust has to be earned, maintained and never to be taken for granted.
Over the last few years, I have thought more about this. How should we build trust in our own public health measures? Too often, we blame people's lack of education or knowledge or awareness. It is easy to say that because people are not educated, they cannot fathom how wonderful modern medicine is, or because they lack higher education they cannot understand what evidence-based interventions are. That, in my view, is simply an elitist argument with layers of anti-poor views that many of us hold dear. The reason people may not trust public health measures is because they have little reason to trust. The reason many choose 'foreign' manufactured medicines over locally made ones cannot simply be blamed on colonial hangover. It is because of a long history of corruption, deception and poor-quality control associated with local medicines. Endorsements by celebrities are less likely to convince a skeptical consumer when there is the weight of history.
I do not have all the answers for the questions that students have asked me about trust, and I am not sure I ever will. But I do know that building and maintaining trust in public health starts not with bombastic claims, but with humility. Trust building requires honest acknowledgement of the errors of the past, a deep commitment to transparency moving forward, and above all treatment of people with dignity and respect. Ultimately, trust too can be infectious, but only in an enabling environment that is built on honesty, reflection and human dignity.

title: Office Space  star Richard Riehle dead at 78
description: Richard Riehle  the veteran character actor known for  Office Space  and  Grounded for Life   has died at 78
content:
Richard Riehle, the veteran character actor known for 'Office Space' and 'Grounded for Life', has died at 78
Richard Riehle, the veteran character actor known for his roles in Office Space and Grounded for Life , has died at the age of 78. The actor reportedly died of natural causes in Los Angeles on October 15, according to TMZ .
PEOPLE reported on October 19 that it had contacted a representative for Riehle for comment.
Born in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin, in 1948, Riehle built a career spanning decades, earning hundreds of film and television credits. He graduated from the University of Notre Dame before earning a Master of Fine Arts degree from the University of Minnesota.
Riehle began his screen career with an appearance in the 1975 John Wayne film Rooster Cogburn . Alongside his work in film and television, he maintained a steady presence in regional theatre, making his Broadway debut in Execution of Justice in 1986. He later appeared in Broadway productions of The Iceman Cometh in 1999 and The Man Who Had All the Luck in 2002.
One of his most recognisable roles came in Mike Judge’s 1999 comedy Office Space , in which he portrayed Tom Smykowski, a software company employee. Riehle also gained recognition for playing Walt Finnerty on the Fox sitcom Grounded for Life , appearing in the series from 2001 to 2005.
His television credits included appearances across the Star Trek franchise and a guest role in Bill Hader’s comedy series Barry in 2023.
Riehle also appeared in several well-known films, including Of Mice and Men (1992), The Fugitive (1993), Jury Duty (1995), Deuce Bigalow: Male Gigolo (1999) and Wedding Crashers (2005).
He frequently portrayed Santa Claus, taking on the character in eight projects, including Our First Christmas and A Very Harold & Kumar 3D Christmas . In 2026, his screen credits included The Cowboy Killer and Boris Is Dead .

title: SpaceX  Tesla earnings to test Musk s AI spending ambitions as merger talk grows
description: Third quarter results will give investors a rare side by side look at Elon Musk s two most valuable companies
content:
Third-quarter results will give investors a rare side-by-side look at Elon Musk's two most valuable companies
SpaceX and Tesla will report third-quarter results on consecutive days this week, giving investors a rare side-by-side look at Elon Musk's two most valuable companies ​as merger speculation gathers momentum.
The results will test whether Starlink's steady growth and Tesla's car profits can fund the AI spending powering the merger debate.
"In ‌terms of metrics, it would have to be Starlink revenue growth more than launch counts and improvement in auto margins for Tesla," said Shawn Campbell, an adviser at Camelthorn Investments who owns shares in both companies, describing what investors will focus on.
Barclays suggested last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting, with SpaceX the more likely acquirer, though neither company nor Musk has officially committed to pursuing a deal.
Tesla ​on Monday said its annual meeting would be held on December 3.
In an all-stock deal, Barclays estimates Musk would hold about 37% of the equity and ​56% of the votes.
"A SpaceX acquisition of Tesla would be cleaner as it would make it easier to deal with the China business ⁠as an asset that is dealt with separately," Campbell said.
Tesla gave the speculation a showpiece on Thursday, unveiling a new Roadster sports car , slated for production in 2028, that can ​jump and turn over mid-air using rocket technology at a SpaceX test site in Texas.
"Musk is blending the future of mobility together by integrating auto and rocket technology; at the very ​least it's a subtle plant in investors' minds making an engineering efficiency argument for a merger," said Bill Birmingham, head of research at REX Financial.
He said the timing, ahead of Tesla's annual shareholders meeting, was no coincidence.
SpaceX absorbed Musk's xAI in February, months before its June IPO, and spending by Tesla and SpaceX now points to the same place: AI.
The businesses still differ, with SpaceX earning from launches, ​Starlink and AI compute, and Tesla from cars and energy storage.
SpaceX reports on Tuesday and Tesla on Wednesday after markets close.
SpaceX reports only its second results ​as a public company, with investors watching whether its surging AI spending is turning into revenue.
The company is expected to report third-quarter revenue of about $12.74 billion and earnings of 14 cents a share, ‌just four ⁠months after going public, according to data compiled by LSEG.
That compares with second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion, a net loss of $541 million, and AI capital spending of $15.8 billion.
Evercore ISI expects SpaceX to exit 2026 at an annualised revenue run-rate of about $104 billion, driven by the AI segment doing "most of the heavy lifting," and estimates capital spending reaching about $151 billion in 2027.
Connectivity revenue, which includes Starlink, rose 66% to $4.3 billion in the second quarter.
SpaceX also agreed on October 8 to buy 800 MHz spectrum from Grain Management for about $8 billion, a deal that needs Federal ​Communications Commission approval and underpins its Starlink ​Mobile push.
Shares closed at $146.03 on Friday, above ⁠the $135 IPO price but well below their post-debut peak.
Tesla is on track to grow deliveries this year for the first time since 2023, but investors are more focused on profits and its robotaxi bets.
Analysts expect Tesla to report adjusted earnings of ​roughly 43 cents a share on revenue of about $27.88 billion, compared with 50 cents a year earlier.
Second-quarter profit fell well short ​of estimates, with negative ⁠free cash flow of $1.1 billion — slipping into the red for the first time in over two years.
Still, Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, beating analysts' estimates.
Tesla has said capital spending will exceed $25 billion this year, and its shares are down about 17% in 2026 as analysts expect the company to post negative free cash flow of $4.92 billion for the third quarter.
Still, Wall Street ⁠has largely focused ​on robotaxis and the Optimus humanoid robot to assess the company's growth, citing them as high-margin product ​lines that could overshadow its traditional car sales business eventually.
While Tesla's robotaxi business and fleet are small compared to Waymo, the company expects to roll out its self-driving taxis widely in the coming years.
Its valuation has largely ​hinged on such long-term ambitions instead of the car business, which contributes the lion's share of the company's revenue.

title: Brazilian court gives Meta 24 hours to prove AI neutrality over looming presidential runoff
description: Meta denies giving preferential treatment to any candidate  says its rules apply equally to all political figures
content:
Meta denies giving preferential treatment to any candidate, says its rules apply equally to all political figures
A Brazilian court gave US tech company Meta 24 hours to prove that its artificial intelligence systems do not favour either candidate ahead of next Sunday’s presidential runoff, local media reported on Monday.
The Superior Electoral Court order, signed by magistrate Marco Aurelio Bellizze Oliveira, covers Meta's algorithmic systems managing social media platforms Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, reported Brazilian outlet Universo Online .
The company must prove that it is not limiting the distribution of political content after President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's campaign alleged that it suppressed material favourable to the incumbent while permitting the spread of hostile AI-generated posts.
Read : Brazil's Lula accuses Meta of election interference
"These inconsistencies in metrics demand explanations and immediate correction," said Michel Bertoni, a lawyer representing Lula’s campaign.
Bertoni argued that when a major digital platform restricts the circulation of political content unevenly, it directly compromises electoral regularity and interferes with national sovereignty.
The measure follows reporting by Brazilian daily Folha de S.Paulo , which cited internal communications indicating that Meta employees acknowledged restrictions affecting Lula's accounts while algorithms recommended the profile and WhatsApp channel of challenger Flavio Bolsonaro.
Read More : AI able to manipulate elections worldwide, expert says
Meta denied giving preferential treatment to any candidate ahead of the October 25 runoff vote, maintaining that its rules apply equally to all political figures and that internal discussions focused on the severity of public technical issues rather than political bias.

title: Gwyneth Paltrow lands major Netflix role in A24 thriller  The Apology
description: Gwyneth Paltrow will lead  The Apology   an A24 thriller series at Netflix  with Thomas Vinterberg directing
content:
Gwyneth Paltrow will lead 'The Apology', an A24 thriller series at Netflix, with Thomas Vinterberg directing
Gwyneth Paltrow is set to star in The Apology , a new thriller series from A24 that has received a two-season straight-to-series order from Netflix.
The project will mark Paltrow’s first series regular role and Oscar-winning filmmaker Thomas Vinterberg’s US television directing debut.
According to Deadline, the series was acquired by Netflix in a competitive deal. Joe Murtagh, known for creating the 2023 series The Woman in the Wall , is writing the thriller and serving as its showrunner.
The Apology follows Evelyn, played by Paltrow, and her husband, Caleb Amspoker, whose son was murdered 18 years earlier in a cold case that attracted national attention. Their lives take an unexpected turn when a stranger arrives and confesses to the crime, raising hopes that the family may finally receive justice.
However, the situation becomes more complicated when the couple learns that the killer could receive a reduced sentence. Faced with the possibility of an outcome they consider unbearable, Evelyn and Caleb decide to take matters into their own hands.
The series will be executive produced by Cut To’s Hipps, Murtagh, Vinterberg and Paltrow. Cut To, which is based at A24, has developed several high-profile television projects, including Discretion , starring Nicole Kidman and Elle Fanning, for Paramount+, as well as Trigger Point , featuring Joel Edgerton, for Netflix.
Paltrow previously appeared in a recurring role on Fox’s musical comedy series Glee . Her television credits also include The Politician , while her film work includes Shakespeare in Love , for which she won the Academy Award for Best Actress. She recently starred in Marty Supreme .
Vinterberg, who won an Oscar for the Danish film Another Round , will direct the Netflix thriller as he makes his debut directing US television. The two-season commitment also represents a significant early move for Netflix as it continues investing in major original programming.
