title: Govt cuts petrol by Rs5.16, diesel by Rs7.69 for Oct 20 | The Express Tribune
description: Petrol price decreases to Rs381.14 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs389.27 under daily price mechanism
content:
Petrol price decreases to Rs381.14 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs389.27 under daily price mechanism
The federal government on Monday decreased the price of petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs5.16 and Rs7.69 per litre, respectively, for October 20.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs381.14 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs389.27 per litre for Tuesday.
The latest revision comes after the government decreased the price of petrol by Rs3.93 per litre, while keeping the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) unchanged from October 17 to October 19.
Read : Govt cuts petrol by Rs3.93, keeps diesel unchanged till Oct 19
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Brent crude futures rose slightly on Monday after attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on a Yemeni ‌military training camp and renewed attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military facilities.
Brent crude futures rose 17 cents, or 0.15%, to 110.03 a barrel at 1:08 pm ET (1708 GMT), after falling more than $3 earlier in the session as investors booked profits following last week's rally to a five-month high .
Yemen's Houthis said on Monday they had carried out attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military targets, ​including an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha airport. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claims, and ​ Reuters could not independently verify them.
Separately, an oil tanker caught fire and exploded after striking a naval mine in the southern Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said, according to Iranian media.
"Ongoing strikes on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz and flows remaining below pre-conflict levels continue to support prices," UBS analyst ‌Giovanni Staunovo ⁠said.

title: Houthi attack kills 53 at Yemen government training camp  officials say
description: US Embassy in Riyadh issues security alert for citizens in Middle East amid Houthi attacks
content:
US Embassy in Riyadh issues security alert for citizens in Middle East amid Houthi attacks
Fifty-three people were killed, and 200 were injured in an attack on Monday by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security ​forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, according to the local authority, ‌as fighting in the impoverished country intensifies.
Video verified by Reuters from Shabwa province showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground.
The Houthis and the internationally recognised government, which is backed by ​a Saudi-led coalition, have been trading attacks since the group advanced in September ​towards territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait , a shipping chokepoint at the ⁠mouth of the Red Sea.
Local authority sources who spoke on condition of anonymity said ​the Houthis had launched three ballistic missiles at security forces during a training exercise.
Shabwa, ​an energy-rich province in south-central coastal Yemen overlooking the Gulf of Aden, is home to the Balhaf liquefied natural gas facility, Yemen's largest industrial investment.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X that ​the group had targeted the training camp, which he said was run by Saudi ​forces. The Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Government forces this month began ‌a ⁠campaign aimed at recapturing areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the strait, while the group besieges Taiz , the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highland area of Yemen.
The conflict in Yemen has become another front line in the ​wider US-Israeli war on Iran ​as the Houthis ⁠have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter, targeting Riyadh's international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco .
War broke ​out in Yemen in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital ​Sanaa, driving ⁠the government south. A Saudi-led military intervention the following year led to a bloody stalemate until the sides agreed to a 2022 truce that held until this year.
Yemen is already one ⁠of the ​world's worst humanitarian crises, with aid agencies warning ​of rapidly deteriorating conditions there.
US embassy issues security alert for citizens in Middle East
Earlier, the United States in Riyadh issued a security alert for Americans in the Middle East "due to the complex security environment," amid attacks by the Houthis on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure.
According to the US Embassy in Riyadh , American citizens should "be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions." It added that the attacks by the Houthis resulted in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions, noting that "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area."
"Americans travelling to or from the Middle East should monitor information about airport and airline operations and develop contingency plans in advance," the embassy advised, adding that "Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions."
Earlier, it was reported that Egypt was ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, potentially raising the stakes in the Middle East war as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on the kingdom.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the Arab world's largest, to help defend its Gulf Arab ally if the kingdom requested its support.
A parliamentary vote had been expected on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said.
Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the north, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming another front in the United States-Israeli war on Iran.
Any Egyptian military backing for Saudi Arabia could mark a major escalation in the wider Iran war, which has threatened global energy supplies and sent oil prices soaring since the US and Israel attacked the Islamic Republic in late February.
Hours after an announcement on further discussions by the parliament, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said in a post on X that he discussed regional developments and the importance of de-escalation during a phone call with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan.
The Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the ​state oil company Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with Saudi-backed forces. The Houthi advances threaten the strategic Bab el-Mandeb oil shipping route, following the collapse of a truce.
"Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement. The statement followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.
Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.
If Egypt weighs in, it could face attacks by the Houthis, ragtag mountain fighters who have emerged as a deadly force of tens of thousands and whose missiles and drones threaten the region.
Arab countries, especially Gulf states hosting US bases, have faced repeated attacks by Iran and its allies, including the Houthis and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq, during the conflict.
Egypt's Mediterranean port of Damietta came under a drone attack in July with no group claiming responsibility. Egypt has not blamed any party for the attack but said it was taking necessary measures to protect the country's national security.
Read: Iran offers help to end Saudi-Houthi conflict through dialogue
Egypt and ​Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi ​Arabia and ⁠other oil-rich Gulf states including the United Arab Emirates provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist President Mohamed ⁠Morsi ​in 2013. Sisi became president a year later.
Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role in the civil war.
Riyadh has turned to regional allies and Pakistan after it sought US President Donald Trump's help to fight the Houthis. Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman visited Abu Dhabi on Sunday and met with UAE President Mohammed bin ​Zayed Al Nahyan, with talks focusing on regional security, according to the Emirati state news agency.
The talks followed a visit to Riyadh last month by UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the first trip by ‌a senior UAE official to the kingdom since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year.

title: Filming through fire
description: Filmed in Gaza shows two Palestinian photojournalists and the human cost of bearing witness in a war with no safe spaces
content:
Filmed in Gaza shows two Palestinian photojournalists and the cost of bearing witness in a war with no safe spaces
No one moved, the room was silent as the last film credit ran. It was comforting to be in a small gathering of friends—I couldn’t imagine a safer group with whom to watch Filmed in Gaza. I had seen many of the video clips shown, but I had followed one of the NBC journalists, Samed Abu Zarifa, for years, reading his work and observing his reporting.
Yet this documentary goes behind the news stories to witness the lives of two NBC News journalists who fought so hard to bravely bring the stories to a reluctant and sometimes ill-informed public. We’re told that journalists have to be objective, detached from the people whose stories they tell. Filmed in Gaza makes one ask: is that possible when your life, your families’ lives, are inextricably bound to the events that you’re filming? And where does truth telling overshadow the elusive “objective” reporting?
From the outset, Filmed in Gaza takes us on a journey through some of the rough days of the current genocidal assault on Palestinian enclave, as it follows the two journalists, Samed Abu Zarifa and Samir Al Boji, who are determined to keep reporting what is happening on the ground despite their own experiences trying to survive as well. The documentary is directed by Samed and captures his video journalism work and that of his colleague and friend, Samir, winner of two News and Documentary Emmy Awards at the 47th Annual Awards in May 2026.
Samed is in his early 30s, married, a father of two young children. He’s been working as an NBC News photojournalist for over 10 years. Samir also has worked as a photojournalist for years. He is 40-years-old, married, and has a family of six. For his part, Samir explained why it was difficult to find a partner—some families were reluctant for their daughters to marry him when they found out his profession—journalism—because in Gaza it’s such a dangerous occupation. He proudly states, it is dangerous, and I love it. Their producer at NBC, Lawahez Jabari, gives us a short introduction: she tells the viewers that Samir is the older of the two, but is the one who brings laughter into their daily work; Samed is more serious. From there, the camera follows these journalists through almost two years of reporting starting in October 2023 when the most recent war against Palestinians began.
Following the Hamas-led attack on Israel that year, Israel banned foreign journalists from entering Gaza to report on Israel’s assaults unless they were accompanied by the IDF. As a result, Palestinian journalists Samed, Samir, and their colleagues have been the major source of news. Against that backdrop, the documentary opens with a scene of Samed in one of a number of tents, getting his hair cut, as the voice over explains, Israel has called for the area to be evacuated, but the people have no idea where to go to be safe, and so they stay, while Samed and the film crew continue filming.
Then Samir told the gripping story. “Samed and I were covering an assault on a house in Khan Younis,” he narrates. “I asked one of the first men that came out of the building what happened, and he said, the IDF bombed without warning. Samed went inside to set up more interviews, and as I was filming, the house collapsed. I knew Samed was inside, so we started searching, day and night. The rescuers were responding to our requests to do more and more, and finally Samed came out, standing tall and strong, confident, and telling the rescuers, there are more guys, more of our crew, still inside. When you see an entire building collapse on your colleague, on your friend, on someone documenting the suffering, you realise you are part of the suffering.”
In other scenes, Samed talks about losing the home he and his family spent years building, destroyed in minutes. “Our work as journalists doesn't negate our feelings. We have feelings.” Later, in April 2025, Israel bombed the tent next to Samed’s tent, and his close friend Yousef was killed.
Samir explained that filming children affected him the most. But they still continue to film. They report, for example, the story of the young father who left his children at home while he went out to the market. When he returned, Israel had bombed his home, and his children had been killed. “Sometimes, I am not sure if I should film or not.” Samir captured the video of a young boy who took on the role of parents for his five siblings after their mother was killed. He would go out to find food, and warm milk for his baby sister. As the film progresses, watching Samed and Samir and their colleagues moving from one location to the next makes it real that there are no safe spaces—not for the journalists or their families, and certainly not for the children, and the families they report on. And still, Samed says letting his wife and children leave Gaza was one of the hardest things he did. But he says it was his duty to continue reporting.
Meanwhile, NBC News producer Lawahez Jabari explains that they send out the videos so that the world can see what's happening. But Samed and Samir and their colleagues—they see and smell the blood, hear the screams, the journalists see the scenes that aren't filmed—and I can see how it has affected them. It has changed their personality, everything. Eventually, she begins to tell them they have to get out. Toward the end, Samir collapses: “I haven't eaten in three days.” And we see them struggle with the decision to leave, watch NBC’s efforts to get them out, and just when it looks as if it will happen, Israel revokes their visas—and there is no explanation. In doing so, Jabari covers the efforts they had to make to get Samed and Samir out.
Told largely from the video segments and voice overs, the photojournalists tell the news stories, but this documentary tells the heart wrenching stories about the storytellers. I had watched many of these stories when they were first reported, now I saw the price the reporters paid to make those videos. I also learned about the team behind Samed and Samir and their crew, as Lawahez Jabari, the NBC News producer in Tel Aviv, relates how she came to work with them and became intricately involved in following their reports and ultimately insisting that they also had to leave Gaza.
Ultimately, the film makes clear: there may be no easy answers when journalists are reporting on and filming stories so intimately connected to their own lives, where there are no breaks, no down time, no safe spaces, and where the only escape routes are controlled by the government responsible for the bombing. Samir and Samed show us this reality—cooking a meal in a tent shared by your colleagues in one moment, reaching for the well-known Press vest, hat, and cameras in the next. What remained with me most are the scenes with the journalists outside of their working roles: Samed saying goodbye to his wife and children as they prepare to leave Gaza, his son asking to carry the suitcase, his daughter Mariam. Samir on the phone with his young children, offering them encouragement, despite what was happening around him.
And yet the reality remains—there is no simple resolution. I wanted a good ending, and the film delivers the scenes when Samir and Samed finally get through the checkpoints, leave Gaza, and meet Lawahez Jabari in person for the first time, sharing a hug and much laughter. But that isn’t the end: the final scenes, when Israel bombs the tent that Samed and Samir share with their colleagues, capture the moment five of the journalists they had only recently left are killed.
In the end, Filmed in Gaza left me with questions I cannot close. How does one return to normal after bearing witness? What happens to the stories you couldn’t tell, the photos you couldn’t share, the memories that refuse to be filed away? How do you carry them so a world grown used to ignoring horror does not forget? According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, 196 journalists and storytellers have been killed in this war. That number is not an answer. It is an accusation. When will this end? How will it end? I don’t know. But I know it cannot end in silence. It cannot end in forgetting. It must end with someone still bearing witness—still filming, still naming, still refusing to look away. When will this end? How will it end? Not with forgetting. Not with silence. It will end only when the world finally refuses to look away.
The writer is an attorney and human rights activist in Chicago who closely follows news about Gaza after a tour to Palestine and Israel in May 2008.

title: US banning Chinese AI DeepSeek from government agency IT systems
description: Use of DeepSeek models by US government employees may result in the transfer of    sensitive data to China
content:
Use of DeepSeek models by US government employees may result in the transfer of ​sensitive data to China
The US Homeland Security Department is ordering the removal of DeepSeek products and third-party services ​using the Chinese AI model from US civilian agency IT systems, according ‌to a notice published on Monday.
The department is also banning the acquisition of DeepSeek products and third-party services developed using DeepSeek by US civilian government agencies. DHS said DeepSeek models pose "multiple threat vectors" ​and raised concerns that use of the product "may result in the transfer of ​sensitive data to the PRC if used by US government employees ⁠or vendors."
DHS also said use of DeepSeek by government agencies "could produce actionable ​intelligence on US persons and/or government agencies. The models themselves may contain malware or ​other security vulnerabilities."
Read : US flags DeepSeek, Chinese firms over AI theft allegations
In a July memo made public on Monday, DHS told federal agencies to monitor flows of traffic in and out of government websites to address potential risks from DeepSeek.
Previously, ​several US agencies, including the Department of Commerce and the Navy, have banned ​the use of DeepSeek on government devices. Multiple states, including New York, Tennessee, and Virginia, have ‌taken ⁠similar steps.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately comment.
The Trump administration has taken a series of steps to crack down on Chinese tech companies.
The Federal Communications Commission will vote on October 29 to bar all Chinese labs from ​testing electronic devices such ​as smartphones, cameras ⁠and computers for use in the US. Last year, 82% of US electronics were tested in China.

In December, the FCC ​banned the import of all new models of Chinese drones and ​also banned ⁠imports of new models of Chinese-made consumer routers, the boxes connecting computers, phones and smart devices to the internet.
In July, the FCC voted to bar sales of devices ⁠in ​the US that contain key hardware from Chinese ​companies deemed to be national security risks and proposed to prohibit US telecommunications carriers from interconnecting with ​Chinese telecom firms deemed national security risks.

Mendes and Rachel Matthews will produce the sequel for Honor Role, the production company they founded to support character-driven storytelling. Mendes has continued working with Amazon MGM Studios on projects including Música and Masters of the Universe . She also appeared in Idiotka , a comedy released in 2026.

title: How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites
description: Cybercriminal outsourced hacking to AI agents  tasking them with spending hours probing  breaking into targeted sites
content:
Cybercriminal outsourced hacking to AI agents, tasking them with spending hours probing, breaking into targeted sites
Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere, home appliance ​company SharkNinja and engine manufacturer Cummins.
Yet the hacker did almost none of the work.
The cybercriminal instead outsourced the hacking spree almost entirely to artificial intelligence, tasking AI agents ‌with spending hours autonomously probing and breaking into targeted sites, according to Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge.
Read : OpenAI agents obscured hacking activity targeting government websites: security firm
In a report provided to Reuters ahead of publication on Monday , Fagerland said the hacker was one of several he discovered while scanning the web for inadvertently exposed instances of Cairn, an open-source AI problem-solving platform popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, Fagerland said he found about two dozen instances of Cairn being used for malicious activity, which allowed him ​to quietly peer over the cybercriminals' shoulders as they set their AI tools loose on the world.
Fagerland's report on the Chinese-speaking hacker did not name the victims, but Reuters was able ​to establish the victims' identities by independently reviewing the hacker's Cairn activity.
At a time of rising anxiety over the power of autonomous AI tools, Fagerland said ⁠his find was real-life evidence that commercially available AI agents could pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention, a dramatic boost to the power of a single malicious actor.
"It's ​a new world now," said Fagerland.
Reuters could not ascertain the degree to which the breaches resulted in unauthorised extraction of data.
Deere told Reuters it had taken "necessary remediation actions" following the incident and had "no indication that ​sensitive information was accessed." SharkNinja said the hack had hit a standalone site carrying only product support information and that the threat had been contained. Cummins said it was "investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors."
Read More : Rogue AI agents broke into Indian firms' live systems, government says
Two smaller businesses also acknowledged being compromised. Other victims listed in the Cairn data did not return messages.
One of the hackers that Fagerland observed stole a trove of credit card data. Another ​tried to get AI agents to rob a cryptocurrency exchange. The Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific. Beginning on September 25, they set their AI army loose against US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese ​e-commerce websites.
Their instructions were terse, sketching out their preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters. As of late last week, their agents had attempted to break into more than 1,200 sites. Successful intrusions typically took around ‌23 hours ⁠of poking and prodding for vulnerabilities. Fagerland estimated that the campaign, which appeared to be using a mixture of China's DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, had chewed up roughly $5,000 worth of tokens, or about $50 per successful hack.
Fagerland — who has worked in cybersecurity for nearly three decades — said he was impressed by some of the techniques the agents used to compromise their victims. In one case, after failing to find any weaknesses in a big company's public-facing application, the AI agents pored through digital records to find associated infrastructure, located a public-facing control panel, discovered a subtle weakness in the way it processed data, and after ​hours of trial and error, reported leveraging it ​to trick the server into executing malicious commands.
"It's ⁠not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland said. "It's not script kiddie stuff."
Cairn's author, whose social media handle is "le1xia0", acknowledged receipt of a Reuters message but did not immediately answer a list of questions. In a recent post on X, they said their platform was "an innovative type of multi-agent architecture and was ​not designed for hacking attacks. If it is used to carry out harmful hacking attacks, that is not my intention."
The ability of ​agentic AI systems to autonomously ⁠discover vulnerabilities, conduct intrusions, and steal data is a source of increasing anxiety around the world. Rogue agents inadvertently unleashed by major AI companies have hacked their way out of computer labs , broken into government websites , and engaged in unsanctioned social engineering attempts . South Korea and Japan have in recent weeks been buffeted by a series of well-publicised hacks attributed to AI-using cybercriminals .
AI agents are increasingly becoming staples of the cybercriminal underground. In August, the Israeli firm ⁠Gambit Security found ​that Russian-speaking extortionists had leveraged SpaceX's Cursor AI tool to break into seven organisations. In September, Gambit documented an AI agent-driven spree that resulted in breaches at 25 companies and the theft of at least 600,000 credit card records. Last week, the cyber intelligence company Bitsight said that discussions about how to use autonomous agents were surging across cybercriminal forums .
Fagerland said he had previously assumed ​hacker-agents would need at least some supervision. He said it was now obvious that the technology had moved past that.
"The development in this field is astounding," he said.

title: Sharjeel says PPP was  last party  to support emergency in K P
description: Says Sindh has made significant progress in public transport over the past four to five years
content:
Says Sindh has made significant progress in public transport over the past four to five years
Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon on Monday stated that the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) was the “last party” to support governor’s rule and the imposition of an emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), further adding that the party had advocated political dialogue and engagement as the first course of action.
The emergency and governor’s rule were declared on October 11 after negotiations between the government and opposition failed , culminating in a PTI long march towards Islamabad that began on October 4.
“PPP was the last party that was in favour of the governor’s rule. We tried to engage them, not once but ten times, and PPP told the federal government that it wanted to resolve issues through political dialogue, but after multiple attempts, if the K-P chief minister himself had an inclination towards the Taliban and terrorists and was not willing to agree, then the government could not let the people of K-P be left on their own at the mercy of the terrorists”. Memon made these remarks during a visit to the Green Line BRT Operations Command and Control Centre, where he received a briefing on the system’s operations, integration with other transport projects, ridership and overall performance.
Transport Secretary Asad Zamin, TransKarachi CEO Zubair Channa, Yellow Line BRT Project Director Kamal Dayo and Sindh Mass Transit Authority Managing Director Behzad Memon accompanied him.
Memon said it was important to connect the Green Line with other BRT projects. The Red and Yellow lines were also being linked, with plans to connect the Orange Line to the Green Line, the Green Line to the Red Line, and the Yellow Line to the Red Line. The links would make it easier for passengers to transfer between services and reach their destinations.
He added that work was continuing on sections of the Yellow Line, including bridges and other construction, further saying that the Sindh government aimed to complete the projects as soon as possible and establish effective connections between them, creating an integrated and modern transport network in the metropolis.
Memon said that Sindh had made significant progress in public transport over the past four to five years, including electric scooters, Pakistan’s first electric buses and Pink Buses for women.
He said the Green Line had been built before Sindh assumed responsibility for it, but it had not included buses reserved for women. Women faced difficulties when using public transport, he said, and better travel facilities could encourage them to travel and help parents feel satisfied about sending their daughters out for education and work. He said the Sindh government had taken several steps to empower women and improve their access to transport.
Asked about Green Line ridership, Memon said that when the service was under the federal government, it carried around 50,000 passengers a day, further noting that since Sindh took over the transport department had worked to improve its performance and the service now carried around 90,000 passengers daily.
The senior minister said the Sindh government aimed to begin road construction in every district across the province within the next six to eight months to improve travel facilities.
Read More : University Road mixed lane to open soon: Sharjeel
Memon said that in Sindh, the government had worked with the Rangers and other law-enforcement agencies to tackle terrorism in Karachi. When conditions worsened in the riverine areas, the government and relevant agencies also conducted operations against bandits. He said kidnapping-for-ransom incidents in Sindh had since declined significantly.
Recalling Karachi’s past, the senior minister said the city had once seen 30 to 40 people killed each day, frequent strikes, closures of businesses and educational institutions, and industries relocating elsewhere. Memon said cooperation between the government and the establishment had helped restore peace, adding that Karachi no longer faced daily strikes on the same scale, and terrorist incidents had declined.
Memon recalled the bombing at the October 18, 2007 homecoming rally for former prime minister Benazir Bhutto, in which hundreds of PPP supporters were killed or injured, and her assassination in Rawalpindi later that year. He said the party’s position against terrorism had always been clear.
He said Benazir had pledged in her final speeches that Pakistan’s flag would again fly in Swat, where Taliban and extremist groups had expanded their influence.
Memon reiterated that the PPP would not remain silent when citizens were suffering from terrorism, innocent people were being killed, and businesses were operating in fear.
He described the recent visit to China as successful and said the chief minister would brief the provincial cabinet on it, further stating that the visit aimed to identify opportunities to benefit Pakistan, particularly Sindh and its people.
Memon said the Sindh government was working democratically across sectors, including health, education, transport, irrigation and local government, to improve people’s lives.

title: I Never Promised You a Rose Garden  gets new film adaptation from Ashley Avis
description: Ashley Avis will direct and produce a film adaptation of Joanne Greenberg   s acclaimed novel about mental illness
content:
Ashley Avis will direct and produce a film adaptation of Joanne Greenberg’s acclaimed novel about mental illness
Filmmaker Ashley Avis has secured the film rights to Joanne Greenberg’s 1964 novel I Never Promised You a Rose Garden after a decade-long effort and will direct a new adaptation based on her own screenplay.
Avis, known for Disney+’s Black Beauty , will also produce the project alongside Edward Winters through her production company, Winterstone Pictures, according to Deadline .
The novel, inspired by Greenberg’s experiences as a young woman diagnosed with schizophrenia, follows Deborah Blau, a gifted Jewish teenager who retreats into an elaborate imaginary kingdom as she struggles with her mental health.
As Deborah’s connection to reality weakens, she is admitted to Chestnut Lodge, where she develops a complex relationship with Dr. Clara Fried, a German psychiatrist whose own past is marked by unresolved trauma. Their relationship becomes central to a story exploring mental illness, recovery, trauma and the challenges of accepting reality.
Avis described Greenberg’s novel as an intimate and imaginative work that invites readers into Deborah’s fictional world, known as the Kingdom of Yr. She said she was particularly moved by the real-life relationship between the two women who inspired the characters.
The book has sold millions of copies worldwide and previously received a film adaptation in 1977. Directed by Anthony Page, the earlier version starred Kathleen Quinlan and earned an Academy Award nomination.
Avis has built her career around projects exploring relationships between people, animals and the natural world. Her credits include the Disney+ adaptation of Black Beauty , starring Kate Winslet and Mackenzie Foy, and the Critics Choice Award-nominated documentary Wild Beauty: Mustang Spirit of the West .
The filmmaker is also developing American Wolf , based on Nate Blakeslee’s book about Yellowstone’s wolves, with Appian Way. Additionally, she has a reimagining of Wim Wenders’ romantic film City of Angels in development at Warner Bros.
Further casting and production details for the new I Never Promised You a Rose Garden adaptation have not been announced.

content:
'Euphoria' star Hunter Schafer reveals she had gender-affirming surgery in December, calling the experience amazing
Euphoria star Hunter Schafer has revealed that she underwent gender-affirming bottom surgery in December 2025, sharing details of the experience in a candid interview with Elle .
The 27-year-old actress, known for playing Jules Vaughn in HBO’s hit drama series, discussed her understanding of queerness, identity and personal growth during the interview, published in connection with her upcoming projects.
“I just had bottom surgery in December, which was amazing, and I love it so much,” Schafer said, explaining why she felt comfortable sharing the experience publicly.
The actress also reflected on the relationship between her personal identity and the broader ideas associated with queerness. She described queerness as an idea centred on possibility, expansion and growth, while acknowledging the challenges of navigating those concepts in everyday life.
“I’m a woman. I’m a girl,” Schafer said, emphasising her identity during the conversation.
She added that there could be tension between exploring queerness as an ideology and understanding how it applies in the context of the world people live in.
Schafer’s comments offer a personal perspective on gender-affirming care, which encompasses medical procedures intended to align a person’s physical characteristics with their gender identity. The specific procedures involved can vary depending on an individual's needs and choices.
The actress has previously spoken about her experiences as a transgender woman and the expectations placed on transgender performers in the entertainment industry. In 2024, she discussed why she had turned down certain transgender roles and reflected on the pressure to serve as a spokesperson for the transgender community.
Through her latest interview, Schafer has continued to share her perspective on identity and representation while discussing her own experiences on her terms.
Her work on Euphoria has brought her international recognition, making her one of the prominent performers associated with the series.

title: Tariq Fazal rubbishes linking governor s rule in K P to mineral extraction
description: Says it is unfortunate attempts are  being made to link the emergency in K P with things other than terrorism
content:
Says it is unfortunate attempts are being made to link the emergency in K-P with things other than terrorism
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry on Monday rubbished linking governor's rule and the imposition of an emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) to mineral extraction in the province.
The emergency and governor’s rule were declared on October 11 after negotiations between the government and opposition failed , culminating in a PTI long march towards Islamabad that began on October 4. Last week, a joint session of parliament adopted two separate resolutions ratifying the presidential proclamations imposing a state of emergency and governor’s rule in K-P for two months, amid protests from the opposition. Before that, both houses of parliament had separately approved the emergency in the province by majority vote under Clause 1 of Article 232 of the Constitution, despite objections from opposition lawmakers.
The opposition has decried the move as an attempt to encroach on the province's mineral wealth and vowed to resist what it has said is the forcible occupation of Pakhtun lands and the appropriation of their natural resources.
Speaking on the private television programme Capital Talk, Chaudhry said political parties were trying to link the emergency to the debate over minerals because they thought the emergency was imposed to gain power as part of a "power game".
"It’s not a power game but a peace game, because of which an emergency has been imposed".
Read : K-P is rich in minerals; we will 'extract and sell them', says Kundi
The minister noted it was unfortunate that attempts were being made to link the emergency in K-P with things other than terrorism, further adding that the emergency had been imposed in extraordinary circumstances and a constitutional option has been used for that purpose.
Chaudhry further said that the "expectations of certain political parties have not been met, including people in my own party who wanted a share of the authority in the new political setup. It was explained to them that the people selected in the advisory council were done so on merit and were experts in their respective fields."
While explaining the reasons for the imposition of an emergency in K-P, the minister underlined that there were differences of opinion between the former provincial government and the federal government on the issue of counterterrorism, further adding that the former chief minister was not even willing to condemn terrorism and the TTP.
On the security situation in K-P, Chaudhry stated that Dera Ismail Khan was among the 12 districts in which operations would be conducted in the first phase. "There is no writ of the government there in DI Khan, and I can provide you the names of parliamentarians who give protection money to safely return to their home."
Talking about US Chargé d'Affaires Natalie Baker’s statement in which she claimed that Pakistan possessed seven trillion dollars of mineral wealth, Chaudhry noted that Pakistan’s partnership with the US was old, further adding that Natalie took the names of both Balochistan and K-P.
Read More : Govt seeks US investment in minerals
“Mines and minerals that have been buried for the past 80 years, should they not be extracted to pay off Pakistan’s loans? The federal government has stressed that people from K-P and Balochistan will have the first right to the mineral wealth of their province, and the money will be spent on provincial development”.
The minister stated that the federal government would provide figures on how much money had been given to K-P and how much of it was actually spent, adding that numbers would also be shared for Balochistan.
On October 17, K-P Governor Faisal Karim Kundi said the province’s mineral resources would be extracted and sold to promote economic prosperity, urging domestic and foreign companies to invest in the sector through joint ventures to generate employment and support local businesses.
The governor defended the proposed exploitation of the province’s mineral resources , arguing that investment in the sector could generate employment, support local businesses and improve economic conditions.
Pakistan's mineral reserves are estimated at around $8 trillion and spread over 600,000 square kilometres, according to the Institute of Cost and Management Accountants (ICMA). The vast mineral resources highlight the massive economic potential of the mining sector. The sector has historically contributed less than 3% to the gross domestic product (GDP). With strong governance and security, annual mineral exports could rise from about $3 billion to $8 billion, and GDP growth could climb from roughly 3% to 6%.
The challenge, however, is to turn the geological potential into bankable projects, exports, jobs and industrial capacity. This requires more than mining and greater focus on exploration, geological data, modern technology, infrastructure, financing, predictable regulation, environmental safeguards and partnerships with international companies.

Actor has addressed comments about her weight, linking stress from running a business to changes in her eating habits
Actor Komal Aziz Khan responded to pregnancy rumours with a witty remark after a social media follower asked whether she was expecting a child.
The exchange took place during an Instagram question-and-answer session, in which Komal shared a picture of herself holding a bouquet of yellow sunflowers. One follower asked, “Are u pregnant again??” Reacting with surprise and amusement, Komal replied, “Hahaha what. I don’t believe in pregnancy before marriage.”
Her playful response appeared to poke fun at the assumption behind the question, turning the awkward exchange into a moment of humour. It also drew attention to her unmarried status and her views on relationships and marriage.
The question came amid discussions about Komal’s recent appearance and weight gain. The entrepreneur has previously faced comments from social media users about changes in her weight, making public scrutiny of her appearance a recurring subject.
On an earlier occasion, Aziz addressed the issue, explaining that running a business could be stressful and that she sometimes found herself eating more during challenging periods. She also disclosed that she did not smoke and might turn to food as a way of coping with stress.
Her candid explanation offered a glimpse into the pressures of running a business and the everyday challenges that can affect a person’s lifestyle. Her latest response, meanwhile, showed her willingness to address personal speculation with humour.
Aziz recently shared pictures from her birthday celebration, showing her marking the occasion with a cake and candles indicating that she had turned 34. The pictures brought renewed attention to the entrepreneur, who has maintained an active social media presence despite stepping away from acting.
Khan rose to prominence through her work in television dramas before turning her attention to entrepreneurship. She later focused on building her clothing business, moving away from the entertainment industry to concentrate on her venture.
Running a business has remained a recurring topic in her conversations with followers. She has also been open about living independently before marriage and has spoken about finding fulfilment in life beyond fame .

title: Mehwish Hayat explains why she limits her social media posts
description: Says she avoids oversharing to maintain privacy  keep fans interested and preserve time for herself away from work
content:
Says she avoids oversharing to maintain privacy, keep fans interested and preserve time for herself away from work
Actor Mehwish Hayat has explained why she maintains a relatively low-key presence on social media, revealing that she prefers to post occasionally rather than share frequent updates with her followers.
During an interview , the Jawani Phir Nahi Ani star said she does not post on social media frequently. “I post every two to three weeks because I feel like people get bored. They should always be wanting more,” Mehwish said.
She added that her approach also stemmed from her personal preference for privacy. While social media allows celebrities to stay connected with their fans, she does not believe in sharing every aspect of her life online.
“It also comes from the fact that I don’t like to overshare,” she said, highlighting her desire to maintain a distinction between her public persona and private life.
Her comments reflect a deliberate approach to managing her online presence. Rather than posting simply to remain visible, the actress prefers to share content selectively, allowing her followers to anticipate her next update.
Beyond maintaining audience interest, Mehwish also emphasised the importance of personal time and preserving space for herself away from work and social media.
She noted that her professional commitments and the time she dedicates to her fans already occupy a substantial part of her life. “Also, I really love my own time because I give so much time to my work and my fans. If I give the rest of my time to social media, what’s left for me?” she said.
Her remarks underline the importance she places on balancing professional responsibilities, engagement with fans and personal time. For Mehwish, being connected with her audience does not mean documenting every moment or remaining constantly active online.
While celebrities increasingly use social media to share professional updates and glimpses into their personal lives, Mehwish’s comments highlight a more selective approach. She appears keen to maintain a connection with her followers without allowing online engagement to dominate her daily routine.
Her perspective also echoes concerns raised by other Pakistani celebrities about privacy and safety on social media.
Actor Kinza Hashmi recently urged women to be cautious about whom they trust, discussing the importance of trusting one’s instincts and avoiding sharing every detail of one’s life in real time. She noted that fans did not need to know where someone was eating or spending time at every moment, particularly given safety concerns in Pakistan.
Mehwish is one of Pakistan’s best-known film and television actresses, recognised for her performances in productions including Punjab Nahi Jaungi , Load Wedding , London Nahi Jaunga and Jawani Phir Nahi Ani .

content:
Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos await their new rescue dog’s homecoming as he receives treatment for a parasite
Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos are delaying the arrival of their newly adopted rescue dog after discovering that the puppy has a parasite and needs treatment.
The Live with Kelly and Mark hosts shared the update exclusively with PEOPLE on Sunday, October 18, while attending the Broadway opening night of Other Desert Cities at the Hudson Theatre in New York City.
“We don’t have him yet because he had a little bit of health issue,” Ripa, 56, told the publication.
“A parasite,” Consuelos, 55, clarified, adding that the dog is receiving treatment before joining the family.
The couple hopes to bring their new pet home soon. “Any day now,” Consuelos said, expressing optimism about the puppy’s arrival.
The adoption was announced less than a week earlier during the hosts’ daytime talk show, Live with Kelly and Mark , as part of its Adopt a Dog Week. The puppy, initially named Lucas, was brought onto the set by rescue organisation Pet ResQ Inc. on October 12.
Consuelos quickly bonded with the dog, who fell asleep in his arms during the broadcast. The couple confirmed the adoption the following day, with Consuelos introducing the puppy as Javi.
However, the name remains undecided. While Consuelos suggested Javi, short for Javier, Ripa revealed that their family was also considering keeping the puppy’s original name, Lucas. Their three adult children, Michael, Lola and Joaquin, have offered suggestions, although the couple joked that their children do not get a vote.
The new puppy will join Lena, their Maltese-Shih Tzu mix adopted in 2020. Ripa previously said the dogs had begun playing together after an initially cautious introduction.
The adoption also comes after the couple lost their beloved dog Chewie in February 2025 at age 17. Ripa said she wondered whether Chewie had somehow led them to their new companion, who reminded her of their late pet.
For now, the couple is preparing to welcome their newest family member once his treatment is complete.

title: Pakistan  Saudi Arabia    satisfied    over progress under Makkah defence agreement
description: CDF Munir and Saudi envoy discuss regional security dynamics  matters of mutual interest during the meeting
content:
CDF Munir and Saudi envoy discuss regional security dynamics, matters of mutual interest during the meeting
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia expressed satisfaction on Monday over progress under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and stressed the need to strengthen defence cooperation, institutional linkages and strategic coordination.
The understanding was reached during a meeting between Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir and Saudi Ambassador to Pakistan Dr Rajeh Tami Albugamy at General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, according to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).
The two sides discussed matters of mutual interest and regional security dynamics, with a focus on further strengthening defence collaboration between the two countries.
Field Marshal Munir congratulated Dr Albugamy on his appointment as Saudi ambassador to Pakistan and expressed confidence that his tenure would contribute to further strengthening the longstanding fraternal ties between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia rooted in shared faith, mutual trust and strategic partnership.
Read: PM vows unwavering support for KSA
The ambassador arrived in Islamabad on September 26 and since then has conducted several meetings with the country’s top civilian and military leadership as Islamabad and Riyadh seek to deepen ties.
On October 14, President Asif Ali Zardari received Dr Albugamy’s credentials at Aiwan-e-Sadr, reaffirming Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security and defence. The president also called for stronger economic ties, highlighted opportunities for greater cooperation and acknowledged Saudi Arabia’s financial assistance and support for oil supplies.
Two days later, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met the Saudi envoy and reiterated Pakistan’s commitment towards the kingdom’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity amid escalating Houthi attacks. During the meeting, PM Shehbaz described the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement and the Makkah Joint Defence framework as significant milestones in bilateral relations. He also pledged to strengthen institutional mechanisms and expand cooperation across various sectors.
On the same day, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also met Dr Albugamy. He also highlighted the countries’ longstanding fraternal ties and shared commitment to closer bilateral cooperation.
Read more: President Zardari receives credentials of French, Saudi ambassadors-designate
These diplomatic engagements follow the September 2025 Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, which established a framework for joint defence, and the subsequent trilateral Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed on August 7 involving Türkiye.
According to the Makkah agreement , an armed attack against any one of the three signatory states would be regarded as an attack against all three, establishing a framework for collective deterrence and expanded defence cooperation.
The agreement has since been followed by efforts to translate its commitments into closer military coordination. In September, senior military commanders from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye met in Riyadh to review the regional security situation and discuss intelligence sharing, military coordination and the integration of defence capabilities.

title: Winning peace more important than winning war   Naqvi on US Iran mediation efforts at Doha security forum
description: Stresses Pakistan chose  path of peace  during critical time  made efforts to bring both sides to negotiating table
content:
Stresses Pakistan chose 'path of peace' during critical time, made efforts to bring both sides to negotiating table
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Monday that "winning peace was more important than winning a war" while discussing Pakistan's mediation efforts between Iran and the United States at the 8th Global Security Forum being held in Doha.
Naqvi stressed that Pakistan chose the "path of peace" during a critical time and made efforts to bring both sides to the negotiating table, highlighting the personal efforts of the Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir to achieve peace.
"I must highlight the remarkable role of our Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir, his personal efforts, his strong relations with world leaders and his continuous engagement with all sides, which has played a key role in opening doors for dialogue," he said.
"The aim of both countries, Pakistan and Qatar, was never to take credit, the only aim was to stop further conflict and to save innocent lives. Pakistan has always believed that dialogue is better than war. We believe that winning peace is far more important than winning a war," he added.
Also Read : Pakistan mediation pulls off elusive deal
Naqvi underlined that a recent example of Pakistan's commitment to regional security was the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement , signed between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, adding that it was a pact for defence and not for war. "We believe that no country can enjoy lasting peace if its neighbours are facing conflict," he stated.
The minister emphasised that the last few months had been difficult for the region, noting that the conflict involving Iran and the US created serious risks not only for the Middle East but for the entire world.
He further said that he was personally involved in the peace efforts along with Field Marshal Munir during their visits to Tehran and meetings with senior Iranian officials, adding that he "saw how difficult these talks were".
"There were moments when the situation was extremely tense, but we never gave up, and we continued talking, listening and working together to build trust. Peace is not achieved in one meeting; it requires patience, trust and continuous efforts," he stated.
Read More : Pakistan helped avert wider conflict through US-Iran mediation, security sources say
Naqvi said that in April, Pakistan hosted the Islamabad talks, adding that in June, Pakistan and Qatar signed the Islamabad MoU , with the two countries sitting together as the mediating parties.
"Days later, at the Lake Lausanne summit, I saw something I will never forget. His Highness, the Prime Minister of Qatar and the Field Marshal worked for more than 16 hours plus without a single break, no cameras, no announcements, only two men who refused to let the talks fail, two countries, one purpose," he added.
The minister further stated, "The recent experience has taught us three important lessons: never close the doors to dialogue, trust is the most important key for any kind of talk, and thirdly, peace requires sincere efforts from everyone. No single country can achieve regional peace alone.” “We do not want credit for stopping wars. We want a future where wars do not start,” he added.
Naqvi said that as Pakistan's interior minister, he understood the price of terrorism and insecurity, adding that since terrorism was a common enemy, "we need stronger cooperation, better intelligence sharing and joint efforts to defeat it".
"Cooperation is not something Pakistan only asks for, it's something that Pakistan has given. For decades, our soldiers and policemen have served in UN peacekeeping missions and helped protect civilians and restore peace in countries affected by conflict. We are proud of their service and their sacrifices," he added.
US and Iran agreed to the Islamabad MoU following months of intense diplomatic efforts by Pakistan. The peace deal was announced by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on June 15. The premier, while announcing the deal, also revealed that the formal signing of the document would be held in Switzerland, though it was signed by the US and Iran electronically. The signing of the 14-point MoU triggered a 60-day window to negotiate the final terms of a deal.
Despite repeated geopolitical pressure points and attempts to disrupt the process, Pakistan maintained its diplomatic channel and ensured continuity of engagement between the two sides. According to former diplomats and international affairs experts, the achievement was not accidental but the result of sustained, discreet and strategically positioned diplomacy.
Also Read : Islamabad credited with rare diplomatic breakthrough
At a time when escalating hostilities between Washington and Tehran had triggered fears of a wider conflict, including concerns over disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global energy route, Pakistan stepped into a space that no other actor was able or willing to occupy.
Experts say Pakistan's credibility stemmed from its unique diplomatic positioning : trusted simultaneously by Washington and Tehran, maintaining constructive ties with Gulf states, and remaining outside direct military entanglements in the conflict zone. This allowed Islamabad to function as a rare bridge between two deeply polarised sides.
Pakistan’s mediation efforts have come under the global spotlight. Trump has repeatedly appreciated the mediating role of Pakistan amid the intense conflict in the Middle East.
Leaders and senior officials from the United Nations, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, Australia, France, Japan, New Zealand, and Germany appreciated Pakistan and expressed support for the agreement that has paved the way for regional stability and ensured diplomatic engagement on Iran’s nuclear programme.

title: Pakistan face stern England test
description: Hosts aim to build on opening victory against Sri Lanka in the ODI tri series
content:
Hosts aim to build on opening victory against Sri Lanka in the ODI tri-series
Pakistan will look to build on their solid performance in the opening match when they take on England in the second show of the ODI tri-series at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Tuesday (today)).
Led by Shaheen Shah Afridi, Pakistan made a bright start to the series on Sunday, making a strong comeback to beat Sri Lanka by 37 runs.
Chasing a target of 306, Sri Lanka were well-placed at 253-5 at one stage. However, Haris Rauf dismissed Janith Liyanage 96), triggering a collapse as the visitors lost their last five wickets for just 15 runs.
Shaheen led from the front with figures of 3-55, while Haris, Faheem Ashraf and Naseem Shah supported him well, taking two wickets each.
Earlier, Salman Ali Agha struck a superb 107, his fourth ODI century, to help Pakistan post 305 all out.
Pakistan were struggling at 118-4 when Agha and Hasan Nawaz, who scored 37, put together a 97-run partnership for the fifth wicket to boost the total.
After losing their openers cheaply, Babar Azam, who scored 45, and debutant wicket-keeper batsman Saad Baig, who made 39, added 74 runs for the third wicket to steady the innings.
However, the subsequent loss of wickets put the hosts under pressure before Agha produced a special knock to strengthen Pakistan's position.
England will pose a tough challenge for Pakistan. The two sides will meet in an ODI for the first time in almost three years.
Their last ODI encounter took place on November 11, 2023, at Eden Gardens in Kolkata during the ICC Men's Cricket World Cup, when England secured a 93-run victory.
The two teams have played 92 ODIs against each other, with England winning 57 matches and Pakistan claiming 32 victories. Three matches ended without a result.
England have enjoyed a strong run in recent times, performing well in the subcontinent. They beat Sri Lanka 2-1 in an away series and also recorded 2-1 series victories over India and Sri Lanka at home.
A major boost for England is the return of premier leg-spinner Adil Rashid, who has rejoined the squad after a hand injury ruled him out of their recent 2-1 ODI series victory over Sri Lanka.
Sam Curran has also returned after recovering from a groin injury. However, premier fast bowler Jofra Archer has been rested for the tour, while Jos Buttler has been ruled out because of a hamstring injury sustained against Sri Lanka.
Glamorgan leg-spinner Mason Crane, who is yet to make his ODI debut, has been called up to the squad. He returns to the England setup eight years after his previous international appearance, in the fifth men's Ashes Test in Sydney in 2018. Crane also played two T20 internationals in 2017.
Uncapped Sussex players James Coles and Henry Crocombe, who were both part of England's white-ball squads this summer, have also been included.
“This will be a massive challenge to play against two really good teams in different conditions,” England captain Harry Brook said at a pre-series news conference.
“We want to be a team that adapts to conditions and can find different ways to win, and this series provides a perfect opportunity to try and do that.”
Brook said England had demonstrated their ability to adapt in recent series, winning in Sri Lanka before beating India and Sri Lanka at home.
Shadab Khan and Sufyan Moqim had missed the previous game due to illness and Pakistan may go against England with at least one of these two bowlers.

content:
The former India coach stresses the importance of preserving the paceman's fitness for next year's tournament
India should keep Jasprit Bumrah fresh for next year's one-day international World Cup by selecting him mainly for test cricket and using the pace spearhead sparingly in ‌other formats, former coach Ravi Shastri said.
Bumrah was recalled to India's test squad for their two-match series in New Zealand last week, but will not play in the five ODIs and five Twenty20 internationals that precede the tests.
Bumrah's career has been ⁠disrupted by back injuries, with the 32-year-old having to undergo surgery in 2023.
He was ruled out of a two-test series against Sri Lanka in August due to a left knee injury, but returned to T20 action at the Asian Games and helped India win gold.
"I don't think he should play all three formats till the ODI World Cup," Shastri, who coached India from 2017 to ‌2021, ⁠told Indian media on Sunday.
"He should play test cricket and should play sporadically between one-day internationals and T20 cricket. He also shouldn't be playing the whole lot.
"I would rather preserve him for the test matches. ⁠That's very important. He becomes a key member of that Indian side. Then he should be used sparingly in the other formats."
Following their tour ⁠of New Zealand, India will host Sri Lanka and Zimbabwe in limited-overs series, before hosting Australia in a five-test series ⁠which concludes in February.
The 2027 World Cup will be held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia from October 2 to November 21.

title: Zubaida Khanum remembered on 13th death anniversary for her musical legacy
description: Playback singer recorded around 250 songs in Urdu and Punjabi before stepping away from the film industry in the 1960s
content:
Playback singer recorded around 250 songs in Urdu and Punjabi before stepping away from the film industry in the 1960s
Pakistani playback singer Zubaida Khanum is being remembered on her 13th death anniversary, with her recordings continuing to represent an important chapter in the country’s film music history.
Khanum, who died in Lahore on October 19, 2013, at the age of 78, was among the prominent female voices of the flourishing film industry of the 1950s. Her work in Urdu and Punjabi cinema helped establish her reputation at a time when songs were central to both storytelling and the commercial appeal of films.
Born in Amritsar in 1935, Khanum moved to Lahore with her family following the Partition of the subcontinent in 1947. She rose to prominence as Pakistan’s emerging film industry developed its own musical identity, drawing on Punjabi folk traditions and the wider musical heritage of the region.
According to IMDb , Khanum began her singing career with the film Billo in 1951 before gaining wider recognition through the Punjabi film Shehri Babu , released in 1953.
Her career flourished during the 1950s, when Lahore was an important centre of Pakistani film production. She became known for her playback singing, in which singers record songs that are later performed on screen by actors. Her voice featured in numerous Urdu and Punjabi films, helping make songs an enduring part of the cinematic experience for audiences of the period.
In an obituary published on October 30, 2013, The Independent reported that Khanum recorded approximately 250 songs, largely in Urdu and Punjabi. The publication also noted her solo performances and duets, as well as recordings that extended beyond film music.
Her film credits included Pattan , Heer and Patay Khan in 1955, followed by Chann Mahi and Dulla Bhatti in 1956. These films belonged to a period when Punjabi cinema was building a strong audience through stories, performances and music rooted in local culture.
Khanum also appeared in a small number of films as an actress, including Patay Khan and Dulla Bhatti , although playback singing remained the principal source of her recognition.
Despite her popularity, Khanum’s career was relatively short. She stepped away from playback singing in the 1960s after marrying film cameraman Riaz Bokhari.
The Independent noted in its obituary that she left the industry to devote herself to family life, leaving behind a body of work concentrated largely in the period when Pakistani cinema was establishing many of its best-known musical traditions.
Her career illustrated the distinctive role of playback singers in South Asian cinema. While actors appeared on screen, singers supplied the voices that conveyed the emotions of romantic sequences, folk-inspired performances and dramatic moments. Their contributions could become widely recognised even when audiences associated the performances visually with the actors.
Khanum’s legacy continued to receive public recognition years after her death.
In 2020 , the Punjab Institute of Language, Art and Culture (PILAC) marked the singer’s seventh death anniversary with an event that included the inauguration of a folk studio and performances of her songs.
PILAC’s then director general, Sughra Sadaf, highlighted Khanum’s importance to Punjabi culture and traditions, noting that her relatively brief career had left behind a significant musical legacy.
Khanum died of a heart attack at her Lahore residence on October 19, 2013. Thirteen years after her death, her place in Pakistan’s musical history remains closely tied to the songs she recorded during the industry’s formative decades. Her career connected the popular cinema of the 1950s with musical traditions that had developed across the Punjab region before and after Partition.
Although her time in the recording industry was relatively brief, Khanum’s work offers a window into an era when film songs played a central role in popular entertainment. Her recordings remain part of the legacy of the singers, composers, lyricists and filmmakers who helped shape Pakistan’s early cinematic identity.

content:
The club backs Puma as authorities ban public gatherings after violent protests
Olympique de Marseille said their official store on La Canebiere, the city's historic main avenue, was looted during weekend unrest in France , with the ‌Ligue 1 club on Monday condemning the incident.
France had some of its worst unrest in years over the weekend, with thousands of people arrested and shops looted or damaged during protests over high prices ⁠and declining public services.
Earlier on Monday, Marseille authorities imposed a ban on public gatherings and demonstrations across the city after violent protests and looting. The measure took effect from midday (1000 GMT) until 8 p.m. (1800 GMT).
"Olympique de Marseille condemns in the strongest possible terms the acts of violence and looting targeting its official store on the Canebiere ‌and ⁠expresses its solidarity with its partner Puma, which operates the store," the club said in a statement.
"These events have caused significant property damage, forcing the club to temporarily close this ⁠store to the public. Fans may, however, continue to visit OM's other official stores in Marseille. The club will inform its ⁠fans as soon as conditions allow for a reopening ..."
Marseille are ninth in Ligue 1 after seven matches and ⁠return to action on Thursday when they visit Austrian side Sturm Graz in the Europa League.

Singer shares photos of their life together, praising his wife’s strength, heart and character in a loving message
Singer Atif Aslam celebrated his wife Sarah Bharwana’s birthday with an affectionate message on Instagram, saying one day was not enough to honour the woman he calls his queen.
In his Instagram post , the singer wrote, “Happy Sarah Day, Week, Month, because one day could never be enough to celebrate you. Obsessed with your strength, your heart, and everything you are my Queen.”
The post featured a collection of photographs capturing moments the couple have shared, including travel memories, dinner dates and selfies, offering fans a glimpse into their life together away from the spotlight.
Known for his soulful voice and romantic songs, Aslam has occasionally shared affectionate messages for Sarah on social media. His latest tribute highlighted his admiration for her strength and character, alongside his birthday wishes.

The couple have since built a family together and have three children: sons Abdul Ahad and Aaryan, and daughter Halima, who was born in March 2023.
Aslam has previously expressed his affection for Sarah in public. In a March anniversary-related post , the singer shared a loving message about wishing he had met her sooner so they could have made even more memories together.
Beyond his personal life, Aslam remains one of Pakistan’s best-known singers, with popular songs including Aadat , Tera Hone Laga Hoon and Dil Diyan Gallan , which have earned him a substantial following across South Asia.

title: Tiger Shroff s car targeted in Mumbai shooting  three arrested
description: Lawrence Bishnoi gang reportedly claim responsibility for attack on Bollywood actor
content:
Lawrence Bishnoi gang reportedly claim responsibility for attack on Bollywood actor
Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff’s BMW was targeted in a shooting outside filmmaker Rohit Shetty’s residence in Mumbai’s Juhu area on Sunday evening, with the actor subsequently rushing his injured driver to hospital.
According to Gulf News , around five rounds were fired at the car, leaving Shroff’s driver, identified in reports as Firdous Ibrahim Baloch, with a bullet wound to his left wrist. The actor escaped the attack without any gunshot injuries.
Shroff reportedly took the wheel after the shooting and drove to Santacruz Police Station before being escorted by police to Nanavati Hospital to ensure his driver received medical attention.
According to India Today , three people have been arrested in connection with the incident. The reported arrests, along with the gang’s alleged claim of responsibility, form part of the developing investigation.
“A firing incident has been reported under Juhu police station. Actor Tiger Shroff is safe and has not sustained any gunshot injuries. Further investigation is underway,” Mumbai police said in a statement quoted by ANI.
According to The Statesman , the Lawrence Bishnoi gang claimed responsibility for the shooting. Anil Pandit, described in the report as a gang member, allegedly said he had carried out the attack with an accomplice, Harman Sandhu.
A video circulating on social media reportedly showed Shroff moving into the driver’s seat after the incident. His actions prompted praise from social media users, who commended him for helping his injured driver in the immediate aftermath of the shooting.
The reported claim of responsibility has also drawn attention to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, which Indian authorities and media reports have linked to several high-profile shootings and killings.
The network has been associated with the 2022 murder of Punjabi singer Sidhu Moosewala and the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique in Mumbai. It has also been linked to a shooting outside actor Salman Khan’s residence in Bandra in April 2024.
Other reported incidents include a shooting at a Delhi gym linked to singer Guru Randhawa and multiple firing incidents targeting comedian Kapil Sharma’s café in Canada in 2025.
According to American prosecutors, the Bishnoi organisation operates as a transnational criminal network that uses public claims of violence to intimidate targets and support extortion activities.
Meanwhile, Mumbai police are investigating the shooting and reviewing available evidence to establish the circumstances of the attack and identify those responsible.

title: Semenyo out for up to eight weeks
description: The Ghana international picked up the injury during Manchester City   s win at Ipswich
content:
The Ghana international picked up the injury during Manchester City’s win at Ipswich
Manchester City's Antoine Semenyo is set to be out of action for up to eight weeks with a leg injury, manager Enzo Maresca said on Monday.
Ghana forward Semenyo suffered the issue during last week's 3-2 win at Ipswich as table-toppers City made it seven wins out of seven in the Premier League this season.
Maresca, speaking ahead of City's Champions League encounter against AEK Athens at the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday, was upbeat about the fitness of Erling Haaland, Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes and Nico O'Reilly, but was less positive regarding Semenyo.
"The rest are more or less all OK," he said. "The only one that will be out for probably eight weeks is Antoine."
Semenyo, however, has had a scan which Maresca said was "not as bad as we expected".
Star striker Haaland was seen limping after the end of the game against Ipswich.
"He can be available, we will see, we have a (training) session now. We have some doubts after Sunday's game. He was quite good yesterday, better. So we will see today," Maresca said.
"First of all to lose Antonine or any player for us, it is not good.
"Then in terms of Erling, we said that we can use Antoine as a nine but also we have different players that we are going to try and find new solutions.
"We will see, again. At the moment it is Erling, why do we need to think about a different nine when Erling is there?
"Then, if something happens and we need a different plan or a different nine, we will see," the Italian added.
Maresca is the first manager to win their opening seven Premier League games at a new club.
But their impressive start to the campaign is taking place against the backdrop of being found guity of more than 100 charges of breaching financial rules in English football's top flight -- all of which City deny, with Maresca having repeatedly insisted he "trusts the club completely".
City, however, were beaten 4-2 by title-holders Paris Saint-Germain in their last Champions League encounter and Maresca insisted there was no question of trying to protect players from possible injury risks against AEK.
"It is a huge game, tomorrow for us," said the Italian.
"It is a Champions League game, unfortunately we lost the last one, we need to win games and we are going to try to win the game with our best players at this moment."
