title: Cable theft leaves traffic signals dysfunctional
description: Cable theft leaves traffic signals dysfunctional
content:
KDA's Traffic Engineering Bureau cites funding shortages and repeated thefts as commuters face daily congestion acros
Theft of cables and other equipment has rendered 33 traffic signals dysfunctional across Karachi, worsening traffic congestion on major roads and adding to commuters' daily difficulties. After targeting iron railings around parks, playgrounds and roadsides, suspected drug addicts have now turned their attention to traffic signals, damaging critical urban infrastructure.
According to the Karachi Development Authority's (KDA) Traffic Engineering Bureau (TEB), 94 traffic signals are installed across the city. However, repeated thefts have left many of them out of order, while the authorities concerned have yet to take effective measures to prevent further incidents.
Cameras installed along major roads have largely been used for issuing traffic challans and monitoring traffic violations, rather than identifying those responsible for damaging public infrastructure.
An Express Tribune survey found that traffic police personnel often resort to manually controlling traffic at intersections where signals are not functioning. In some instances, however, traffic officials are also absent from these locations. The deteriorating condition of roads, with several stretches damaged and broken, further compounds the problem.
As a result, traffic congestion has become a daily occurrence on major thoroughfares as well as roads within residential and commercial areas.
Traffic Engineering Bureau (TEB) sources said repairs had been suspended for over a year due to funding shortages, with more than Rs10 million in contractor payments outstanding. The Sindh government allocated funds to the Karachi commissioner's office for repairs, lane marking and road signs.
Using the funds and TEB's technical support, 20 signals were repaired, including five automated ones. However, cables were subsequently stolen from seven signals, including those in Red Zone areas monitored by surveillance cameras, forcing them to shut down again.
These locations included Ziauddin Road near Lily Bridge, Boat Basin Chowrangi, Sir Syed Khalid bin Walid Road intersection, Akbar Road, Court Road and Singer Chowrangi. Cables on Ziauddin Road were reportedly stolen on three separate occasions.
At Boat Basin, a private security guard foiled an attempt to steal a newly installed road sign. TEB sources said police had repeatedly been informed about the thefts but had taken no effective action.
A police officer, speaking anonymously, said Safe City cameras were monitored through a centralised control room and used for traffic enforcement, tracing stolen vehicles and monitoring suspicious activity in Red Zone areas.
District police can obtain footage through formal requests, while community policing cameras installed with private donations are monitored at local stations. The officer said footage could help identify the culprits, blaming police negligence for the lack of action. The South district police spokesperson sought a day to comment but did not respond to subsequent calls.
TEB sources said signals at another 26 locations were dysfunctional due to cable and equipment thefts, including Makki Masjid, Yaseenabad, Atrium Mall, Karachi Grammar School, Shahrah-e-Iraq, Albela Chowrangi, Guru Mandir, Banuri Town Mosque, I.I. Chundrigar Road near Denso Hall, Aram Bagh and Shalimar Chowk.
Ghaus Bakhsh Abbasi, project director at the Karachi commissioner's office, confirmed an increase in traffic signal cable thefts, saying FIRs had been registered and the commissioner had taken up the matter with senior police officials.
He said repairs had been delayed due to a funding shortage at the Traffic Engineering Bureau. Following the chief minister's directives, the Sindh government released Rs100 million to the Karachi commissioner's office, enabling the repair of 20 signals, including five automated ones, along with lane marking and road sign installation.
However, some repaired signals were damaged again by cable thefts. Abbasi said a request for additional funds to repair the remaining faulty signals had been submitted to the provincial government.

Residents of Tando Jam and other parts of Hyderabad Rural taluka appealed for immediate relief measures, saying authorities must ensure flour remains affordable and accessible to ordinary families.
They said their demand was simple: affordable food so that household kitchens could keep running and chil-dren could receive two meals a day.

title: Construction along Nehr e Khayyam slammed
description: Construction along Nehr e Khayyam slammed
content:
A nehr (canal) that residents say should remain a lifeline for the city's drainage system is now at the centre of a growing battle over commercialisation, with Clifton residents warning that construction along Nehr-e-Khayyam could come at a heavy environmental cost.
From fears of urban flooding to concerns over marine pollution, protesters say the concrete structures emerging along the waterway raise troubling questions about the project's purpose, legality and long-term impact on the metropolis.
Carrying placards and banners declaring "No to commercial activities at Nehr-e-Khayyam", residents and civil society representatives took to the streets on Sunday, demanding an immediate halt to construction and the disclosure of approved plans, environmental clearances, contracts and project costs.
The protesters alleged that the construction could pave the way for shops, commercial buildings and a food street along the canal, potentially narrowing the waterway and reducing its capacity to carry rainwater towards the sea. They said the government had yet to adequately explain the project or share its detailed plans with affected residents.
Rasha Tariq, a representative of Clifton Residents, said the authorities had failed to answer residents' questions despite repeated protests.
"This is a potentially disastrous project that could cause serious harm to the city," she said, adding that civil society members, elected representatives, lawyers, showbiz personalities and people from other walks of life had joined the campaign.
Residents recalled that a similar attempt to construct a building along the canal in 2005 had been challenged in court, eventually resulting in the structure's demolition. They alleged that work had resumed in 2019 and expressed concern over the latest construction activity.
The protesters questioned whether the Sindh government had obtained the necessary environmental approvals, how much the project would cost and whether residents had been consulted before work began.
Amber, a representative of a citizens' organisation, said residents who had opposed commercial activities along Nehr-e-Khayyam in 2005 would continue to resist what they described as encroachments on the waterway.

The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) has renewed its call for new administrative units in Sindh, arguing that the devolution of powers and authority is essential to address longstanding civic problems in Karachi, Hyderabad and other urban areas.
"Establishing new and empowered administrative units is the biggest challenge and the solution to ensuring that people receive their rights at their doorstep," MQM-P Chairman Dr Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui said during a meeting with legal experts at the party's Bahadurabad headquarters.
The meeting brought together members of the Muttahida Lawyers Forum, the party's Legal Aid Committee and prominent legal experts to discuss urban Sindh's civic challenges, constitutional and legal reforms, judicial performance and strategies for securing the release of party activists in detention.
Senior MQM-P leader Wasim Akhtar and other party leaders attended the meeting, while former judge Qazi Khalid was also present.
Addressing the gathering, Siddiqui said the lack of basic facilities and the failure to devolve powers had fuelled public discontent in Karachi, Hyderabad and other urban districts. He called for a new administrative arrangement to restore balance in governance and ensure that citizens could access their rights and essential services more effectively.
Legal experts briefed the party leadership on what they described as shortcomings in existing laws and regulations that could be exploited to deprive citizens of their rights. They presented legal proposals and draft amendments aimed at addressing procedural and constitutional gaps.
The participants also discussed the need for far-reaching judicial reforms to ensure timely, affordable and transparent justice, particularly for disadvantaged and marginalised communities.
Members of the Legal Aid Committee pledged to expand and strengthen legal assistance for citizens facing difficulties in accessing justice. The meeting also considered legal strategies concerning detained party workers and efforts to secure their release.
At the conclusion of the meeting, MQM-P leaders and legal experts reiterated their commitment to pursuing the party's demands through political, constitutional and legal means, including advocating new administrative units and reforms to existing laws.

title: KDA s cash crunch fails to stop perks for favoured officials

content:
Four advance increments approved for former DG's personal secretary, while 24 officers reportedly receive two each
At the cash-strapped Karachi Development Authority (KDA), the wait for pensions and retirement dues continues for former employees, even as serving officials appear to have secured a generous share of the financial pie.
Two official orders granting special salary increments to dozens of officers have surfaced, raising questions about the authority's priorities at a time when it relies on Sindh government grants to meet salaries and operational expenses.
The first order, dated September 7, 2026, approved four advance increments for Riyaz Ahmed Rashid, the senior personal secretary to the director general, effective July 1, 2026. The approval was granted on the stated grounds of his performance in accounts and exceptional work, according to the document.
Sources alleged that the decision was among the special favours extended by former KDA director general Asif Jan Siddiqui before his departure. The four increments, they said, had drawn particular attention given the authority's financial difficulties and the outstanding dues of retired employees.
A second order, dated March 16, 2026, reportedly granted two increments each to 24 officials on the recommendation of the then member administration. The list includes former member administration and current Senior Director Master Plan Muhammad Shakeel Ahmed Siddiqui, former Secretary Arshad Khan, Senior Director Land Management Jameel Ahmed and Director Finance and Accounts Nasir Khan.
Other officials named in the order include Shakeel Ahmed Khan, Naveed Anwar Siddiqui, Kashif Siddiqui, Syed Atif Hussain Naqvi, Muhammad Meraj, Mir Imran Jokhio, Syed Shah Muhammad Arif, Muhammad Zubair, Nadeem Shabbir, Nadeem Taj, Nasir Saleem Siddiqui, Syed Arif Abbas, Hamza, Muhammad Atif, Muhammad Waseem, Muhammad Ali Khan, Arsalan Shariq, Muhammad Kamran and Syed Shujaat Hussain, among others.
The order reportedly cites the officials' contribution to increasing the authority's revenue through public auctions conducted in 2025 as the justification for the additional increments.
Both orders base the benefits on performance, with the increments reportedly incorporated into the recipients' salaries, increasing their monthly earnings.
The approvals have raised concerns about financial discipline and the equitable distribution of benefits within an organisation facing persistent resource constraints. While the authority depends on government grants to cover its running costs, retired employees continue to await pensions and other post-retirement payments.
The contrast between the reported salary benefits for serving officers and the financial difficulties faced by pensioners has brought the authority's spending priorities under scrutiny.
The circumstances surrounding the approvals, including their financial implications and the criteria used to award the additional increments, warrant clarification from the KDA administration. The authority's response to the allegations was not available at the time of filing this report.

title: Medic urges timely flu vaccination
description: Medic urges timely flu vaccination
content:
Paediatrician Dr Faiza Jahan has advised timely vaccination and preventive measures, particularly for children, older adults and people with chronic diseases, as cases of seasonal flu-like illnesses, including colds and coughs are increasing with the change in weather.
Speaking to the media, Dr Jahan said influenza could become more prevalent during November and December, particularly in cold and dry weather. She added that the flu vaccine should have ideally been administered before the season reached its peak, as it takes about two weeks for immunity to develop after vaccination.
The paediatrician cautioned against the unnecessary use of antibiotics, explaining that they were ineffective against viral infections. "If symptoms persist for five to seven days, antibiotics should only be used on a doctor's advice," she said, adding that children required medical assessment if they stopped eating or developed rapid breathing.
The doctor stressed that people with chronic conditions, including heart disease and asthma, as well as heavy smokers, should consider getting vaccinated against influenza after consulting their healthcare providers. Highlighting the risks to children, she said viral infections could sometimes lead to complications, including bacterial pneumonia.

title: Capital embraces traditional beverage
description: Capital embraces traditional beverage
content:
Nabeez, a centuries-old Sunnah drink, is experiencing a revival in the federal capital as residents increasingly turn towards natural and traditional beverages as healthier alternatives to sugary soft drinks and artificially flavoured products.
Prepared by soaking dates or raisins in water overnight, Nabeez has gained renewed popularity in homes and religious gatherings across the federal capital.
The drink is particularly attracting health-conscious consumers seeking a combination of traditional values, natural nourishment and spiritual significance.
Local grocery stores and dry-fruit retailers have reported a rise in demand for premium dates and raisins, with traders attributing the trend to growing awareness through social media, religious scholars and wellness communities.
Zahir, a dry-fruit trader in Aabpara Market, said customers were increasingly purchasing Ajwa and other varieties of dates and raisins specifically for preparing Nabeez. He added that demand rises during Muharram, Ramazan and other religious occasions when people show greater interest in traditional Sunnah practices.
Islamic scholar and Jamaat-e-Islami Women Wing Islamabad Information Secretary Sadia Saif said Nabeez held religious significance, citing authentic Hadith references. She explained that the Holy Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) consumed Nabeez prepared from dates or raisins before fermentation occurred.

title: Punjab cops to get specialised training in China
description: Punjab cops to get specialised training in China
content:
Programme to focus on detecting illicit financial transfers, trade-based money laundering
To strengthen Pakistan's system for combating money laundering, the inspector general of Punjab police has nominated 14 officers for high-level training in China.
From October 28 to November 10, experts in detecting and preventing money laundering will train the Punjab police officers in China.
The officers will receive training aimed at preventing the movement of illicit funds and precious minerals that could be used to finance terrorism or other illegal activities in Pakistan, particularly in Punjab.
Pakistan was placed on the grey list of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), an international body operating under a global framework to combat money laundering and terrorist financing, because of concerns over the movement of illegal funds within and outside the country.
However, Pakistan was subsequently removed from the FATF grey list following improved performance and effective measures against money laundering.
The training will be held at a police training institute in China from October 28 to November 10. As China currently holds the FATF presidency, it will familiarise Pakistani officers with modern methods being used to transfer illicit funds.
The programme will also cover ways to prevent different forms of money laundering, including trade-based money laundering.
The officers nominated by the Punjab inspector general to participate in the training and seminar include DIG Commandant Punjab Constabulary Hassan Habib Imtiaz; DIG Special Protection Unit Punjab Muhammad Tayyab Hafeez; SSP and Chief Traffic Officer Lahore Syed Abdul Rahim Shirazi; SSP and Additional Director Operations Punjab Muhammad Usman Bajwa; SSP Investigation Lahore Muhammad Naveed; SSP CTD Intelligence Punjab Lahore Asif Amin Awan; SSP Intelligence Special Branch Punjab Lahore Muhammad Faraz Ahmed; SSP Administration CTD Punjab Lahore Noshiwan Ali; SSP RO CTD Lahore Shameer Khalid; SP Training-I, Police College Sihala, Rawalpindi Saad Arshad; Additional SP Cantt Division Multan Dr Khadija Umar; SP Investigation Sialkot Muhammad Haseeb Raja; and ASP SDPO Sialkot City Bushra Aziz.

title: Cantt residents face water shortage
description: Cantt residents face water shortage
content:
Residents of Rawalpindi Cantonment have complained of a severe shortage of water, saying they receive supplies for only 15 to 25 minutes after intervals of up to 48 hours despite paying monthly water bills. They have urged senior authorities to take immediate notice of the situation and ensure a regular and fair water supply.
One of the residents, Muhammad Shafique, said the shortage had forced households to store water in drums, tanks and other containers. He expressed concern that water stored in open containers could provide breeding grounds for dengue mosquitoes, increasing the risk of the spread of dengue in the area.
Another complainant Naeem Qureshi pointed out that millions of rupees had been allocated over the past three years for water supply projects, including the construction of underground water tanks, rehabilitation of tube wells and installation of new distribution pipelines.
He questioned why the water shortage persisted despite these investments and demanded an inquiry into the management and distribution of water across the cantonment.
Residents also alleged that some lower-level officials in the Cantonment Board's water supply wing were favouring influential individuals in the distribution of water. They claimed that selected people were informed before supply valves were opened or pumps switched on, while other households continued to face shortages.
They further claimed that the Cantonment Board's water bowsers and smaller supply vehicles, often remained out of service for three to four days a week.

title: Twin cities shift gears to electric vehicles
description: Twin cities shift gears to electric vehicles
content:
Rising fuel costs drive a shift towards EVs in Islamabad and Rawalpindi
Amid soaring fuel prices driven by Middle East tensions and growing environmental concerns, the twin cities of Islamabad and Rawalpindi are witnessing a silent but swift shift towards electric mobility, as more and more citizens are opting for electric vehicles as a cost-effective and eco-friendly alternative to conventional fuel-run transport.
From electric bikes and scooters to cars and rickshaws, the roads of Islamabad and Rawalpindi are witnessing a visible surge in EVs, particularly among students, office-goers and delivery riders.
The trend is being driven by low running cost, low maintenance and government support for EV charging infrastructure. Several charging stations have been set up at fuel stations and in commercial areas of the twin cities.
A resident of Islamabad Sohail Tanveer who recently bought an electric bike, said, "My monthly petrol expense was around Rs12,000. Now my electricity charging cost is less than Rs1,500. It is very economical."
He said that it is easy to handle, no noise and no need to stand in queues at petrol pumps. "For students, electric scooter is the best as no petrol tension and very low maintenance noting that he charge it at home at night and use it whole day," he added.
Ride-hailing rider, Sultan said EV has doubled his savings as he used to spend half of his earning on petrol adding that with an electric bike, he save more and earn more. "EV has changed my life as a delivery rider, fuel was my biggest expense. Now my savings have almost doubled. I just charge it for 3 hours and ride 100 kilometres," he commented.
A car owner, Saba Ahmed from Rawalpindi, said she switched to an electric car for a smooth and environment-friendly drive. "There is no engine noise, no smoke and it is very comfortable for city driving," she said.
