title: Four killed in fire at Canadian military base
description: Four killed in fire at Canadian military base
content:
The Canadian government said on Sunday that a weekend fire at an Alberta military base killed at least four people and seriously injured dozens in what Prime Minister Mark Carney called one of the worst peacetime tragedies ever for Canada's armed forces on home soil.
"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost," Carney said Sunday, adding that he had ordered flags on federal buildings across the country to be lowered to half-staff to honor the victims.
CBC, the government-funded national broadcaster, previously reported seven ?deaths at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, citing unnamed sources.
Canadian authorities have said the situation continues to evolve, and that they will not confirm casualty figures until next of kin have been notified.
CFB Wainwright had 1,310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The base, one of Canada's largest, is ?about 210 km (130 miles) east of Edmonton in Alberta. National Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Sunday he would go to the city for briefings on the situation.
The base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which runs training scenarios and exercises for the army.
Carney said those affected in Saturday's fire came from military bases across the country. Few details have been released about the cause of the fire, which took place at about 4 p.m. (2200 GMT) on Saturday in a training area at the base as winds gusted up to 60 miles per hour (96 kilometers per hour).
Military and civilian firefighters fought the fire through the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable," Carney said.

title: Paris police in new battles with protesters
description: Paris police in new battles with protesters
content:
2,000 arrested nationwide during 'cost-of-living' protests
French police battled protesters and looters for a second day Sunday as the country reeled from the violent chaos left by a day of cost-of-living demonstrations in which 2,000 people were arrested nationwide.
Paris city workers had not finished clearing up the torched cars, smashed shopfronts and burnt debris from Saturday's unrest when the new troubles started and political recriminations erupted.
AFP journalists said several hundred people gathered in the Republique square in the capital following social media calls for a gathering that authorities said had not been approved.
Television footage showed the looting of a clothing store and bikes were also set alight nearby.
The Paris police prefecture said security forces moved in when "faced with the initial signs of tension".
AFP journalists saw police firing tear gas and stun grenades at hundreds of people gathered in the square. Bottles and rocks were hurled at police who made several arrests.
Some 550 people out of 855 arrested in Paris remained in detention from Saturday's troubles and police stations were struggling to cope, according to the Legal Team Paris group of lawyers.
Six months from a presidential election, the government faced opposition attacks over preparations for the nationwide day of action that followed weeks of mounting student
President Emmanuel Macron, who Saturday vowed that anyone who engaged in vandalism or looting would be prosecuted, was to address the nation Sunday evening at 1800 GMT.
Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, said the troubles showed that Macron's administration was "running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented".

title: Pope addresses crowd after cancer surgery
description: Pope addresses crowd after cancer surgery
content:
Pope Leo XIV addressed thousands of people in St Peter's Square on Sunday, smiling and saying he would resume work "gradually" in his first major public appearance since undergoing lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old pope had part of his right lung removed in the surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli hospital and he was discharged on Saturday.
"I would like to thank all the people who have been praying for me in these days," the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics told the crowd.
"Having overcome this delicate phase, as you know I will now gradually resume my activities," said the pope, who looked well and spoke normally.
A chorus of "Viva il papa!" (Hooray for the pope!) had reverberated across the square as he appeared at the window of his Apostolic Palace for his traditional Angelus prayer and address.
People in the square welcomed the pope's speedy return.
Christopher Butler, 68, a parish priest from Leeds in northern England called Leo a "great shepherd for the Catholic Church".
"I'm concerned he needs to take time to make a full recovery but he's obviously a very resilient man and keen to return to work, to lead the Church and to be a world leader," Butler said.
Soledad Espinosa, 59, from Ecuador, said she was happy to hear that the pope would be allowed by his doctors to visit Latin America next month.
"We are all hoping for his recovery and that he has gotten through the situation well. We know that he is ok and we're pleased," she said.
Norma Grasso, 76, from Argentina, said: "We are waiting for him".

title: Two killed in Saudi copter crash near Yemen border
description: Two killed in Saudi copter crash near Yemen border
content:
Authorities close major landmark in Riyadh
The Saudi-led coalition said on Sunday two crew members were killed when a helicopter crashed in the southern Najran region near the Yemeni border, while authorities in Riyadh closed major landmark to order mandatory remote working in the wake of escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has recently faced attacks on strategic infrastructure, including Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco. Amid increasing attacks, Egypt said it was prepared to consider possible military support, while Saudi and Emirati officials held talks on regional security.
The coalition attributed the AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter crash to a technical malfunction, but the Houthis claimed they had shot down a Saudi helicopter in the same area. The claims could not immediately be reconciled.
The Houthis, however, released footage that they said showed a Saudi AH-6i helicopter being struck by a missile while conducting what they described as hostile activities near Najran. The footage did not clearly establish how the helicopter had crashed.
The Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement the helicopter crashed in an area under the jurisdiction ?of the Saudi National Guard Ministry. Al-Maliki rejected Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree's X post on Saturday that the group had shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter.
Najran has been hit ?by attacks from the Houthis in recent weeks as fighting between the coalition and the Yemen-based group escalated. On Sunday six people were injured after a projectile fired by the Houthis fell on a residential area in Najran, the Saudi civil defence said.
In Riyadh, meanwhile, the management of the 99-storey Kingdom Centre skyscraper ordered all office tenants to work remotely until further notice. The landmark houses offices used by financial services giant Merrill Lynch, management consultancy McKinsey and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
"Please be advised that remote working arrangements are mandatory for all office employees at Kingdom Centre, effective immediately and until further notice," the building's management said in an email. However, the shopping mall at the foot of the building remained open.
The measure followed a Houthi attack on Riyadh's international airport a week earlier that killed 13 people, according to the AFP report. The airport remained closed, while schools had recently extended remote-learning arrangements.
The coalition also reported intercepting two drones in the Riyadh area and another over the oil-rich Eastern Province. Saudi authorities had earlier issued a threat alert in the capital, while the coalition said two ballistic missiles were intercepted in the kingdom's south.
The Houthis have also declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a strategic Red Sea chokepoint and vital route for international shipping. The disruption threatens a key trade corridor linking Asia and Europe through Egypt's Suez Canal.
Against this backdrop, Egypt moved towards a possible role in supporting Saudi Arabia's defence. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi asked parliament to authorise military assistance to the kingdom if Riyadh requested it, saying Cairo was prepared to take measures to protect its close regional partner.
The Egyptian presidency said on Sunday that Egypt was ready to provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources and territorial integrity, and safeguard Islamic holy sites.
Earlier, Sisi chaired a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council, attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief. A parliamentary vote on authorising the military support had been expected on Sunday, but local media reports said discussions would continue on Monday.
Meanwhile, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman held talks in Abu Dhabi with UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on regional developments and ways to strengthen security, according to the Emirati state news agency WAM.
The meeting followed a visit to Riyadh last month by UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the first trip by a senior Emirati official to Saudi Arabia since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year.

title: Shehbaz urges future ready education for all
description: Shehbaz urges future ready education for all
content:
PM calls on educational institutions to promote IT, robotics and artificial intelligence
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Sunday underscored the importance of preparing students for the demands of the modern world by promoting information technology, robotics, artificial intelligence and other emerging fields in educational institutions.
Addressing the inauguration ceremony of Daanish School Kuri in Islamabad, the prime minister stressed the need to ensure equal opportunities in education and healthcare for all citizens, regardless of their socioeconomic background, to realise the vision of Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah.
"No talented child should be deprived of quality education merely because of financial constraints," he said. "Pakistan cannot fully realise its founding ideals unless every child, from Karachi to Peshawar and from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to Gilgit-Baltistan, has access to quality education and healthcare."
Shehbaz said the Daanish Schools initiative aimed to provide children from underprivileged families with educational opportunities comparable to those available at the country's leading institutions, enabling them to develop their potential and contribute to national progress.
"After 80 years down the line, we must pause and honestly introspect about what we dreamt of in 1947," he remarked, questioning whether the prevailing disparities in the education system reflected the Pakistan envisioned by Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah.
The prime minister observed that affluent families could afford to send their children to prestigious educational institutions in Pakistan and abroad, while exceptionally talented children from poor families often struggled to access even basic educational facilities.
Referring to students who had overcome financial hardships to achieve academic success, he said Pakistan had countless gifted boys and girls whose abilities could help transform the country's future if they were provided with the right opportunities.
He cited the example of a specially-abled girl from K-P who had continued her education despite considerable challenges. He also highlighted the achievement of a girl from a disadvantaged area of Punjab who, after studying at a Daanish School, became a doctor and was now able to serve humanity.
Shehbaz said these achievements reinforced the vision behind establishing the Daanish Schools network in 2010, during his tenure as chief minister of Punjab, to bridge the educational divide between privileged and disadvantaged sections of society.
The initiative, he said, was intended to provide children from remote and underserved areas, including Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, with access to high-quality education and the opportunity to compete on merit with students from affluent families.
The prime minister said the Punjab Education Endowment Fund, now transformed into the Pakistan Education Endowment Fund, was also helping realise Quaid-i-Azam's vision by enabling talented students to pursue education regardless of their financial circumstances.
He expressed confidence that Daanish School graduates would not only transform their own lives through education but also contribute to Pakistan's development through their ingenuity, hard work and sustained efforts.
"I am standing before you today not merely as the prime minister of Pakistan, but as a servant of the people," he said, describing the students' stories and achievements presented at the ceremony as deeply moving and inspiring.
He stressed that every child deserved a fair chance to succeed, whether born into a wealthy family or a household struggling to meet basic needs. Expanding access to education, he added, was essential to building a more equitable society and enabling young people to play a meaningful role in the country's progress.
Earlier, the prime minister visited different sections of Daanish School Kuri, interacted with students and staff members, reviewed the educational facilities and encouraged students to pursue their ambitions despite the challenges they might face.
Federal Education Minister Dr Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui described the occasion as an important milestone in the country's education sector, reflecting a renewed focus on preparing younger generations for the future.
Chairman of the Prime Minister's Youth Programme Rana Mashhood appreciated the prime minister's initiatives, including scholarships for deserving students, the Punjab Education Endowment Fund and the Punjab Daanish Authority.
According to a briefing at the ceremony, more than 40,000 students were receiving education in Daanish Schools, while 28 schools were under construction in different parts of the country, including nine in Balochistan, six in K-P, three in Sindh, five in Azad Jammu and Kashmir and four in Gilgit-Baltistan.
Sharing their experiences at the ceremony, students Zahid Gul from Kurram and Aiman Ali Gul spoke about the financial hardships that had threatened their educational aspirations. They expressed gratitude for the opportunities provided by the Daanish Schools system, which had enabled them to continue their studies.
Daanish School graduates Amanat Ali, Ansa, Irfan Ullah, Dr Aleena and Naeem Asghar also shared their experiences, highlighting how educational opportunities had helped them overcome financial barriers and pursue their chosen careers.

title: Maldives president arrives tomorrow | The Express Tribune

content:
Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu will visit Pakistan from October 20 to 22, with the two countries set to explore wider cooperation in trade, investment, defence and maritime security as they mark 60 years of diplomatic relations, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Sunday.
"The State Visit, the first by a President of Maldives to Pakistan in eleven years, assumes special significance as the two countries commemorate the 60th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1966," the FO said in a statement shared on its X account.
Muizzu will visit Pakistan at the invitation of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, accompanied by First Lady Sajidha Mohamed and a high-level delegation
comprising cabinet ministers and senior officials, according to the statement.
During the visit, Muizzu will meet President Asif Ali Zardari, who will host a state banquet in his honour, and hold restricted and delegation-level talks with PM Shehbaz.
"The two leaders will review the entire spectrum of bilateral relations and explore avenues for further strengthening cooperation in trade, investment, health, education, tourism, agriculture, defence, maritime security, climate change and people-to-people exchanges," the statement said.
"They will also exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest," it added.
The visit will also feature a PakistanMaldives Business Forum, "aimed at promoting greater interaction between the business communities of the two countries and exploring new opportunities for trade and investment," the statement read.
A number of agreements and memorandums of understanding covering different areas of bilateral cooperation are also expected to be signed during the visit.
Highlighting the longstanding ties between the two countries, the statement said, "Pakistan and Maldives enjoy warm and fraternal relations rooted in shared faith, mutual respect, longstanding goodwill and close cooperation at regional and international forums."
"The forthcoming visit reflects the shared commitment of both countries to further strengthening their bilateral partnership and opening new avenues of mutually beneficial cooperation," the statement concluded.
The Speaker of the Maldives' People's Majlis, Abdul Raheem Abdullah, also visited Pakistan for five days in September at the invitation of National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq. During the visit, the two sides agreed to strengthen parliamentary cooperation and people-to-people contacts.
Abdullah praised Pakistan's "clear and consistent" stance on Palestine and Kashmir and reaffirmed the Maldives' commitment to expanding legislative and institutional cooperation with Islamabad.

title: Bilawal says dialogue can end K P emergency
description: Bilawal says dialogue can end K P emergency
content:
PPP chairman asks opp to engage with Centre Says PPP working on new National Action Plan JUI-F chief can help br
Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) Chairman Bilawal Bhutto Zardari on Sunday defended the imposition of governor's rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) and urged the opposition parties to engage with the federal government if they want the emergency arrangements to end.
Speaking to the media after visiting the Karsaz tragedy memorial with First Lady Aseefa Bhutto Zardari, Bilawal said eliminating terrorism was the mission of Shaheed Benazir Bhutto. He added that the PPP was working towards a new National Action Plan (NAP) and a fresh national consensus against terrorism.
The two laid flowers at the memorial and offered Fateha for those killed in the October 18, 2007, attack that Bilawal described as one of the worst terrorist attacks in Pakistan's history. He paid tribute to the armed forces, police and civilians targeted by terrorists.
Bilawal said the PPP-led federal government launched operations against terrorists in Swat and other parts of K-P after coming to power in 2008. He said Pakistan had defeated terrorists after enormous sacrifices, but the decision to allow terrorists from Afghanistan to settle in the former tribal areas reversed those gains.
"Today, Pakistan is paying the price for those wrong decisions. We have once again reached a point where certain forces want to remove Pakistan's flag from Swat," he said, adding that terrorist attacks were taking place across the country, from Khyber to Khuzdar.
Criticising K-P Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, Bilawal called him a "coward" for refusing to confront terrorists and defend his province. "The PPP was prepared to fight terrorism if the provincial leadership was unwilling to do so," he said, adding that the PPP had supported the Centre's decision to impose the governor's rule.
Bilawal maintained that the PPP had always imposed emergencies in accordance with the Constitution and the law. He cited the imposition of governor's rule in Balochistan during the party's 2008-2013 government, arguing that the PPP had acted against its own provincial government because of the security situation.
He urged all political parties not to politicise terrorism or make counterterrorism measures controversial.
Referring to Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, Bilawal said the opposition leader had every right to criticise the government but should also openly condemn terrorist attacks, noting that members of his own party had been killed in such incidents.
"If they want the emergency arrangements and governor's rule in K-P to end, they should engage with the federal government," Bilawal said, adding that Fazl could help bridge differences between the government and opposition.
Turning to the economy, Bilawal said Pakistan was facing a historic economic crisis and warned that conditions appeared likely to worsen. He said the country needed collective efforts to address economic hardship, combat terrorism and improve the electoral system.
The PPP, he added, was working towards a new National Action Plan (NAP) and a fresh national consensus against terrorism. He also welcomed the federal government's agreement to establish an electoral reforms committee and invited opposition parties to participate in its work.
Bilawal said the PPP government from 2008 to 2013 had focused on employment, economic difficulties and terrorism, reflecting the priorities associated with Benazir Bhutto's political legacy. He said her assassination had placed an even greater responsibility on the party to pursue those objectives.
On the creation of new provinces, Bilawal said Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi was aware of the PPP's position and that of President Asif Ali Zardari. He stressed that new provinces could be created through constitutional and legal procedures, with the president's signature required for the process.
"If this is not merely a political stunt, why are provinces not being created where there is consensus?" he asked, citing Gilgit-Baltistan as an example where he said consensus existed.
Bilawal also defended political reconciliation, saying compromise was an essential part of democratic politics. He recalled that Benazir Bhutto had prioritised the country, the people and party workers over personal interests, making compromises when necessary. He said the 18th Constitutional Amendment had likewise been achieved through negotiations and consensus among political stakeholders.
Asked about K-P Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, Bilawal said the PPP had nominated him for the post, but he was now constitutionally a representative of the federal government. He added that he would continue speaking to Kundi and offering advice while recognising his present responsibilities.
Bilawal said the PPP was continuing its struggle to realise Benazir Bhutto's vision of a Pakistan that could address economic hardship, provide employment, strengthen democracy and defeat terrorism.
PPP Sindh President Nisar Ahmed Khuhro, Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah, provincial ministers, lawmakers, local government representatives, party office-bearers and workers were also present at the memorial.

title: Eight terrorists killed in Balochistan
description: Eight terrorists killed in Balochistan
content:
Security forces killed eight terrorists belonging to the Indian proxy, Fitna al-Hindustan, in three intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan and recovered 490 kilogrammes of explosives, the military's media wing said on Sunday.
According to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), on October 17, security forces conducted three IBOs in Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts of Balochistan, on the reported presence of terrorists belonging to the Indian proxy, Fitna al-Hindustan.
The federal government last year officially designated all terrorist groups operating in Balochistan as Fitna al-Hindustan, accusing India of sponsoring a proxy war through the outfits.
In Quetta's Panjpai area, security forces intercepted an attempt by terrorists to establish a roadblock to disrupt local traffic, resulting in the killing of five Indian sponsored terrorists, the ISPR said.

In a separate intelligence-based operation in Khuzdar, security forces engaged a terrorist hideout and killed one Indian-sponsored terrorist, according to the statement. A large quantity of explosives, weighing 490 kilogrammes, was also recovered.
The ISPR said sanitisation operations were underway to eliminate any other Indian-sponsored terrorists found in the areas.
"Relentless counter terrorism campaign under vision "Azm-e-Istehkam" (as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country," the statement concluded.
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif lauded the security forces for successfully eliminating eight India-sponsored terrorists during three separate IBOs in Quetta, Naushki and Khuzdar.
The president reiterated that the conspiracies hatched by terrorists' foreign patrons and their local facilitators would be decisively thwarted.

title: PTI panel to probe long march failure
description: Most participants point to inadequate preparations  poor coordination  a lack of consultation
content:
Most participants point to inadequate preparations, poor coordination, a lack of consultation
The PTI core and political committees on Sunday constituted a fact-finding committee to investigate the long march's failure, with several participants reportedly holding suspended Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi responsible for shortcomings in its arrangements.
According to sources, the committees also discussed assigning Barrister Muhammad Ali Saif responsibility for matters relating to access to jailed PTI founder Imran Khan.
Some participants also called for giving party members responsibilities currently held by Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas. Achakzai and Abbas respectively serve as the leaders of opposition in the National Assembly and the Senate.
The meeting of the PTI core and political committees was held following the removal of the party's provincial government in K-P on October 11 to review the imposition of governor's rule and the emergency situation in K-P and discuss the party's future strategy.
The PTI announced holding a long march to Islamabad on September 27. The party later deferred the march until October 4, prior to which the federal government and the PTI held a long session of talks.
The federal government on October 11 announced imposing emergency in the province citing the rising incidents of terrorism in K-P and the provincial government's alleged failure to deal with the menace.
Sources said the Sunday meeting saw an extensive discussion on the long march, with most participants pointing to inadequate preparations, poor coordination and a lack of consultation with party leaders and members of the provincial assembly.
PTI Secretary-General Salman Akram Raja reportedly told the meeting that participation in the march was particularly low in Charsadda and Mardan. He also highlighted inadequate arrangements for overnight stays, noting that tents and other essential preparations had not been made.
According to sources, several participants consequently blamed Afridi for the shortcomings in organising the march. Raja, however, later defended Afridi, describing him as a courageous young leader committed to Imran Khan's ideology.
He said a critical review of the march's organisational arrangements was necessary but warned against presenting core committee discussions out of context to advance what he described as conspiratorial narratives against Afridi.
Some participants reportedly argued that the activity had effectively become a street movement rather than a properly organised long march, lacking clearly defined points of advance, logistical arrangements or strategy.

title: Lahore park set to open giraffe caf
description: Lahore park set to open giraffe caf
content:
Pakistan's first giraffe café has been established at Lahore Safari Park, offering visitors the opportunity to feed giraffes by hand and enjoy tea or coffee in close proximity to the animals. Designed around a wildlife theme, the café is part of the park's revamping project. According to the administration, preparations are under way to open the facility to the public soon.
Zainab Ali, a member of a family visiting the safari park, said sitting near giraffes, drinking coffee and feeding the animals by hand would be a unique experience. She expressed the hope that the café would open soon so visitors could benefit from the new facility.
Another visitor, Abdul Rehman, said he had toured the giraffe enclosure in an electric vehicle. He described the experience as feeling like being in an African forest. He said he was looking forward to feeding the giraffes by hand and enjoying tea in the wildlife-themed setting.
Lahore Safari Park currently houses 10 giraffes, including two males and eight females. The animals were brought to Pakistan from South Africa in September 2025. Special rooms and enclosures have been built to accommodate them, with round-the-clock monitoring to ensure their well-being. The temperature in their housing blocks is maintained at 25 degrees Celsius because giraffes cannot tolerate excessive heat.
According to Dr Warda Gul, a veterinary officer at Lahore Safari Zoo, giraffes are social animals that prefer to live in groups. They can gradually adapt to their surroundings and become accustomed to human presence.
She said the animals were provided with a balanced diet comprising green fodder, minerals and other essential nutrients. Giraffes also enjoy feeding on leaves from tree branches.
Dr Gul said the growth and development of all the giraffes at the park were satisfactory, with their height increasing rapidly. The administration hopes that the animals may eventually breed at the facility. If successful, this would mark an important development for giraffe breeding in Pakistan.

title: SC allows appeals without jail surrender
description: SC allows appeals without jail surrender
content:
Ex-MNA Jamshed Dasti granted protective bail; arrest barred
The Supreme Court has made it clear that a convict's petition could be entertained without their surrender before the police or jail authorities.
A division bench led by Justice Malik Shahzad Ahmad Khan, referring to the proviso to Rule 8 of Order XXIV of the Supreme Court Rules, 2025, noted that if a convict surrenders before the court, then the court may entertain his petition/application/appeal without requiring surrender to the police/jail authorities.
"Therefore, it is held that under the amended Supreme Court Rules 2025, it is for the court to decide that as to whether the surrender of the petitioner/applicant/appellant before the Court is sufficient or he has to be sent to the jail in compliance of the orders/judgments of his imprisonment," said the order issued in matter related to ex-MNA Jamshed Dasti who is facing dozens of criminal cases.
It further clarified that in the future, such petitions/applications/appeals filed by the convicts against their convictions shall be numbered and directly placed before the court. The bench subsequently overruled objections raised by the SC registrar office on November 18, 2025, regarding Dasti's petition.
It directed that, upon request by the petitioners/appellants/their advocate on records (AORs) or their counsels in such like cases, the registrar office shall fix the case before the court on the same day or on any date noted by the petitioners/appellants/their counsels or AOR, along with any office objections.
Subsequently, the bench granted protective bail to Dasti. It also sought details from Punjab government related to registration of total cases against him in the province. The court also directed the police departments not to arrest Dasti till next date of hearing. The court adjourned hearing of case till Oct 22.

title: Prison term should reflect  crime s gravity
description: Prison term should reflect  crime s gravity
content:
Punjab urges SC to discourage concurrent sentences
The Punjab prosecution department has told the Supreme Court that sentences should not routinely run concurrently in every criminal case, including cases involving multiple murders.
It has argued that consecutive sentences should be imposed in exceptional cases involving extremely brutal, inhuman and heinous crimes that shock the public conscience, particularly murder, kidnapping, sexual assault and terrorism.
In a written response submitted through Punjab Additional Prosecutor General Tariq Siddique, the provincial government argued that consecutive sentences for multiple murders would reflect the gravity of each offence, reinforce public confidence in the criminal justice system and serve the deterrent and retributive purposes of punishment.
A seven-member larger bench, headed by Justice Jamal Khan Mandokhail, is examining two questions: whether a person convicted of multiple murders should serve life sentences concurrently or consecutively, and how the term of life imprisonment should be determined under Pakistani law.
The next hearing is scheduled for November 10.
The Punjab government maintained that courts should issue reasoned and explicit orders when directing sentences to run consecutively, particularly in exceptional cases involving crimes committed in an exceptionally cruel, barbaric or inhuman manner.
Referring to Section 4 of the Punjab Sentencing Act, 2019, the written response said the objectives of sentencing included punishing offenders, preventing and reducing crime, deterring criminal conduct, rehabilitating offenders and protecting the public.
The government argued that automatically ordering concurrent sentences in cases involving multiple victims could diminish the seriousness of additional offences and create an artificial equivalence between killing one person and murdering several.
"If courts continue to order different sentences to run concurrently in an unguarded and casual manner, a message will be conveyed to society that our criminal justice system makes no distinction between the murder of one person and the murder of several persons," the response stated.
It added that every unlawful taking of a human life should attract a distinct and meaningful legal consequence. Merging multiple sentences into a single concurrent term, the government argued, could undermine the gravity of additional murders.
The response also raised concerns about the practical duration of life imprisonment in Pakistan. It stated that, after accounting for government remissions and sentence reductions, a life sentence could effectively be reduced to around 15 years.

title: Western brands feel the pinch amid Chinese economic crunch
description: Western brands feel the pinch amid Chinese economic crunch
content:
China's consumers turn to second-hand market to save money, causing sharp downturns in sales for global fashion brand
With China's economy still struggling to recover from the pandemic, even global fashion icons are beginning to feel the pinch as consumers turn instead to the second-hand market or buy upstart new homegrown brands.
Chinese were once massive buyers of luxury Western brands, accounting for around a third of worldwide spending and earning firms such as LVMH and Hermes billions of dollars.
But consumers' belt-tightening has forced them to rethink their strategies, with Louis Vuitton closing five stores in mainland China in the past two years -- including a chocolate boutique in Shanghai -- while Galeries Lafayette shut its Beijing flagship in May.
"People used to compare who had spent more," dance teacher Yuan told AFP at a new retail space in central Shanghai filled with luxury handbags, belts and jewellery items -- all second hand.
"But now everyone compares who got a better deal and spent less," the 24-year-old said at the two-storey warehouse-style store in the centre of the Chinese financial hub.
After plunging as much as 19 percent in 2024, mainland China's personal luxury market contracted another three to five percent in 2025, according to consultancy Bain & Company.
LVMH recently blamed a "slowdown in demand in China" for a drop in organic sales in the third quarter in its fashion and leather goods unit, a slump expected to be mirrored in its peers' results.
China's second-hand luxury market meanwhile exploded 15-20 percent in 2025, according to Bain & Company.
And domestic industry consultancy Insight & Info Consulting estimates total sales reached 38.4 billion yuan ($5.7 billion) in 2025, while forecasting it could top 100 billion yuan by 2030.
At the new Shanghai store Super Zhuanzhuan, shoppers have to wear black gloves to avoid their greasy fingers touching the products.
Customer Phoebe Ma, 24, said that when her mother's generation was young, China "wasn't so developed" and people were initially familiar with only a handful of luxury brands.
"Consequently, they formed a deep-seated impression that, OK, Louis Vuitton was the absolute best and most prestigious," the freelancer told AFP.
"I just feel that the [LV] monogram is dated. It suits my mother's generation, but Gen Z would rather buy trendy Korean brands," she said.
Chen Luo, head of China consumer research at Bank of America, said shoppers were moving away from associating luxury solely with social status and towards "self-identity, distinction, experience, quality, emotional value (and) cultural relevance".
"Apart from that, China's retail landscape is very digital/social media driven, and China's digital ecosystem is also very unique," Luo told AFP. "Foreign brands should work very hard to stay relevant in this context."
Adding to the headwinds for Western brands is growing cultural and legal friction.
LVMH recently successfully sued Chinese beverage chain Molly Tea for trademark infringement over a four-petal floral pattern resembling the French firm's monogram.
But the lawsuit sparked an online backlash after Chinese internet users and state media pointed out that the motif shares roots with ancient Chinese traditional patterns.
"It feels a bit absurd," said shopper Echo Wang, 31, who works in marketing.
"Molly Tea may be doing well in China, but it's nowhere near Louis Vuitton's global profile... I think some people feel the lawsuit was inappropriate," she told AFP.
LVMH management called its intellectual property "an absolute key asset", but admitted the furore had "had a negative impact".
Analysts emphasise that China remains vital for the global luxury industry.
"In our view, China will still be an important market, although it may not be a growth engine in two to three years," said Luo.
"Luxury spending is normally rebounding in sync with the economy, as usually the wealthy class will be among the first to benefit from economic recovery."

title: Hollywood turns tech heroes into villains | The Express Tribune
description:
Hollywood turns tech 
heroes into villains
content:
In departure from past, Tinseltown is now portraying Silicon Valley icons like Elon Musk and Sam Altman in a more crit
Hollywood has found its new favorite villain: the onetime heroes of Silicon Valley.
From convicted biotech fraudster Elizabeth Holmes to tech giants Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman, the marquees are dominated by the headline makers who have wowed the world -- and the markets -- with promises of innovation.
"These figures used to be more on the aspirational side," Monica Castillo, the film critic for the pop culture website The A.V. Club, told AFP.
"They were larger-than-life figures who bootstrapped their way to multibillion dollar companies, and they were kind of seen as heroes who were like changing the world," Castillo said.
"Then now... there's sort of a level of disillusionment."
Castillo said the world is now asking "harder questions" of its tech heroes, adding: "There's a little bit more reflection because of what's happened with this generation."
Silicon Valley was once seen as a breeding ground for progressive-minded entrepreneurs, their politics running in parallel with their innovative solutions.
But lately, many of the industry's A-listers have switched allegiance to US President Donald Trump and his "America First" policies.
"Musk," Alex Gibney's searing four-hour documentary about the world's richest man, dissects the career of the South Africa-born head of SpaceX and Tesla, from his beginnings as a tech genius to his alliance with Trump and the Republican Party.
Also in theaters is "The Social Reckoning," Aaron Sorkin's follow-up to his Oscar-winning 2010 film "The Social Network."
This time around, rather than trace the meteoric rise of the Facebook wunderkind, writer-director Sorkin tells the story of company whistleblower Frances Haugen (Oscar winner Mikey Madison) and how she revealed some of its more nefarious practices.
One of those was how its algorithms amplified hate speech by keeping users on the platform for as long as possible, and the dramatic consequences of that decision.
The films highlight how Musk and Zuckerberg amassed so much power that they were affecting US government policy, and how that reverberated around the world.
No one is seen with a more skeptical and critical eye in Big Tech than Holmes, who once upended the biotechnology sector with Theranos, which pledged that it could perform a host of medical tests using only a few drops of blood.
But the now-defunct company couldn't deliver, Holmes was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison for fraud and conspiracy, and her fall from grace is chronicled in the buzzy documentary "You Can See Everything."
Holmes unexpectedly opened her home to co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim in the 34 days before heading to a Texas prison in a bid to tell her story in her own words. They eventually moved in.
The result -- a strange mix of documentary and reality television -- is earning serious Oscars buzz.
Back on the fiction side, Italian director Luca Guadagnino's "Artificial" stars Andrew Garfield as OpenAI chief Altman, who changed the world with his generative artificial intelligence tool ChatGPT.
Matt Neglia, the editor in chief of the weekly audio and video show Next Best Picture, called the film "as entertaining as it is terrifying."
"It's a brilliantly written human story about power, control, ambition and greed that might be the most urgently relevant film of our time," Neglia said.
For J.M. Tyree, a professor of cinema at Virginia Commonwealth University and the editor in chief of Film Quarterly, "popular movies always are reflecting these social anxieties of the day."
"Right now, people are really worried about power being concentrated into the hands of just a few individuals at the expense of most of the rest of the citizens," Tyree told AFP.
People have lost faith in "zillionaire tech moguls," and are starting to see their flaws, he added.
"That's maybe a common thread of these films, is that they're not just holding wealth for themselves, but also their products don't seem to be very good for society," Tyree said.
This group of films attempts to showcase the tech titan, not their products.
Castillo says the directors appear to be seeking "some sort of accountability for all the damage" that these tech titans have wrought on society.
"The only way that they can punch back is through their movies," she said.

title: Solar is our saviour  capacity charge our drain
description: Solar is our saviour  capacity charge our drain
content:
Around $40b paid in capacity charges since 2019; pro-seller PPAs need renegotiation
Pakistan's power sector has been in crisis since 2004, when oil prices spiked by around 56% in a single year. The trend continued until 2008, when prices peaked at almost five times of their initial value in 2004. The country was then heavily dependent upon furnace oil for power generation. As a result, between 2004 and 2008, the annual energy import bill of Pakistan increased by around 2.5 times.
The government attempted to accommodate the impact on the power supply chain through subsidies. But the lack of required fiscal depth and the consequential delayed payments towards the independent power producers (IPPs) resulted in an acute crunch of working capital. This in turn gave birth to the venomous serpent we all know by the name of circular debt. The same pushed the country into the worst power crisis it has ever seen.
The new government in 2013, driven by highly ambitious growth targets and corresponding requirements of power on the grid, launched a new power policy and a massive plan for generation capacity augmentation. Consumption increased promisingly during the period but not as rapidly as capacity. The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra)'s State of the Industry report of 2017 aptly forewarned about the fast-emerging monster of capacity charge due to the increasing gap between generation capacity and consumption.
As per the report, the capacity payments made in FY2015-16 and FY2016-17 were, respectively, Rs280 billion and Rs350 billion. In the same paragraph, it also tells us that for the value to remain at that of FY2015-16 in FY2018-19, the power sold was required to be 57% higher than its preceding year, ie 2017-18. However, the actual gain was even less than 2%.
Unfortunately, since 2019 till 2026, GDP growth has generally remained sluggish. The same in turn has continued to further increase the ratio of the capacity charge in the payments to the sellers. As a result, we have already paid around $40 billion in this respect during the period. This could, of course, have been largely avoided by incorporating informed and stringent qualifiers, for situations triggering capacity payments, in the "take or pay" clauses of the power purchase agreements (PPAs).
A major catalyst was the introduction of the Net Metering Regulations in September 2015, associated with solar power. Due to the economic benefits it offered, it virtually caused an exodus of users from the grid. For example, industrial power consumption from the grid was 29,885 gigawatt hours (GWh) in FY2020-21 and 29,114 GWh by 2024-25, despite a 7.5% increment in users in this category on the DISCO grid during the period.
To me, the magnitude of the impact solar ingress has caused in our economy is that out of its aggregate installed solar capacity, hardly 13% is integrated with the grid. After applying the commonly used capacity utilisation factor in the range of 18% to 22%, the estimated maximum net capacity of the off-grid system alone comes out to be above 10,000MW. The utilisation factor is primarily a function of a solar panel's efficiency, its exposure to sunlight hours and associated irradiance in each such hour. The above deduced capacity is already 42% of the average power demand which prevails on our grid in summers. Solar batteries are also improving this off-grid capacity further by keeping the power available from the same source even after sunset.
While the above transformation continues along with the augmentation of installed grid capacity, the utility bills of those on the grid continue to balloon with the impact of the increasing capacity charge. Yet the tariff structure still largely operates in the mode of power scarcity by charging higher per unit for higher consumption. Otherwise, widespread use of electricity for domestic and commercial cooking and heating may help a lot in this regard. Additionally, even partial diversion of the pertaining gas to industry can also reduce imports of expensive liquefied natural gas (LNG).
A highly encouraging development, though initiated under International Monetary Fund (IMF) pressure, is the effort which is under way since early last year to eliminate captive power and divert the associated load to the grid. This would, of course, also result in sparing around 280 million standard cubic feet per day (mmscfd) of processed gas for more efficient applications. Available data for the past fiscal year also indicates the effort is on the right track. However, its long-term success is largely conditional on the dependability of power supply to industrial units as per their stringent operational requirements.
The above measures can definitely go a long way in increasing the consumption of the grid's load and minimising capacity charge. However, I apprehend that the recent introduction of net-billing may not prove to be of much use. The fact that purchase of solar batteries in FY2025-26 increased by around 2.5 times compared with the preceding year rather indicates that even those partially on the grid now may soon be 100% off-grid.
This trend of opting for alternative avenues is visible in energy uses other than electricity too. For example, as per the Energy Yearbook 2025, the aggregate conventionally documented consumption of energy by the industrial sector experienced marked reduction of around 46% since 2020 till 2025. Solar ingress is not the only factor accounting for the entire gap. Higher utility costs have compelled industry to adopt alternative fuels like coal and wood too. As per a recent study, coal contributes 20% of the textile sector's energy mix. No wonder use of solid fuel boilers has increased considerably in recent years.
Similarly, the Energy Yearbook reports decline of 58% by volume in the use of coal since 2021 till 2025 in the brick-kilns industry. Probably, to accommodate economic factors, it is being used together with crop residues and in some cases even fuels like used tyres, lube oil, plastic and textile waste.
Based on the above, it is evident that we should be very cautious while intervening in solarisation. It has proven to be the biggest saviour for our economy. In addition to its contribution in savings in energy imports, the GDP it is annually shouldering is many times more. Secondly, the perennially open drain on the economy called capacity charge continues to widen. Therefore, there is a clear and urgent requirement for renegotiating the evidently pro-sellers' power purchase agreements and bringing the required balance to them.
Thirdly, we need to keep an eye on the changes in our energy fabric in the context of our carbon footprint and commitments to the United Nations regarding reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
THE WRITER IS A PETROLEUM ENGINEER AND AN OIL AND GAS MANAGEMENT PROFESSIONAL

title: Hidden cost of street politics
description: Hidden cost of street politics
content:
When protest stretches over a week, cumulative shock shaves 0.2-0.5% off GDP
At dawn on a weekday that should have hummed with commerce, the GT Road and Motorway stand frozen. Multi-ton shipping containers, requisitioned overnight by relevant authorities and dropped onto thoroughfares like giant iron dominoes, choke the entry arteries to Islamabad. Barbed wire glints under streetlights, police vans idle with tear-gas launchers primed, and millions of workers across the urban corridor wake to severed cellular data networks and shuttered transit terminals.
This is the recurring anatomy of modern political agitation; the "Long March." Once conceived as a symbolic pilgrimage to air public grievances, the long march has mutated into an instrument of economic leverage. In contemporary power struggles, leverage is measured not merely by headcounts or speeches, but by the magnitude of paralysis an opposition can force, and the level of economic bleeding a government can endure before conceding ground.
Yet behind the rhetoric of constitutional rights and state sovereignty lies an unyielding ledger. In an economy operating on razor-thin fiscal margins, every day of political blockade, shuttered bazaar, and halted supply chain extracts an irreversible toll, one that strikes hardest not at the political elite negotiating in fortified compounds, but at the daily-wage labourer whose dinner depends on a single day's physical toil.
When national arteries are severed, the macroeconomic damage is immediate, severe, and compounding. According to official estimates compiled by the Ministry of Finance and economic research think tanks, a single day of nationwide disruption, strikes, and capital-bound long marches drains approximately Rs120 billion from national output.
A breakdown of this daily drain illustrates how comprehensively a modern strike metastasizes across sectors:
The services collapse (Rs86 billion/day): Wholesale trade, retail markets, banking clearing houses, urban transport and hospitality absorb over 70% of total output losses. When shopping districts lock their shutters and urban logistics freeze, transactions cannot simply be postponed; many vanish entirely. Industrial paralysis (Rs25 billion/day): Large-scale manufacturing plants grind to a halt as shifts fail to report, export consignments miss feeder vessels at regional ports and raw materials remain stranded inside locked transit corridors.
Agricultural wastage (Rs9 billion/day): Perishable agricultural goods – milk, vegetables, poultry and fresh fruit – rot in stranded trucks along provincial highways, inflicting direct capital losses on farmers and sparking localised food inflation in besieged urban centres.
Fiscal haemorrhage (Rs17 billion/day in lost revenue): The state exchequer suffers a direct blow in missed customs tariffs, sales taxes and withholding receipts. Concurrently, the state burns public funds on tear gas munitions, logistical support and security deployments costing upward of Rs5 to Rs10 billion per threat cycle.
When a march or sit-in stretches over a week or recurs across a volatile quarter, the cumulative shock shaves between 0.2% and 0.5% off the annual real GDP. For Pakistan, striving to transition from emergency stabilisation to sustainable growth under tight multilateral debt covenants, such losses are catastrophic. They wipe out fiscal headroom, suppress quarterly revenue targets and undermine sovereign credit ratings.
The contemporary fallout of street agitation extends far beyond blocked asphalt. In a bid to restrict coordination and quell unrest, authorities routinely deploy blanket mobile internet suspensions and bandwidth throttling. While state managers treat the digital "kill switch" as a low-cost security lever, the modern economy treats it as an unmitigated disaster. Over the past five years, freelance digital services, business process outsourcing (BPO) and software exports have emerged as rare bright spots for foreign exchange earnings.
Industry data indicates that prolonged connectivity disruptions during protest cycles cause software house billings and digital services exports to plunge by as much as 80% during outage windows. Global enterprise clients, operating on rigid Service Level Agreements (SLAs), do not accommodate geopolitical friction; an unrendered software patch or missed offshore support shift leads to cancelled retainers and blacklisted vendors. Similarly, physical exporters face prohibitive penalties. Textile mills, the backbone of export receipts, operate on unforgiving fashion calendar cycles. Stranded containers mean missed shipping windows, forcing manufacturers to charter emergency airfreight at five to eight times standard ocean transit costs, or face outright cancellation of seasonal purchase orders. Foreign buyers, observing chronic instability, quietly reallocate future supply chains to more predictable regional competitors in Vietnam, Bangladesh and India.
While macro figures outline national erosion, the human crisis plays out on the sidewalks. The most perverse reality of the protest economy is its regressive incidence: those who hold no stake in the political contest pay the highest price. In Pakistan's sprawling urban centres, between 70% and 80% of the non-agricultural labour force works within the informal economy. These are the pushcart vendors, port porters, auto-rickshaw drivers, construction day-labourers and loading dock coolies. They do not have remote-work contingencies, severance packages or salaried bank deposits. They live in a cash-in-hand ecosystem where missing a single shift means an empty cooking pot at night.
Beyond immediate transaction loss, repeated long marches inflict deep structural damage on the psychology of capital. Domestic businesses scale back capital expenditure, choosing cash preservation over modernisation or hiring. For foreign direct investors, predictable rule of law and unhindered movement of goods are non-negotiable prerequisites. When international headlines repeatedly broadcast images of capital encircled by freight containers, commercial confidence dissolves. Corporate planning horizons shrink from five-year capital deployments to 90-day survival tactics. The economy falls into a low-level equilibrium trap: investment stalls, job creation collapses, underemployment deepens and the resulting economic discontent fuels the very popular unrest that leaders mobilise for the next round of protests.
The right to peaceful assembly and free political expression is an indispensable pillar of any functioning democracy. No state can suppress political contestation without sliding into authoritarianism. Conversely, no fragile economy can survive a paradigm where every political disagreement is settled by weaponising public mobility and taking urban commerce hostage. Breaking this destructive feedback loop requires structural reform from both the political class and state managers. Following may be considered in this context.
First, to earmark the designated protest enclaves. Modern democracies channel large-scale demonstrations into dedicated rally grounds equipped with civic facilities, outside critical transit and commercial corridors. The politics of claiming "D-Chowk" or central business arteries must be replaced by structured conventions that allow political display without crippling logistics.
Second, ending the "Container Doctrine". Law enforcement's reflex to immobilise entire provinces with freight blockades and blanket telecommunications shutdowns often causes more economic damage than the marches themselves. Proportional policing, intelligence-led crowd management and targeted security must replace systemic paralysis. Third, institutionalising an Economic Red Line. Political actors must establish a cross-party "Charter of the Economy" – a formal consensus that critical infrastructure, digital connectivity, export supply chains and the livelihoods of informal labourers remain off-limits from partisan warfare.
When political movements measure their strength by how deeply they can paralyse a nation's pulse, victory is an illusion. The state loses revenue, businesses shed markets and democracy loses moral authority. But above all, it is the daily-wage worker, walking miles past cold shipping containers to an empty market, who quietly pays the ransom for political power.

title: A US bond shock will reach Pakistan s doorstep
description: A US bond shock will reach Pakistan s doorstep
content:
Oil is the largest risk, bonds are amplifiers; Islamabad's best defence is to protect reserves
Heavy borrowing to build AI infrastructure, and an oil price that has surged since the Iran war began, have created a shock in the US bond markets that has raised US long-term borrowing costs to levels not seen in almost two decades. The Trump administration's attempts to cap them, including expanded buybacks of long-dated debt and coordinated yen support with Japan, have failed to turn yields lower.
Brent crude, around $70 a barrel in early July, has since climbed above $110. The Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan have all raised rates this summer. Because US yields anchor bond markets everywhere, the effects travel, though unevenly. Economies closely tied to America, or with fragile external finances, feel them most. Pakistan, an importer of both energy and capital, belongs to the second group.
However, this is not a sign of global recession fuelled by the Gulf crisis. The combined trade surplus of China, South Korea and Taiwan alone in September was a staggering $200 billion. What has changed is that this money is not flowing into the US bond market. The US needs the massive East Asian surplus to fund its deficit, but the surplus is landing in US equities instead. This phenomenon is known as de-reservification, where sovereign countries move dollars from traditional reserves to pension funds, banks and other investment funds.
Apparently, the dollar's role globally, and particularly in Asia, is increasingly driven by returns rather than safety. For Pakistan, higher yields matter less than what is driving them. The country sources roughly 90% of its energy from abroad, so every move in crude passes quickly into petrol, diesel, power tariffs, transport and food.
This year has already shown how fast it works. Domestic fuel prices were raised about 20% in early March as the conflict escalated. Headline inflation then rose from 7.3% in March to 10.9% in April and 11.1% in August, driven by energy, transport costs and food. Hence, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) raised its policy rate by 100 basis points to 11.5% in April and has held it there since, including at its September meeting. Officials have told the International Monetary Fund (IMF) that even with oil near $95, average inflation this fiscal year could stay below 9%, keeping real rates comfortably positive, but only if oil holds near $100. With Brent now above that level, the projection is being tested. A heavier fuel bill also eats into an import budget of roughly $69 billion to $70 billion, leaving less room for the machinery and raw materials that exporters need.
This removes the option of easing in the near future. That matters for the government, whose interest bill already absorbs a large share of the budget, and for businesses that need affordable credit to expand. It also complicates the official goal of 4% growth, after 3.7% in the last fiscal year. Despite that, Pakistan must keep borrowing abroad. It recently raised $3 billion through a Eurobond, a sign that market access has returned. But as US yields rise, investors demand wider spreads on frontier credits, so the next issuance, rollover or commercial loan will cost more. Capital also tends to drift towards the safety of dollar assets in such episodes, putting pressure on the rupee.
That pressure arrives at a delicate moment. Islamabad and the IMF remain divided over exchange-rate policy. The Fund wants a more market-determined rupee, while the government argues that stability contains imported inflation. Moreover, Pakistan is not entering this shock empty-handed. Reserves have been rebuilt, the current account has stayed relatively contained, and successive IMF reviews have unlocked official inflows. Dollar remittances stretch further when the rupee weakens, and domestic bond yields respond mostly to local inflation and SBP policy, so the pass-through from Washington is partial rather than automatic escalation.
Three priorities stand out. Firstly, continue to pass through fuel prices honestly and shield the poorest with targeted support rather than blanket subsidies, which would jeopardise fiscal targets the IMF is watching. Secondly, allow the rupee reasonable flexibility instead of burning reserves to hold a line the market doubts. Thirdly, use calm windows to lock in longer-dated financing and accelerate energy substitution, from solar to domestic gas and efficiency, because every dollar of avoided oil imports is also a dollar of avoided exposure to global rates.
Pakistan's recovery is intact but newly fragile. The sell-off in US Treasuries, which has pushed 30-year yields to a 19-year high of 5.36%, will make dollars costlier, narrow SBP's room to manoeuvre and raise the price of fuel that Pakistan cannot produce itself. Oil is the largest risk. The bond market is the amplifier. Islamabad's best defence is to protect reserves, avoid spending them on an unsustainable rupee, and use the breathing room it has to cut its dependence on imported energy. If oil falls and yields stabilise, Pakistan's recovery stays on track. If both keep climbing into 2027, just as large external repayments fall due, the margin for error will shrink quickly.
THE WRITER IS A CAMBRIDGE GRADUATE AND WORKS AS A STRATEGY CONSULTANT

title: Customs duty is not the barrier  GST is
description: Customs duty is not the barrier  GST is
content:
Industry admits 18% GST, not tariffs, hands the informal sector its edge, as import-based revenue falls below 40%
The National Tariff Policy 2025-30 has remained in the news for the right reasons recently, and it is time to offer a provisional assessment in the light of recent data. The good news first: the policy is working.
One of the underlying objectives of the policy was to stop treating customs tariff as a source of revenue and start treating it as a tool of industrial policy – to provide signals to industry and consumers. One year of experience indicates that the policy is succeeding, as the contribution of import-based revenue has come down from above 50% of overall tax revenue to less than 40%. This has happened despite an increase in import volume and customs revenue, while overall tariffs have gone down – exactly as the research had predicted.
Now the more difficult question is the impact of the tariff policy on industrial output, competitiveness and the overall trade balance. It is too early to comment on a policy that is designed for five years. However, some trends can be observed without necessarily establishing causal relationships. During the first quarter of fiscal year 2026-27 (1QFY27), Pakistan's provisional total goods exports reached $8.42 billion. This marks a 10.84% year-on-year growth compared with $7.59 billion during the first quarter of fiscal year 2025-26 (1QFY26). Agriculture and food rose by 23%, manufacturing, mining and energy by 17%, and textiles and apparel by 6%. This is broadly aligned with the goal of 14% growth due to tariff reforms by 2030.
However, there are strong headwinds against the National Tariff Policy. Pakistan's tariff debate is often framed as a choice between protecting domestic industry and exposing it to foreign competition. The real choice is different. It is whether the state should continue allocating resources through taxes, layers of customs duties, regulatory duties (RD) and additional customs duties (ACD), or establish a predictable, low and broadly uniform regime across industries and value chains.
If the state maintains different rates of taxes and tariffs, including ACD and RD, for different sectors of the economy, we are effectively selecting certain markets over others and obstructing competition. The durable principle is straightforward. Move towards low and uniform taxes and tariffs across industries and within value chains. Customs duties, regulatory duties and additional customs duties should cease to be instruments for selecting sectors, directing resources or shaping investment decisions. Firms should compete on productivity, quality and export capability rather than on their access to protection. A gradual transition may be necessary, but its destination must remain clear, and no sector should be treated as a favourite.
The discussion on whether we should include ACD or RD in our estimates of customs duty is peripheral at best. We should be discussing effective rates of tariffs in all cases. The argument from industry against tariff reduction can be summed up as follows. The local industry is at a cost disadvantage of around 20% to 30% against its foreign competitors on account of energy cost, bad infrastructure, expensive capital, deteriorating rule of law and other frictions like poor regulation. Therefore, to provide a level playing field, the state must provide a tariff protection wall to local firms by the same degree. Hence, some sectors get 10% protection, some get 20%. This is the underlying philosophy of all protectionists. The National Tariff Policy essentially puts a stop to this philosophy and provides a framework towards free and competitive markets.
For the sake of argument, let us consider this point of view sympathetically and extend the argument to include other problems of governance. The problem of corruption, for example, is very "taxing" and "tarrifying". We can add a few percentage points of tariff protection on its account. This is an unending debate. Also, no firm in the same market faces the same cost structure.
However, I want to acknowledge one point made recently at a seminar. The industry says customs duty is now less of a problem, and that they face a greater problem due to the high rate of General Sales Tax (GST), which is 18%, as it provides a huge advantage to the informal sector that does not pay any GST. The solution is not to seek protection from customs duty. The solution is to bring GST down to 5% across the board. This will wipe out the informal market as it will lose the incentive to stay undocumented.
The push for continuation of protective tariffs is not universal. Some sectors, like the steel industry, are adjusting well to the changing dynamics, where all other factors remain the same. A significant reduction in the cost of capital and the emergence of alternative sources of electricity are two major developments of the last two years. This can compensate for higher costs in other factors of production.
Another moot point is the cascading structure. Continuation of the existing cascading structure in tariffs is likely to preserve the existing inefficient structure of the economy. The new tariff policy is gradually reducing overall tariff rates, but it is broadly preserving the cascading. It retains tariff escalation by continuing to apply higher protection at later stages of processing. An overall reduction in tariff rates will reduce the impact of cascading but will not dismantle it.
The industrial policy idea that we should import components, assemble them locally and provide advantage to assemblers by erecting tariff walls on finished goods is deeply flawed. As the failure of the mobile phone device manufacturing policy has shown, a country cannot achieve competitive advantage through assembly and protection only. It must first establish an ecosystem around certain products where it has comparative advantage, and then establish value-chain linkages with leading global producers. This needs removal of tariff walls and investment in research and development (R&D), not support for the emergence of new classes of auto-assemblers.
THE WRITER IS CEO OF PRIME INSTITUTE, AN INDEPENDENT ECONOMIC POLICY THINK TANK

title: Was Pakistan ever an open economy
description: Was Pakistan ever an open economy
content:
Highest tariff among 70 major exporters; 40% of tariff lines above 15%
Pakistan's National Tariff Policy 2025-30 is now in its second year of implementation. Yet questions persist about whether tariff reforms were necessary, whether the underlying data were reliable, and whether reducing import duties will benefit the economy. These are legitimate questions. But before judging the reforms, we must address a more fundamental issue: was Pakistan genuinely an open economy, or had decades of protectionism weakened its competitiveness and export potential?
Much of the confusion appears to stem from a misinterpretation of the tariff indicators published by the World Trade Organisation (WTO). These indicators are useful, but they must be understood in context. Headline figures on applied customs duties do not necessarily capture the full burden of protection created by Pakistan's regulatory duties (RDs), additional customs duties (ACDs) and other import taxes. Nor does a relatively low trade-weighted average tariff necessarily mean that an economy is open to international competition.
The distinction is important. A trade-weighted average reflects tariff rates weighted by the value of actual imports. Products imported in large quantities, such as petroleum, edible oil and machinery, have a greater influence on the average, while goods facing prohibitively high duties, such as cars and consumer goods, account for a relatively small share of imports precisely because those duties discourage their importation. A proper assessment must therefore examine not only average tariffs but also tariff peaks, additional duties and the overall tax burden on imports.
The evidence from government ministries, international financial institutions and independent researchers leaves little doubt that Pakistan needed to address its restrictive trade regime.
In 2019, the then government's National Tariff Policy for 2019-24 acknowledged the extent of Pakistan's tariff protection. It noted that Pakistan had the highest weighted average tariff among 70 countries with annual exports exceeding $20 billion. It also observed that, while all 20 of the fastest-growing export economies had reduced import tariffs during the preceding decade, Pakistan's tariffs had increased by 11%. While successful export economies were opening up to international competition, Pakistan was moving in the opposite direction.
The case for reform, therefore, did not originate with the current policy. For years, multilateral institutions, Pakistani think tanks and academic researchers had identified high import taxes as a major reason for the country's persistently weak export performance. The World Bank placed Pakistan among the world's most protected economies, ranking it seventh on the Overall Trade Restrictiveness Index. It highlighted how a complicated tariff structure, comprising customs duties alongside additional customs duties, regulatory duties and other measures, distorted investment decisions and favoured heavily protected industries over more competitive businesses. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) similarly identified persistently high tariffs and an increasingly complex tariff structure as important factors behind Pakistan's poor export performance.
The WTO's 2022 Trade Policy Review provides further evidence. More than 40% of Pakistan's tariff lines carried duties exceeding 15%, a threshold commonly used to identify tariff peaks. The corresponding proportions for peer countries were considerably lower. If the total burden of regulatory and additional duties were also included, this figure would have been much higher.
The Economic Advisory Group, comprising independent Pakistani economists, highlighted another striking distortion. In 2023, trade-related taxes accounted for more than 40% of Pakistan's total tax revenue, compared with a global average of approximately 5%. The need for tariff reform, therefore, was not based on questionable data or an arbitrary preference for liberalisation. It was recognised by successive governments and supported by a substantial body of national and international research.
When the current reforms were debated in 2024-25, dire predictions were made. Critics warned that reducing tariffs would devastate domestic manufacturing, severely damage government revenues and trigger a balance-of-payments crisis. Some estimates suggested that the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) could lose more than Rs2,000 billion annually in import-related revenue.
Fifteen months into the reform process, the evidence does not support the predicted doomsday scenario. Although it is still too early to assess the full impact of the five-year National Tariff Policy, Pakistan's manufacturing sector has recorded growth of more than 6.5% after years of weak performance. Pakistan now has its highest-ever foreign exchange reserves and its balance-of-payments situation is positive for the first time in over two decades. Exports typically take time to respond to changes in trade policy, but they recorded growth of 10% in the first quarter of the current financial year.
These developments should be interpreted cautiously. Manufacturing growth, export performance and the external account are influenced by many factors beyond import tariffs. Nevertheless, one conclusion is already warranted: the predicted collapse of manufacturing and the anticipated balance-of-payments crisis have not materialised.
Tariff liberalisation is not about opening the economy indiscriminately or abandoning domestic industry. It is about changing the incentives that shape investment and production. Businesses should be encouraged to compete through productivity, technology, quality and innovation rather than depend indefinitely on high import barriers.
No country can build a competitive export economy by insulating its industries indefinitely from international competition. Successful industrialisers have followed different paths and used different policy instruments, but integration with international markets has been central to their long-term success.
The National Tariff Policy should ultimately be judged by whether it helps Pakistan raise productivity, expand exports and create sustainable employment. These outcomes will take time, and the government must remain willing to correct implementation problems as evidence emerges.
But the starting point for this debate must be the facts. Pakistan's trade regime was not as open as some suggest, and the case for reform was established long before the current policy was introduced. The real choice is not between protecting Pakistani industry and opening the economy. It is between protecting industries from competition indefinitely and helping them become competitive enough to succeed in the world.
THE WRITER IS A SENIOR FELLOW WITH THE PAKISTAN INSTITUTE OF DEVELOPMENT ECONOMICS. PREVIOUSLY, HE SERVED AS PAKISTAN'S AMBASSADOR TO THE WORLD TRADE ORGANISATION
