title: Jesse Eisenberg develops new A24 TV series with Peter Rice
description: Jesse Eisenberg develops an A24 TV series on culture wars  with former Disney executive Peter Rice as producer
content:
Jesse Eisenberg develops an A24 TV series on culture wars, with former Disney executive Peter Rice as producer
Jesse Eisenberg is preparing to return to television with a new series for A24, with former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice attached as an executive producer.
The untitled TV project is written, executive produced and set to be directed by Eisenberg. According to Deadline , the series is expected to be presented to potential buyers in the coming weeks under Eisenberg’s deal with A24.
The story is based on one of Eisenberg’s short stories and follows a young woman whose beliefs are challenged by new ideas and relationships. Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter at the London Film Festival premiere of his latest film, The Debut , Eisenberg said the story explores the beginnings of the culture wars through the perspective of an 18-year-old girl in autumn 2002.
It remains unclear whether the series adapts the story of Harper Jablonski, a college freshman featured in Eisenberg’s 2016 short-story collection, Bream Gives Me Hiccups .
Rice’s involvement comes shortly after he was named Netflix’s chief content officer. Although Netflix could become a potential buyer for the A24 series, Rice is not expected to take an active role in the project following his appointment. He is, however, likely to retain his executive producer credit.
Eisenberg initially gained attention as a child actor before joining the main cast of Fox’s comedy-drama Get Real in 1999. He subsequently focused on films, earning an Academy Award nomination for playing Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network . He later won an Oscar for writing the 2024 film A Real Pain .
The Debut , starring Julianne Moore, marks Eisenberg’s third feature as a writer-director, following When You Finish Saving the World and A Real Pain .
His previous television work includes the FX limited series Fleishman Is in Trouble , released in 2022. The new A24 project marks another step in his return to television, although a title, cast and release date have not yet been announced.

title: Meghan Markle reportedly drops out of Netflix   s  The Gentlemen
description: Meghan Markle is out of Netflix   s  The Gentlemen  talks as sources claim her name was used to promote season two
content:
Meghan Markle is out of Netflix’s 'The Gentlemen' talks as sources claim her name was used to promote season two
Meghan Markle is reportedly no longer in talks to join Netflix’s The Gentlemen , despite earlier reports that she was being considered for a role in the show’s third season.
Sources close to the Duchess of Sussex told The Telegraph that they believe her potential involvement was publicised to help promote the series’ second season. One insider alleged that Netflix benefited from the publicity surrounding Meghan’s possible casting, although the claims have not been independently confirmed.
“Some people in her camp feel she was used to help promote season two,” a source told the publication, suggesting that reports of discussions may have emerged before negotiations had progressed significantly.
Representatives for Meghan and Netflix did not immediately respond to PEOPLE’s request for comment on October 18.
The reports follow earlier coverage in August that Meghan was in the very early stages of discussions to join The Gentlemen . According to Deadline , talks were at an initial stage, while T he Hollywood Reporter reported that the role was being written and her potential episode count remained unclear.
The crime drama, created by Guy Ritchie, stars Theo James and Kaya Scodelario. Its second season premiered on Netflix on September 3, while the streaming platform renewed the series for a third season earlier this year. Variety reported in August that the upcoming instalment was already in pre-production, with scripts still being finalised.
A role in The Gentlemen would have marked Meghan’s most significant acting project since leaving Suits , where she played Rachel Zane for seven seasons. In a 2022 interview with Variety , she said she was finished with acting, although she has since filmed a cameo in the upcoming film Close Personal Friends . Its release date has not been announced.
Meghan has also continued working on screen through her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan , which premiered in 2025.
According to PEOPLE, Meghan is interested in returning to acting and has been exploring opportunities, though her reported involvement in The Gentlemen now appears to have stalled.

content:
'Growing Pains' actress Betty McGuire dies at 100, following a career spanning television, film and Broadway theatre
Betty McGuire, the actress known for playing Kate Malone on the ABC sitcom Growing Pains , has died at the age of 100.
She died on October 8, 2026, from natural causes at the Motion Picture & Television Fund’s Wasserman Campus in Woodland Hills, California.
Keith Gerchak, McGuire’s power of attorney, confirmed her death, according to Variety .
McGuire became familiar to television audiences through her seven-year association with Growing Pains . She played Kate Malone, the mother of Joanna Kerns’ character, Maggie Seaver. The actress appeared as a recurring character in the sitcom’s first two seasons before returning for Seasons 4 through 7.
Her television career extended well beyond the family sitcom. McGuire appeared in several popular series, including Falcon Crest , The Doris Day Show , Columbo , Star Trek: Deep Space Nine , Hill Street Blues , ER , CSI: Miami , MacGyver , Moonlighting and Charlie’s Angels .
McGuire also appeared in feature films, including Cheech & Chong’s Up in Smoke and Coma , the medical thriller directed by Michael Crichton.
Alongside her screen work, McGuire had an extensive theatre career. She performed with prominent Broadway figures such as Ethel Merman, Barbara Cook, Bea Arthur and Tony Randall in original productions of Plain and Fancy , Happy Hunting and Oh, Captain! She later headlined Mame at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas and toured in productions of Gypsy , Auntie Mame , Oliver! , How to Succeed in Business… and The Ziegfeld Follies of 1956 .
In her later years, McGuire volunteered at the Coalition for Economic Survival legal clinic in Los Angeles, helping low-income tenants facing eviction. She also hosted GabFest , a talk show on Channel 22 at the Motion Picture & Television Fund Home, where she lived.
According to Variety, McGuire had no surviving family members.

title: The Dick Van Dyke Show  almost had a second Petrie child
description: The Dick Van Dyke Show  creator Carl Reiner originally planned a second Petrie child  according to a series historian
content:
'The Dick Van Dyke Show' creator Carl Reiner originally planned a second Petrie child, according to a series historian
The Dick Van Dyke Show could have taken a different direction if creator Carl Reiner had followed his original plan to introduce a second child to the Petrie family during the sitcom’s first season.
David Van Deusen, an archivist and historian who has spent decades researching the classic television series, revealed the little-known detail in his book From Fandom to Friendships: My Adventures with The Dick Van Dyke Show Cast .
According to Van Deusen, Reiner’s original character descriptions included a baby who would join Rob and Laura Petrie’s household alongside their son, Ritchie. The planned addition was intended to inspire storylines exploring sibling rivalry and the challenges older children face when a new baby arrives.
Reiner reportedly envisioned episodes examining how Ritchie would adjust to having a younger sibling. However, the second child never became part of the family’s story, leaving the original concept as an intriguing piece of the show’s history.
The Dick Van Dyke Show premiered on CBS in October 1961 and ran for five seasons. The sitcom starred Dick Van Dyke as Rob Petrie, a comedy writer working on a television variety programme, and Mary Tyler Moore as his wife, Laura.
Larry Mathews played their son, Ritchie, whose family life provided an important part of the show’s domestic comedy. The series also followed Rob’s professional experiences alongside fellow writers Sally Rogers and Buddy Sorrell.
Van Deusen has dedicated years to preserving the sitcom’s legacy, including publishing The Walnut Times newsletter for two decades. His latest book shares behind-the-scenes stories and experiences involving cast members and guest stars.
As the beloved sitcom marks its 65th anniversary, Van Deusen’s discovery offers fans a fresh look at Carl Reiner’s original creative vision and the family storyline that never made it to television.

title: A24   s Elizabeth Holmes documentary scores  15 million in surprise debut
description: A24   s Elizabeth Holmes documentary scores  15 million in surprise debut
content:
A24’s 'You Can See Everything' earns $15 million as Elizabeth Holmes memes fuel its viral box office success.
A24’s documentary You Can See Everything , featuring disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and comedian Nathan Fielder, has made a strong debut at the domestic box office, earning $15 million in its opening weekend.
Directed by Lance Oppenheim and co-directed by Fielder, the three-hour documentary follows Holmes and her controversial business history. Its unexpected release, secretive production and viral social media campaign helped attract audiences, particularly younger moviegoers.
According to Deadline, the film recorded more than 2,000 sold-out screenings and delivered the second-biggest opening weekend for a documentary in the domestic box office market, behind Michael Moore’s 2004 film Fahrenheit 9/11 , which opened with $23.9 million.
The documentary also achieved the strongest opening for a film released in fewer than 1,000 locations since Borat debuted in 2006. Its success comes as A24 continues to build a reputation for unconventional marketing strategies that encourage audiences to drive online conversations.
Around 70% of the film’s opening-weekend audience was under 25, according to Deadline. The audience was also split 56% men and 44% women, while 44% of viewers attended with a partner.
Social media memes featuring Fielder and Holmes helped fuel interest in the documentary, drawing comparisons with the online excitement surrounding Barbie and the Barbenheimer phenomenon.
The film was developed largely in secrecy over four years and premiered at the Telluride Film Festival on September 6, with its teaser released as the screening took place. A24 later released a trailer featuring Fielder questioning Holmes about whether she believed she had done anything wrong.
Critical reception has also been strong, with the documentary earning a 99% critics’ score and a 98% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, according to Deadline.
Following its limited release, You Can See Everything is set to expand into more theatres, as A24 looks to build on its unexpected box office success.

title: Real parliamentarians  where democracy meets everyday life
description: Real parliamentarians  where democracy meets everyday life
content:
When rainwater enters a street, a sewer overflows, garbage remains uncollected, or drinking water stops flowing, an ordinary citizen rarely thinks of Parliament, a provincial secretariat, or a ministry. He looks for someone closer, someone he knows, someone whose door he can knock on. Very often, that person is his elected local representative.
This simple relationship explains something fundamental about democracy. Governments may formulate policies in capitals, but people experience governance where they live. For them, the State is not merely the Constitution, Parliament or a government office. It is also the clean street outside their home, water reaching their tap, the functioning school in their neighbourhood, drainage after heavy rain, and the public representative who listens when something goes wrong.
This is why elected local representatives may rightly be described as the real parliamentarians of everyday life. Their parliament is the neighbourhood. Their constituents do not need an appointment to tell them that a streetlight has stopped working, a drain is blocked, or a family has been left without a basic service. They meet people in markets, on streets, at community gatherings, and sometimes at their own doors. They hear public problems before those problems become official files or statistics. Local representatives are, in this sense, the first responders of democracy.
This idea has long been recognised internationally. Former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon observed that just as politics is local, development ultimately becomes local too. This captures the essence of grassroots governance: development becomes meaningful when it changes life in a village, town, union council or neighbourhood.
Pakistan's Constitution provides its own foundation for this relationship. Article 140A requires each province to establish a local government system and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility and authority to elected local representatives. The constitutional promise is significant because responsibility alone is not devolution. Local representatives cannot meaningfully respond to citizens if responsibilities travel downward while authority and resources remain elsewhere.
Imagine the frustration of an elected councillor approached every morning by residents complaining about sanitation, water, roads or other municipal problems, yet lacking the authority or financial resources to respond. To the citizen, that councillor represents government. Within the system, however, the same representative may have little power to act. The result is a damaging gap between public expectation and institutional capacity. Real devolution therefore requires more than elections. Functions, finances and authority must move together.
Pakistan acknowledged this connection at the Local Government Summit on the Sustainable Development Goals in Islamabad in 2017. The discussions emphasised stronger local institutions, adequate human and financial resources, community participation and meaningful political and administrative empowerment. Pakistan's subsequent reporting on the 2030 Agenda also recognised the importance of effective local government in embedding sustainable development at the grassroots. But the case for local government goes deeper than development targets and institutional arrangements. At its heart, it is about human dignity and democratic ownership.
An ordinary citizen should not need connections in a distant office to have sewage removed from outside his home. An elderly person should not have to navigate layers of bureaucracy to report a broken water line. A neighbourhood should not become invisible simply because its problem is too small to attract attention at the provincial or national level. For the family living with it, that "small" problem may be the most immediate failure of government in their lives.
This is where the principle of subsidiarity acquires human meaning. Decisions should, wherever practical, be taken as close as possible to the people affected by them. Local representatives understand not only what a community needs, but often where the problem lies, whom it affects, and who risks being left behind. The realities of a neighbourhood cannot be fully understood from a file in a distant office.
Empowerment, however, must travel with accountability. Bringing authority closer to citizens should also bring responsibility closer to scrutiny. Local representatives are visible and accessible. People know whether a drain was cleared, a road was repaired, water was restored, or a promise was honoured. Local democracy can therefore shorten the distance not only between citizen and State, but also between a problem, responsibility and accountability for the result.
None of this diminishes the importance of Parliament, provincial assemblies or higher levels of government. Their constitutional and policy roles are indispensable. The argument is different: democracy is incomplete when meaningful representation ends at the national or provincial capital. It becomes tangible when governance reaches the street, village, union council and neighbourhood.
Perhaps that is the deeper meaning of calling elected local representatives the real parliamentarians of everyday life. Their constituency is within walking distance. Their questions come not through formal notices but from citizens standing at their doors. Their performance is judged not only at election time, but every day, when a citizen asks a simple question: when I need my government, is there someone close enough to hear me?
Strengthening local government, therefore, is not simply about creating another layer of administration or periodically holding local elections. It is about shortening the distance between the State and the citizen and ensuring that the nearest door of government has the authority, resources and capacity to respond when people need it.
Ultimately, the true test of democracy is not how powerful government appears from afar, but how responsive, accessible and humane it feels when an ordinary citizen knocks on its nearest door.

title: Canada s troubling conflation of anti Zionism and antisemitism
description: Canada s troubling conflation of anti Zionism and antisemitism
content:
Canada's Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree and Justice Minister and Attorney General Sean Fraser released the federal government's first progress report on its National Commitments to Combat Anti-Semitism on Sept 24, 2026. Buried in the report is a significant assertion: "Anti-Semitism, which includes anti-Zionism, is not always obvious." Elsewhere, it calls for institutions to recognise "contemporary manifestations of anti-Semitism, including anti-Zionism".
The government is right to take antisemitism seriously. Jewish Canadians should not face threats, harassment or violence because they are Jewish. Anti-Zionism can also become a vehicle for antisemitism: "Zionist" can substitute for "Jew", Jews can be blamed collectively for Israel's actions, and old conspiracies can be repackaged as political commentary.
But saying anti-Zionism can be antisemitic is different from saying antisemitism includes anti-Zionism.
For many Jews, Zionism is closely connected to history, identity and self-determination. It is also a political movement involving sovereignty, territory and competing claims to land. Jews themselves have disagreed about Zionism since its emergence. For Palestinians, it is inseparable from displacement, dispossession and the Nakba. Opposition to Zionism, by itself, does not establish hostility towards Jews.
The wording matters because this is not merely an academic debate. The report discusses training for police, prosecutors, educators and public servants. It identifies the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition and Canadian handbook as foundations for federal efforts against antisemitism.
The government stresses that IHRA is not legally binding and does not criminalise expression. Nevertheless, definitions acquire practical force when institutions use them to investigate complaints, discipline students or assess employees. Institutions can constrain free speech and academic freedom without criminal prosecution.
A report released four days later by the US Commission on Civil Rights offers a striking contrast. Its bipartisan investigation unanimously concluded that campus antisemitism is a serious civil-rights problem, documenting harassment, threats, vandalism and exclusion.
Yet the commission also drew a line Ottawa is blurring. It distinguished discrimination based on Jewish ancestry or national origin from opposition to Israel or Zionism. Even offensive anti-Israel or anti-Zionist rhetoric, it recognised, can remain protected speech.
Kenneth Stern, who led the drafting of the predecessor text to IHRA, has warned about this problem. In material submitted to a Canadian Senate committee, he criticised the binary proposition that "anti-Zionism is anti-Semitism", alongside its mirror image, "Zionism is racism". He also questioned governments treating Zionism as essential to Judaism.
He is concerned that institutions may place a contested phrase on the "bad side of a line" and condemn anyone who uses it. Antisemitism is too complicated to address by consulting a glossary of politically contested words.
Courts have encountered similar problems. In Students for Justice in Palestine v. Abbott, a federal court in Texas found that students were likely to succeed in showing that university policies incorporating IHRA imposed unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination and chilled protected speech. The court did not invalidate IHRA; it questioned the connection between political viewpoints and disciplinary rules.
In Britain, former University of Bristol professor David Miller successfully argued that his anti-Zionism constituted a philosophical belief protected under the Equality Act. The university's appeal failed in 2026. It neither endorsed his politics nor protected everything said in anti-Zionism's name. Protecting a belief is different from endorsing it.
The Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism and the Nexus Document likewise recognise that discourse about Israel and Zionism can become antisemitic without treating opposition to Zionism as inherently so.
In their UCLA Law Review article, "Defending Jews From the Definition of Anti-Semitism", law professors Itamar Mann and Lihi Yona identify another danger: definitions tying Jewish identity too closely to Zionism can marginalise anti-Zionist and non-Zionist Jewish traditions. The possibility of antisemitism does not establish its presence.
Government should also avoid reinforcing an association it ought to challenge. Treating Jews as collectively responsible for Israel, or assuming they necessarily identify with the Israeli state, is itself a familiar feature of antisemitism. Equating opposition to Zionism with hostility towards Jews risks reproducing that assumption.
Canadian universities illustrate the institutional stakes. Justice Mary Lou Benotto's external review of Toronto Metropolitan University recommended IHRA as an educational and policy framework. Yet she declined to recommend formal adoption of the Arab Canadian Lawyers Association's definition of anti-Palestinian racism, partly because it incorporates contested historical and political propositions.
There is an asymmetry here. If institutions should hesitate before incorporating contested propositions about the Nakba and Palestinian indigeneity into policy, the same caution should apply to Zionism.
Canadian law already addresses hate propaganda, discrimination and harassment. In Saskatchewan (Human Rights Commission) v. Whatcott, the Supreme Court distinguished expression exposing a protected group to "detestation" and "vilification" from expression that is merely offensive or repugnant.
None of this gives anti-Zionism a free pass. Threatening Jews, blaming them collectively for Israel's actions or recycling antisemitic stereotypes demands a response. But the conclusion requires examining what was said, who was targeted, the circumstances and the evidence. An accusation should not substitute for proof.
These distinctions protect democratic rights. Students, academics and citizens must be able to debate political ideologies and advocate Palestinian rights without opposition to Zionism alone establishing bigotry. Equally, political language cannot excuse anti-Jewish hatred.
Ottawa could avoid much of the problem by changing a few words. Instead of saying antisemitism "includes anti-Zionism", it could say anti-Zionism can manifest as antisemitism.
Canada can confront anti-Jewish hatred without having the government declare opposition to a contested political ideology inherently bigoted.

title: Teaching grammar and bilingualism
description: Teaching grammar and bilingualism
content:
The bilingual sentence-wise translation in learning English tenses always remains elusive for the students of English as a second language. I frequently quote sentences to expose the incompatibility of syntax and grammar of two languages: 'Wo 1980 se mujay janta hey.' As per the formulas of tenses ingrained in students' minds, the Urdu sentences ending with 'ta hey, tii hey, tey hein' belong to the first tense, present indefinite, while the time marker '1980 se' seduces the young learners of English to translate it under the rules of present perfect continuous. However, the sentence belongs to neither. It is translated according to the present perfect tense. Mechanical search for a single Urdu marker cannot make grammar learning easier. Urdu markers become a misleading compass when learning of tenses is targeted.
Such disparities perplex the students because they have been taught grammar as a separate entity. In early classes, teachers don't have sufficient time to explain which tense and why it has been used in the text they are teaching. Or, they have to teach the language for exam preparation. Surprisingly, from middle to graduation level, only five to fifteen marks are allocated to Urdu to English translation. As learning of tenses requires a long concerted effort, they are deprioritised as per marks allocation and segregated to be taught as a separate entity.
Another fallout of bifurcating the teaching of grammar and reading of text is that students find it near impossible to grasp the passive voice of the English verb. At almost all levels of education in Pakistan, students are asked to change the voice of given English sentences from active to passive and vice versa. That's why students fail in specifying the voice of the Urdu sentences.
Today, students don't consult a dictionary to find the word's meanings. The dictionary also shows the part of speech the word falls under. Students can learn much grammar through osmosis. Then, when they are tutored in grammar, they cringe at the very words adjective, adverb or conjunction.
In lesson-planning the teaching of tenses, teachers must focus on the meaning to be expressed. A simple timeline must be used to represent the time of the action: present, past and future. Further, students must be asked whether the action is habitual, continuing, completed or expected to occur. Sentences like 'Ossay bhook lagi huii hey' should be quoted to illustrate the illusive nature of Urdu action markers. As the sentence alludes to the continuity of action, that's why it is translated according to the present continuous tense. Therefore, contrastive teaching can turn bilingualism into an advantage.
Similarly, a generalisation can be quite handy in teaching grammar in general and tenses in particular. The present simple is used for general truths and habitual actions. Modal verbs help express recommendations. Conditional constructions are used to show outcomes. Passive voice can shift the focus from who is doing it to what is being done.
Grammar is not difficult to learn; it is made difficult by misteaching it. Errors in learning grammar are of two types: the errors that distort meaning and the errors that are self-corrected through gradual refinement over time. Tenses fall in the first category, while articles, prepositions and spellings fall in the second. Students must also welcome corrections, as a 2015 meta-analysis by Eun Young Kang and Zhaohong Han finds that 'written corrective feedback can improve grammatical accuracy in second language writing.'
A two-pronged practical strategy requires x-ray reading first and then extensive reading. I always go for English newspaper reading for x-reading and classics for extensive reading. How grammatical constructions are employed to enhance the impact of expression and communication of thoughts can be learned by reading editorials, while the flow and rhythm in writing are acquired through osmosis by reading classics.
The linguist Richard Schmidt proposes in his 'noticing' hypothesis that darting close attention to both the form and meaning of language items contributes immensely to one's language learning. The input of the text must be converted into the intake of the learner.

title: Passport reform
description: Passport reform
content:
Pakistan's decision to phase out machine-readable passports in favour of electronic passports is a welcome step towards modernising its immigration infrastructure. The transition, expected to be completed within a month, should strengthen document security and bring the country closer to international standards. However, technological advancement must be accompanied by administrative efficiency and affordability. For millions of Pakistanis, obtaining a passport has often been an unnecessarily cumbersome exercise marked by bureaucratic hurdles and delays.
Electronic passports are hardly a new development in Pakistan. Introduced in 2022 and subsequently made available nationwide in 2023, they contain embedded chips that store biometric information and enable more reliable identity verification. Their wider adoption is overdue, particularly as international travel increasingly relies on digital authentication. Yet the government's assertion that the new technology would make forgery impossible is an exaggeration. No security system is entirely immune to manipulation, and the effectiveness of electronic passports depends as much on secure databases and verification mechanisms as on the sophistication of the documents themselves. Pakistan must therefore ensure that the transition is supported by robust cybersecurity safeguards and adequate protection of citizens' sensitive personal information.
Of greater concern is the financial burden this transition could impose. Under the existing official fee structure, a standard five-year electronic passport costs Rs9,000, twice the Rs4,500 charged for its machine-readable equivalent. A passport is an essential identification document, not a luxury reserved for those who can afford increasingly expensive government services. The authorities must also ensure that the changeover does not disrupt applications or recreate the backlogs that have previously plagued passport offices. The government must also demonstrate that its administrative machinery is capable of supporting the transition.

title: 10 million hungry mouths
description: 10 million hungry mouths
content:
With destitution on the rise as global economies enter a phase of contraction, hunger is raising its ugly head in at least 10 countries. It is quite unfortunate that Pakistan is one of them, with more than 10 million people malnourished and living below the poverty line. A new report by "Action Against Hunger", released in connection with World Food Day, warns that an estimated 10.6 million people in Pakistan will require humanitarian assistance. This report comes weeks after the South Asian country was ranked among nations with the lowest Human Development Index scores, while also remaining a prime victim of terrorism.
The report cautions that more than 177 million people around the world are in hunger-concentrated zones. Likewise, "acute hunger" has doubled over the past decade, affecting 266 million people across 47 countries. There is a host of reasons behind this decay, many of which stem from environmental degradation, institutional ad-hocism, and rampant corruption among developing countries. As far as Pakistan is concerned, climate-related disasters, economic hardship, displacement and shrinking humanitarian funding are responsible for this sordid state of affairs.
It is also worth noting that Pakistan has a dismal record in terms of budgetary allocations to education and health; according to UNICEF and the WHO, around 55% of the population lacks access to clean drinking water. Moreover, high food inflation, soaring unemployment, and declining household incomes continue to erode the quality of life for millions every year. Pakistan, despite being an agrarian state, has one of the lowest yields per acre. Similarly, unfavourable prices for farmers' crops and the lack of a vibrant farm-industry nexus have amplified the food crisis.
The report should serve as an eye-opener for policymakers. An instant damage-control strategy must be ushered in to feed the hungry and undo the trend of societal disenfranchisement. Food insecurity can only be addressed by tackling water scarcity, salinity and waterlogging, and by introducing mechanised farming.

title: Russia s reconnect
description: Russia s reconnect
content:
As regional dynamics remain in a state of flux, Russia appears to be recalibrating its strategic posture. Central to this evolving landscape is Pakistan, which, given its geopolitical significance, has a pivotal role to play and remains highly adaptive to shifting ground realities. The suspension of maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, alongside ongoing instability in the Red Sea, poses a threat to Pakistan's interests. Furthermore, escalating terrorism - fueled by Afghanistan's emergence as a hub for non-state actors - presents a growing concern for nations that have engaged with the Taliban regime. Consequently, Russia's proactive efforts to bridge regional rifts are increasingly evident and signal a positive turn for long-term peace and security.
Russia, of late, has shown its cards. It wants perpetual peace in Afghanistan and is also wary of the simmering tensions between Kabul and Islamabad. While Moscow praises the Taliban for "putting up a brave fight against ISIS", it is more than eager to strengthen Kabul's counter-terrorism capabilities. The Kremlin believes that the mushrooming terror nexus inside Afghanistan could have a spillover effect on its own security. The unending imbroglio in Ukraine, coupled with Afghanistan slipping back into the abyss of lawlessness, poses direct strategic threats to Russia. Thus, the back-to-back visits of high-powered Russian delegations to Islamabad, Kabul and New Delhi are no coincidence; something is cooking as a strategic deterrent.
The million-dollar question is whether Moscow is aiming to stage a comeback on the global stage while Washington is essentially in retreat. Russia's advice to the Iranians is also one of strategic restraint, urging them not to escalate the war beyond its current borders. This serves as a mechanism to keep Tehran on its side as a bargaining chip in an evolving landscape of realpolitik. The Makkah Pact, however, is a new development in the scheme of things, and this is where Russia will have to reposition itself if it wants to lead from the front. The sudden rise of the Houthis and their precision attacks on Saudi Arabia appear to be a telling tale of deception and re-engagement.

title: Russia s Pakistan signal
description: Russia s Pakistan signal
content:
Three Russian security visits to three regional capitals last week deserve attention, particularly from Pakistan. On October 14, Russian Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev held crucial talks with Pakistan's civilian and military leadership in Islamabad and Rawalpindi. The same day, Sergei Naryshkin, director of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, was in Kabul for talks with Taliban intelligence chief Abdul Haq Wasiq. In New Delhi, Aleksandr Venediktov, deputy secretary of Russia's Security Council, co-chaired security talks with Indian Deputy National Security Adviser Pavan Kapoor.
The timing is difficult to ignore. Russia is a major power with deep historical connections across the region. India remains its longstanding strategic partner. Pakistan was on the opposite side during the Cold War, while Afghanistan carries its own complicated history for Moscow. What makes the latest diplomatic activity significant is that it comes as Indo-Pak tensions remain high and relations between Islamabad and Kabul have deteriorated sharply.
The starting point for understanding Moscow's moves is Afghanistan. Russia remains the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government. That decision itself departed from the regional approach Pakistan had hoped countries would follow towards Kabul. The shift became even more visible at the Moscow Format meeting on October 5. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov offered a markedly different assessment of Afghanistan from Pakistan. While Islamabad accuses the Taliban authorities of harbouring the banned TTP, Lavrov praised Kabul's efforts against terrorist groups and described the Taliban-led administration as a "national government" that was governing the country successfully.
The differences surfaced dramatically when participants failed to issue a joint statement. Russian officials said Afghan objections to language relating to terrorism and Pak-Afghan tensions prevented consensus. Moscow still acknowledges that terrorist groups operating from Afghanistan threaten Russia and its allies. The crucial difference is that it increasingly separates that threat from the Taliban government itself.
It is against this background that last week's visits become significant. Kolokoltsev, the first Russian interior minister to visit Pakistan, received an unusually warm welcome. He met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and Field Marshal Asim Munir. Pakistan and Russia also signed an agreement to strengthen cooperation against organised crime. Yet the public warmth should not obscure potential differences over Afghanistan. Pakistani officials privately play down Moscow's growing proximity to the Taliban, arguing that Russia believes engagement can prevent Kabul from again opening the door to Western influence.
That explanation may only tell part of the story. Some diplomats also link Moscow's calculations to changing strategic alignments following the Makkah pact. Russia may be assessing what the new arrangement means for its interests in the Gulf and the wider region. One diplomat went further, alleging Russian assistance to the Houthis and arguing that a prolonged Gulf conflict benefits Moscow through higher energy prices. Such assertions remain difficult to independently verify, but they illustrate the suspicions surrounding Russia's regional moves. Perhaps most intriguing was Venediktov's visit to New Delhi. He and Kapoor chaired the seventh round of the India-Russia Special Mechanism on Pakistan and Afghanistan, a dedicated bilateral forum whose very title is noteworthy at a moment of acute Pakistan-Afghanistan tensions.
None of this proves that Moscow's simultaneous engagement with Islamabad, Kabul and New Delhi represents a coordinated strategy aimed at Pakistan or the Makkah agreement. But neither should the timing be dismissed as coincidence. Russia is clearly becoming more active across a region where old fault lines are widening and new alliances are emerging. Watch Moscow's next moves carefully; they may be the message for Islamabad and its allies.

title: China proposes export controls on solar manufacturing technologies
description: Seeks tighter control of solar technology exports  citing national security and growing use in aerospace and defence
content:
Seeks tighter control of solar technology exports, citing national security and growing use in aerospace and defence
China has proposed export controls on 12 technologies used to make solar equipment, citing national security concerns, as part ​of a broader revision that also covers AI and biotechnology.
The Ministry of Commerce proposed adding the photovoltaic technologies to China's export-control list, it said in a statement on Friday, adding that greater oversight is needed because solar technologies are ​increasingly being used in sensitive areas like aerospace and national ​defense.
Chinese officials held initial talks with manufacturers about potential curbs on ⁠advanced solar-panel manufacturing technologies, Reuters reported in April, a move that could ​threaten plans by US firms such as Tesla to expand production in the ​US.
Beijing has also curbed exports of solar-manufacturing technology to India, Reuters has reported. Analysts say China is seeking to preserve its dominance as India tries to build up domestic ​manufacturing and shake off reliance on China.
Export restrictions aim to "guard against ​the risks of technologies from running out of control or being improperly disseminated, while ‌safeguarding normal ⁠international exchanges and cooperation in science and technology," the ministry said.
Exporters must now register certain overseas technology transfers until the export-control catalogue is formally updated. Public consultation on the proposal will close on November 15.
China would ​ban technologies including ​those used to ⁠make some thin wafers, perovskite and tandem solar cells, as well as large-scale fluidized-bed polysilicon production technologies.
Perovskite is ​an emerging technology that offers the potential of increased ​conversion efficiency. ⁠Tandem cells combine perovskite and silicon layers to capture more of the sunlight spectrum.
Fluidized-bed technology for producing polysilicon — a key building block for solar panels — ⁠is ​less expensive and more energy-efficient than the ​dominant Siemens process.
China would also restrict, but not prohibit, exports of advanced solar cell manufacturing technologies, ​including TOPCon, HJT and XBC.

title: Leaders weigh  huge benefit   risks of AI for global economy
description: IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva notes any slowdown in the AI industry  would be felt across the world
content:
IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva notes any slowdown in the AI industry 'would be felt across the world'
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has been a key driver of global growth, but also poses economic risks should investment in the technology falter, experts and policymakers said this week at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
Propelled by spending on data centres and microchips, AI has helped cushion the economic shock of rising global energy prices caused by war in the Middle East, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in a report on Tuesday.
The fund's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro noted this week that global trade rose 8.3 per cent between 2023 and 2025 -- a figure she said would be closer to 4.6 per cent without AI-related products.
"It is everywhere in the global economy," Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said of AI on Friday.
"You see it in GDP. You see it in the stock market. You see it in the bond market... So it is here, and it's just the beginning."
But some top officials gathered in Bangkok this week cautioned against relying too heavily on AI investment.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh called AI the "most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime, and said it had "a huge benefit". Still, he warned the road ahead would be "bumpy".
"The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don't know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies," he said.
IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva similarly noted the AI boom's boost to global growth, but she told AFP that any slowdown in the industry "would be felt across the world".
"If there is loss of confidence and money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks," Georgieva said.
An IMF report released this week projected that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4 per cent by 2028.
"Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction," the report said.
While AI investment and trade have softened the global economic impact of the Middle East war, economists at Moody's Analytics have warned that if the conflict drags on, it could "puncture" the boom.
They said higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions could push up operating costs and interest rates, adding to doubts over "the long-term profitability and viability of AI business models".
"A drawn-out conflict would put serious strain on the economics behind AI investment," the group said.
The uncertainty around regulation has also clouded the technology's outlook.
Leaders like US President Donald Trump have urged more limited government regulation, even as some in the industry have called for legislation to mitigate risks.
Georgieva, the IMF chief, appeared on Friday to link such regulation to future investment.
"If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities," she said in Bangkok.

The education adviser also expressed gratitude to citizens who had recorded videos highlighting unsafe school buildings and shared them with the relevant authorities. title: Lahore Zoo   s adoption scheme raises questions over animal welfare
description: As citizens  schools and companies sponsor wild animals  experts call for better facilities  improved animal care
content:
As citizens, schools and companies sponsor wild animals, experts call for better facilities, improved animal care
Lahore Zoo’s new adoption scheme puts a price on wildlife sponsorship, but will it do enough to improve life behind the enclosures?
A private school recently adopted a male hippopotamus, named “Gabo” by its students. Under the new scheme, adopters can visit their animals, learn about their health and diet, and offer care suggestions, but cannot take them home. They receive certificates and educational material, while their names may appear on enclosures.
Deputy Director Shahzaib Khurshid said individuals and institutions could adopt animals for one, three or six months, or a year. Veterinary Officer Dr Muhammad Azhar said zoo staff remained responsible for their feeding, health and care.
Read : Lahore Zoo welcomes 29 new animals
According to the zoo administration, annual adoption fees vary by species. Sponsoring lions, tigers and other big cats costs Rs1 million, while the annual fee for a hippopotamus is Rs600,000. A giraffe costs Rs300,000, a fawn Rs100,000 and other antelopes Rs150,000. Interested individuals can contact the administration for details of fees for shorter periods.
The programme has attracted celebrities and educational institutions in the past. Actress Reema adopted two fawns after becoming a goodwill ambassador, while Babra Sharif sponsored a lion cub named “Shainko”. Actress Meera, the University of the Punjab, Government College University and several private educational institutions have also participated in animal adoption initiatives.
Citizen Abdul Rehman said the programme offered an opportunity for people interested in wildlife but lacking space to keep animals at home. Through adoption at the zoo, he said, enthusiasts could support animals while allowing them to remain in an appropriate environment.
Student Nida Fatima suggested extending the initiative to birds, saying it would encourage students and citizens to contribute to the conservation of a wider range of species.
Similar programmes operate at zoos across the region. Mysore Zoo in India has reportedly generated crores of rupees in a single year through its adoption scheme. Its annual fees include approximately Rs300,000 for an elephant, Rs100,000 for a lion or tiger and Rs50,000 for a hippopotamus, while deer can be adopted at lower rates. Zoos in Delhi and Hyderabad also allow families, schools and companies to sponsor animals such as lions, tigers and elephants.
The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) distinguishes domestic animal sponsorship from commercial wildlife trade. The World Association of Zoos and Aquariums (WAZA) stresses that animal welfare includes suitable habitats, good health, social needs and natural behaviours, with adoption funds supporting these needs.
Animal rights activist and lawyer Altamash Saeed said keeping wild animals at home was wrong and illegal. He supported zoo-based adoption but called for better facilities, larger enclosures and stricter monitoring to ensure animal welfare. Animals, he said, should not be treated merely as a source of entertainment, and their welfare must remain a priority.
Wildlife laws restrict keeping large wild animals in urban homes. Experts say the adoption programme can support conservation, provided funds are used transparently to improve animal care and living conditions.
Additional Chief Wildlife Ranger for Central Punjab Mudassar Hassan said the initiative was not limited to Lahore Zoo. Citizens and institutions could adopt animals at any zoo or safari park in Punjab.
He warned that keeping large cats, including lions and tigers, in homes posed serious risks to public safety and animal welfare. Such animals require specialised enclosures, appropriate diets, veterinary facilities and trained handlers. Adoption at recognised facilities, he said, provides a safer alternative for people wishing to support wildlife.

title: Agha  Shaheen star in Pakistan   s solid win
description: Seasoned batsman blasts his fourth ODI century before bowlers do well to seal victory  against SL
content:
Seasoned batsman blasts his fourth ODI century before bowlers do well to seal victory against SL
KARACHI: Salman Ali Agha slammed a solid century while Shaheen Afridi bowled extremely well as Pakistan took a golden start when they defeated Sri Lanka by 37 runs in their opener of ODI tri-series at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Sunday. Agha struck 107 to guide Pakistan to 305 all out in the allotted 50 overs. Shaheen (3-55) then bowled well alongside his other pacers to fold Sri Lanka for 268 in 48.1 overs. Set to chase a seemingly stiff target, Pavan Rathnayake and Janith Liyanage did a glorious job with the bat to keep Sri Lanka alive. After losing four wickets for 91 in the 20thover the due shared an incredible 119-run partnership for the fifth wicket to put pressure on the hosts. Faheem Ashraf broke the vital stand when he got rid of Rathnayake, held by Salman Ali Agha to bring Pakistan back into the game. Rathnayake, who brought in his fifty off 54 balls, smashed two sixes and six fours in his 74-ball knock. When Sri Lanka were needed 53 off 38 balls Haris Rauf gave a much-needed breakthrough when he had Janith Liyanage, held in the deep by Babar Azam. Liyanage, who completed his fifty off 62 balls, struck five fours in his 74-ball 60. In the next over Shaheen removed Dasun Shanaka (28) to keep Pakistan’s hopes alive. Shanaka hit three fours and one six from 18 balls and Sri Lanka now were 256-7 in the 45th over. Naseem Shah then removed Sachindu Colombage (1) and Eshan Malinga (2) got run out to leave the visitors at 260-9. Haris then had Asitha Fernando (7) to end Sri Lanka innings. Earlier opener Kamindu Mendis played a composed innings of 50-ball 44 to provide a good base to the visitors. He hit four fours in his nice knock before being dismissed by Shaheen Afridi. Naseem Shah, Haris Rauf and Faheem Ashraf ably backed their skipper with two wickets each. Earlier Salman Ali Agha struck his fourth one-day international century to propel Pakistan to 305 all out. Agha scored 107 off 90 balls, hitting ten fours and a six, to anchor Pakistan's innings after Sri Lanka elected to field. Pakistan lost both openers early, with Fakhar Zaman making 16 and Saim Ayub scoring seven, before Babar Azam and debutant Saad Baig steadied the innings. Babar made 45 off 57 balls, striking six fours, while Baig contributed 39 from 40 deliveries, including three fours and two sixes. The pair added 74 runs for the third wicket before Babar fell to Eshan Malinga. Baig followed soon after, dismissed by Malinga, leaving Pakistan needing a substantial partnership to build a competitive total. Agha and Hasan Nawaz provided the foundation, adding 97 runs for the fifth wicket. Hasan scored 37 off 49 balls, hitting two fours and two sixes, before falling to Asitha Fernando. Agha continued to accelerate, reaching his century off 82 balls with ten fours and a six. He survived a Sri Lanka review, with the appeal against him unsuccessful. Arafat Minhas added 18 off 15 balls, including two fours, in a sixth-wicket stand that helped Pakistan push towards 300. Agha was eventually dismissed by Fernando for 107 in the 47th over. Sri Lanka's bowlers struck regularly at the death to prevent Pakistan from batting out their full quota. Malinga finished with 4-46 runs, while Fernando claimed 3-59. Dilshan Madushanka took 2-67 in his ten overs. Pakistan now will meet England in their second show at the same venue on Tuesday.

title: Six injured as Houthi projectile hits Najran  says Saudi Civil Defence
description: Three homes and three vehicles also sustain material damage as projectile strikes residential area in the city
content:
Three homes and three vehicles also sustain material damage as projectile strikes residential area in the city
Six Saudi citizens were injured, and three homes and three vehicles sustained material damage when a projectile launched by the Houthis struck a residential area in the city of Najran, Saudi Arabia's General Directorate of Civil Defence stated, the Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported on Sunday.
According to the SPA, the directorate stressed that attempts to target civilian objects were a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law, further adding that teams responded to the incident and followed standard procedures.
Saudi-led coalition says helicopter crash in Najran kills two crew members
A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday.
The helicopter crashed due to a technical malfunction in an area under the jurisdiction of the Saudi National Guard Ministry, the statement added.
Yemen's Houthis released footage later on Sunday of what they said was a Saudi AH-6i helicopter being shot down by a missile while carrying out what they described as hostile activities near Najran.
The footage did not clearly show the incident, and Reuters could not immediately verify the Houthis' claim. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.
On Saturday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X that the group had shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter near Najran. It was not clear if that referred to the same incident.
Al-Maliki commented on Saree's post on Sunday with a photo of several Apaches lined up, saying: "You claim to have shot it down, but it will enter the battlefield soon."
Egypt says it will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary support
Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible support to defend its security and stability, its presidency said on Sunday.
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted 2 Houthi ballistic missiles headed for southwestern Saudi Arabia
The Saudi-led coalition said on early Sunday that it intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by Yemen's Houthi group toward Khamis Mushait in southwestern Saudi Arabia.
Coalition spokesman Turkial-Maliki announced the interceptions in a statement on US social media platform X.
Shortly before the announcement, Saudi Civil Defense issued "potential danger" alerts in the capital Riyadh and the southwestern cities of Abha and Khamis Mushait through its national early warning system.
The agency later announced that the danger had passed.
Read: Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, calls for immediate halt at UN
On Saturday, al-Maliki said coalition forces had intercepted and destroyed four drones over several hours in the Riyadh region, Eastern Province and southern Saudi Arabia.
The coalition also released footage it claimed showed strikes destroying two ballistic missile launchers in Saada, northern Yemen, after they had been used to fire missiles toward Saudi Arabia.
Houthis claim to have shot down Saudi Apache helicopter near Yemen border
Yemen's Houthi group claimed on Saturday that it shot down a Saudi Apache military helicopter near the Najran region in southern Saudi Arabia while it was targeting Houthi positions.
In a statement carried by the Houthi-run version of Yemen's Saba news agency, the group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, claimed that Houthi forces shot down the helicopter while it was carrying out "hostile operations" against their positions along the border.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi officials on Saree's remarks.
The claim came amid continued military escalation in Yemen and strikes by the Houthis against Saudi Arabia since July, including attacks on civilian aviation facilities and energy infrastructure inside the kingdom.

Faisal Town Group marked another significant milestone in community development with the inauguration of Jamia Masjid Hazrat Ali (R.A.) at Faisal Hills on Friday, October 9, 2026.
With a capacity to accommodate more than 22,000 worshippers, the mosque is described by the developer as the second-largest in the Islamabad–Rawalpindi region after Faisal Mosque.
The mosque was formally opened ahead of Friday prayers. Chairman of Faisal Town Group, Chaudhry Abdul Majeed, attended the inauguration and joined worshippers in offering special prayers for Pakistan’s peace, progress and prosperity.
The magnificent mosque combines traditional Islamic architecture with contemporary design, offering a spacious and peaceful environment for worshippers. Its striking golden dome, intricate gold-foil detailing and exquisite chandeliers reflect the richness of Islamic art and craftsmanship. The thoughtfully designed interiors and spacious prayer halls create an atmosphere of serenity, grandeur and spiritual reflection.
Designed to accommodate the spiritual needs of the wider community, the mosque features a dedicated prayer hall for women with a separate entrance, ensuring privacy, comfort and convenient access for female worshippers. Additional facilities include parking for approximately 300 vehicles, ablution arrangements for 200 worshippers at a time and a designated area for funeral prayers.
Beyond daily prayers, the mosque complex also houses a madrassa , an Islamic library and dedicated community spaces, establishing it as a centre for religious education, spiritual learning and community engagement.

title: La Bola Negra    earns  277 500 at Box Office as Netflix reports grosses for first time
description: La Bola Negra  is a historical drama exploring the lives of gay men across different generations in Spain
content:
'La Bola Negra' is a historical drama exploring the lives of gay men across different generations in Spain
Netflix has reported box office figures for the first time in its history, with Spanish-language drama La Bola Negra earning $277,500 during its opening weekend in a limited release across four cinemas in Los Angeles and New York.
According to Variety, the film averaged $69,375 per screen, marking a significant moment for the streaming giant, which has historically declined to disclose theatrical box office figures for its releases. The decision represents a shift in Netflix’s approach to theatrical distribution as it prepares to give several upcoming films more extensive cinema runs.
Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, collectively known as Los Javis, La Bola Negra is a historical drama exploring the lives of gay men across different generations in Spain. The film features an ensemble cast including Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close, alongside Guitarricadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau, Carlos González and Milo Quifes.
The story spans three timelines, set in 1932, 1937 and 2017, examining sexuality, identity, desire and the lasting effects of social and political repression. Inspired in part by the unfinished writings of Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca, the film connects the experiences of different generations against the backdrop of Spain’s history.
The film reportedly had a production budget of between $15 million and $17 million. Netflix acquired its US distribution rights for approximately $5 million following its presentation at the Cannes Film Festival, where Calvo and Ambrossi received the Best Director award.
Netflix’s decision to publish the film’s grosses follows reports that the company plans to disclose box office figures for a select group of upcoming theatrical releases. These include David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , Danny Boyle’s Ink , Peter Berg’s The Mosquito Bowl , Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew and the animated Charlie and the Chocolate Factory film.
The move comes as Netflix experiments with longer theatrical release windows. La Bola Negra opened in US cinemas on October 16 and is scheduled to arrive on the streaming platform on December 2, giving it an extended period in theatres before its streaming debut.
The company’s approach to theatrical releases has historically differed from that of traditional Hollywood studios, with Netflix prioritising streaming availability and often limiting cinema runs. Its decision to report box office figures could provide greater transparency about the performance of its theatrical releases while offering filmmakers and cinema operators more insight into audience demand.
With La Bola Negra leading Netflix’s new reporting approach, its theatrical performance will be closely watched as the company prepares to release more films in cinemas before bringing them to its global streaming audience.

title: Georgina Cates  An Awfully Big Adventure actress  dies at 51

content:
Georgina Cates, known for An Awfully Big Adventure and Clay Pigeons, has died at 51, her daughter revealed
British actress Georgina Cates, best known for her roles in An Awfully Big Adventure and Clay Pigeons , has died aged 51. Her death occurred on May 6, according to an Instagram tribute shared by her daughter, Naiia, although the news was not widely reported until recently.
Naiia remembered her mother as beautiful and free-spirited, praising her creativity, curiosity and courage to remain true to herself. Further details surrounding Cates’ death have not been disclosed.
Born Clare Elaine Woodgate on April 4, 1975, in Colchester, Essex, England, Cates began her acting career under her birth name. She first gained recognition playing Jenny Porter in the BBC sitcom 2point4 Children during its first two seasons from 1991 to 1992.
Her breakthrough came with Mike Newell’s 1995 coming-of-age film An Awfully Big Adventure , adapted from Beryl Bainbridge’s novel. Cates portrayed Stella Bradshaw, an impressionable young woman who joins a Liverpool repertory theatre company after the Second World War and falls for its director, played by Hugh Grant.
Cates initially failed to secure the role but auditioned again under the name Georgina Cates. She dyed her hair red and adopted a Liverpool accent to better embody the character.
She later appeared alongside Joaquin Phoenix and Vince Vaughn in the 1998 black comedy Clay Pigeons . Her other credits included Illuminata , Frankie Starlight , Stiff Upper Lips , Sinner , and Jackass: Bad Grandpa . Her final onscreen credit was the 2016 film Everlasting .
Cates married American actor Skeet Ulrich, known for Scream and Riverdale , in 1997. The couple divorced in 2005 and had twins, Naiia and Jakob, born in 2001.
After building a varied acting career, Cates also worked as a photographer. She had previously spoken about her desire to explore different roles rather than repeat the same performances.

title: Japan to launch historic round trip mission to Mars moons
description: Mission to reveal how Mars  its two moons formed  a key piece of knowledge in working out how Solar System was born
content:
Mission to reveal how Mars, its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how Solar System was born
Japanese scientists are preparing a mission to Mars’s moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region.
The unmanned Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.
The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Centre Tuesday at 4:41 am (1941 GMT Monday), according to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).
Read : NASA's Perseverance rover breaks record for off-planet driving on Mars
“Being able to be involved in such a grand mission is incredibly exciting,” Makoto Arita, project manager of JAXA’s H3 rocket team, told reporters two days before the launch.
The spacecraft will arrive near Mars around August next year, where it will orbit one of its moons, Phobos, before landing and collecting at least 10 grams (0.35 ounces) of material from the surface during three years of operating within the Martian sphere.
A rover dubbed IDEFIX -- the French name for the comic hero Asterix’s dog -- will first conduct surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing.
“The sampling (from) Phobos is of course the world’s first, but it means... this is the first round trip to the Martian system,” MMX’s project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu told AFP .
JAXA said the mission will also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a “natural space station” by establishing the requirements for a round trip to Mars -- something “essential for crewed Mars exploration”.
It will also observe the Red Planet’s moon Deimos, although it will not land on it, before returning to Earth.
JAXA hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how the Solar System was born.
One theory for the origin of the Martian moons -- the “giant impact” hypothesis -- is that they formed after a celestial body collided with Mars.
The “capture” hypothesis, meanwhile, postulates that the moons are asteroids captured by Mars’s gravity.
Determining which theory is correct will help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets”, JAXA said, referring to the four rocky worlds closest to the Sun -- Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
“MMX will shed light on the transport mechanisms that delivered water, volatiles, and organic compounds from the outer Solar System to the inner rocky planet region -- processes that may have played a key role in making these worlds habitable,” said Patrick Michel, a French astrophysicist working on IDEFIX.
“If Phobos and Deimos are indeed remnants of these early delivery systems, they may hold clues to the origins of life itself, or, to be more correct, to the transport of the materials that were key to the emergence of life on rocky planets,” he told AFP .
MMX is a collaboration with France’s National Centre for Space Studies (CNES), the German Aerospace Centre (DLR), NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA), and about 20 universities and tech companies.
The development of the spacecraft’s landing legs was particularly difficult, as gravity on Phobos is extremely weak, JAXA scientists say.
Japan’s unmanned Smart Lander for Investigating Moon (SLIM) -- the “Moon Sniper” -- tipped over after touching down on Earth’s Moon in 2024, but still transmitted data and survived several two-week lunar nights.
Japan also has experience in bringing back samples from space, including JAXA’s unmanned Hayabusa-2, which returned 5.4 grams of rock and dust collected from an asteroid several hundred million kilometres from Earth in 2020.
On the upcoming mission, “we have to travel very close to Mars and return”, which means escaping the planet’s heavy gravity, Kawakatsu told reporters.
Phobos orbits about 6,000 kilometres above the Martian surface.
“Going deep into what we call the ‘gravity well’ is difficult,” Kawakatsu said.
US and Chinese space agencies have been racing to be the first to return rock samples from Mars’s surface back to Earth.
NASA’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming the Red Planet since 2021, has already collected samples.
The mission, however, was effectively cancelled by the administration of President Donald Trump following a vote by the US Congress in January.
China, meanwhile, has announced its Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled for launch around 2028 and hopes to return Mars samples to Earth as early as 2031 -- potentially before the MMX’s return.
JAXA scientists say sand and rocks from Phobos may offer a wider variety of samples than those on the planet itself, especially if it was formed by a collision between a celestial body and Mars.

title: Jessica Biel and Justin Timberlake make rare red carpet appearance at Academy Museum Gala
description: The couple  who have been married for 14 years  posed together for photographers at the Academy Museum
content:
The couple, who have been married for 14 years, posed together for photographers at the Academy Museum
Jessica Biel and Justin Timberlake made a rare red carpet appearance together at the sixth annual Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles on October 17, stepping out in coordinated black ensembles for the star-studded event.
The couple, who have been married for 14 years, posed together for photographers at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. Biel wore a dramatic black feathered gown by designer Tamara Ralph, while Timberlake opted for a black patterned double-breasted suit. Their appearance offered a glimpse of the couple together at a major Hollywood event, as they generally keep their public outings relatively low-key.
The outing came just weeks after Biel and Timberlake celebrated their 14th wedding anniversary. The singer marked the occasion on social media with affectionate messages for his wife, calling her his “favorite person in every lifetime” and praising her as “the greatest mom”. In another post, he wrote, “14 down, forever to go.”
Biel also shared a tribute to her husband, writing, “Happy anniversary my love,” alongside photographs celebrating their relationship.
The pair first began dating in 2007 and married in October 2012. They share two sons, Silas and Phineas, and have occasionally offered fans glimpses of their family life through social media. Despite their high-profile careers, the couple tend to keep their children out of the public spotlight.
Biel is known for her acting roles in 7th Heaven , The Sinner and Candy . In addition to acting, she has worked as a producer on several projects, including the crime drama The Sinner , which earned her recognition for her work behind the camera.
Timberlake first rose to fame as a member of the boy band *NSYNC before establishing a successful solo music career. His hits include Cry Me a River , SexyBack , Mirrors and Can't Stop the Feeling! . He has also pursued acting, appearing in films such as The Social Network , Friends with Benefits and Trolls .
The Academy Museum Gala brought together prominent figures from film, television and music to raise funds for the museum's exhibitions, screenings and educational programmes. This year's honourees included Charlize Theron, who received the Icon Award, Colman Domingo, who received the Vantage Award, and filmmaker John Carpenter, who received the Luminary Award.
Other attendees included Taylor Swift, Kim Kardashian, Kendall Jenner, Connor Storrie and Rosé. Swift also performed during the evening, making the gala a major gathering for stars across the entertainment industry.
The event raised more than $14 million to support the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and its mission to celebrate and preserve the history of cinema.

title: AI rapidly improving  could vastly boost US GDP  Anthropic s Clark tells policymakers
description: Clark says there is growing evidence of a  singularity  where AI development outpaces human control
content:
Clark says there is growing evidence of a 'singularity' where AI development outpaces human control
Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will ​bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models ‌forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030.
Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology, and there was a shrinking window for policymakers to act.
Clark said that the estimated potential US GDP of $44 trillion, which compares ​to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery.
He said the forecast ​assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that ⁠new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion".
Clark's remarks come as the company prepares for an initial ​public offering expected in November that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion.
Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about ​the speed of AI development, saying there was growing evidence of a "singularity" where AI development outpaces human control.
"We should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially ​great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials.
AI was a major topic at the IMF and World ​Bank meetings, as both a source of growth offsetting high energy prices and a potential threat to stability if it falls short of its promise as a productivity game-changer ‌and stock ⁠valuations crash.
Officials also expressed worries about AI destroying certain jobs and leaving some countries behind.
But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic's "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants.
More countries can participate in the AI revolution by helping to build the ​data center computing capacity needed to ​power AI, he said.
Strictest controls ⁠on biological research
Clark cautioned that global leaders need to understand how powerful AI will become and make urgent choices about how to regulate the technology.
"Being able to use AI for science opens us up to the ​misuses of science as well, biological and cyber weapons and things we cannot yet imagine, and we have ​many choices to make," ⁠he said.
Biological research, where AI has already created new viruses, is an area "where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety."
Despite some recent high-profile incidents where rogue AI systems have escaped testing environments and hacked websites and databases, he said AI was still under human control. But the window to ⁠impose safeguards ​was shrinking as AI became more capable and was now "a small number of years."
Read : Artificial Intelligence: Dawn of a new global order
Clark ​also acknowledged that AI was causing job losses in some fields with "high AI exposure" such as call centers and customer service personnel. But for other fields, such as scientific research, he ​said AI was enhancing employment and a major unknown was its potential to create jobs in completely new industries.

title: Joe Manganiello reveals what led to 13 year estrangement from his father
description: Manganiello also reflected on the absence of his father during a particularly difficult period in his life
content:
Manganiello also reflected on the absence of his father during a particularly difficult period in his life
Joe Manganiello has opened up about the incident that led to a 13-year estrangement from his father, Charles Manganiello, revealing how a comment he made about his childhood during an interview ultimately fractured their relationship. The actor recounts the painful family rift in his newly released memoir, Bloodlines , explaining that he never intended to hurt his father by speaking about his upbringing.
The disagreement began when Manganiello was playing Stanley Kowalski in a production of A Streetcar Named Desire at Yale Repertory Theatre. During an interview about why he was frequently cast in intense roles, the actor explained that his understanding of anger came from witnessing volatility while growing up. Although he did not name any family members or reveal specific details, his father reportedly took issue with the comments, believing his son was publicly discussing private family matters.
According to Manganiello's account in Bloodlines , Charles changed his phone number without telling him rather than attending one of his performances. The actor subsequently called his father's new number and left a message, hoping to resolve the situation. When that did not work, he sent an email apologising for any hurt his remarks might have caused.
However, the response he received only deepened the rift. Manganiello described his father's email as one of the most disturbing messages he had ever read, recalling that Charles called him “a disappointment and a teenage girl”.
The actor wrote that he could never imagine sending such a message to his own child. Their relationship deteriorated further, and Charles ultimately became the only member of Manganiello's family who was not invited to his wedding to actress Sofía Vergara. The former couple married in 2015 and finalised their divorce in 2024.
Manganiello also reflected on the absence of his father during a particularly difficult period in his life. The actor has described a seven-year battle with an autoimmune illness that left him seriously unwell and required major surgery, including the removal of his large intestine. According to his memoir, his father did not call, write or visit him in hospital during that period.
“For years afterward while I was fighting for my life, he never came to see me the way I did for him,” Manganiello wrote, reflecting on the painful lack of contact.
Despite the length of their estrangement, Manganiello's account makes clear that he did not set out to damage his relationship with his father. He said he had attempted to apologise after learning that his comments had caused hurt, but the exchange that followed made reconciliation more difficult.
Through Bloodlines , the True Blood and Magic Mike actor is sharing a more personal account of his life beyond Hollywood, including his complicated family history, health struggles and experiences away from the screen. His revelations offer insight into a relationship that has remained fractured for more than a decade.
