title: Five K dramas that couldn   t stick the landing
description: Overcomplicated storylines  underdeveloped characters  too many loose ends leave viewers divided
content:
Overcomplicated storylines, underdeveloped characters, too many loose ends leave viewers divided
Some Korean dramas have all the ingredients for a memorable series, only to lose their way as the story unfolds.
Few things are as frustrating for a K-drama fan as watching a series with a brilliant premise gradually lose its momentum. A promising beginning does not always guarantee a satisfying ending. Whether through overcomplicated storylines, underdeveloped characters or finales that leave too many loose ends, some K-dramas have struggled to live up to their early potential.
Below are five K-dramas whose promising starts were followed by storytelling choices that divided viewers.
When the Phone Rings initially appeared to be a gripping psychological drama wrapped in the story of a troubled marriage.
Starring Yoo Yeon-seok and Chae Soo-bin, the series follows Baek Sa-eon and Hong Hee-joo, a couple whose relationship has been defined by emotional distance and years of silence. Their carefully maintained arrangement takes a dramatic turn after a mysterious phone call introduces a threat that could unravel their lives.
The early episodes build suspense around Hee-joo's silence, Sa-eon's cold behaviour and the possibility that their marriage conceals far more than either is willing to admit. The setup leaves plenty of room for a tense exploration of power, resentment and secrets.
However, the narrative gradually shifts towards romance, reframing Sa-eon's behaviour through the lens of concealed affection and misunderstanding. For viewers drawn in by the darker psychological elements, this change in direction could feel like a missed opportunity.
As the story progresses, increasingly dramatic developments compete with the central relationship, and the search for a missing spouse eventually takes the drama into a war-zone setting.
The result is a series that begins with the ingredients for an intriguing thriller but struggles to maintain that focus. Its strongest hook is the mystery surrounding the couple; the later storytelling does not always make the most of it.
A chance encounter, an unforgettable kiss and a workplace romance provide the foundation for Dynamite Kiss , a series that initially embraces the lighter side of Korean romantic comedy.
Jang Ki-yong plays Gong Ji-hyeok, a team leader who becomes preoccupied with a woman he meets in Jeju. Kim Ji-an plays Go Da-rim, who takes on the identity of a married mother to secure a position at a baby-products company. Their professional relationship becomes increasingly complicated as the truth threatens to surface.
The early episodes benefit from playful misunderstandings, romantic tension and the familiar appeal of two people struggling to make sense of their feelings. The straightforward premise also offers a welcome alternative to romances burdened by unnecessarily dark subplots.
As the series moves towards its conclusion, however, the story becomes increasingly crowded. Kidnappings, fires, financial trouble, romantic complications and long-held secrets begin to compete for attention, making the original workplace-romance premise feel less central.
A particularly dramatic confrontation involving Da-rim adds to the escalating tension, while a late accident and memory-loss storyline introduce another obstacle just as the series should be preparing to resolve its central romance.
The ending had to move rapidly through the reunion and proposal before jumping ahead in time, leaving little room for the emotional payoff that the earlier episodes seemed to promise.
For viewers who prefer uncomplicated romantic comedies, Dynamite Kiss illustrates how adding more drama is not necessarily the same as developing a better story.
With Hyun Bin and Park Shin-hye leading the cast, Memories of the Alhambra had the potential to become one of Korean television's most distinctive fantasy thrillers.
The series follows Yoo Jin-woo, a technology executive who travels to Spain after learning about an ambitious augmented-reality game. What begins as a business opportunity soon becomes a frightening experience as the boundaries between the digital world and reality begin to collapse.
The show's early episodes are among its most intriguing features. The Spanish setting lends the drama a distinctive atmosphere, while the game's immersive mechanics create an unusual blend of technology, suspense and fantasy. The possibility that an apparently harmless game could have deadly consequences gives the story a strong central mystery.
However, the concept becomes harder to sustain as the narrative progresses. Repeated encounters with enemies and increasingly familiar action sequences begin to reduce the sense of danger that initially made the premise so compelling.
The balance between the two leads also becomes uneven. Park Shin-hye's character, Jung Hee-joo, often has less to do than the mystery seems to warrant, leaving the relationship and its wider emotional stakes underdeveloped.
Most frustratingly, the finale leaves several important questions unresolved. The ambiguity may invite interpretation, but it also risks leaving viewers feeling that the series has stopped short of delivering a complete payoff.
Memories of the Alhambra remains an ambitious experiment in genre storytelling, even if its execution does not consistently match the promise of its opening episodes.
Few recent K-dramas generated as much conversation as Queen of Tears , led by Kim Soo-hyun and Kim Ji-won. Its central premise combines marital breakdown, family wealth and a medical crisis, creating opportunities for both sharp comedy and genuine emotional drama.
Baek Hyun-woo, a lawyer from a modest background, is married to Hong Hae-in, an heiress whose powerful family makes their already strained relationship even more complicated. When Hae-in receives devastating medical news, Hyun-woo's plans for separation are thrown into turmoil.
The early episodes explore the couple's resentment, buried affection and gradual rediscovery of one another. Their contrasting backgrounds provide much of the humour, while their painful history gives the romance an emotional foundation.
However, the series increasingly relies on an antagonist whose schemes repeatedly push the protagonists into fresh crises. Yoon Eun-sung's interference, the family's financial troubles and a succession of dangerous confrontations gradually shift attention away from the marriage that anchors the drama.
Hae-in's memory loss following surgery adds another major complication, forcing the relationship to revisit familiar emotional territory. Although the device creates opportunities for poignant scenes, it also risks making the couple's progress feel cyclical rather than decisive.
The final stretch attempts to resolve the story while covering an enormous amount of emotional ground, culminating in a substantial leap forward in time.
For some, the conclusion provides the closure the couple deserves, while for others, the relentless succession of villains and crises overshadows the intimate relationship that made the series so engaging in the first place.
Twenty-Five Twenty-One is remembered by many viewers as a moving coming-of-age story whose bittersweet conclusion was also its most contentious element.
Kim Tae-ri stars as Na Hee-do, an ambitious young fencer determined to pursue her dreams despite financial and personal obstacles. Nam Joo-hyuk plays Baek Yi-jin, whose family's fortunes collapse during South Korea's 1998 financial crisis.
Their relationship develops against a backdrop of youthful ambition, friendship and uncertainty. The series captures the intensity of growing up, when relationships can feel permanent even as life continues to pull people in different directions.
The show's ensemble of friends, memorable conversations and a nostalgic atmosphere help establish an emotional connection that extends beyond the central romance. The fencing storyline also gives Hee-do a goal of her own, allowing the series to explore personal achievement alongside love.
The difficulty emerges as the drama approaches its final episodes. Because the story is framed through the adult Hee-do's past and her daughter's discovery of old diaries, viewers are encouraged to wonder how the events of her youth connect to her present life.
Instead of offering the romantic resolution many had hoped for, the story follows Hee-do and Yi-jin as professional commitments, distance and changing circumstances gradually separate them. Their breakup is painful precisely because the series has spent so much time establishing the importance of their relationship.
The ending's refusal to provide a conventional romantic payoff divided audiences. Some appreciated its recognition that not every formative love lasts, while others felt the final episodes did not sufficiently prepare them for the outcome.
Regardless, Twenty-Five Twenty-One remains a powerful story about youth, ambition and the people who shape us, even for viewers who wish its central couple had found a different future.
For some viewers, an unconventional ending can be part of a show's appeal. For others, repeated plot twists, unresolved mysteries or a sudden shift in tone can undermine the emotional investment built over many episodes. Ultimately, the most memorable K-dramas are not necessarily those with the most dramatic twists but the ones whose endings feel true to the stories they set out to tell.

title: 12 killed as truck runs over devotees near temple in central India  police
description: At least 39 taken to hospital after truck crashes into temple wall  gate
content:
At least 39 taken to hospital after truck crashes into temple wall, gate
At least 12 people were killed and dozens of others injured when a truck hit devotees near a temple in India's central Madhya Pradesh state, a police official said early Sunday.
The accident occurred in Gwalior when a truck loaded with paddy lost control on a steep road and crashed into the outer wall and gate of the Sheetla Mata Temple, senior police official Dharmveer Singh said.
He said 39 people were taken to a hospital, of whom 12 died. Ruchika Chauhan, a local civil official, said an investigation was underway to determine the cause of the accident.
A day earlier, at least 17 people were killed and several others injured in a stampede at a religious festival in north Kolkata in India, NDTV reported.
Read: Two killed, including 6-year-old, when truck drives through Kansas youth soccer game, police say
Durga Puja, the biggest annual festival of Hindus in India's eastern state of West Bengal, draws thousands of devotees to temporary structures known as pandals, which house idols of the goddess Durga.
A police statement said the stampede occurred in the evening due to "heavy crowds of pandal hoppers amid rainfall." All injured persons were rescued and shifted to hospital.
Besides the dead, 25 people were injured, according to West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari.
According to eyewitnesses, many festivalgoers lost consciousness, and some were taken to the hospital on motorcycles. One witness said that the entrance to and exit from the pavilion were very narrow and that there was no lighting there.

title: FM Dar  Iranian FM discuss regional situation  OIC meeting in Baghdad
description: Dar  Egyptian counterpart discuss upcoming R 4 meeting involving during phone call
content:
Dar, Egyptian counterpart discuss upcoming R-4 meeting involving during phone call
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Sunday held a telephone conversation with his Iranian counterpart, Seyyed Abbas Araghchi, to discuss the evolving regional situation and an ongoing meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation’s (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad, the FO said.
In a post on X, the FO said the two leaders had discussed “the evolving regional situation” and “the ongoing OIC Council of Foreign Ministers meeting in Baghdad”.
FM Dar “underscored the importance of continued dialogue and diplomacy in addressing regional challenges”, the statement said. The two foreign ministers also “agreed to maintain close contact."
Pakistan and Iran were expected to hold further consultations on regional peace efforts on the sidelines of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation’s (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers meeting in Baghdad on October 17–18.
Iranian state news agency IRNA reported that the meeting would provide an opportunity for consultations between key regional players, including Islamabad and Tehran.
Pakistan has continued to advocate a negotiated settlement to the conflict involving Iran and the United States. On October 9, the military’s media wing chief, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, said Pakistan remained committed to a “negotiated and peaceful outcome” and warned against the conflict spreading further across the region.
He said Pakistan had condemned attacks on Iran by the United States and Israel, as well as Iranian attacks on Arab and Gulf countries.
Dar, Egyptian counterpart discuss upcoming R-4 meeting
Earlier today, FM Dar also held a telephone conversation with his Egyptian counterpart, Badr Abdelatty, and strongly condemned the Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, reaffirming their full solidarity with the Kingdom and support for its sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.
In a post on X, the FO said the two leaders also discussed the next meeting of the R-4 grouping, comprising Pakistan, Egypt, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, during a telephone conversation.
“The two leaders exchanged views on recent regional developments," the ministry added. Both looked forward to holding the next R-4 meeting soon to “further strengthen mutual ties and to coordinate on the regional issues."
According to the FO, the R-4 framework brings together Pakistan, Egypt, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia to strengthen ties and coordinate on regional issues.
Read: PM reaffirms Pakistan’s support for Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks in meeting with newly appointed envoy
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Egypt held the latest round of high-level consultations in Istanbul late last month, as Islamabad stepped up diplomatic coordination with key regional powers following the signing of a landmark defence agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye.
The four countries have been coordinating under the R-4 framework, which was launched earlier this year to intensify consultations on regional crises, particularly the conflict involving the United States and Iran and broader efforts to promote regional stability. The grouping has held several meetings since March, with its fourth ministerial meeting taking place in Cairo in June.
The attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group on Saudi Arabia escalated in October , with missile and drone strikes targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport, killing and injuring civilians and disrupting air traffic.
Saudi authorities reported that at least 12 people were killed and more than 300 injured in a strike on Riyadh’s airport on October 10. Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, under the R-4 framework, condemned the attacks and backed the kingdom’s right to take legitimate measures to counter the threat.
Read more: Gaza: Muslim states seek coordination
The foreign ministers of Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye last met on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 22 to discuss regional developments and efforts to promote peace and stability.
During the meeting, the four countries condemned attacks against Saudi Arabia, including recent Houthi attacks, and reaffirmed their support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security. They also stressed the importance of dialogue and diplomacy , called for the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding to be upheld to help secure lasting regional peace and stability, and reiterated support for the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination.
The Istanbul meeting, however, assumes added significance because it will be the first major R-4 engagement since Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on August 7.
The agreement commits the three countries to collective defence, with an armed attack against one member to be treated as an attack against all. Pakistan and Türkiye have stressed that the pact is defensive in nature and is not directed against any particular country. The agreement also envisages deeper military coordination, joint exercises and cooperation in defence technology.
Egypt's potential participation had emerged as an important question in the run-up to the Makkah agreement. Turkish officials had indicated that Cairo could eventually join the new defence arrangement, given its military weight and strategic importance in the region. However, Egypt did not become a signatory when Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye concluded the pact in Makkah.

title: Imran Khan challenges  unconstitutional  exit notice in Bombay High Court
description: Indian actor says OCI status provides statutory basis for residence  lawyers expected to seek Monday hearing
content:
Indian actor says OCI status provides statutory basis for residence, lawyers expected to seek Monday hearing
Indian actor Imran Khan challenged a notice directing him to leave India by October 28, arguing that the order was unconstitutional and that authorities failed to properly consider his Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) status.
According to Gulf News , the 44-year-old actor filed a writ petition in the Bombay High Court on Saturday against the Leave India Notice issued by the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) on October 14.
The notice followed the actor's detention near Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan during a student-led protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on October 10 after Khan allegedly violated immigration rules by joining the political protest.
The actor, a United States citizen who said he has lived in India since the age of two, argued that authorities had treated him solely as an American national while failing to account for his OCI registration. According to Gulf News , he contended that his OCI status provided a statutory basis for his residence in India and that his removal without due process would violate his rights, including protections under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution.
In his petition, he described the notice as an excessive use of official power. He argued that simply being present near a protest site or expressing concern about restrictions on movement should not be grounds for ordering his departure from India.
According to Gulf News , the actor maintained that he had no organisational links to the demonstration and had gone to the area out of curiosity about the protests. He said he complied when police informed him that the area was restricted.
Khan also disputed allegations that he had incited the crowd, claiming that authorities had overlooked CCTV footage relevant to the incident. According to the petition, he was returning to his car when he was apprehended after media personnel gathered around him.
The petition also questioned the FRRO's authority to issue the notice under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025. Khan argued that the restrictions around the protest had been imposed by local police and that the site was not a location formally designated as prohibited by the central government.
The FRRO also issued a show-cause notice asking the actor to explain why his OCI registration should not be cancelled under Section 7D(e) of the Citizenship Act, 1955. The provision allows the government to cancel OCI registration on specified grounds, including national security, sovereignty and public interest, subject to applicable procedural safeguards.
According to Gulf News , Khan was given 15 days to respond. The notice also warned that authorities could proceed with further action if Khan failed to submit an explanation within the stipulated period.
The actor asked the Bombay High Court to quash the notice and suspend its implementation while the case is heard. Khan sought an interim stay on the order, with his lawyers expected to seek a hearing before a Bombay High Court division bench on Monday.

title: You Can See Everything  sets Rotten Tomatoes and Letterboxd review records
description: Nathan Fielder s latest project  centred on Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes  has received strong praise
content:
Nathan Fielder's latest project, centred on Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has received strong praise
You Can See Everything has achieved some of the highest review scores of 2026, setting new records on Rotten Tomatoes and Letterboxd during its opening weekend.
The documentary-style project from Nathan Fielder, centred on Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has received strong praise from both critics and audiences.
According to Forbes , the film initially earned a 100% critics’ score on Rotten Tomatoes , becoming the only film of the year to reach that mark with more than 80 reviews.
After one negative review was added, its score fell to 99%, based on 101 reviews.
The film has also secured a 99% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, placing it ahead of other highly rated releases, including Spider-Man: Brand New Day , at 97%, and Project Hail Mary , at 95%.
On Letterboxd , You Can See Everything has reached an average rating of 4.7 out of five, making it the platform’s fourth-highest-rated entry at the time of reporting.
The ranking reportedly includes television series and a live Radiohead concert, meaning the film could be considered the highest-rated movie on the list.
However, the ratings remain subject to change as more viewers submit reviews.
Attention is now turning to the film’s box office performance.
Early estimates placed its opening weekend earnings at between $7 million and $8 million, while its reported production budget is approximately $5 million to $7 million.
With strong reviews and growing audience interest, the film could exceed initial commercial expectations.
Its critical reception raises the possibility of an Academy Award nomination for Best Picture, which would be a significant achievement for a documentary.

title: US vice president says he has yet to decide on 2028 presidential run
description: Vance says  of course there s a chance  he will not seek Republican nomination
content:
Vance says 'of course there's a chance' he will not seek Republican nomination
United States Vice President JD Vance said he has not decided whether to run for president in 2028, acknowledging he could ultimately opt out despite being widely viewed as a leading contender to succeed President Donald Trump.
Asked by CBS News ' Tony Dokoupil during an hour-long town hall in Michigan, released Saturday night, whether he might not run, Vance replied: "Of course there's a chance."
He described himself as a procrastinator when facing major life decisions and said he would "have to think about it," citing his four young children and his wife, Usha Vance, who "has never loved politics" but "loves public service."
Trump has called Vance his "most likely" Republican successor.
Read: Vance suggests disagreement with Trump over Iran war
Vance also defended the administration's economic and foreign policies, blaming former President Joe Biden's administration for neglecting manufacturing while acknowledging that reversing its decline would take time.
On the Iran conflict and elevated fuel costs , he said: "I recognise that gas prices are too high right now," adding: "When this conflict is over, we are going to see gas prices come down."
Defending Trump's Iran strategy, Vance argued that the US had "in some ways ... won decisively," but added that "the enemy gets a vote here." He said Washington was seeking a "final firm commitment from the Iranians that they're not going to rebuild their nuclear program."
Vance also rejected allegations of presidential corruption, saying he had not seen "a single shred of evidence that (Trump) participates or sanctions in that corruption."

title: Maldivian president to visit Pakistan on Oct 20 22 as ties mark 60 years  FO
description: Several agreements  MoUs covering different areas expected to be signed during the visit
content:
Several agreements, MoUs covering different areas expected to be signed during the visit
Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu will visit Pakistan from October 20 to 22, with the two countries set to explore wider cooperation in trade, investment, defence and maritime security as they mark 60 years of diplomatic relations, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Sunday.
“The State Visit, the first by a President of Maldives to Pakistan in eleven years, assumes special significance as the two countries commemorate the 60th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1966,” the FO said in a statement shared on its X account.
Muizzu will visit Pakistan at the invitation of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, accompanied by First Lady Sajidha Mohamed and a high-level delegation comprising cabinet ministers and senior officials, according to the statement.
During the visit, Muizzu will meet President Asif Ali Zardari, who will host a state banquet in his honour, and hold restricted and delegation-level talks with PM Shehbaz.
“The two leaders will review the entire spectrum of bilateral relations and explore avenues for further strengthening cooperation in trade, investment, health, education, tourism, agriculture, defence, maritime security, climate change and people-to-people exchanges,” the statement said.
Read: CDF Munir, Maldives parliament speaker discuss bilateral cooperation and regional security
“They will also exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest,” it added.
The visit will also feature a Pakistan–Maldives Business Forum, "aimed at promoting greater interaction between the business communities of the two countries and exploring new opportunities for trade and investment,” the statement read.
A number of agreements and memorandums of understanding covering different areas of bilateral cooperation are also expected to be signed during the visit.
Highlighting the longstanding ties between the two countries, the statement said, “Pakistan and Maldives enjoy warm and fraternal relations rooted in shared faith, mutual respect, longstanding goodwill and close cooperation at regional and international forums.”
“The forthcoming visit reflects the shared commitment of both countries to further strengthening their bilateral partnership and opening new avenues of mutually beneficial cooperation,” the statement concluded.
The Speaker of the Maldives’ People’s Majlis, Abdul Raheem Abdullah, also visited Pakistan for five days in September at the invitation of National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq. During the visit, the two sides agreed to strengthen parliamentary cooperation and people-to-people contacts.
Abdullah praised Pakistan’s “clear and consistent” stance on Palestine and Kashmir and reaffirmed the Maldives’ commitment to expanding legislative and institutional cooperation with Islamabad.

title: James McAvoy reveals    Split    is the only film that consistently pays him residuals
description: McAvoy added that horror actors still do not receive recognition for the quality of work being produced in the genre
content:
McAvoy added that horror actors still do not receive recognition for the quality of work being produced in the genre
James McAvoy has revealed that Split , his 2016 psychological thriller directed by M. Night Shyamalan, is the only film in his career that consistently earns him residual payments, despite starring in several major box office hits.
The actor shared the revelation during an appearance on Josh Horowitz’s Happy Sad Confused podcast on October 15, while discussing his career and directorial debut, California Schemin’ .
McAvoy explained that residual payments from his films are usually unpredictable, with some cheques amounting to only a few hundred pounds and others worth as little as 25 cents.
“You get the odd check for, you know, a couple 100 quid here or sometimes you get checks for, like, 25 cents,” he told Horowitz. “But the only one that really consistently pays me is Split .”
Released in 2016, Split follows Kevin Wendell Crumb, a man with dissociative identity disorder who has 23 distinct personalities. McAvoy portrays the character, delivering a performance that required him to switch between numerous identities, each with its own mannerisms and characteristics.
The film also stars Anya Taylor-Joy as Casey Cooke, alongside Betty Buckley and Haley Lu Richardson. Its commercial success proved particularly lucrative, with McAvoy attributing the continuing residual payments to the film’s relatively modest production budget and strong box office performance.
“I think it was made for like $6 million or something like that,” he said, estimating that the marketing campaign cost around $30 million. “And in our first weekend, we made 40, so we were in profit.”
McAvoy recalled receiving his first residual payment at the end of the film’s opening weekend, describing the experience as “bonkers”. The film ultimately grossed approximately $278 million worldwide, making it a significant commercial success relative to its production costs.
The actor credited Shyamalan’s filmmaking approach for helping make the project financially successful. He praised the director’s preparation and ability to maximise limited resources, noting that Shyamalan also made the 2019 sequel Glass on a relatively modest budget.
“The thing I took away from him is his preparedness,” McAvoy said, explaining that Shyamalan was focused on making the most of each filming day and communicating his vision clearly to the crew.
McAvoy said he consciously and subconsciously adopted lessons from directors he had worked with when making California Schemin’ , his own directorial debut. The film marks a new chapter in his career as he explores work behind the camera.
Despite Split receiving positive reviews and generating awards-season discussion around McAvoy’s performance, the actor said he had not expected a horror film to receive significant recognition from major awards bodies.
“I didn't think it would get welcomed into that sphere much,” he said, referring to awards consideration for genre performances. He added that horror actors still do not receive enough recognition for the quality of work being produced in the genre, although he believes attitudes are gradually changing.
McAvoy also praised actress Inde Navarrette for her performance in the psychological thriller Obsession , highlighting her ability to shift between emotional states and describing her work as both impressive and unsettling.
The actor's comments offer a glimpse into the financial realities of a film career, where box office success does not necessarily translate into substantial residual income for performers. For McAvoy, Split remains a notable exception, continuing to generate payments years after its theatrical release.

title: California governor says US military aid to Israel must be conditioned
description: Newsom says position is becoming Democratic Party consensus  calls Israel s war in Gaza  moral catastrophe
content:
Newsom says position is becoming Democratic Party consensus, calls Israel's war in Gaza 'moral catastrophe'
California Governor Gavin Newsom said Saturday that United States military aid to Israel "has to be conditioned," describing the position as increasingly becoming the Democratic Party's consensus as he campaigns in New Hampshire ahead of a potential 2028 presidential run.
"Aid has to be conditioned," Newsom told the Washington Examiner , citing settler violence in the occupied West Bank and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies, which he said undermine prospects for a two-state solution.
"Bibi Netanyahu has done a remarkable job of really isolating himself from the rest of the world and increasingly from the American people," Newsom said, adding that "the damage he's done is incalculable."
Read: Pakistan, others walk out as Israeli president speaks at CICA summit in Azerbaijan
Newsom called Israel's war in Gaza a "moral catastrophe" but declined to specify which forms of military assistance should face conditions, noting the distinctions between defensive systems such as Iron Dome and offensive weapons.
He said US aid should advance human rights principles, including under the Leahy framework — a 1997 federal rule prohibiting the US government from funding foreign military units linked to "credible information" of severe human rights violations .
His remarks come amid growing Democratic opposition to arms transfers to Israel.
Most Senate Democrats voted in the spring to block a weapons sale , while more than 100 House Democrats opposed a separate measure in July.
Israel is scheduled to hold elections on October 27, which Newsom said could influence the debate.
Newsom has previously criticised Netanyahu while expressing support for Israel, including visiting the country in 2023 to meet survivors of the Hamas attack. In March, he called his description of Israel as an "apartheid state" a "regret."

title: Pakistan to launch first astronaut into space from China on Nov 25  Ahsan Iqbal
description: Announces plans to establish Pakistan   s first Space Museum at University of Narowal to promote scientific awareness
content:
Announces plans to establish Pakistan’s first Space Museum at University of Narowal to promote scientific awareness
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal announced on Sunday that Pakistan’s first astronaut would embark on a space mission from China on November 25, as he set out the country’s ambitions for a lunar mission by 2035, state-run Radio Pakistan reported.
Addressing the concluding ceremony of World Space Week 2026 in Narowal, Iqbal said cooperation with China would help Pakistan reach new heights in space exploration.
He also announced plans to establish Pakistan’s first Space Museum at the University of Narowal to promote scientific awareness and encourage young people to pursue space science and technology.
The planning minister said World Space Week had been celebrated in Narowal for the first time in collaboration with Suparco under his vision, with the aim of raising awareness among young people about space science, scientific research, and modern technology.
The proposed Space Museum at the University of Narowal is also intended to inspire students to explore scientific fields and pursue careers in space research and technology.
Pakistan’s first astronaut is expected to travel to China’s Tiangong space station under a bilateral human spaceflight programme . Two Pakistani candidates, Khurram Daud and Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, have been undergoing training in China, with one to be selected for the mission.
According to Reuters , the selected astronaut will serve as a payload specialist and conduct scientific experiments aboard the space station. The mission is part of wider cooperation between Pakistan and China in space science and technology.
Pakistan’s space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (Suparco), signed an agreement with the China Manned Space Agency in February 2025 to prepare a Pakistani astronaut for the mission.
Iqbal also reiterated Pakistan’s ambition to reach the Moon by 2035, with China’s support expected to play a significant role in advancing the country’s space programme.
The two countries are also collaborating on a Pakistani lunar rover planned for China’s Chang’e-8 mission, expected around 2028, Reuters reported. The rover is intended to contribute to lunar exploration through autonomous navigation and imaging technology.

title: Paul Bettany addresses public perceptions of friendship with Johnny Depp after private texts emerged in court
description: He explained that he chose not to comment publicly  believing people understood his private nature and personal life
content:
He explained that he chose not to comment publicly, believing people understood his private nature and personal life
Paul Bettany has spoken about the public reaction to his private text messages with Johnny Depp, revealing that the pair had not spoken for years when their exchanges became public during Depp's libel trial.
In a recent interview with The Times , the British actor said he was surprised by how their relationship was portrayed after the messages were read in court during Depp's 2020 legal battle against The Sun.
"I hadn't spoken to Johnny in years when that happened and I haven't spoken to him since. I was being painted as this close friend of a guy I hadn't spoken to in years and, honestly, amid all the shit two celebrities threw at each other, that bit was the most odd," Bettany said.
He explained that he chose not to comment publicly, believing people understood his private nature and personal life.
"So I decided to say nothing because, I think, people know me," he continued. "I've been married 23 years and, for what I do, I live an incredibly quiet life. Everybody kind of thought this is probably a nothing burger – and left it alone."
The text exchange, originally sent in 2013, became public during a February 2020 court hearing.
The messages included disturbing remarks about Depp's then-wife, Amber Heard, and attracted significant attention during the proceedings.
Depp sued News Group Newspapers, publisher of The Sun, over an article describing him as a "wife beater".
In November 2020, Judge Andrew Nicol ruled against Depp, finding the publication's allegation substantially true.
Bettany and Depp previously worked together on several films, including The Tourist (2010), Transcendence (2014) and Mortdecai (2015).
Bettany's latest comments offer insight into the distance between the actors when their private correspondence became a public issue.

title: Security forces kill eight terrorists in three operations across Balochistan  ISPR
description: A large quantity of explosives  weighing 490 kilogrammes  also recovered in Khuzdar
content:
ISPR says a large quantity of explosives, weighing 490 kilogrammes, was also recovered in Khuzdar
Security forces killed eight terrorists belonging to the Indian proxy, Fitna al - Hindustan, in three intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan and recovered 490 kilogrammes of explosives, the military’s media wing said on Sunday.
According to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), on October 17, security forces conducted three IBOs in Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts of Balochistan, on the reported presence of terrorists belonging to the Indian proxy, Fitna al - Hindustan.
The federal government last year officially designated all terrorist groups operating in Balochistan as Fitna al-Hindustan , accusing India of sponsoring a proxy war through the outfits.
In Quetta’s Panjpai area, security forces intercepted an attempt by terrorists to establish a roadblock to disrupt local traffic, resulting in the killing of five Indian sponsored terrorists, the ISPR said.
The statement added that “during sanitisation operation in Nushki district, security forces busted terrorists' hideout, and after an intense fire exchange, two Indian sponsored terrorists were sent to hell,” the ISPR said, adding that weapons and ammunition were also recovered.
In a separate intelligence-based operation in Khuzdar, security forces engaged a terrorist hideout and killed one Indian-sponsored terrorist, according to the statement. A large quantity of explosives, weighing 490 kilogrammes, was also recovered.
Read: Five terrorists killed in Balochistan's Washuk IBO: ISPR
The ISPR said sanitisation operations were underway to eliminate any other Indian-sponsored terrorists found in the areas.
“Relentless counter terrorism campaign under vision " Azm-e-Istehkam" (as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country,” the statement concluded.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi praised the security forces for conducting successful intelligence-based operations against terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Hindustan in Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar. He lauded the professionalism and courage of the security forces for killing eight Indian-sponsored terrorists.
Naqvi said, “The significant successes achieved by the security forces against Fitna al-Hindustan terrorists and their facilitators are commendable."
He added that the terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Hindustan and their facilitators would find no place to hide. “The nation stands shoulder to shoulder with the security forces to eliminate the menace of terrorism,” Naqvi said.
On Thursday , security forces killed five terrorists belonging to the Indian proxy, Fitna al-Hindustan, during an IBO in the Washuk district of Balochistan, the military’s media wing said.
According to the ISPR, the operation was conducted on the night of October 12-13 following reports of the presence of terrorists
On Wednesday , security forces also killed five terrorists and injured four others during an IBO against Fitna al-Hindustan in the same district of Balochistan. During the operation, advanced weapons and ammunition were recovered.
Read more: 49 terrorists killed in Balochistan, K-P IBOs
Pakistan has witnessed a surge in terrorist activity over the past three months, with a series of attacks across the country resulting in the martyrdom of security personnel and civilians.
Last week, 12 people were killed and 35 others injured when a blast struck a joint checkpoint near Aman Mela in the Darazinda area of Dera Ismail Khan, with the TTP claiming responsibility for the attack.
On September 19, 23 people, including 15 police personnel, were martyred in a blast at a mosque in Kohat’s Police Lines during Friday prayers. Eight terrorists were also killed during a subsequent search and clearance operation. Later, the Ittihadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), led by Afghanistan-based Hafiz Gul Bahadur, claimed responsibility for the deadly bombing and rampage involving multiple attackers.
In a separate incident, a captain and a lieutenant were among six security personnel martyred in an exchange of fire in Hangu district, while eight terrorists were killed.
On September 1, six personnel, including two officers, and a customs department official were martyred as security forces thwarted an attempt to breach the Customs House in Balochistan.
In July, at least 30 people , including 27 police personnel, were martyred when terrorists identified by the state as the Indian proxy Fitna al-Hindustan ambushed police personnel deployed in the Kach Mangi Phase III area of Ziarat, triggering hours-long gun battles. The attackers also abducted several civilians and police personnel after the assault.

title: Explosion  fire at Canadian military base leave multiple fatalities  injuries
description: Defence minister confirms fatalities as strong winds spread flames  prompt large scale emergency response
content:
Defence minister confirms fatalities as strong winds spread flames, prompt large-scale emergency response
An explosion and major fire at a Canadian military base in Alberta on Saturday left people dead and injured, Defence Minister David McGuinty confirmed, while local authorities later said the blaze was under control after strong winds spread flames beyond the facility.
"I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base," McGuinty told reporters. He was referring to Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, east of the provincial capital Edmonton, but did not provide casualty figures.
McGuinty also did not disclose the circumstances surrounding the incident, including whether the explosion involved weapons or ammunition, describing the situation as “active and delicate.”
The Canadian Armed Forces said the fire was first reported around 4pm local time (2200GMT) on a training range at the base before spreading beyond the training area's boundary.
Read: Explosion at Bolivia military base kills at least 10, dozens injured
He said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were investigating, while the Canadian Armed Forces and federal, provincial, and municipal authorities were coordinating their response.
Local media cited an email by the Mounted Police that said officers were called to assist shortly after 4pm following reports of a fire in a training area. Multiple police resources were deployed, with their initial emergency response winding down but personnel remaining available if needed.
General Jennie Carignan, chief of the Defence Staff, said the military was fully engaged with federal, provincial, and local authorities. "Our priority remains the welfare of our members, their families and their community, and my thoughts are with all those affected by this incident," she said on US social media company X.
Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier described the incident as "serious," saying it had caused a major fire at the base. "Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Carney wrote on the US social media platform Facebook, adding that federal authorities were working closely with provincial and local officials.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the blaze as "significant and tragic," saying it had affected many military personnel. Canadian lawmaker Dane Lloyd earlier reported hearing of "significant casualties" following the explosion and fire.
Read More: Trump says men arrested at US air base in UK were looking to do 'big damage'
The Municipal District of Wainwright said strong winds had caused the fire to spread beyond the base perimeter, prompting emergency crews from multiple jurisdictions to respond.
In the latest update, municipal authorities said the wildfire south of the community was "being held" and that a fire watch would remain in place to monitor the affected area and respond to changing conditions.
Local authorities said no evacuation orders had been issued but urged residents to avoid the area and keep roads clear for emergency vehicles.
McGuinty said the nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting assistance and that authorities were closely monitoring the blaze. "I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," he said, pledging to release further information as it became available.
The base, located about 200 kilometres (124 miles) southeast of Edmonton, is one of Canada's busiest military training facilities.

title: Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
description: Groups target public buildings  loot supermarkets as police arrest around 1 200 people
content:
Groups target public buildings, loot supermarkets as police arrest around 1,200 people
Rioting erupted in cities across France on Saturday as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze; in Marseille, black-clad protesters broke into city hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city's tourist office.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year.
"To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X .
Read: France protests: demonstrators vow to shake government
Some 1,200 people had been arrested as part of the protests, Lecornu added while visiting the sites in the evening.
Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. The CGT union told Reuters it estimated protesters at 800,000 people.
President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had carried out the attacks. "We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so," he wrote in a post on X .
Belgium , Portugal and Italy also faced smaller-scale protests on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president and the wealthy.
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.
Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations.
In some parts of Paris, police fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas.
Rioters tried to break into the Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store as well as other boutiques and looted an SFR mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars.
In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
Read More: Teenager shoots headmaster, teacher at French school
In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe.
In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported.
The protests in France began last ‌month at high schools in Paris' working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.
In Paris on Saturday, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked Macron's previous term in office. Saturday's protests eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron's pension overhaul.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France's efforts to reduce public debt have not reassured investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades.
Also Read: Trump blames France unrest on 'mass migration', Islam
Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.
Lecornu said more than 150 police officers had been injured in Saturday's protests, but did not say whether any protesters had been hurt. Nunez confirmed reports that one person had his hand torn off in clashes with police on Saturday. French media reported he tried to pick up a stun grenade.
The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point.
"Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes," the union said. "Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum."

title: Public opinion triumphs over Trump   s spectacle
description: After condemnation from all quarters  the plan to livestream Nidal Malik Hasan   s execution has been called off
content:
After condemnation from all quarters, the plan to livestream Nidal Malik Hasan’s execution has been called off
Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas, seventeen years ago, is still scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3 at the military post where he carried out the attack. What has changed, however, is the audience. After a public outcry, President Donald Trump withdrew the administration’s plan to televise the execution.
In a social media post, Trump presented the reversal as a concession to people who did not want to see a man die. “Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” he wrote. Earlier, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had defended the proposed broadcast by arguing that “people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things”.
Despite weeks of debate over whether the execution should be broadcast, the administration has never explained why the public needs to watch Hasan die to understand that he has been sentenced to death. From the onset, the proposal drew opposition from an unusually broad coalition. Democrats and Republicans in Congress criticised it, religious leaders questioned its morality, and dozens of retired admirals, generals and other military officers warned that broadcasting the killing would damage the armed forces and the country they serve.
Even Vice-President JD Vance expressed doubts. “I’m not going to be watching it,” he told members of the media, adding that he did not know whether the broadcast would actually happen. House Speaker Mike Johnson, one of Trump’s most loyal allies, also said the country should not be doing this.
For an administration accustomed to brushing aside criticism as partisan hostility, the breadth of the opposition made the proposed live execution harder to defend. These were not simply Democrats objecting to a Republican president. Former senior officers, religious figures and lawmakers from both parties were raising concerns about what the government was proposing to do in the country’s name.
In an open letter, dozens of retired military officers said the broadcast “would clearly violate the basic human dignity of the condemned prisoner”. It would turn “what should be the solemn and grave punishment of a member of our society for committing the most serious crimes into a carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators”, they wrote. Their concern was not limited to Hasan. “This type of exploitative broadcasting that debases human dignity will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it,” the letter said.
Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island also criticised the judgment behind the proposal, describing it as evidence of “the impulsive and dysfunctional civilian leadership from the White House and US Department of Defense”. Hegseth, the senator added, deserved criticism for his judgment, strategy and communication, not only over the proposed broadcast but throughout his tenure as defence secretary.
Human rights experts argue that the government already had the authority to carry out Hasan’s sentence. Broadcasting his death, they said, would not have changed the punishment or made the conviction any more conclusive. “It would simply have allowed the state to display its power before an audience on a scale that would have been impossible in an earlier era.”
Public executions have served a purpose for centuries. The Romans made death a form of public entertainment, while authoritarian governments have used executions to intimidate opponents and demonstrate control. The Taliban and Islamic State have also circulated footage of killings to terrorise audiences and project an image of power.
A livestream would have given the American government a role in a practice it has long condemned when carried out by others. The images would not have remained under the administration’s control, either. They could have been copied, edited and redistributed by extremist groups and hostile governments, potentially reaching audiences far removed from those the Pentagon intended to influence.
The administration’s claim that the broadcast would deter future attacks was particularly difficult to establish and reason. A public execution might frighten some people, but there is no guarantee that the intended audience would interpret it as a warning. Images of state violence can also provoke anger, reinforce existing grievances and become propaganda for movements seeking recruits.
If anything, history has a few lessons on these grand executions. More recently, the hanging of former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein served as a cautionary example. His execution was filmed, and footage of the event circulated widely. Taunts directed at the former Iraqi dictator by witnesses became part of the recording, which fed into the sectarian tensions surrounding the American-led occupation of Iraq. The broadcast did not just communicate the fact that a sentence had been carried out, but it became part of the political struggle over how that killing would be remembered.
The circumstances of Hasan’s case are different, but the risks are familiar even now. Extremist groups could have used the footage to portray the US as hypocritical, while governments hostile to Washington would have had an easy way to attack its claims to defend human rights. A broadcast intended to demonstrate American authority could have served precisely the audiences the administration would want to discredit and Hasan may have emerged as a martyr for extremists and their audiences.
There is also a wider concern about how the Trump administration presents military force. Hegseth has shared footage emphasising the lethality of American operations, while the White House and Pentagon have circulated videos of aircraft destroying boats in the Caribbean and striking Iranian targets. Some clips have been set to popular music, giving military action the treatment of online entertainment.
Military operations and an execution are not the same thing. But the growing use of violence as material for public consumption raises questions about the message the Trump White House wants to send. The armed forces must be able to use force when necessary, but experts argue that they must also retain the public’s confidence that decisions about its use are made with judgment and restraint.
Retired admiral William H McRaven, who oversaw the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, made a similar argument in a recent piece in Foreign Affairs: “Although the moral high ground does not guarantee military victory, it is a foundation on which success rests.”
The retired officers who opposed the livestream were defending more than the dignity of a condemned prisoner. They were warning that the military’s reputation could suffer if its authority were used to stage a public spectacle without any clear operational purpose.
The US has kept executions out of public view for generations. The last widely recognised public execution in the country took place in Kentucky in 1936, when the execution of Rainey Bethea attracted an estimated crowd of 20,000. Capital punishment continued after public executions disappeared, but the practice of gathering spectators to watch a person die ended and for good reason.
The proposed livestream of Hasan’s execution would have brought that practice back through technology capable of carrying images around the world almost instantly. The fact that the broadcast would have been digital rather than a gathering in a town square would not have changed its essential character. The public would still have been invited to watch the state kill a prisoner.
All that said, Hasan’s crimes were appalling, and nothing about opposing the broadcast of his execution requires anyone to minimise the suffering of his victims or their families. But a person’s conviction does not remove every obligation the state has towards them. The severity of a crime cannot be the sole measure of whether a human being retains dignity, particularly when that person is entirely in the state’s power.
People can support capital punishment and still oppose turning an execution into entertainment. Others may reject the death penalty altogether, but neither position requires the public to accept that a condemned person’s final moments should be made available for mass consumption.
On the other hand, the prisoner has no meaningful say in whether the government broadcasts his death. The state decides how the sentence is carried out, who may witness it and what information is made public. If nothing else does, that imbalance makes restraint especially important.
There are also unresolved legal questions and critics have argued that livestreaming the execution could raise concerns under the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment. There is no established ruling directly addressing the constitutionality of a broadcast in these circumstances, so it remains uncertain whether such a challenge would succeed.
The moral objection does not depend on a court settling that question. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, the Catholic archbishop for the military services, said the proposal “flies in the face of the moral and ethical and theological basis on which we operate”. His criticism reflected a concern that the state could carry out its lawful duties without turning a person’s death into a public event.
The campaign against the livestream was never meant to save Hasan’s life. Its achievement was narrower, it prevented the government from making his death a spectacle. If anything, it tells us that public opinion, organised across political and religious divisions, proved capable of imposing a limit on a decision that the administration had initially defended with confidence.
Military veterans worried about the honour of the armed forces. Religious leaders challenged the morality of the proposal. Lawmakers from both parties questioned its wisdom. Their combined opposition made it more difficult for the White House to dismiss the criticism or proceed without paying a political and institutional price.
That said, there is no guarantee that the administration has learned a broader lesson. The cancellation does not mean it has changed its approach to human rights, abandoned its punitive politics or ruled out similar proposals in the future. Still, the retreat shows what can happen when opposition extends beyond one political camp and refuses to let an outrageous proposal pass as regular business. Public outrage, when it cuts across political divides, can still add pressure even on governments that display all the trappings of an authoritarian regime.

title: Two killed  including 6 year old  when truck drives through Kansas youth soccer game  police say
description: 10 people hospitalised with traumatic injuries as 34 year old  female driver taken into custody
content:
10 people hospitalised with traumatic injuries as 34-year-old female driver taken into custody
A truck drove into a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, leaving a six-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man dead, and 10 others hospitalised with traumatic injuries, police said on Saturday.
The injuries ranged from minor to severe, but none appear to be life threatening, Wichita police Captain Aaron Moses said at a news conference. The two people killed were pronounced dead at the scene, he said.
Moses said a 34-year-old woman was driving the truck, which ended up in a field at the west end of the Stryker Sports Complex. She has been cooperating with investigators, he said, but when asked whether she had been arrested, he said only that she was in custody.
Read: New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says
"We know what happened, but now we're working very hard to find out why it happened, and we're not there yet," Wichita police Chief Joe Sullivan said.
The injured include two youths aged five, two aged eight, a 9-year-old and five adults, police said. In addition to those 10 people, one adult was hospitalised for non-traumatic medical issues.
The driver had a child playing soccer at the complex, but not on the field where the incident took place, Moses said. The truck involved had two juveniles as passengers, he said.
Emergency dispatchers started getting calls about the incident at 3:25pm local time (2025 GMT), Moses said.
"Today is a heartbreaking day for Wichita," Mayor Lily Wu said. "Families came to Stryker Sports Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon, watching their children play soccer and no one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold."

content:
Swift arrived at the event in a pale blue Dior dress and changed into a cobalt blue number for her performances
Taylor Swift brought elegance and music to the Academy Museum Gala 2026 in Los Angeles on Saturday, October 17, wearing a pale blue Dior gown before delivering a special performance at the prestigious event.
The 14-time Grammy winner arrived on the red carpet in a strapless, pale blue pleated silk dress featuring a beaded bow.
She completed the look with Chopard diamond jewellery and Aquazzura shoes, while her softly curled hair and pale pink lipstick added to the ensemble.
Swift also took to the stage, performing "The Fate of Ophelia" from The Life of a Showgirl for the first time with acoustic accompaniment.
Wearing a sequined cobalt blue dress, she also performed some of her old hits "Love Story" and "Blank Space" as well as her recent release from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack, "I Knew It, I Knew You" .
Several celebrities attended the gala, with Rosé, Connor Storrie, Jessica Alba and Charlize Theron among those seen enjoying the performances and singing along.

title: Cinema across borders
description: A veteran educator reflects on the power of cinema to build lasting ties between Pakistan and Russia
content:
A veteran educator reflects on the power of cinema to build lasting ties between Pakistan and Russia
I will begin with a confession. I have loved Russian cinema since my young days, when it was still Soviet cinema. If that makes me biased, so be it. Some biases are simply the truth, held with affection.
I came to these films as a young admirer and later came to know them more deeply as a student of Russian. There was Gaidai's Kidnapping, Caucasian Style and The Twelve Chairs, and Motyl's White Sun of the Desert, which cosmonauts still watch before flying, a ritual that has now travelled with them to American launch sites. In Russia, lines from these comedies became household phrases, quoted at dinner tables and in offices to this day. Once you know them, you hear them everywhere. It was a cinema that could make you laugh, make you weep and make you think, often in the same film. So when I sat down to watch four new Russian films recently, I carried a heavy question with me: does today's Russian cinema live up to that legacy? I walked out certain that it does.
I am not alone in that view. The celebrated American critic Roger Ebert called Russian Ark, a film shot in a single unbroken take through St Petersburg's Hermitage Museum, "one of the best-sustained ideas I have ever seen on the screen”. The New York Times found the Russian sci-fi thriller Sputnik "a genuinely scary and satisfying experience”.
Pakistani audiences got to judge for themselves at the end of this summer. Four recent films were screened at Centaurus Cineplex in Islamabad at the end of August and at Raiha Cinegold Plex in Bahria Town, Rawalpindi, in early September, all in Russian with English subtitles. They could hardly have been more different from one another, and that range was itself a statement.
The first, The Golden Key, is a new screen version of Buratino, Alexei Tolstoy's much-loved Russian retelling of Pinocchio, the story of a wooden boy that every Soviet child knew. It is lavish and stylish, with a star cast and beautiful camerawork. Russian critics compared it favourably with the classic Soviet version, and one wrote that among the many remakes of old favourites, this one truly shines. What stayed with me was Papa Carlo, a lonely old craftsman who carves a puppet to earn his bread and ends up with a son. In Pakistan, where parents still look to a son to support them in old age, that story needs no translation.
Chebi 2: My Fluffy Friend gave families the same warmth, and even more laughter. Ask a Russian about Cheburashka and you get the look a Pakistani gets at the mention of Uncle Sargam: instant, fond recognition. Russian audiences were clearly waiting for him. The film has become the highest-grossing film in Russian box-office history, and critics found the sequel funny, lively and touching almost to tears. The story is simple and true. Cheburashka is growing up and testing limits, and his friend Gena struggles to raise him. The lesson is that families survive by listening to each other. It was a film Pakistani parents and children could watch together without a single awkward moment.
If these two films offered laughter, the other two brought tears. Baby is the most intense of the four. It follows Dima, an 18-year-old who lives for rap music and wants nothing to do with politics, until he learns that his mother is trapped in a besieged city. It is not an easy film, and it is not meant to be. At its heart lies something universal: a son's love for his mother, and how quickly circumstances can force a boy to become a man.
It was the last film, however, that I have not been able to stop thinking about. As a student of Russian, I learned about the siege of Leningrad long before I ever saw it on screen. I read the diary of 11-year-old Tanya Savicheva: a few small pages, each marking the death of someone she loved, ending with the words "Only Tanya is left." I read poems by Olga Berggolts, the voice that kept starving Leningrad alive by radio through the siege, whose words, "No one is forgotten, and nothing is forgotten," are now carved at the cemetery where its victims lie. The blockade lasted nearly 900 days. Its lifeline was the Road of Life across the frozen Lake Ladoga: ice that carried bread in and children out, and too often gave way beneath the lorries.
Angels of Ladoga took us onto that ice in November 1941. A group of young ice-yacht racers, once rivals, set out to deliver ammunition across the frozen lake. Their sails appeared so suddenly out of the winter haze, and moved so fast, that people called them the angels of Ladoga. Then they learn of an orphanage whose children were left behind when the city was evacuated, and their mission becomes a rescue. What touched me most is that they are not soldiers. They are ordinary young people who, at the worst possible moment, become a team and carry children they don't know across ice that could break at any step.
I am not ashamed to say I wept. I wept for the children, and for the young people who became their angels. I also wept because the film confirmed something I have always believed about the Russian people: their memory of suffering has made them not bitter but deeply humane. The director never lets spectacle overwhelm the people on screen. Every frame of white, cracking ice carries dread, and every small kindness lands like a blessing. I left the cinema quiet and stayed quiet for a long time. If I could recommend only one of these films to young Pakistanis, it would be this one. We, too, are a nation that knows sacrifice, and Angels of Ladoga speaks our language, even in Russian.
What united all four films, beyond their stories, was their craft. The cinematography, sound design, visual effects and editing meet every international technical standard. On the big screen they held their own against anything Hollywood sends us. That is no small achievement. It reflects serious investment in studios, technology and film education, and a generation of filmmakers who know exactly what they are doing.
This matters well beyond the cinema hall. Most Pakistanis know Russia through headlines. These screenings showed them the Russia that headlines leave out: its humour, its family values, its fairy tales and its memory of war. After a lifetime of teaching Russian, I can say that one good film often teaches more about a culture than a semester of lectures. Our two peoples share more than they realise: respect for elders, the centrality of family, and a deep memory of sacrifice. Cinema makes those bonds visible.
That is why this initiative must not remain a one-off. Russian film days should travel to Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar and Quetta, and to our universities, where curiosity runs highest. Urdu subtitles would widen the audience further. The exchange should also run both ways, with Pakistani films shown to Russian viewers. Co-productions between our two industries are not a distant dream. They are a natural next step.
The Soviet films of my youth taught me to love a language and a people. Today's Russian cinema is ready to do the same for a new generation of Pakistanis. Let us give it every screen we can.
The writer is Head of the Department of Russian Language at the National University of Modern Languages (NUML), Islamabad, and a recipient of the Pushkin Medal
