title: The institutional alibi
description: Do universities shield predators to protect their brand
content:
Do universities shield predators to protect their brand?
Outside the stone facade of the Toni Morrison Dining Hall, at Cornell University in upstate New York, a large crowd of students gathered for a seven-hour-long sit-in. Each passing hour represented a harrowing crime that took place on campus two years ago. A fellow undergraduate—identified in public court records only as Jane Doe—alleges she was raped for seven hours one night at the Chi Phi fraternity house.
What started as an alleged assault using drugs, alcohol, and sedatives quickly became a major international controversy for universities. The institutional fallout was immediate and chaotic: emergency fraternity suspensions, a national outcry regarding administrative transparency, and a high-profile civil lawsuit that exposed a dirty secret long whispered in academic quadrangles.
Behind the ivy-covered brick, the manicured lawns, and the lofty rhetoric of moral leadership lies a universal and brutal reality: when a sex crime shatters the illusion of campus safety, elite university administrations are fundamentally wired to protect the institution's brand, financial endowment, and public reputation long before they seek justice for the survivor. It is a crisis underscored by the sobering reality that approximately 1 in 5 undergraduate women experience sexual assault or attempted rape during their college years.
The shockwaves the Cornell 7 case sent through the American educational establishment trace directly back to the labyrinthine bureaucratic machinery governing US campuses: Title IX. Enacted as part of the US Education Amendments of 1972, Title IX was originally designed to prevent sex discrimination in educational programs receiving federal financial assistance. For decades, its cultural footprint was defined almost entirely by athletics—opening collegiate locker rooms and playing fields to female athletes and levelling the playing field for women in sports. However, a major paradigm shift occurred under the Obama administration in 2011, when federal guidance explicitly reinterpreted the statute to mandate how schools must handle sexual assault and harassment.
In theory, Title IX creates a parallel track to the US criminal justice system. While local police investigate offenses that carry the threat of prison time, campus-run Title IX tribunals are empowered to hand down internal institutional discipline, up to and including expulsion. In practice, however, this two-pronged structure is an administrative quagmire that frequently fails victims on both fronts.
Over the last decade, these rules have kept changing dramatically with every new administration. Under Donald Trump’s first term, the US Department of Education rules narrowed the legal definition of sexual harassment and mandated live cross-examinations, causing reporting numbers to dip across the country as victims struggled against the complex, adversarial hurdles required to seek accountability. When Joe Biden assumed office, his administration overhauled the regulations once more, expanding definitions, incorporating explicit protections for LGBTQ+ students, and making live hearings optional. Almost immediately, a coalition of federal judges pushed back, blocking and altering implementations across hundreds of campuses—including Cornell—leaving administrators and students alike navigating a legal maze without a reliable map.
More damningly, historical data demonstrates that this dual-track maze rarely delivers meaningful accountability. Research compiled by community psychologists and higher education watchdogs reveals a sobering statistical gap: only a fraction of reported cases ever lead to formal prosecution or conviction in criminal courts.
At Cornell specifically, institutional data covering 2018 through 2024 shows that out of 1,216 reported Title IX complaints, a staggering 96 per cent were dismissed or closed without a formal finding of responsibility against the accused. A mere handful—just 14 suspensions and seven total expulsions or dismissals—resulted from five years of complaints. Survivors of sexual assault are told they have robust options, yet they frequently find themselves caught in a cruel administrative purgatory. In the ongoing case at Cornell, a district attorney declined to prosecute due to high evidentiary barriers, and a university disciplinary committee quietly prioritised risk mitigation over institutional truth.
As reports of sexual assault and harassment on campuses in India and Pakistan surface with increasing frequency—turning up in headlines with grim regularity—South Asia reveals an architecture of institutional self-protection that looks hauntingly familiar. Whether examining elite private liberal arts institutions in urban centres or sprawling, heavily securitised public universities across Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh, the institutional playbook for handling campus sexual misconduct is strikingly uniform: denial, minimisation, victim-blaming, and aggressive image control.
When major scandals erupt in the region—ranging from dormitory security breaches and administrative cover-ups to digital blackmail rings and surveillance exploitation—university administrations routinely treat the crisis as a public relations disaster threatening the moral prestige and cultural standing of the institution. Only if the students protest does it take on the urgency of human rights failure.
Yet, the parallels between Ithaca and South Asia go far deeper than mere administrative cowardice. In South Asian academic spaces, the structural and societal obstacles facing survivors are magnified by deeply entrenched cultural realities. Namely, while Western students navigate bureaucratic red tape, South Asian students frequently face immense familial and communal pressure to stay silent to protect family honour. In patriarchal social frameworks, a survivor's trauma is routinely weaponised by society as a reflection on family honour, forcing many to bear their pain in isolation rather than risk public exposure.
University syndicates and administrative bodies in South Asia have historically relied on heavy-handed retaliation. Student activists demanding safer campuses, transparent inquiries, or administrative accountability are frequently met with expulsion or suspension, disciplinary hearings, or physical intimidation by campus security forces.
The social penalty for speaking out weighs heavy on the survivor, not the perpetrator. In an environment where institutional authorities control degrees, housing, and career recommendations, reporting misconduct is often viewed by students as jeopardising their academic futures.
Furthermore, public universities in South Asia often operate under state-funded bureaucratic webs where political appointments dictate administrative boards. Vice-chancellors and syndicate heads are frequently political appointees whose primary directive from higher-ups is maintaining public calm and political stability, rather than championing progressive internal accountability. Consequently, sweeping allegations under the rug becomes an institutional survival strategy, protecting influential alumni, faculty members, or politically connected student wings at the direct expense of student welfare.
In both America’s Ivy Leagues and South Asia's prestigious universities, the core issue is identical: institutional hierarchy that treats student safety as secondary to the preservation of the brand. Whether protecting a centuries-old endowment in New York or guarding the moral reputation of a historic state university in Punjab, the institution’s first instinct is always self-preservation.
Why do these cases so routinely collapse across every known legal and administrative system? The answer lies in the devastating psychological and evidentiary complexity inherent to prosecuting sex crimes.
Unlike financial fraud, embezzlement, or property theft, sexual violence almost never leaves clean paper trails. Drug-induced incapacitation—such as the fast-acting sedatives and dissociative drugs referenced in the Cornell litigation—compounds this nightmare. Drugs and alcohol wipe away clear recollection, induce amnesia, trigger delayed trauma responses, and leave survivors grappling with fragmented memories. In hostile cross-examinations, these natural trauma responses are routinely weaponised by defense attorneys and institutional investigators to dismantle a survivor's credibility. By the time a case reaches a hearing or court, the rules are often stacked to protect the status quo.
The Cornell 7 case highlighted one structural codependence prevalent in American campuses: universities that rely heavily on fraternities and their alumni networks to drive fundraising, maintain housing networks, and sustain a party circuit that underpins campus social life. When misconduct occurs within these spaces, administrators face a perverse incentive to sweep it under the rug to shield the university’s brand and financial interests. This institutional self-protection was laid bare when the university’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, issued a public apology acknowledging a profound "loss of trust" on campus. Students and faculty widely dismissed the gesture as a defensive image control exercise, pointing out that the administration only acted after national public outrage forced their hand. Whether dealing with an opaque internal review process in the West or an overworked university disciplinary committee in South Asia eager to avoid government scrutiny, the apparatuses ostensibly constructed to dispense justice frequently end up acting as gatekeepers protecting the powerful.
The widespread public backlash at Cornell—culminating in massive student sit-ins, a no-confidence debate surrounding the university administration, the suspension of fraternity social events, and the unprecedented intervention of state law enforcement task forces taking over sex crime investigations—signals that public tolerance for institutional negligence is finally wearing thin.
Yet, appointing special prosecutors, drafting temporary emergency rules, and commissioning external review boards are ultimately mere band-aids on a globally fractured system. Lasting reform demands that universities everywhere permanently strip away their own self-policing powers.
Until academic institutions accept that their moral legitimacy depends on protecting human lives rather than guarding their endowments, campus safety will remain nothing more than an institutional alibi until the next survivor's voice exposes the dark underbelly of academic citadels.

title: The return of offline fun
description: From board game nights to reading circles  people are finding new ways to unwind  make friends and enjoy time
content:
From board-game nights to reading circles, people are finding new ways to unwind, make friends and enjoy time
For Zainul Hassan Siddiqui, making friends in a new city turned out to be harder than expected. He had lived in Quetta, Lahore and even the United States before moving to Karachi in 2022. Naturally sociable, he was used to being around people, but building a social circle in a city where work occupied much of his time was another matter.
A corporate lawyer pursuing an executive MBA over the weekends, Siddiqui had little trouble keeping himself busy. What he missed was having people to spend time with outside work, without needing a particular occasion to meet.
Earlier this year, he began looking for activities that would help him meet people. Alongside padel, he discovered organised board-game nights, including one hosted by a community-driven board game group which hosts events in Karachi. He went along hoping to socialise. What followed was more than an occasional evening of entertainment.
Some of the strangers he met at those gatherings are now close friends. They meet outside organised events, visit one another's homes and spend four or five hours playing strategy games, often accompanied by friendly taunts and arguments over moves.
Siddiqui now attends board-game gatherings at least twice a week, despite his demanding schedule.
His experience is part of a wider picture of people finding ways to spend their leisure time together, whether around a board game, a book or a conversation that doesn't begin and end on a screen.
For some, these gatherings offer an opportunity to make friends. For others, they provide a few hours away from work, family responsibilities or the familiar habit of scrolling through social media. And sometimes, as Siddiqui discovered, a game is simply an excuse to find people worth meeting again.
Taha Jawed had been playing board games for six or seven years, but finding others who shared his interest wasn't always easy. Most people he came across knew Ludo, Monopoly or Sequence. There was a whole range of games beyond those familiar titles, but not enough people to play them with.
Six months ago, he and his wife, Yusra, decided to do something about it. They started Boardgame Baithak, a community built around bringing people together to play.
Recalling how difficult it had been to find people familiar with different board games, Jawed says, “We set out to change that through action.”
Their first gathering attracted five people. Today, Jawed says, the community has more than 200 members, although a typical game night brings together around 15 to 20 players.
The format is straightforward. People turn up, the organisers explain the rules in about five minutes, and the games begin. Flip 7, Feed the Kraken and Mafia are among the favourites. Some involve as many as 12 players, and there is no limit on how many games someone can try during the evening.
Jawed estimates that 90 per cent of participants are newcomers. Many attend alone initially and bring their spouses or friends the next time.
“Digital entertainment is overrated in my honest opinion,” he says. “There's nothing like forming connections and engaging with people in real time.”
He has watched people who first met at these events go out for dinners, arrange padel games and even form business connections. Once, a participant brought along their own collection of games and told the organisers, “Let me host you now.”
Another participant, Sidrah Ramzan, a 31-year-old copywriter, who also has a three-year-old child, says free time is difficult to come by. When she does get some, she often ends up scrolling through social media.
She and her husband were initially cautious about meeting strangers, but found the organisers welcoming. They now attend roughly every other week.
“My favourite part is the friendly banter that goes on,” she says.
Sidrah has made friends there, although she doesn't attach too much significance to it.
“I have made a ton of friends through these events and it's fun to learn about new people. Wouldn't say meaningful connection because it's more for unwinding and not deep conversations.”
For Sidrah, that is reason enough to keep going.
Not everyone looking for company wants to spend an evening competing over a board game. For some, sitting around a table discussing a book is enough.
Saniya Imtiaz started Pakistan Book Readers Club in 2016, at a time when she felt conversations around books and literature were becoming less common. She remembers an earlier culture of people gathering to discuss ideas, writers and what they had been reading. She wanted to create a space for those conversations again.
What began as a Facebook group now holds reading sessions in Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad, Gujranwala, Faisalabad and Hyderabad. The physical gatherings are deliberately small, usually bringing together 10 to 15 people.
Imtiaz says larger gatherings can make it difficult for everyone to contribute. With fewer people, discussions are easier to manage and participants have more opportunities to share their views.
The conversations are not always limited to a particular book. Sometimes there is a theme, while other sessions bring authors and readers together.
“If we are discussing one book, then everyone's interpretation will be different,” Imtiaz explains. A reader might notice something another has missed, or understand a character or idea differently. For her, that exchange is what makes reading together worthwhile.
Over the years, she has seen these meetings develop into something beyond literary discussions. Members exchange books, recommend unfamiliar authors and sometimes send books to readers who cannot afford to buy them.
In smaller towns, where finding books can be difficult, members have also helped get books to one another through people travelling between cities.
One gathering that stayed with Imtiaz was with women writers and aspiring authors in Karachi. Some participants spoke about the difficulty of expressing themselves openly. Hearing published authors discuss their experiences encouraged others to consider writing themselves, even if only a short poem.
But not every reader is looking for a club.
Saadia Khan, a marketing executive who reads almost daily, prefers the experience of reading alone.
“I'd rather read alone, because I cannot stand slow readers (no offense),” she says.
She does, however, enjoy discussing books afterwards, particularly when someone else's interpretation challenges her own.
Saadia has considered joining a reading club but struggles to find the time to commit regularly. For now, conversations with fellow readers are enough to introduce her to books she might otherwise never discover.
Sidrah was scrolling through Instagram when she came across a post about board game gatherings and thought it might be something she and her husband would enjoy. They went, met a few people and have been returning ever since.
The irony isn't lost on her. An activity she discovered through social media has become one of the few occasions when she barely looks at her phone.
“We barely use our mobile phones, maybe just to take a picture or two. Other than that, it is all about socialising and playing games,” she says.
Siddiqui has noticed a difference in his habits too. Before he started attending board-game events, he would often spend his spare time playing mobile games or scrolling through Instagram. It kept him occupied, but he didn't always feel relaxed afterwards.
He explains that watching reels can distract someone for half an hour without doing much about the stress they were trying to escape. At a game night, there is something to react to, someone to argue with over a move, or a joke being made at another player's expense.
His overall phone use, he says, has reduced considerably since he began making time for these activities.
For Saadia, an avid reader since childhood, putting the phone aside comes more naturally. She doesn't need a gathering or a scheduled activity to do it.
“Sure, scrolling through reels can be fun. But nothing beats getting lost in a book for hours. The storytelling, world-building, and character arcs are really immersive. It's like watching a movie only I can see.”
Saadia says reading hasn't completely changed her screen time. She still uses social media, but often finds herself choosing a book instead.
Saniya, meanwhile, has encountered readers who specifically want printed books because they already spend much of their day looking at screens. But she also knows people who rely on PDFs because buying physical books isn't always affordable.
Pakistan Book Readers Club itself uses WhatsApp and Google Meet to keep discussions going, particularly for members who cannot attend in person because of travel expenses or responsibilities at home.
For them, being online isn't necessarily a habit they are trying to break. It is how they remain part of a reading community.
Finding an activity you enjoy is one thing. Making room for it in an already crowded week is another.
For Siddiqui, time is the biggest challenge. His work as a corporate lawyer sometimes involves long hours and even all-nighters. Add weekend classes to the mix, and there are weeks when attending a game night means sacrificing a little sleep.
Yet missing a gathering brings its own frustration. Siddiqui says seeing photographs and messages in group chats after an event he couldn't attend leaves him with a genuine fear of missing out. The people he met through these activities have become such a regular part of his life that he doesn't particularly enjoy being absent.
Organisers have their own difficulties. Jawed says maintaining a consistent booking system has been the main challenge for him and his wife. Getting people interested is no longer the problem it was when he started.
For Saniya, who has spent a decade running her book club, the obstacles are considerably broader. Finding affordable venues remains difficult, particularly when the intention is to keep participation free.
She has approached organisations for collaborations, hoping some might offer space for meetings. Removing the venue expense, she explains, makes it easier to arrange gatherings without passing the cost on to readers.
There is also the question of access to books themselves. Imtiaz points to the ease with which people can find places to eat or shop, even in smaller towns, compared with the effort sometimes required to find a bookshop.
She believes reading communities still need greater support, both from institutions and private organisations.
Yet running the club has also brought an unexpected source of help. Imtiaz says homemakers in their forties, fifties and sixties, along with retired people, have volunteered their time to organise activities and support the community.
For some, it has become an opportunity to contribute after years spent managing households or completing their working lives.
Saadia understands the difficulty of committing to a regular gathering. Although she likes the idea of joining a reading club, finding time for it has kept her from taking that step.
It is a reminder that an interest in something does not always translate into attendance. Between work, family, travel and other commitments, even a few hours of leisure can require planning.
There is one thing Saniya has noticed over the years. People who cannot attend every reading session still try to remain involved. Some return after missing several meetings, while others keep up with the discussions whenever they can. For her, that continued interest matters as much as the number of people in the room.
Jawed has seen something similar. People who initially came to learn a board game eventually become familiar faces, comfortable enough to bring their own games and introduce others to something new.
For Siddiqui, what began as an attempt to find something to do outside work has become a regular part of his week. There are still deadlines, classes and family commitments to manage. But there are also people he looks forward to seeing.
The games may change from one evening to another. Some take only a few minutes to learn; others can occupy an entire afternoon. What Siddiqui has gained, though, is a group of people he can call when he wants to play.
And that is something he didn't have when he first moved to the city.

title: The school at home
description: Growing interest in homeschooling reflects parents    concerns about safety and education  but home learning brings responsibilities of its own
content:
Growing interest in homeschooling shows parents' safety concerns, but home learning brings its own responsibilities
For most of the last century, the picture of childhood education was simple: children put on a uniform, walked or rode to a school building, sat in a classroom with dozens of classmates, and returned home in the afternoon. Today that picture is changing. In countries as different as Pakistan, a growing number of parents are deciding that the best classroom for their child is the one in their own living room. Homeschooling, once seen as an unusual choice made by a handful of families, has become a serious and increasingly visible alternative to traditional schooling.
Having spent the last twelve years in the teaching profession, I have seen first-hand both the strengths and the limits of the classroom. I have taught children who blossomed with a little individual attention, and I have also watched capable students slip through the cracks in a room of forty because no one had the time to notice them. For this reason, I understand why parents turn to homeschooling, and I do not dismiss their concerns.
At the same time, my experience has taught me that school is more than lessons and examinations. It is where children learn to share, disagree, compete, cooperate and grow in confidence among people who are not their family. Homeschooling can give a child warmth and focus, but it works best when parents are committed, organised and willing to give the child regular contact with teachers, peers and the wider community. In my view, the real question is not whether home or school is better, but whether each child is receiving a complete education, academic, social and moral, in the setting that suits him or her best.
Homeschooling, also called home education, is the practice of educating children at home or in community settings arranged by the family, rather than in a conventional public or private school. Parents may teach the child themselves, hire private tutors, enroll the child in online courses, or combine several of these methods. Some families follow a formal curriculum that closely resembles what a school would teach. Others prefer a flexible approach in which learning grows out of the child's interests, daily life, travel and projects.
No single reason explains the growth of homeschooling. Families arrive at the decision for many different reasons, and often several of them overlap. The most common are described below.
The most frequent reason is simple disappointment. Parents look at the education their children are receiving and feel it is not good enough. In many public systems, classrooms are overcrowded, teachers are overworked and under-supported, and lessons depend heavily on memorisation for examinations. Even in some expensive private schools, parents complain that results matter more than real understanding. When families lose confidence in the local schools and cannot afford or find a better one, teaching at home starts to look like a realistic option.
Concerns about bullying, violence, peer pressure, and harassment lead some parents to choose homeschooling. It can provide children with a safer environment and give parents greater control over their social surroundings.
In Pakistan, safety is a major reason some parents choose homeschooling. Concerns about terrorism, unsafe transport, bullying, harassment and corporal punishment can make schools feel risky. For some families, home education offers greater physical and emotional security, despite fewer social opportunities.
In a traditional classroom, one teacher must move a whole group through the same material at the same pace. Some children find this too slow and become bored; others find it too fast and quietly fall behind. Homeschooling lets parents match the pace and style of teaching to the individual child. A student who loves mathematics can move ahead, while a student who struggles with reading can spend extra time until the skill is secure. For many parents, this flexibility is the strongest argument in favour of home education.
Some families want education to reflect their faith, moral outlook or cultural traditions. They may feel that mainstream schools either ignore these values or teach ideas that conflict with them. By teaching at home, parents can weave religious study, language, ethics and family traditions into the child's daily education rather than leaving them for evenings and weekends.
Children with learning differences, disabilities or other challenges may struggle in mainstream schools. Homeschooling allows parents to adjust the environment, schedule and teaching methods to meet their needs. It can also benefit gifted children who need more challenging learning.
Homeschooling suits families who travel, move often, or live in remote areas. It also allows children to balance education with activities like sports, music, acting, or entrepreneurship.
Twenty years ago, a parent who wanted to teach advanced science or a foreign language at home would have faced a difficult task. Today, free video lessons, interactive platforms, digital libraries, online tutors and complete virtual curricula are available to anyone with an internet connection. This has lowered the barrier dramatically.
The pandemic closed schools around the world and forced millions of families to teach at home, at least temporarily. For many, the experience was difficult. For others, it was a revelation: they saw how their children learned, discovered that the school day could be much shorter and more focused than they had assumed, and enjoyed the closer family relationship.
In some regions, there is simply no good school within reach, or the available private schools charge fees that families cannot afford. Homeschooling, though not free, can sometimes cost less than private tuition, especially when parents use free online materials and community resources.
Supporters of homeschooling point to several real strengths. A teacher with one or two students can notice immediately when a child is confused, tired or bored, and can respond at once. The learning plan can follow the child's strengths, interests and speed. This one-to-one attention is often cited as the reason homeschooled children can cover material efficiently and develop confidence in their abilities.
Homeschooling is not bound by bells, fixed terms or rigid timetables. Lessons can take place in the morning or evening, on weekdays or weekends, and holidays can be taken when it suits the family. Learning can happen in museums, farms, markets and nature as easily as at a desk. This flexibility can reduce stress and make learning feel more natural and enjoyable.
Spending more time together gives parents and children the chance to build deeper relationships. Parents are more aware of their children's progress, worries and character. Brothers and sisters often learn to cooperate and help one another. Many homeschooling families report a closer, more communicative family life.
At home, children are generally protected from bullying, constant peer comparison and the pressure to fit in. Children who are shy or sensitive may find it easier to ask questions and make mistakes without fear of embarrassment.
Parents can include practical skills that schools often neglect: cooking, budgeting, gardening, basic repairs, first aid and communication. They can also guide moral and character development in a consistent way, connecting what is learned to how the family lives.
Because there is no pressure to cover a fixed syllabus in a fixed time, children can explore subjects in depth. A child fascinated by astronomy, history or coding can spend weeks on it. This depth can build real curiosity and independent thinking, qualities that examinations alone do not measure.
A large part of the school day is spent on registration, transitions, waiting and managing large groups. Homeschooled children often complete their core academic work in a few focused hours, leaving time for reading, hobbies, exercise and creative projects.
Homeschooling is not a perfect solution, and honest discussion must include its limits and risks. A common concern is that homeschooled children may have fewer opportunities to interact with diverse peers. Schools help children develop teamwork, conflict resolution and social skills. Homeschooling families can provide these experiences through sports, community groups, cooperative classes and friendships, but it requires regular effort.
Teaching is a demanding profession. A parent who homeschools must plan lessons, find resources, assess progress and keep the child motivated, often while also managing the household. This is tiring and time-consuming, and the work usually falls most heavily on one parent, who may have to give up a career or reduce working hours. Burnout is a real risk.
Loss of one income, together with the cost of books, materials, online courses, tutors and activities, can place a strain on the family budget. Homeschooling can be inexpensive, but doing it well often is not.
No parent is an expert in every subject. Advanced mathematics, laboratory science and foreign languages can be especially difficult. Without outside checks, gaps in a child's knowledge may go unnoticed for years. Parents may also be tempted to avoid subjects they find difficult or dislike. Tutors, online courses and regular external assessments can reduce the risk, but they require time and money.
Schools provide science laboratories, libraries, sports grounds, music rooms, drama stages and competitions. Replicating these at home is difficult. Children may miss the experience of team sports, school plays, debating contests and group projects unless parents find alternatives elsewhere.
Formal qualifications are often required for university and employment. Homeschooled students may need to take exams as private candidates, which can involve extra costs and paperwork. Families should plan the qualification pathway early.
Spending most of the day with the same few people can create emotional intensity. Without other adults and mentors, a child's view of the world may be narrower. Some children also find it harder to adapt later to the structure of university, workplaces or large organisations. Even a supportive family cannot fully replace the variety of voices and experiences a school provides.
Where regulation is light, there is little to ensure that every homeschooled child is actually receiving a good education or is safe and well. Most homeschooling parents are dedicated and responsible, but the absence of external checks leaves a small number of children at risk of neglect. This is why many educators argue for reasonable registration and periodic assessment.
Is homeschooling right for every family?
Homeschooling can succeed, but it does not suit everyone. Several questions can help a family decide. Can at least one parent commit seriously to planning and supervising the child's learning over many years? Can the family manage on the available income and cover materials and outside classes? Does the child respond well to learning at home, or does he or she thrive on the energy of a classroom? Is there a realistic plan for regular contact with friends and other adults? Are the registration requirements, examinations and future university plans understood?
Many families choose a middle path through part-time homeschooling, hybrid schools or online education. Successful homeschooling usually involves a regular routine, varied learning resources, progress checks and support from other homeschoolers. Most importantly, parents should listen to their children and adapt learning to their changing needs.
Moreover, Erum Khan, who has taught for 14 years, firmly opposes homeschooling. “Children need more than a parent as a teacher because they learn best when exposed to different teachers, ideas and classmates,” she says. Although she acknowledges that individual attention is valuable, she warns that parents may lack training in teaching methods, assessment and certain subjects, which can lead to hidden learning gaps. “Parents cannot handle the children at home,” she adds.
On the issue of safety, Khan understands parents’ concerns but believes the solution should be to make schools safer rather than remove children from them. She also argues that schools teach important life skills such as sharing, teamwork, handling disagreements; waiting for a turn and accepting different opinions; lessons that cannot be fully learned from textbooks.
Homeschooling has become popular because it offers personalised learning, safety, flexibility and greater family involvement. Children can receive individual attention, learn at their own pace and study in a calm, supportive environment.
However, homeschooling has challenges, including limited social interaction, parental pressure, costs and possible learning gaps. Without proper planning, children may miss important skills, qualifications and school experiences.
The wisest conclusion is that homeschooling is neither a miracle nor a mistake. It is a serious responsibility that works best for families who are well prepared, well informed and willing to adapt. Whether a child learns at a school desk or at a kitchen table, the goal is the same: to raise a curious, capable and confident young person ready to take part in the world. The best choice is the one that serves that goal for the particular child in front of us.
Rabia Khan is a freelance writer and researcher focusing on social issues, gender rights, and current affairs. She can be reached at rabiayousufzai26@gmail.com

title: Vows under trial
description: As Christian family law reform gains ground  colonial era statutes leave minority women trapped in broken marriages
content:
As Christian family law reform gains ground, colonial-era statutes leave minority women trapped in broken marriages
For years, Asiya Bibi has lived separately from her husband in the quiet residential pockets of Lahore, bound to a marriage that exists only on paper. She no longer wishes to remain in the union, yet obtaining a legal divorce remains an uphill, almost insurmountable battle. Under current statutory requirements, she must present and prove specific, highly restrictive grounds in court—a process that is not only emotionally exhausting but often legally impossible to establish after years of complete estrangement.
“We have been living completely separate lives for a very long time,” Asiya says, reflecting on the prolonged legal limbo that has defined her recent years. In every practical sense, the marriage ended long ago. “But the law demands that I go to court and publicly prove specific faults or accusations. Why should a woman be forced into lengthy, degrading court battles when both parties know the relationship is irretrievably broken?” Asiya asks.
Asiya calls for a legal framework that grants women the right to dissolve a marriage with dignity, particularly when separation has persisted for years and any prospect of reconciliation has vanished. Her experience highlights the painful disconnect between administrative legal procedures and the lived realities of individuals trapped in unworkable marriages. Asiya’s dilemma reflects a broader structural crisis across Pakistan, where millions of Christian citizens remain governed by colonial-era family laws that have failed to evolve alongside contemporary society.
Marriage, divorce, and inheritance form the bedrock of personal status and family life, yet the legal framework governing these matters for Pakistan’s Christian community dates back to the peak of the British colonial era. The primary statutes—the Christian Marriage Act of 1872, the Divorce Act of 1869, and the Succession Act of 1925—were enacted more than a century ago under the British Raj.
Over the decades, family structures, gender roles, economic dynamics, and social expectations across Pakistan have undergone radical transformations. Yet, these foundational legal statutes remain frozen in time, leaving lawmakers, judges, legal practitioners, and community members continually grappling with provisions that no longer reflect modern social conditions or basic constitutional rights.
While superior courts have occasionally reinterpreted archaic clauses to address pressing grievances, legal experts emphasise that piecemeal judicial interpretation cannot substitute for a comprehensive, legislative overhaul. Relying on courts to bend outdated statutes to fit modern needs creates inconsistency across different jurisdictions, leaving litigating families in state-wide legal uncertainty.
Advocates for reform argue that a modernised family law framework must establish clear, straightforward procedures, safeguard human dignity, and provide effective, accessible remedies when marital or inheritance disputes arise. Crucially, reformers contend that the law should explicitly recognise situations where a marriage has irretrievably broken down, rather than forcing estranged spouses to remain legally bound to a union that has ceased to exist in practice.
Divorce remains the single most formidable legal hurdle for Christian women in Pakistan. Under Section 10 of the Divorce Act of 1869, dissolving a Christian marriage requires fulfilling rigid, narrowly defined grounds. Historically, this meant that grounds for divorce were exceptionally restrictive, leaving women trapped in hostile or abusive households even after years of physical separation, severe domestic conflict, or complete emotional abandonment.
Peter Jacob, executive director of the Centre for Social Justice, points out that the 1869 statute is fundamentally incompatible with contemporary international human rights standards and constitutional guarantees of equal protection. According to Jacob, legal protections for Christian women will remain critically incomplete unless Section 10 is comprehensively amended to incorporate explicit grounds such as mental and physical cruelty, failure to provide financial maintenance, and the irretrievable breakdown of marriage.
“The Divorce Act of 1869 is a colonial-era law and is no longer compatible with contemporary social conditions,” Jacob says. It was drafted for a completely different social milieu. “Judicial interpretations can provide temporary relief in individual cases, but comprehensive reform can only be achieved through legislation by Parliament. A modernised law,” he argues, “should provide clear procedures and safeguards while ensuring that women are not forced to remain in marriages that have effectively ended.”
According to him, women’s legal protection will remain incomplete unless Section 10 of the Divorce Act includes grounds such as cruelty, failure to provide maintenance and irretrievable breakdown of the marriage.
In recent years, superior courts have attempted to bridge this statutory gap through landmark judicial precedents. Lahore High Court advocate Samuel Pyara highlights a crucial ruling delivered in February 2026. In that case, the Lahore High Court held that if a husband and wife have been living apart continuously for two years, the continuous breakdown of the marital relationship and abandonment by a spouse can serve as valid legal grounds for divorce.
Commenting on the landmark decision, Lahore High Court advocate Samuel Pyara points out that judicial recognition of prolonged separation offers much-needed relief to women in unworkable marriages. While progressive rulings set valuable precedents, he maintains that only a comprehensive legislative amendment can deliver lasting, uniform protection across the country.
Recognising the growing urgency of statutory updates, provincial assemblies across Pakistan have initiated steps toward reform, though progress across regions remains fragmented and uneven.
In Punjab, where a significant proportion of Pakistan’s Christian population resides, concrete legislative steps were taken earlier this year. A draft amendment to the Christian Marriage Act was introduced in the Punjab Assembly aimed at overhauling registration standards and age restrictions. In September 2026, the Punjab Assembly’s Standing Committee on Human Rights and Minority Affairs formally approved the draft amendment.
Key provisions of the Punjab draft include setting the uniform minimum marriageable age for both Christian men and women at 18 years, mandating compulsory registration of all Christian marriages, and establishing modern, standardised systems for record-keeping. To support these statutory changes, the Punjab provincial government has also begun developing an online digital portal for marriage registration, aiming to make the process transparent, accessible, and less vulnerable to record tampering or fraud.
Similar legislative stirrings have occurred in other provinces. In Sindh, provincial authorities introduced a draft Christian family law framework to review age, registration, and dissolution standards. Similarly, in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), a draft amendment to the Christian Marriage Act was submitted to the provincial assembly for consideration.
However, despite these encouraging regional efforts, no provincial assembly has yet passed a fully integrated, comprehensive Christian family law code. The absence of a single, unified legal framework means that different aspects of family life—marriage, divorce, child custody, guardianship, and inheritance—continue to be governed by separate, fragmented statutes enacted in different centuries, creating legal ambiguity for families and attorneys alike.
Beyond marriage and divorce, the question of inheritance and property rights remains a vital battleground for Christian women in Pakistan. Matters of succession and inheritance for Christians are primarily governed by the Succession Act of 1925.
While Pakistani courts have repeatedly affirmed that Christian women possess an indisputable legal right to inherit ancestral and acquired property, the real-world execution of these rights is fraught with severe obstacles. In practice, legal rights guaranteed on paper rarely translate automatically into actual property ownership.
Christian women frequently encounter daunting procedural delays when applying for succession certificates, administrative inertia within land revenue departments, and intense socio-cultural pressure or resistance from male relatives. In many cases, property disputes linger in lower courts for years, during which women are deprived of financial security and income generated by inherited assets.
Legal scholars and human rights advocates emphasise that any broad-based reform of Christian family laws must include robust administrative mechanisms to enforce inheritance rights. Streamlining the issuance of succession certificates, penalising coercive property waivers, and creating specialised legal aid mechanisms are critical steps toward ensuring that women can claim their rightful economic shares without fear of intimidation or financial ruin.
As legislative momentum builds, the debate over family law reform has highlighted delicate tensions between civil rights modernisation and religious tradition. Within the Christian community, marriage is viewed not merely as a civil contract recognised by the state, but as a sacred, lifelong spiritual sacrament.
The Church of Pakistan and various denominational leaders have expressed lingering reservations regarding legislative processes that do not fully engage church authorities. Church representatives maintain that because Christian matrimony involves deep theological principles, any alterations to statutory rules governing marriage and dissolution must carefully respect ecclesiastical traditions.
Church leaders argue that while administrative improvements—such as raising the marriage age to 18 and implementing digital registration—are widely welcomed, changes surrounding divorce standards require careful theological nuance. They stress that comprehensive, structured consultations between state lawmakers, legal experts, women's rights organisations, and church leadership are essential to ensure that new laws align with constitutional guarantees without impinging upon religious doctrine.
Falbous Christopher, a Christian member of the Punjab Assembly, emphasises the necessity of building broad consensus among all stakeholders before finalising legislation.
He calls for bringing marriage age, registration, divorce, custody, and inheritance under one comprehensive legal framework, but cautions that all stakeholders—including clergy, legal experts, and civil society—must be taken into confidence to ensure reforms solve real-world problems while respecting the community's religious identity.
The ongoing debate surrounding Christian family laws in Pakistan extends far beyond technical legislative editing. At its core, the drive for reform is about fundamental human rights, gender equality, institutional protection for vulnerable women and children, and equal access to justice under the constitution.
While recent judicial decisions from the Lahore High Court and draft legislative proposals in Punjab, Sindh, and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa mark important steps forward, temporary remedies and piecemeal drafts are not enough. Without a unified, nation-wide or fully enacted provincial legislative framework, thousands of women like Asiya Bibi will remain trapped in legal uncertainty, caught between antiquated nineteenth-century statutes and twenty-first-century social realities.
Achieving meaningful, lasting reform will require sustained political will, parliamentary commitment, and collaborative dialogue among provincial assemblies, higher courts, religious institutions, and civil society advocates. Only through a balanced, comprehensive legislative framework can Pakistan ensure that its Christian citizens are granted the legal certainty, dignity, and rights they deserve.

title: The unseen killer
description: Pakistan faces a growing Hepatitis D challenge as gaps in Hepatitis B diagnosis  follow up and routine screening leave thousands vulnerable to silent liver damage
author_name: Tufail Ahmed, Wisal Yousafzai, Muhammad Ilyas
content:
Pakistan faces growing Hepatitis D challenge as gaps in Hep B diagnosis & screening leave thousands vulnerable
Hepatitis D does not announce itself loudly. The virus can remain hidden for years, quietly accelerating liver damage in people already infected with Hepatitis B, before cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer finally brings the disease to medical attention. For thousands of Pakistanis, the danger may not simply be the virus itself but the gaps that allow it to remain undiagnosed.
Unlike other forms of viral hepatitis, Hepatitis D virus (HDV) cannot infect a person independently. It requires the presence of Hepatitis B virus (HBV) to survive and reproduce. A person can acquire both viruses at the same time, known as coinfection, or develop HDV after already having chronic HBV, known as superinfection. The latter can follow a particularly aggressive course.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) describes chronic Hepatitis D as the most severe form of chronic viral hepatitis because HDV infection can accelerate liver damage and substantially increase the risk of cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer.
Yet Pakistan does not currently have a reliable, up-to-date nationwide estimate of the prevalence of HDV. Available studies have produced widely varying figures because they have generally been conducted among selected hospital or HBV-positive populations rather than through representative national surveys.
A recent WHO-supported survey in Sindh found that 32.8 per cent of HBsAg-positive participants were also positive for anti-HDV antibodies, highlighting the substantial burden in parts of the country. Earlier studies have also reported high rates in Sindh and Balochistan, while lower but still significant levels have been reported in Punjab and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P).
For experts, the absence of reliable nationwide surveillance is itself part of the problem.
Dr Yasar Yousafzai, Professor of Haematology at the Institute of Pathology and Diagnostic Medicine at Khyber Medical University, said HDV was certainly present in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa but its current provincial burden could not be determined because no province-wide survey had been conducted.
“Older studies from K-P have generally found HDV in approximately 10 to 15 per cent of hepatitis-B-positive patients, while one molecular study found HBV-HDV coinfection in around 14 to 15 per cent of patients,” he said.
However, he cautioned that these figures were based on older studies and selected patient groups and could not be used to establish the current prevalence across the province.
“The important issue is that we are not routinely monitoring HDV because testing is not widely available in government or local private-sector facilities,” Dr Yousafzai said.
The problem begins even before HDV testing. A large proportion of people living with Hepatitis B in Pakistan remain undiagnosed, while many of those who are diagnosed do not enter or remain in long-term care. Patients may discover they are infected incidentally during blood donation screening, pre-surgical testing or investigations for another illness, but detection does not always lead to registration, specialist assessment or continued follow-up.
“Many of these patients are identified accidentally, but they are not properly registered or followed up,” Dr Yousafzai said. “They may be lost from the system without confirmation, HDV detection or registration under the provincial programme.”
This creates a critical gap between finding Hepatitis B and completing the diagnostic pathway needed to determine whether a patient also has Hepatitis D.
Both infections can remain silent for years. By the time symptoms such as worsening liver function or other complications become apparent, significant damage may already have occurred.
“By the time obvious symptoms develop, significant liver damage may already have occurred,” Dr Yousafzai said.
He added that tertiary-care hospitals and private gastroenterologists frequently encounter patients with advanced liver disease who were previously unaware that they had HBV or HDV.
Without a provincial patient registry, he said, authorities also cannot determine what proportion of HDV patients eventually develop cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer.
Although specialised HDV testing is technically available in Pakistan, access remains limited.
Current clinical recommendations support screening people who are HBsAg-positive for anti-HDV antibodies at least once. Where antibodies are detected, an HDV RNA PCR test can confirm active infection and determine whether the virus is replicating.
But these tests are not routinely accessible to every Hepatitis B patient, particularly outside major cities.
Dr Yousafzai said some specialised private laboratories could perform HDV RNA testing, while the Public Health Reference Laboratory in K-P did not currently offer Hepatitis D testing.
“The biggest problem is the gap between detecting hepatitis B and completing the HBV-HDV diagnostic pathway,” he said.
The problem is not only availability but affordability. Patients in remote districts may have to travel to larger cities or specialised centres for molecular testing, while the cost of PCR and other investigations can place diagnosis beyond the reach of low-income families.
A recent survey of Pakistani liver specialists similarly highlighted the financial barrier. Around 83 per cent of experts surveyed said HDV diagnostic tests were available but unaffordable for many patients. Only about half reported routinely ordering the specific PCR test for HDV among their Hepatitis B patients.
For patients already struggling with the cost of repeated consultations, liver-function tests, imaging and antiviral medicines, an additional molecular test can become a significant burden.
The problem is particularly visible in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, where the provincial hepatitis programme provides services for Hepatitis B and C but HDV has not been systematically incorporated into routine surveillance and diagnostic systems.
Dr Tariq Mehmood, Director of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa's Integrated Programme on HIV, Hepatitis and Thalassaemia, confirmed that the programme's current mandate primarily covers Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C.
“Under our programme, our mandate is focused on hepatitis B and hepatitis C,” he said.
For specialists, this omission is significant because the consequences of missing HDV can be severe.
Dr Mushtaq Ahmad, Assistant Professor of Gastroenterology and Hepatology at KMU Hospital and Research Centre, described HDV as an aggressive infection that can significantly increase the risk of severe liver damage, cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer.
“Superinfection can follow an especially aggressive course,” he said, explaining that it can lead to rapid progression of liver fibrosis and cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation and liver failure, while also increasing the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
HDV is primarily transmitted through exposure to infected blood and body fluids. Unsafe injections, contaminated needles, inadequately sterilised medical or dental equipment, unsafe blood transfusions and contaminated sharp instruments can all create a risk. Sharing razors and other objects contaminated with blood can also transmit the virus, while sexual transmission is possible.
The virus does not spread through food or water or through ordinary social contact. Shaking hands, hugging, sharing meals or sitting with someone infected with HDV does not transmit the disease.
Dr Imran Ali Syed, consultant gastroenterologist and hepatologist, said the presence of HBV was fundamental to HDV infection.
“Hepatitis D is a viral liver infection that can only occur in people who have Hepatitis B,” he said, adding that HDV can make HBV infection more severe and accelerate progression to cirrhosis and liver cancer.
He said HDV had been reported particularly in Balochistan and Sindh, followed by Punjab, but stressed that there was no reliable current nationwide estimate.
Punjab has established a network of hepatitis clinics through its provincial programme, providing services including registration, testing, vaccination and treatment for Hepatitis B and C. District and tehsil-level hospitals are also part of the system.
However, the situation is less clear when it comes to Hepatitis D. Available government information does not indicate a comparable province-wide programme specifically providing free and routine HDV screening and treatment. This creates a potential gap for patients who have already tested positive for HBV.
Dr Salman Kazmi, a Lahore-based internal medicine specialist, believed that expensive diagnostic tests, limited availability, low public awareness and the absence of a clear national screening policy remained important obstacles.
The issue is particularly important because Hepatitis B patients can require long-term monitoring even when they have few or no symptoms. If HDV is not considered during this follow-up, a potentially serious additional infection can remain undetected.
Managing HDV is considerably more challenging than preventing it.
The objectives of treatment are to suppress HDV replication, reduce liver inflammation and prevent progression to cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer.
Pegylated interferon-alpha remains an option for carefully selected patients under specialist supervision. Newer treatments, including bulevirtide, have emerged internationally but remain of limited availability in Pakistan.
Medicines such as tenofovir and entecavir may be prescribed to control Hepatitis B when clinically indicated, but they do not directly suppress HDV replication.
For patients, this can mean prolonged specialist follow-up, repeated blood tests and monitoring for liver complications.
The burden extends beyond medicine. Patients may need to travel repeatedly to tertiary-care hospitals, while families face transport, accommodation and lost-income costs.
In Punjab, patients interviewed for an investigation described being referred to major centres such as the Pakistan Kidney and Liver Institute in Lahore, sometimes after first seeking treatment closer to home. Their experiences highlighted the financial and logistical difficulties of repeated testing and hospital visits.
The medical principle, however, is that not every hepatitis patient necessarily requires referral to a specialised liver centre. Patients with uncomplicated disease can often be managed through appropriate district-level services, while those with advanced cirrhosis, liver failure, complex procedures or transplantation needs require specialised care.
The key question, therefore, is whether referrals are being made because of genuine clinical need or because appropriate diagnostic and treatment facilities are unavailable closer to patients' homes.
Because HDV depends on HBV, preventing Hepatitis B is also the most effective way to prevent Hepatitis D.
Dr Imran Ali Syed said vaccination against Hepatitis B was the most important preventive measure. Safe injections, screened blood, sterile medical and dental equipment, safe sexual practices and testing of people living with HBV were also essential.
This makes strengthening HBV diagnosis and vaccination a central part of any national HDV strategy.
Experts also believe that people already diagnosed with Hepatitis B should not be lost from the healthcare system. They should receive appropriate follow-up, and HDV screening should become part of their clinical assessment.
A recent survey of Pakistani specialists found strong support for formally incorporating HDV into national hepatitis programmes. More than 83 per cent of experts supported treating HDV as a distinct component of the national response, alongside clearer screening guidelines, awareness campaigns and improved access to treatment.
For a country already carrying a substantial Hepatitis B burden, the failure to identify how many patients are also living with HDV creates a dangerous blind spot.
The absence of reliable nationwide data does not mean the disease is absent. Instead, it means Pakistan cannot accurately determine where the burden is highest, how many patients require treatment or how many are progressing towards cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer.
Experts believe the response should begin with routine anti-HDV screening for people diagnosed with Hepatitis B, followed by HDV RNA PCR confirmation where appropriate. Testing should be made affordable and available beyond major tertiary-care hospitals.
A stronger response would also require a patient registry, integration of HDV into provincial hepatitis programmes, continuous availability of medicines, decentralised diagnostic services and clear referral pathways for complicated cases.
Public awareness is equally important. Patients need to know that a Hepatitis B diagnosis is not the end of the diagnostic process and that Hepatitis D can significantly alter the course of their illness.
Most importantly, prevention must remain at the centre of the strategy. Every Hepatitis B infection prevented through vaccination is also an HDV infection that cannot occur.
For Pakistan, the challenge is therefore not simply treating Hepatitis D after it appears. It is closing the gaps that allow Hepatitis B and HDV to remain undiagnosed, unmonitored and untreated until irreversible liver damage has already begun.

title: Peshawar pilot dies in plane crash
description: Qazi Zafar of renowned flying family succumbs to injuries  companion critically hurt
content:
Qazi Zafar of renowned flying family succumbs to injuries; companion critically hurt
Another pilot from the well-known Qazi family, long associated with the Peshawar Flying Club, has lost his life in a microlight aircraft accident. Qazi Zafar was killed when his aircraft crashed during a flight in Punjab's Jhang district on Saturday.
According to local sources, Qazi Zafar was piloting the microlight when the aircraft met with the accident. A friend travelling with him was also on board and sustained serious injuries in the crash. Qazi Zafar, however, could not survive his wounds and succumbed soon afterwards. Sources said the pilot had returned to Pakistan from abroad only a short while ago.
The tragic incident has cast a shadow of grief over the Qazi family and the wider community in Landi Arbab, Peshawar, from where the late pilot hailed.
Former Member of the Provincial Assembly Malik Wajidullah Khan expressed deep sorrow over the untimely death. In a statement, he described Qazi Zafar's sudden demise as a painful tragedy that has left the pilot's family, relatives and local residents in mourning.
"The sudden death of Qazi Zafar is a deeply unfortunate incident. His family, loved ones and the people of the area are grief-stricken. In this hour of sorrow we stand shoulder to shoulder with the bereaved family," Malik Wajidullah Khan said.
He prayed that Almighty Allah grant the late pilot complete forgiveness, elevate him to a high rank in Paradise, and bestow patience upon all those left behind.
The accident has once again highlighted the risks faced by light-aircraft enthusiasts in the country. Further details about the cause of the crash are awaited.
It may be recalled that the renowned Qazi family of Peshawar (Landi Arbab) has a history of passion for amateur aviation, manufacturing gliders, and piloting aircraft, but this pursuit has unfortunately resulted in multiple tragic and fatal accidents rather than injuries.
Historically, the family's amateur aviation journey began in the late 1980s when Qazi Sajjad and his brothers started building home-made gliders out of parachute material and bamboo sticks. Early on, their maiden flight crashed into trees, leaving the pilot seriously injured. Later, the family suffered a string of devastating losses:
Qazi Ajmal lost his life in December 2021 when his small gyrocopter crashed into the mountains near Kund Malir in Balochistan. His family noted that he was compelled to take off in pitch darkness due to security threats in the area, leading to the fatal crash. Following this incident, the family announced they would quit their flying practices.

title: Armed attack on police post foiled in Sibi
description: Armed attack on police post foiled in Sibi
content:
An attempted assault by armed militants on a police checkpoint near Dosa Cross in Sibi was thwarted on Saturday when security forces responded swiftly, killing one terrorist and injuring two others in an exchange of fire.
According to security sources, a group of armed individuals launched an attack on the police post located along National Highway N-65 near Dosa Cross in Sibi district. Acting on immediate information, the Frontier Corps Quick Response Force rushed to the scene and engaged the attackers. In the ensuing gun battle, one terrorist was killed while two others sustained injuries. Security personnel recovered a substantial cache of arms and ammunition from the site. A search and clearance operation remains underway in the surrounding area to eliminate any remaining threat.
In a separate development, Sardar Shah Zaman Khan Alizai, a prominent tribal figure from Mastung, and his son have been safely recovered nearly a month after their abduction. Local administration officials confirmed that the pair returned home on Friday.
The two were kidnapped on August 19 by armed men near Sorgaz while travelling from Quetta to Mastung. Efforts for their recovery had continued over the intervening period. Their safe return has brought relief to the family and the local community.
Security officials have not released further details regarding the identity of the slain militant or the condition of the injured attackers. Investigations into both incidents are continuing, with forces maintaining heightened vigilance along the highway and in the wider region.

title: PESHAWAR | The Express Tribune
description:
UoP reclaims Rs5b bungalow after 
22-year battle
content:
Property to fund scholarships for needy students
After a 22-year legal struggle, the University of Peshawar has finally taken possession of a bungalow worth Rs5 billion located on Gul Maher Lane in University Town.
The property, spread over more than nine kanals, was dedicated through a registered waqf deed dated January 2, 1974, by the late Begum Kulsoom Amin Durrani. She had endowed it for the welfare of students and the provision of scholarships to deserving students. Income generated from the property is expected to support up to 350 scholarships for needy students of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa.
The university approached a civil court on September 21, 2004, seeking legal title and possession of the property. After prolonged proceedings, the civil court on June 22, 2013, declared the property a waqf, recognised the UoP as its mutawalli (trustee), and restrained the defendants from selling or transferring it.
An appeal against the decision was dismissed by the Additional District Judge-II, Peshawar, on November 15, 2023. The Peshawar High Court vacated the stay order on March 23, 2025, and later dismissed civil revision petitions filed by the opposing party on October 15, 2026.
To enforce the court orders, the executing court's civil judge directed the SSP Operations, Peshawar, on October 9, 2026, to provide police force along with the court bailiff so that possession could be handed over to the university's authorised officer. On Friday, October 16, the court bailiff transferred possession of the bungalow to the Registrar of the UoP in compliance with the judicial directives.

title: Kundi moves to curb dengue as cases surge
description: Kundi moves to curb dengue as cases surge
content:
Kohat worst-hit with 2,319 infections; two deaths reported province-wide
An important high-level meeting was held under the chairmanship of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi to review the dengue situation in the province, assess measures to prevent its further spread and evaluate the overall anti-dengue response.
Advisor for Health Lieutenant General (retired) Nigar Johar, the Secretary Health and other senior officials of relevant departments attended the meeting. Officials gave the Governor a detailed briefing on the latest dengue statistics, the implementation status of the anti-dengue action plan, the functioning of the reporting and surveillance system, and other steps being taken to contain the disease.
According to the briefing, a total of 3,771 dengue cases have so far been reported across the province, while two deaths have been attributed to the disease. District Kohat remains the worst-affected area, accounting for 2,319 of the confirmed cases. Officials informed the meeting that climate change, unplanned growth of urban populations, poor sanitation conditions, electricity load-shedding and several other contributing factors are facilitating the spread of dengue.
A comprehensive action plan has been prepared to combat the disease. The plan clearly assigns responsibilities to all relevant departments and district administrations. Steps are under way to further strengthen the reporting and surveillance system so that cases can be detected and monitored in a timely manner.
In parallel, an awareness campaign is being conducted with the support of concerned departments to educate the public about dengue prevention and control. To handle any emergency, isolation wards with a total capacity of 1,666 beds have been established across the province.
Governor Faisal Karim Kundi directed the Kohat district administration to take effective measures on an emergency basis to bring the outbreak under control and to keep him continuously informed of the progress. He further instructed that immediate and effective steps be taken in other affected districts as well, in close coordination with the respective district administrations.
The Governor emphasised that the resources required by district administrations for an effective anti-dengue campaign must be provided on a priority basis so that the spread of the epidemic can be checked and the public protected from its harmful effects.

title: Haze triggers highest level alert in parts of Southeast Asia  monitor
description: Haze triggers highest level alert in parts of Southeast Asia  monitor
content:
Fires in Indonesia that have sent toxic smoke disrupting daily life across Southeast Asia has triggered the highest-level alert by the regional bloc's meteorological monitor.
The months-long pollution spell has closed schools, fuelled a surge in respiratory conditions and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.
"This thing needs to stop," Zul Hafiz, a 39-year-old teacher cycling from the Malaysian city of Shah Alam to the capital, told AFP on Saturday, calling on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to take action.
The 11-country organisation's ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) said in a notice on its website on Friday that it had activated "Alert Level 3 for the Southern ASEAN region" -- the highest rung of a four-tiered alert system.
The alert level is triggered when there is a "high risk of severe transboundary haze in the region" and is reserved for widespread moderate to dense smoke haze, observed over two or more consecutive days.
The ASMC has already issued two Level 3 alerts this year, according to its website.
Singapore ranked second on IQAir's live ranking of the world's most polluted major cities behind Baghdad on Saturday, with Kuala Lumpur third. All readings showed "very hazardous" levels."
Indonesia said Saturday it had been using dry ice at one of South Sumatra province's main airports in an attempt to disperse the haze.
The country's national disaster mitigation agency said that 2.4 tonnes of dry ice were dispersed by plane.
"The smoke not only reduces visibility and disrupts aircraft operations, but also affects residents' health," the agency warned.
The haze has disrupted life across Southeast Asia, sparking fresh calls for action from residents in Kuala Lumpur.
"It's a bit unfair on Malaysia because of the irresponsible behaviour of our neighbouring country," Khairul Azhar, a 33-year-old bank officer told AFP.
"This is affecting our weekend routine -- not just for us but many Malaysians," he said.
In East Timor, unhealthy air pollution persisted on Saturday, including in the capital Dili, according to IQAir.

title: Brazil s Bolsonaro says not considering father for govt post
description: Brazil s Bolsonaro says not considering father for govt post
content:
Brazil's right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro said on Friday that he had not considered giving his father a government position in the event of victory, though he did not rule out the possibility.
Bolsonaro will face leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on October 25 in the country's presidential election runoff.
Former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio's father, is currently under house arrest for planning a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula.
"He has never suggested that he would like to work in the government... he has never raised the subject with me, so it's not on the radar," Flavio Bolsonaro said in an interview with TV Globo.
He did not close the door on the possibility of his father's involvement in government should he win, though the 45-year-old ruled out appointing his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro as foreign minister.
Eduardo, 42, gave up his seat as a lawmaker in Brazil when he moved to the United States last year.
He was sentenced in absentia in June to four years and two months in prison after urging US sanctions on his country during his father's coup trial.
During the interview, Flavio Bolsonaro described the incumbent government as "chaos" and insisted that the "Lula era is about to end."
"There are only nine days left before the election, before we can turn this sad page of history," the senator said.
Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula by 47 percent to 45 percent in the first round of voting on October 4.
A Datafolha poll published on Thursday showed his lead in the runoff narrowing from four percentage points to two, putting the rivals in a statistical tie.
Bolsonaro was on 51 percent of valid votes against Lula's 49 percent, within the survey's two-point margin of error.

title: US budget deficit grows to nearly  2 trillion  highest since 2021
description: US budget deficit grows to nearly  2 trillion  highest since 2021
content:
The US budget deficit grew to almost $2 trillion over the past year, government data showed Friday, reaching its highest level since 2021 despite President Donald Trump's promises to cut public spending.
The expansion comes amid growing worries over the massive $40.3 trillion US debt load and rising inflation, as the cost of borrowing climbs.
Refunds of Trump's tariffs after they were overturned have further fueled the budget gap.
The federal deficit, which occurs when government spending exceeds its revenues, rose to $1.99 trillion in fiscal year 2026, the Treasury Department said.
This marked a 12-percent increase from the prior year, when the shortfall came in at $1.78 trillion.
A key driver of expenditures was the rising interest paid on public debt, which jumped $144 billion to a record $1.36 trillion.
Interest costs on around $32 trillion in publicly held US debt have been ballooning in recent years, and climbing bond yields have sparked further concerns.
Treasury bond yields, which influence interest rates for mortgages and auto loans, have jumped this year, with steeper borrowing costs adding to pressures that US voters face ahead of November's midterm elections.
Meanwhile, an expected influx of revenue from Trump's sweeping tariffs have failed to fully materialize during his second term.
The Supreme Court struck down his global duties in February, triggering a wave of refunds.
Treasury data released Friday reflected $145 billion in customs refunds over the year -- primarily due to tariffs -- erasing significant gains from Trump's duties.
Overall, government revenues climbed by three percent to $5.40 trillion in the latest fiscal year, which ended September 30.
But spending was much higher, rising by six percent to $7.40 trillion.
The deficit will likely be similar for the next year, said Nancy Vanden Houten of Oxford Economics.
But she warned "the risk may be for a larger budget gap if the war with Iran persists well into the fiscal year."
The Trump administration has pledged to cut deficits and government spending since he returned to the White House last year.
Besides slashing the federal workforce and foreign aid, the Republican-controlled Congress pushed through cuts to the Medicaid health insurance scheme and moved to shrink the federal food assistance program too.
But they also extended expiring tax cuts and provided fresh funding for Trump's migrant deportation drive.
The latest data released Friday showed that upticks in tax collection from individuals and customs revenues were offset by higher refunds and lower corporate tax collection.
Among other sectors, spending on defense military programs increased by $48 billion, or six percent, over the year to $917 billion.
Taken together, a Treasury official estimates the US deficit-to-GDP ratio is around 6.2 percent, up from 5.8 percent last year.
This stands in contrast to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's previously stated goal of bringing the deficit down to three percent of GDP, alongside other targets like spurring economic growth of three percent.
The latest budget figures come less than three weeks before US midterm elections, where Trump's Republican party is fighting to retain control of Congress.
Ahead of the crucial vote, both Republicans and Democrats have raised ideas that could widen the budget shortfall further.
Trump recently promised $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans maintained control of Congress, a plan that would cost over $1 trillion.
Democrats say they are looking to reverse Medicaid cuts and revive health care tax breaks.

title: Food security goes beyond availability
