title: PSX struggles on weak indicators
description: PSX struggles on weak indicators
content:
Benchmark KSE-100 index recovers late, ends week lower by 670 points
Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) fell 0.4% during the outgoing week, shedding 670 points, as persistent geopolitical tensions, elevated crude oil prices and concerns over a possible rate hike dampened investor sentiment.
On a day-on-day basis, political clouds kept sentiment subdued on Monday, with the benchmark KSE-100 index declining 1,965 points (-1.18%) to close at 165,124. On the next day, the PSX witnessed a mixed and volatile session, when the index declined 348 points (-0.21%) to close at 164,776, slipping below the key psychological support level of 165,000.
On Wednesday, the market tentatively rebounded amid geopolitical uncertainty, with the benchmark index gaining 641 points (+0.39%) to close at 165,418, reclaiming the psychological level of 165,000. Positive momentum continued on the second last day of the trading week as the PSX held ground above 166k. The index gained 769 points (+0.46%) and closed at 166,186. The market concluded the week with a range-bound session, modestly rising by 234 points (+0.14%) at 166,420.
"The KSE-100 declined marginally by 0.4% week-on-week to 166,419 points, shedding 670 points, primarily due to persistent geopolitical uncertainty," said Arif Habib Limited (AHL) in its weekly report.
Among major economic data, Pakistan's trade deficit widened 5% year-on-year (YoY) and 7% month-on-month (MoM) to $3.53 billion in September 2026 as exports increased 18% YoY and 17% MoM to $2.96 billion, while imports grew 11% YoY and MoM to $6.49 billion. During 1QFY27, the trade deficit expanded 15% YoY to $10.77 billion, with exports rising 11% to $8.45 billion, while imports increased 13% to $19.21 billion.
AHL mentioned that the government raised Rs685.5 billion in T-bills' auction against the target of Rs550 billion, with cut-off yields inching up 0.5 basis point in three-month and 12-month tenors, while declining 5.1 basis points in the one-month and 17.9 basis points in the six-month tenor. The largest amount of Rs310.1 billion was raised via three-month papers.
The PSX recorded its highest-ever monthly addition of 25,280 new investor accounts in September, bringing total UINs to a record 656k, up 55% YoY from 423k in September 2025, reflecting growing investor confidence and broader participation in Pakistan's capital market.
Pakistan's gross Roshan Digital Account (RDA) inflows reached $14,157 million as of Sept'26. Out of the total received funds, $2,146 million has been repatriated while $8,937 million has been utilised locally. With this, the net repatriable liability stood at $3,074 million.
Oil production declined 1.7% WoW to 62.5k barrels per day, mainly due to lower flows from northern fields, while gas production decreased slightly by 0.2% WoW to 2,992 mmcfd, driven by lower production from Uch, Nashpa and Sharf.
Auto sales (cars, LCVs, vans and jeeps) decreased 3% MoM to 15.1k units during Sept'26, reflecting a decline of 12% YoY, while cumulative sales during 1QFY27 increased 19% YoY to reach 50.5k units.
Pakistan recorded a current account deficit of $356 million in September, compared to a surplus of $133 million in September last year and a deficit of $73 million in Aug'26, taking cumulative deficit for 1QFY27 to $874 million, up from $755 million in the same period of last year. Among petroleum prices, motor spirit recorded a 2.1% WoW decline to Rs390.23/litre, while high-speed diesel rose 0.3% to Rs396.96/litre, AHL added.
Topline's weekly review noted that the KSE-100 index continued its downward trajectory, declining 0.4% WoW, primarily driven by elevated crude oil prices amid US-Iran geopolitical tensions and expectations of a potential policy rate hike by the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) at its upcoming monetary policy meeting to contain inflationary pressures.
Key developments during the outgoing week included: (1) automobile sales, as reported by PAMA, totalled 15,104 units in September 2026, down 12% YoY and 3% MoM; (2) the Large-Scale Manufacturing (LSM) Index increased 0.7% YoY in August 2026 but declined 5% MoM; (3) the current account recorded a deficit of $356 million in September 2026, widening from $73 million in August 2026; and (4) Pakistan's Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) rose to 108.93 in September from 107.92 in August. Average daily traded volume and value during the week stood at 449 million shares and Rs18 billion, respectively, Topline said.

title: Govt moves to revive small industry
description: Govt moves to revive small industry
content:
Approves Rs2 billion for interventions under revamping plan
The government has approved the release of Rs2 billion to revive the small industry, which is considered a vital pillar of an economy but it has been virtually wiped out of the country.
Small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs) have been contributing to the economic growth of developed countries for decades but in Pakistan the big industry has turned into giants while swallowing the small ones.
Considering the significant importance of SMEs, the present government is working on a plan of reviving the small industry, which can give a push to the modest annual economic growth, described as insufficient to absorb new entrants in the workforce every year.
The Ministry of Industries and Production briefed the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) in a recent meeting that the prime minister had approved a business plan for revamping and transforming the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Authority (Smeda) into a dynamic, responsive and result-oriented institution with a strengthened focus on promoting sustainable growth, modernisation, productivity and competitiveness of Pakistan's small, medium and micro enterprises.
The Ministry of Industries apprised the ECC that pursuant to approval from the prime minister, Rs2 billion had been provided in the federal budget for financial year 2026-27, specifically for approved interventions under the Smeda business plan. It was informed that the proposed funding was supported by a comprehensive cash plan, which set out intervention-wise implementation targets and the estimated expenditure and corresponding funding requirements during the current financial year.
In order to ensure transparent, accountable and purpose-specific utilisation of funds allocated for implementation of the prime minister's revamping plan, a dedicated assignment account had been kept in the NBP main branch, Lahore under the Accountant General Pakistan Revenues (AGPR) sub-office, Lahore.
The Ministry of Industries further informed the meeting that the Finance Division had conveyed its agreement to the release of Rs2 billion in favour of Smeda for approved interventions under the revamping plan. However, as the requisite provision was to be made through a technical supplementary grant, the approval of the ECC was required for incorporation/provision of the budgetary allocation.
Accordingly, a summary for consideration of the ECC was being submitted to obtain its approval for the release of the supplementary grant. It was pointed out that a draft summary was also shared with the Finance Division for its views and comments.
The Ministry of Industries said that the prime minister, both in his capacity as the PM and the minister in charge of Industries and Production Division, had accorded his approval for submission of the summary to the ECC. The ministry solicited approval of the ECC for provision of the technical supplementary grant amounting to Rs2 billion in favour of Smeda during financial year 2026-27 for making approved interventions under the business plan.
The ECC considered the summary submitted by the Ministry of Industries titled "Technical Supplementary Grant for Implementation of the Business Plan under Prime Minister's Revamping Plan for Small and Medium Enterprises Development Authority (Smeda) during Current Financial Year 2026-27" and approved the proposal.

title: SBP rebuilt reserves without new debt
description: SBP rebuilt reserves without new debt
content:
Forward liabilities cut to under $1b from $5.7b; external debt barely rose in three years
State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) foreign exchange reserves recovered from less than $3 billion in February 2023 to $21.5 billion by October 9, 2026, and the build came from the central bank's own foreign exchange purchases rather than new borrowing, with the external debt stock rising only marginally over the last three years, Governor Jameel Ahmad told foreign investors at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
SBP's forward liabilities were reduced from over $5.7 billion to less than $1 billion, he said, according to a statement issued on Saturday. The FX purchases were facilitated by an almost balanced current account in FY26.
The governor held meetings with senior executives from JP Morgan, Citibank, Jefferies, Deutsche Bank, Barclays, Bank of America, MSCI, Standard Chartered and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group from October 12 to 17, along with bilateral and multilateral partners, other central banks and global credit rating agencies.
He said the economy has become more resilient to domestic and external shocks as a result of sustained macroeconomic policies and structural reforms. Inflation declined sharply from elevated levels in FY23 to almost within the target range in FY26 despite the significant oil price shock. Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth, after contracting in FY23, reached 3.7% in FY26 and is projected at 3.5% to 4.5% in FY27.
Regulatory reforms, especially for exchange companies and to encourage channelling of remittances through formal channels, have improved interbank foreign exchange liquidity, he said. Foreign exchange purchases are expected to continue, with the current account deficit projected to remain within 0% to 1% of GDP in FY27.
The fiscal position has also strengthened, with the primary fiscal balance posting a third consecutive annual surplus in FY26, putting the public debt-to-GDP ratio on a downward trajectory.
A staff-level agreement has been reached with the IMF for the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF) reviews. Continued implementation of the reform agenda has improved investor confidence, led to sovereign credit rating upgrades and facilitated Pakistan's access to global capital markets despite a challenging global environment.
He emphasised that Pakistan's economic fundamentals remain strong, supported by a prudent policy mix that has cushioned the impact of multiple shocks over the last three years. While ongoing geopolitical developments pose challenges, he said the economy is in a significantly better position to withstand this shock than during previous periods of external stress.
The governor reaffirmed SBP's commitment to safeguarding hard-earned macroeconomic stability, strengthening external buffers and advancing structural reforms for sustainable economic growth.

title: No gas queues  no shortage  FinMin
description: No gas queues  no shortage  FinMin
content:
Says Pakistan prepared for winter but attacks on Gulf infrastructure worrying
Pakistan's finance minister has told Agence France-Presse (AFP) the country has so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices caused by the Iran war, but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook, according to a report published by AFP.
In an interview on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Muhammad Aurangzeb said the South Asian country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.
"The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan," he said. "We've had no shortage, no queues at the gas stations, and no law and order situation, which at times we have seen in some of the countries."
He added that unless the government saw "an absolute dire need", it would not be procuring spot cargoes on the liquefied natural gas (LNG) front, which tend to be far more expensive than previously contracted shipments.
Since the United States and ally Israel launched the war on Iran in February, global energy prices have surged as Tehran's retaliatory action has targeted Washington's Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies. With Yemen's civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure, including energy facilities and airports, in recent days.
Aurangzeb expressed alarm at the escalation, saying damage to such sites would delay a return to economic normalcy. "What is now the worrying part of it is when the energy infrastructure starts getting hit," he said. "I, to be very honest, I don't know where that would go. But one thing is very clear: that if the infrastructure continues to get hit, the return to normalcy, even if things subside, will take longer."
Pakistan has been a frequent customer at the IMF, the lender of last resort to countries on the brink of default. It is currently in the midst of its 25th programme with the Fund, at least 11 of which have been outright bailouts, since gaining independence in 1947. The current programme totals around $7 billion over three years, with the Fund reaching an agreement this month to release a $1.2 billion tranche.
With global debt stocks running high, the Fund has called at this year's annual meetings on all economies, even those most vulnerable to the Iran war shock, to engage in fiscal consolidation to avoid a potential crisis. "Fortunately for us, we have been on this fiscal consolidation path for a while," Aurangzeb said with a rueful smile.
The country's tax revenues have grown significantly in recent years, and the finance minister said the government was targeting the theft of taxes by private sector businesses that collected sales tax from consumers but never deposited it in government accounts. Such theft accounted for billions of dollars, he said, adding that there remained "room for improvement" on increasing income tax collection as well.
He said the government's reform agenda had faced resistance from industry, lobbying groups and vested interests. "Every reform, everything that you try to do when you try to change the status quo, there is pushback," he said.
One of the major pillars of the IMF's programme criteria is privatising state-owned assets in Pakistan, where the military runs a vast empire of businesses in sectors from real estate to fertiliser. Asked about those companies, Aurangzeb denied that they were receiving state funding. "As far as we are concerned, whichever commercial enterprises the military are running, they are running on a standalone basis and profitable on their own basis," he said. "So, I can confirm to you, we are not providing any funds from the exchequer."
Pakistan's military has directly ruled the country for roughly two-fifths of its history, and under current Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir it has tightened its grip over key pillars of power, even as a civilian government remains nominally in charge of the state.
Separately, Aurangzeb held a series of engagements with international development partners, financial institutions and the IMF to discuss development financing, sovereign debt management, capital market access, investment opportunities and Pakistan's economic resilience amid regional and global uncertainty, according to a statement issued on Saturday.
With Alexander De Croo, Administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and UN Under-Secretary-General, he discussed development financing, climate resilience and employment generation, emphasising the need to strengthen implementation capacity to translate financing and policy frameworks into bankable projects. Discussions covered UNDP's Implementation Bridge, an investable pipeline through the SDG Investment Fair and V20 platform, blended finance, public-private partnerships and closer UNDP-World Bank cooperation, alongside biodiversity financing and potential debt-for-nature and debt-for-climate swaps.
The finance minister met delegations from Sharjah Islamic Bank, Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, Ajman Bank and JP Morgan, highlighting progress under the IMF programme, fiscal consolidation, stronger foreign exchange reserves, improved sovereign credit ratings and restored access to international capital markets. Discussions covered prospective Sukuk issuances, rupee-denominated dollar-settled instruments, further Panda Bond issuance and possible Eurobond tokenisation, with emphasis on replacing costly short-term debt and extending maturities without increasing overall external debt.
With Jihad Azour, Director of the IMF's Middle East and Central Asia Department, the finance minister reviewed Pakistan's economic performance, including revenue mobilisation, inflation, growth and the current account. He outlined energy procurement and winter preparedness measures and highlighted adequate fertiliser supplies to safeguard food security, alongside stronger reserves, reduced forward liabilities and longer debt maturities. Both sides discussed privatisation, greater private-sector participation and export-oriented growth, emphasising reform momentum, political commitment and effective communication.

title: Pakistan extends airspace ban for Indian aircraft until October 23
description: Restriction applies to all civil and military aircraft of Indian airlines  marking the 19th consecutive month of the airspace ban
content:
Restriction applies to all civil and military aircraft of Indian airlines, marking 19th consecutive month of ban
Pakistan extended the closure of its airspace to Indian aircraft for another month, with the restriction remaining in place until November 24, the Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA) said on Saturday.
“Pakistan’s airspace will remain closed to Indian aircraft until November 24,” the PAA said in a new Notice to Airmen (NOTAM), making it the 19th consecutive month of the closure.
The restriction applies to all civil and military aircraft of Indian-registered airlines, the notice says. The authority added that under the extended restriction, no Indian-registered aircraft can use Pakistan's airspace, even if the aircraft has been taken on lease.
Read : Iran war deals double blow to Indian airlines already hit by Pakistan airspace ban
PAA issued the new NOTAM on the government’s directions.
Earlier, the PAA extended the restriction on Indian aircraft using its airspace until October 23 .
Pakistan has kept its airspace closed to Indian aircraft since April 2025, when tensions between Islamabad and New Delhi sharply escalated after an attack in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir’s Pahalgam.
The attack killed 26 people; India immediately blamed Pakistan for the incident. Pakistan, however, categorically rejected the blame and offered to support a neutral investigation.
In response, India undertook a series of hostile actions the day after the incident. On April 23, 2025, it suspended the 65-year-old Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), cancelling visas for Pakistani citizens, closing the Wagah-Attari border crossing, ordering the shutdown of the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi, and reducing diplomatic staff at each other's embassies.
Tensions further escalated in May, when missile strikes hit six cities in Punjab and Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), destroying a mosque and killing dozens of civilians, including women, children, and the elderly.
Read More: Air India feels the heat of Pak airspace ban
In response, Pakistan’s armed forces shot down Indian warplanes, including three Rafale jets. India then targeted several Pakistani airbases with missile strikes. In retaliation, Pakistan launched Operation Bunyanum Marsoos , damaging Indian military installations, including missile storage sites, airbases, and other strategic targets.
On May 10, 2025, United States President Donald Trump announced that a ceasefire had been reached following intense diplomatic efforts. Minutes later, the agreement was confirmed separately by Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and the Indian foreign secretary.

title: Am I brave  or a falsified feminist  Or was it a British insult  sir
description: Am I brave  or a falsified feminist  Or was it a British insult  sir
content:
'Brave' can be praise; it can be solidarity. In British usage, depending on the tone
A short scroll through social media and some of Pakistan's leading newspapers has made me realise, once again, that perhaps we are becoming a little more "mature" as a society.
The quotation marks matter. For years, some of the most visible disclosures of childhood sexual abuse by well-known women, particularly from showbusiness, involved chowkidaars, maalis and other men who entered the household through work. Those disclosures were important and should never be belittled. But have we quietly created a mental map in which abuse belongs to that constituency? A perpetrator has no particular occupation, beard or bank balance. He can be a driver or a doctor, a cook or a civil servant. Respectability is not a risk assessment.
Recently, senior civil servant Maliha Sehr, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Headquarters), Rawalpindi, filed a police complaint alleging prolonged domestic violence by her husband. He is on judicial remand. The allegations remain to be tested in court. In her complaint, she said she had remained silent for a long time in the hope of saving her marriage and family. Her photograph travelled. In the coverage that reached my own feeds, I saw her face and not his. I was relieved she was heard, and uneasy about what comes next. Because what happens after we call a woman brave?
"Brave" can be praise. It can be solidarity. In British usage, depending on the tone, it can even carry a faint sting: You are brave to do that. Meaning, perhaps, I certainly would not.
I have spent decades supporting disadvantaged women from different backgrounds to name what happened to them. Yet I have also stayed silent when many respectable men wronged me in many ways, including matters of money. I knew how paperwork and friendships could line up. Was that cowardice or calculation?
What I keep wondering about is the afterward. The remand ends. The news cycle moves on. Who sits beside her at work on a Monday? Who asks what she did to provoke it? What does a woman owe the public once she has become a headline? These questions have followed me under a title I gave myself: falsified feminist.
By "falsified" I mean the self that edits, conceals and weighs every word. It is not an accusation against feminism. I turn it on myself because I notice the distance between the woman who speaks in public and the woman who measures her language when the subject comes too close to home. That distance is rarely forgiven. The intimacy is always forbidden.
We do not ask every man who writes about morality to be a saint at home, or every human rights lawyer to have a flawless family life. Yet a woman who speaks about equality is expected to demonstrate it perfectly in the most private corners of her life. I do not believe every private truth must become public. Confidentiality and secrecy are not the same thing. Confidentiality can be an ethical choice, a protection offered to another person or to oneself. Secrecy can be imposed by shame, fear or the demand to protect the family's reputation.
Aik chup sau sukh: one silence, a hundred comforts. Taali dono haathon se bajti hai: it takes two hands to clap. We teach the "good girl" not to speak, and expect her to carry the khandaan ki izzat on her shoulders, as though family honour were packed into the few inches of her female body. I know women raising children born of rape, and that is before we count marital rape.
In many homes, even today, a dead daughter is preferred to a divorced one. There are exceptions, but they remain exceptions.
When a woman screams, someone does the math. What will it cost her family, her job, her children's marriages, her name? In our part of the world izzat (honour) works like currency, and it is the woman who pays, whether she speaks or keeps quiet. Whatever she does, a label is waiting. Call it my shorthand history: say no in the 1600s and you were a witch; in the 1800s, unladylike; in the 1900s, hysterical; in the 1970s, frigid; by the nineties, a bitch; in the 2010s, bossy. In 2026, we have become gentler and simply say "difficult" and leave it there.
Violence against women is everywhere, and many countries treat it as their own private embarrassment. What gets reported is only the tip. The distance between what happens and what gets counted is where izzat does its work. Even the tip has a class. A few cases become names we all know; the rest remain a line in a report. The woman with a surname, a lobby, a donor, who speaks the language of the press club, is more likely to be remembered. I am not against anyone's fame. Every scream that gets heard helps all of us.
Behind the activist, researcher and inspirational survivor is a more inconvenient woman. She may still be angry. She may not yet know what she thinks.
Women should not need to be "allowed" that unfinished state. So which feminism do we need? The visible kind, which gives other women courage but can cost the speaker her safety? Or the careful kind, which protects her and leaves the silence intact? Should I suspect we need both? I believe we also need to question feminism more loudly, beyond the restrictions of sanitised Urdu, immaculate English and rigid frameworks for getting donors' funds. And perhaps we need to stop judging women by which one they can afford. Visibility is easiest for those who can survive it. A photograph, once published, cannot be taken back.
So, am I brave, or a falsified feminist? I do not know yet. Or was it a British insult, sir? Survivors are not diplomats. They do not have to be politically correct. I would rather be as truthful as I can, even when some truths must stay private.

title: Civilisationalism and the future of the world order
description: Civilisationalism and the future of the world order
content:
Modern world came to believe that innovation and globalisation had diminished geography's constraints
Sir Halford Mackinder argued in the early 20th century that geography matters because location shapes power. More than a century later, this fundamental principle of geopolitics remains as relevant as ever. As far back as the fifth century BC, during the Peloponnesian War, Sparta occupied the Dardanelles to deny Athens access to imported grain. The strategic logic of controlling geographical chokepoints has endured across centuries, even as technology has transformed warfare, communication and commerce.
The modern world came to believe that innovation and globalisation had diminished geography's constraints. That assumption is now being challenged. Geography is returning with a vengeance. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the prospect of disrupted maritime traffic through Bab-el-Mandeb expose the vulnerability of a globalised economy that depends on the uninterrupted flow of energy, goods and trade. These geographic chokepoints suggest that while globalisation has integrated economies across borders, the great powers have struggled to reconcile their pursuit of national interests with their responsibility for sustaining the global order on which their own prosperity depends.
The US and its allies constructed the post-war international order around the twin principles of primacy and restraint. Today, however, the limits of American power in the Persian Gulf have raised fundamental questions about the credibility of US primacy. The inability to guarantee the security of American military installations in the region, coupled with the difficulties of confronting Iran through conventional military means, has exposed a widening gap between Washington's global ambitions and its capacity to translate military superiority into strategic outcomes. The US now faces the formidable task of reshaping the global economic and geopolitical order, a challenge increasingly framed as the basis of a new American grand strategy. But does Washington possess the political resolve, economic resources and military capacity to undertake such a project? And can it secure the cooperation of allies and partners whose support would be indispensable to its success? During the Cold War, the containment of communism provided a strategic purpose around which the US mobilised an extensive network of international support. The global war on terror subsequently offered another organising framework for American power, with achievement of varying degrees of results. Can Washington generate comparable support for a strategy aimed at reconfiguring global geoeconomics and geopolitics in an era when hybrid warfare, grey-zone competition and the weaponisation of economic interdependence are increasingly shaping international relations? The challenge is no longer simply whether the US can exercise primacy, but whether it can convert that primacy into a sustainable global order.
American grand strategy has historically been organised around an identifiable adversary. During the Cold War, it was the Soviet Union and the ideological challenge of communism. In the aftermath of 9/11, it was the threat of terrorism, increasingly framed through the lens of the Islamic world. Today, Iran, as the principal state representing Persian civilisation, and Russia, engaged in a war on the European theatre, appear to occupy central positions in a broader strategic contest over the future of the global geopolitical and geoeconomic order. When Marco Rubio declared that "we must fight to defend Western civilization with the same passion as our forefathers did", his words evoked the language of a civilisational struggle reminiscent of the Crusades. Yet the question that such rhetoric raises is whether the defence of civilisation is being invoked to uphold universal principles or to legitimise the pursuit of geopolitical interests. The conduct of any civilisation must ultimately be measured against the professed principles of the pursuit of truth, the recognition of human dignity and worth, and the rule of law. By these standards, the US, despite its unrivalled position during the unipolar moment, has repeatedly faced questions about the consistency between its declared values and its actions as a global hegemon. Meanwhile, Washington's defence and security strategies have identified China as a major geopolitical challenge of the 21st century. Beijing, therefore, has reason to view the unfolding crises in the Middle East and Ukraine not merely as separate regional conflicts, but as potential stages in a wider strategic contest. Once Washington has addressed these theatres, China may find itself at the centre of the next phase of American strategic competition. The dilemma is that a strategy intended to preserve a particular vision of global order may instead widen the divisions between civilisations and accelerate the very geopolitical fragmentation it seeks to prevent.
The Cold War demonstrated that the world can remain relatively peaceful when deterrence holds and competing powers recognise the costs of confrontation. Deterrence, however, rests on two essential elements: capacity and credibility of will. Both are increasingly under strain in the present international order. The difficulties faced by the US and its allies in deterring Iran, alongside their reluctance to confront Russia directly, have raised questions about the credibility of Western deterrence and Washington's ability to dictate the outcomes of these conflicts. How the US responds to these challenges will help determine the kind of international order that emerges.
It is in this context that I propose civilisationalism as a work in progress, a potential theoretical framework for understanding a less hegemonic and more pluralistic world. Its central proposition is that major powers should recognise the civilisational spheres within which their historical, cultural and strategic interests are concentrated, pursue peaceful coexistence and cooperation across these spheres, and abandon the ambition of imposing a single model of global leadership. No civilisation should claim an exclusive right to organise the world in its own image. The irony facing the US is that it may strengthen its claim to leadership not by insisting on being first, but by accepting that it cannot, and perhaps should not, lead everywhere. America may have to learn to put itself second in the pursuit of a shared global order. If it insists on remaining first, it must relinquish the ambition of exercising universal leadership and make room for a civilisational order founded on mutual restraint, sovereign equality and peaceful coexistence. Such a transition would not eliminate competition or conflict, but it could offer the world a more sustainable alternative to the endless struggle for global primacy.

title: The hidden burden of being a man
description: The hidden burden of being a man
content:
Every morning, on my way to work, I notice a shopkeeper from the neighbourhood dropping a woman off nearby. One day, out of curiosity, I asked him who she was. He replied that she was his sister, who worked as a schoolteacher. Knowing that he worked long hours, I casually asked when he usually closed his shop. His answer surprised me: "Around 3 am."
Yet, every morning, at approximately 7:20 am, he was there to drop his sister off at work.
For a moment, I was speechless. Here was a man who barely had time to rest, yet made sure his sister reached her workplace safely. What struck me even more was his reaction when I appreciated his efforts. His face lit up. A simple acknowledgment seemed to mean more to him than I had imagined.
That encounter stayed with me. It reminded me how many sacrifices men make for their families without seeking recognition. Sometimes, even a few words of appreciation can reveal how rarely their efforts are acknowledged.
In our society, the pressure to provide begins early. By adolescence, boys are often reminded that they must eventually support their parents, siblings, spouses and children. While women's economic roles are changing and many also carry financial burdens, earning is still treated as a non-negotiable duty for men. The freedom to explore interests and dream about the future can give way to worries about employment, income and dependants.
For many middle-class men, most of what they earn goes towards rent, groceries, education, healthcare and family obligations. They may keep little for themselves, yet take pride in sharing what they have. Their contribution becomes so routine that the sacrifices behind it disappear from view. Not every man fulfils these responsibilities, of course, but many quietly do.
This expectation also shapes career choices. A young man may abandon an ambition, not because he lacks talent or passion, but because a safer profession promises financial stability. What others call a sensible decision may involve the loss of a deeply cherished dream.
We increasingly tell men to express their emotions. Films and public conversations challenge the image of the endlessly strong, silent man. Yet our everyday reactions often deliver the opposite message. A man who speaks about financial difficulties risks being labelled incompetent; one who discusses marital problems may be mocked. Men who experience domestic violence may remain silent for fear of humiliation or threats to their masculinity. Even physical illness, anxiety and emotional exhaustion can become subjects they feel obliged to conceal.
How can we ask men to be emotionally open while punishing them for vulnerability? Silence may look like strength, but sometimes it is simply self-protection.
The expectations continue after work. Men should share parenting and household responsibilities; that is essential to fair and caring families. But we can recognise women's unpaid labour without overlooking a father's long working day, his involvement in raising children, or his care for ageing parents. Many men move between being employees, husbands, fathers, brothers and sons, while also hearing that they must contribute to the progress of society.
This is not about denying women's struggles or competing over who suffers more. Women and men face different pressures, often simultaneously. Recognising men's burdens should expand our compassion, not diminish anyone else's experience.
I am thinking of ordinary men around us: shopkeepers, teachers, office workers, fathers, brothers and neighbours. We value what they provide, but how often do we ask how they are coping? A society that praises male responsibility must also make room for male vulnerability.
We need homes where boys can admit fear without ridicule, relationships where men can discuss conflict without shame, and communities where asking for psychological support is not seen as weakness. Acknowledgment cannot solve every hardship, but it can make a person feel seen.
I return to that shopkeeper in my thoughts. His kindness towards his sister was ordinary to him, yet it revealed something important to me: some of the greatest acts of care are the ones we have stopped noticing. Men, too, deserve appreciation, dignity and support - not only for what they provide, but for who they are.

title: Ceasefire fa  ade
description: Ceasefire fa  ade
content:
Israel's continued military aggression has rendered the ceasefire little more than a diplomatic facade
A ceasefire under which children continue to be slaughtered is an affront to humanity and a mockery of international diplomacy. More than 340 Palestinian children have reportedly been killed in Gaza since the cessation of hostilities was announced over a year ago. Hundreds more have been wounded, some permanently maimed. That Israeli strikes and gunfire continue to claim innocent lives while the world speaks of peace is a disgrace that should weigh heavily on the conscience of every government that endorsed the agreement.
Israel's continued military aggression has rendered the ceasefire little more than a diplomatic facade. Its repeated invocation of security concerns cannot justify the killing of children or diminish its obligations under international humanitarian law. The very idea that a ceasefire can coexist with the routine killing of civilians exposes the dangerous double standards governing the treatment of Palestinian lives. Particularly disturbing is UNICEF's finding that nearly half of the children reportedly killed since the truce have died near the so-called Yellow Line demarcating Israel's military presence. A boundary drawn on a military map cannot become a licence to kill. Nor can the alleged violations of a ceasefire by one party provide the other with immunity from accountability. Equally reprehensible is the international community's willingness to tolerate this continuing brutality. The powers that brokered and celebrated the ceasefire cannot absolve themselves of responsibility merely because an agreement was signed.
What is required is sustained diplomatic pressure and credible consequences for violations of international law. Above all, Israel must be compelled to cease unlawful attacks and permit the unrestricted delivery of essential humanitarian assistance. The world cannot continue congratulating itself on a peace process that has left Palestinian children exposed to death and deprivation.

title: New name plate
description: New nameplate
content:
The government's reported plan to create a new tax collection agency - or at least restructure the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) - may be the best example of 'old wine in a new bottle' that we have seen in years. The FBR has many problems. It is on course to miss this year's target by an estimated Rs650 billion, its tax-to-GDP ratio is stuck at 10.3%, and it fell short of last year's original goal by over Rs1.1 trillion. The agency also needs better leadership. But it doesn't need a new name, just as the 2007 name change in 2007 - from Central Board of Revenue to FBR - only massaged a dictator's ego with little net gain in the eyes of the public.
Other half-baked attempts at change have included a Rs55 billion "transformation plan" launched in 2024, and the caretaker government's efforts to carve out Customs from Inland Revenue. Each exercise promised efficiency, even though it left the core problem intact - the tax base is still narrow, enforcement against powerful interests remains weak, and the compliance culture punishes the documented while the undocumented flourish. Critics have also noted that reforms often include glaring loopholes, since honest efforts to fix the system would also mean withdrawing billions of rupees worth of unnecessary perks and privileges.
Instead of the massive overhaul needed to improve the workings of the tax authority, we are getting the same dynamism from 2007 that saw the FBR Act introduced with no attempt to actually make the agency more effective.
But at least the FBR has put one concerning rumour to bed - namely, that tax collection could be outsourced. As for the perceived positives in the proposal, there is a case to be made for structurally separating audit, assessment and enforcement to curb collusion. But these things can be done within the existing framework. Instead of new organisation charts, the FBR and policymakers need to focus on enforcing the law equally, digitising without loopholes and stopping treating tax reform as a donor-pleasing ritual.

title: Sisyphus in the land of saviours
description: Sisyphus in the land of saviours
content:
Saviours make yet another of two groups - the rulers and the ruled - in the country
Ever since humankind has been on Earth, people across time and space have tried to overcome trials and make life worthwhile. In their respective times and contexts, societies attained a relative stability. As a result, the trials that the earliest humans underwent have largely gone, only to be replaced by new sets of challenges today. Notwithstanding the universality of hardship, societies tend to navigate it and attain shared prosperity. They abhor hardship and tend to selflessly lend a voice and a helping hand should any individual or group have their rights usurped or marginalised. For them, crises are opportunities in disguise, should they be learnt from. And gradually, these societies, however plagued by crisis, overcome them.
Why have we, as a society, failed to navigate, let alone address, the crises in our 79 years of existence? Why does the country's struggle throughout its history resemble Sisyphus's struggle, with the boulder repeatedly tumbling back into the abyss? Much like elsewhere, crises and issues are deemed opportunities in our part of the world as well, though for a different purpose. Elsewhere, miseries might be abhorred, pitied and empathised with; here they are manufactured, celebrated and cashed in on. This makes the issues facing individuals and society not only a source of ascent to power but also of locking the people's fate in crisis. That is, a society that tends to seek and cash in on issues, both at the individual and collective level, is set to multiply and deepen them. This is because issues serve multiple purposes.
First, they offer the ruling elite a justification to scapegoat their predecessors and an exemption from addressing them. Second, the endurance of issues is a pretext for the policy failures of the government. Third, they offer a chance to exploit them and allocate funds for redressal only to squander them. Fourth, issues afford a ploy to enact self-serving policies under the pretext of necessity. Fifth, they help secure and sustain the stakes of the ruling elite and shield them from potential accountability. Sixth, masking the existing issues paves the way for new ones to be created and exploited. Seventh, the perpetuity of the crises facing the country ensures the people keep struggling for survival, neutralising any threat to elite capture. Last but not least, crises spawn a class of opportunists disguised as saviours, who, owing to their proximity to people, serve the interests of the elite by keeping people in check at the grassroots level.
The saviours make yet another of two groups - the rulers and the ruled - in the country. These include the bureaucracy, pliant media-persons, clergy, pirs, feudal and tribal warlords, civil society, feminists, supposed human rights activists, liberals and the intelligentsia, labour and civil rights movements, nationalists' groups and unions at different levels. Notwithstanding their promises, most are embedded in the system. They bargain away the rights of the people they pretend to represent and thereby strengthen the stakes of the elite capture. This, over time, worsens the plight of the oppressed and simultaneously adds to the stakes of the mediating redeemers and their patrons.
Also, Fake saviours trap people in a state of helplessness. They act as a firewall between the oppressors and the oppressed and ensure that the aggrieved neither seek redressal against their oppressors on their own nor come out of dependence on them. This way, the saviours keep them struggling at the bottom of Maslow's hierarchy of needs. The ones who truly care for the people either lose any meaningful position from which to serve the oppressed or get branded with heresy or unpatriotic awards.
The damage runs deeper than the original oppression. The aggressor takes away rights, but the fake saviour takes away the hope of having them defended. Where there is grievance, there is now a market for its representation. The victim's pain is the raw material, and the saviour is the broker who processes it, packages it and sells it upward.
The one thing the victim never receives is the finished product: justice.

title: Ambassador Sheikh calls for stronger Pakistan US tech collaboration
description: Highlights Pakistan   s IT sector potential and calls for greater US investment in emerging technologies
content:
Highlights Pakistan’s IT sector potential and calls for greater US investment in emerging technologies.
Pakistan’s Ambassador to the United States, Rizwan Saeed Sheikh, has highlighted the potential for mutually beneficial investment and cooperation in emerging technologies, urging Pakistani and American businesses to strengthen partnerships and expand collaboration in the technology sector.
Speaking at Pak-US Tech Connect 2026 in Silicon Valley, Sheikh underscored the importance of strengthening economic engagement between the two countries through technology, innovation and entrepreneurship.
He highlighted Pakistan’s information technology sector and encouraged greater collaboration between businesses in the two countries to develop mutually beneficial partnerships, expand market access and promote investment in emerging technologies.
Read : Ambassador Sheikh urges Pakistani-Americans to drive 'mutually rewarding' economic engagement
The event was aimed at promoting cooperation between Pakistan and the United States in technology, innovation and digital enterprises.
Tech Connect 2026 marked the third edition of the Tech Investment Conference series launched by the Embassy of Pakistan and Pakistani consulates general in the United States in coordination with the Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB).
The latest edition began in Silicon Valley, with subsequent events scheduled in Dallas, Washington, D.C., and Chicago on Oct 19, 21 and 23, respectively.
The Silicon Valley event brought together representatives of Pakistani technology companies, industry leaders, entrepreneurs and other stakeholders to explore business opportunities and strengthen links between Pakistan’s technology sector and the Silicon Valley ecosystem.
The programme featured presentations by leading Pakistani IT companies, discussions on potential collaborations and an exchange of experiences on promoting and scaling technology businesses in the US market.
Discussions highlighted Pakistan’s growing IT sector and its potential as a destination for technology partnerships, investment and digital innovation.
A panel discussion titled “Pakistan to Silicon Valley — Building and Scaling Global Tech Companies” examined the challenges and opportunities involved in entering the US market, securing enterprise customers, scaling global teams and adopting emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.
Also Read : Pakistan envoy to US briefs University of Hartford students on diplomacy, peacebuilding
A fireside chat also explored business opportunities in the US technology sector.
In his closing remarks and keynote address, Sheikh reaffirmed the embassy’s commitment to facilitating long-term links between businesses and technology stakeholders in both countries.
He said initiatives such as Pak-US Tech Connect provided a valuable platform to showcase Pakistan’s technological capabilities, supported by its demographic advantages, and foster innovation-driven partnerships as a pillar of sustainable economic ties between the two countries.
The ambassador also urged members of the Pakistani diaspora and professionals in Silicon Valley and the US West Coast to join efforts to position Pakistan as a cost- and quality-competitive technology destination.

title: 50 Cent opens up about Diddy  Trump and his fallout with  Power  creator Courtney Kemp
description: The interview comes as Jackson continues to draw attention for  Sean Combs  The Reckoning
content:
The interview comes as Jackson continues to draw attention for 'Sean Combs: The Reckoning'
50 Cent is reflecting on some of the most controversial relationships and defining moments of his career, discussing his long-running feud with Sean “Diddy” Combs, his falling-out with Power creator Courtney Kemp and the discovery that his late mother was gay.
In a new interview with Variety, the rapper and television producer, whose real name is Curtis Jackson, also discussed his expanding entertainment empire and his role as Balrog in the upcoming Street Fighter film. Now 51, Jackson has moved beyond his music career to become a major television producer, with projects spanning scripted dramas, documentaries and several networks.
The interview comes as Jackson continues to draw attention for Sean Combs: The Reckoning, the Netflix documentary series he executive produced about Combs. Jackson said he was not surprised by the impact of the project and credited showrunner Alex Stapleton with shaping the documentary into a compelling account of the allegations and perspectives surrounding the former music mogul.
Jackson also discussed his strained relationship with Combs, claiming the music mogul had attempted to damage his reputation behind the scenes. He alleged that Combs sought to find people who would make what he described as “frivolous accusations” against him, suggesting the efforts were intended to undermine his credibility as scrutiny of Combs intensified.
Jackson has been a vocal critic of Combs for years, and their feud gained renewed attention following the release of Sean Combs: The Reckoning. Jackson said the documentary could have become overly aggressive but credited Stapleton with allowing people to share their own perspectives. Combs has faced multiple allegations of sexual misconduct, which he has denied in various legal proceedings. Jackson's claims about an alleged smear campaign remain his account of events.
The rapper was equally candid about his falling-out with Courtney Kemp, who created Power and worked with Jackson as an executive producer. He credited himself with helping secure the series' success through his music, promotional efforts and business decisions, arguing that their partnership became increasingly difficult after the show became a hit.
Jackson said he felt Kemp had begun to minimise his contributions to the series, despite his involvement in pitching the project and developing its musical identity. He also discussed disagreements over the direction of the wider Power franchise, including the decision to expand the original series into multiple spin-offs.
Kemp disputed Jackson's recollection in a statement to Variety, saying he was rarely involved in budget meetings and describing his account of production requirements as uninformed. She acknowledged his importance to the show's beginnings but stressed that he did not write or create Power. Kemp added that she had moved on professionally and questioned why Jackson continued bringing her up in interviews.
The interview also touched on Jackson's childhood and the loss of his mother, who died when he was eight. He described the experience as one of the most painful periods of his life, explaining that he struggled to understand that she would not return.
Jackson additionally reflected on learning from his grandmother that his mother was a lesbian. He said that, as a child, he had simply viewed the women around his mother as friends before later understanding their relationship.
“I'm not ashamed of that in any way,” Jackson said, adding that growing up around those relationships had shaped his perspective. He also discussed expressing that experience through his music, including the lyrics of “Hate It or Love It”, which touch on the confusion he experienced as a child.l
On politics, Jackson discussed his approach to navigating relationships with both sides of the political divide. Asked about Donald Trump reportedly offering him millions of dollars to attend or perform at rallies, Jackson said he tries to remain politically independent and does not necessarily understand every position taken by either party. He explained that his perspective on politics is also influenced by the realities of running businesses and creating jobs.
Alongside these personal revelations, Jackson discussed his expanding slate of television and film projects. He is preparing a Hulu docuseries about his own life and continues to develop projects connected to the Power franchise, while also working on Fightland, his British boxing drama.
His latest film role is Balrog in the upcoming live-action adaptation of Street Fighter. Jackson revealed that he trained for three hours a day over nine weeks to prepare for the part, dropping from 238 pounds to 200 pounds. He also discussed the character's distinctive hairstyle and the physical demands of filming the fight sequences.
The interview offers a glimpse into how Jackson has built a business empire while remaining an outspoken figure in entertainment. From his disputes with fellow industry figures to his reflections on family and identity, the rapper continues to draw on his personal experiences as he expands his work across music, television and film.

title: Mahershala Ali breaks down recalling emotional Moonlight scene
description: You see this like crisis for this young boy who s already in crisis     Ali said
content:
“You see this like crisis for this young boy who's already in crisis,” Ali said
Mahershala Ali became emotional while revisiting one of the most heartbreaking scenes from Moonlight during a conversation at the BFI London Film Festival, where the Oscar-winning actor reflected on the film's enduring impact and offered a cautious update on his role in Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse.
Speaking during a Screen Talk hosted by Amon Warmann on October 17, Ali discussed the 2016 drama directed by Barry Jenkins, which earned him his first Academy Award for his portrayal of Juan, a drug dealer who becomes a father figure to a young boy named Chiron. As he recalled one of the film's most powerful moments, the actor struggled to hold back tears.
The scene that moved Ali features Chiron asking Juan during a dinner-table conversation whether he sells drugs. Reflecting on the moment, Ali described the heartbreak of watching a child already struggling with his circumstances confront the reality of the adult he has come to trust.
“You see this like crisis for this young boy who's already in crisis,” Ali said, describing the scene as heartbreaking.
When Warmann asked why Moonlight continues to resonate with audiences a decade after its release, Ali paused as he became overwhelmed with emotion, wiping away tears before continuing.
The actor explained that the film's ability to give humanity and depth to people whose experiences are often overlooked is part of what makes it so meaningful. He also drew on personal memories when developing Juan, using the example of a man he had known since childhood who served as a father-like figure in his neighbourhood.
Ali recalled that the man, who had played basketball with him and worked as a substitute teacher, was eventually imprisoned while Ali was still in college. The experience influenced how he approached Juan, helping him understand the complexity of people whose lives cannot be reduced to a single label.
The conversation also touched on Ali's experience following his success with Moonlight and his subsequent role in Green Book, for which he won his second Academy Award. The actor acknowledged the controversy surrounding the 2018 film, particularly criticism related to its portrayal of pianist Don Shirley and the concerns raised by Shirley's family.
Despite the backlash, Ali said he continues to stand by his work on the film and the experience of making it. He also reflected on the difference between professional achievement and personal fulfilment, explaining that winning consecutive Oscars gave him a sense of accomplishment without necessarily providing lasting satisfaction.
The discussion eventually turned to Ali's upcoming animated project, Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse, in which he is expected to reprise his voice role as Aaron Davis, also known as the Prowler.
Ali was careful not to reveal details about the highly anticipated sequel, particularly when asked how he distinguishes between different versions of the character in the Spider-Verse. “I don't want to give anything away or spoil anything, I've got to be careful,” he said.
When pressed about whether he had completed his voice-recording sessions, Ali jokingly replied, “I might not even be in it, man! I don't know, man! I don't know!”
The comments offered little concrete information about the film but highlighted the secrecy surrounding the next instalment of Sony's animated superhero franchise. Ali previously voiced Aaron Davis in Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, while a different version of the character appeared towards the end of Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse.
Ali also discussed the demanding production schedule of HBO's True Detective, recalling how filming the first season's three timelines required extensive hours and lengthy sessions in the make-up chair. He described the experience as exhausting, particularly while balancing the demands of the production with family life.
The actor is currently appearing in HBO's crime drama Task alongside Mark Ruffalo and has also been promoting his film Your Mother, Your Mother, Your Mother, directed by Bassam Tariq.
As Moonlight marks its 10th anniversary, Ali's emotional recollection serves as a reminder of the film's lasting influence and the deeply personal experiences that can shape an actor's performance. Meanwhile, his guarded comments about Beyond the Spider-Verse leave fans waiting for more details about his return to the animated franchise.

title: French police clash with protesters as tens of thousands rally over cost of living
description: Interior Ministry says 272 people had been arrested by mid afternoon
content:
Interior Ministry says 272 people had been arrested by mid-afternoon
Clashes broke out between police and protesters in cities across France on Saturday as tens ​of thousands of people angered by rising costs and declining public services took to the streets in some of the country's most violent protests in years.
The ‌Interior Ministry said 272 people had been arrested by mid-afternoon after violent incidents involving hooded individuals, including in Paris, Marseille in the south, Toulouse in the southwest, Angers in the west and Lyon in east-central France.
The protesters said most people were protesting peacefully and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police.
The ministry said, however, that violence ​was increasing, and that there had been "confrontations with law enforcement, looting or attempted looting of shops, attacks on and damage to public buildings". It blamed the ​unrest on what it described as the "ultra-left".
In some parts of Paris, police occasionally fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face ⁠of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas.
Read: India's 'cockroach' movement founder released a day after detention
Some tourists at a fashionable department store near the ​Paris opera were seen spluttering when they were caught in clouds of tear gas, and shops nearby were hastily shuttered. Windows of many shops and restaurants in the capital were ​smashed, and cars and trash cans were set on fire.
In Lyon, protesters torched the tourist office.
In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalised and that additional police were being sent to the city following talks with the government.
In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people also protested in Brussels on Saturday, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they ​are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
Albania also faced more protests on Saturday, with police firing what appeared to be ​rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
The protests in France began last month at high schools ‌in Paris' ⁠poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.
Read more: Greta Thunberg joins French teens on new day of school protests
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.
A large police presence had been deployed in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as ​the Champs-Elysees and the Arc de Triomphe, ​which were excluded from the routes of ⁠two authorised demonstrations.
Protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked President Emmanuel Macron's previous term in office.
Macron, who urged calm on Friday, is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France's ​efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than two ​decades.
Police tactics have drawn ⁠criticism following a series of injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said more than 900 police officers had also been injured in previous protests.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence. France suspended the use of stun grenades during the student demonstrations, but Interior Minister Laurent ⁠Nunez said ​they could be used on Saturday.
The Yellow Vest movement emerged in 2018 in opposition to diesel taxes before ​expanding into a wider protest against living costs and inequality. The movement subsided after Macron announced billions of euros in tax cuts.

title: Islamabad ATC sends former G B CM Khalid Khurshid to jail on 14 day judicial remand
description: Rejects police request for 30 day physical remand in case over Nov 26 protest
content:
Rejects police request for 30-day physical remand in case over Nov 26 protest
An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Saturday rejected the police’s request for physical remand of former Gilgit-Baltistan chief minister and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) leader Khalid Khurshid and sent him to jail on a 14-day judicial remand.
Khurshid, who was arrested by the federal police, was produced before ATC Judge Abul Hasnat Muhammad Zulqarnain. The police had sought a 30-day physical remand, but the court rejected the request and ordered that he be sent to jail on judicial remand.
A case has been registered against Khurshid at Islamabad’s Aabpara police station in connection with a protest held on Nov 26.
Read : Former G-B CM Khalid Khurshid sentenced to 34 years
In December 2024, an ATC sentenced Khurshid to 34 years in prison on charges of threatening security agencies.
The charges stemmed from an incident on May 26, 2024, during a PTI public gathering, where Khurshid allegedly threatened G-B’s chief secretary, chief election commissioner and security agencies.
Khurshid had served as the chief minister of the region from 2020 until his disqualification in July 2023. His removal from office followed a ruling by the G-B Chief Court, which disqualified him for submitting a fake degree during his nomination process.
The degree, purportedly from the University of London, was later verified as fake by the Higher Education Commission after a formal inquiry.
Khurshid, who joined PTI in 2018, had risen to the position of divisional president of Diamer-Astore. His involvement with PTI has also led to his booking in multiple cases, including charges related to the party’s protests at D-Chowk in Islamabad in October.

title: ATC summons Islamabad IGP in Imaan  Hadi bail case on November 3
description: Issues show cause notices to SP  DSP for failure to produce case record
content:
Issues show-cause notices to SP, DSP for failure to produce case record
An Islamabad anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Saturday summoned the Islamabad inspector general of police (IGP) for the November 3 hearing of a post-arrest bail petition filed by Imaan Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha and issued show-cause notices to the superintendent of police (SP) and a deputy superintendent of police (DSP) over the investigating officer’s repeated absence and failure to produce the case record.
The ATC was convening a hearing of a post-arrest bail petition filed by Imaan and Hadi in a case involving protests and interference in official duties in Islamabad.
The court also warned that the concerned officers could face proceedings leading to imprisonment if the record was not presented at the next hearing.
Judge Abul Hasanat Muhammad Zulqarnain heard the bail petitions of Imaan and Hadi. Their lawyers, Raja Ali Azad and Eimal Khan Mandokhail, appeared before the court, while Special Public Prosecutor Raja Naveed Hussain was also present during the hearing.
Read: Ministry of Law issues notification for jail trial for Imaan, Hadi
During the case proceedings, the court grilled the prosecutor about the investigating officer’s absence, asking where he was and why he was not present. The court’s reader informed the judge that the IO had gone to Gilgit-Baltistan and had not yet returned.
The court subsequently summoned the SP investigation.
Islamabad Bar Council Vice Chairman Advocate Asif Irfan told the court that it was not helpless and yet it had been unable to summon the case record.
During the hearing, Advocate Azad stressed that the bail petition had been filed on October 29 and the court had issued notices, but proceedings could not move forward because of the IO’s long absence. He said that in several similar cases, when the IO was unavailable, another police official brought the record to court.
“How long would the court wait for the record?” he asked.
He then presented arguments before the judge and reminded the court about its own order that the suspects' physical remand was not required and all the charges against his clients were bailable.
He further highlighted that section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had also been added to the case and urged the court to decide the matter in accordance with the law.
During the hearing, the lawyers also referred to judicial policy, citing that bail petitions should be decided within four to five days. They said the delay was creating the impression that the accused would first be convicted in the trial of another case and then the bail petition would be decided. They stressed that the impression needed to be dispelled.
Read more: Imaan, Hadi boycott proceedings as ATC records witness statements
Advocate Aleem Abbasi urged the court to exercise its powers and decide the matter on merit.
He said the legal fraternity stood with the judiciary for its independence and warned that if the courts did not exercise their powers, everything would be taken away.
“Lawyers raise slogans for justice but are unable to secure justice for their own children,” he said, urging the court to decide the case according to its conscience.
During the case hearing, Advocate Zafar Khokhar also asserted that the lawyers would present their arguments and leave, but the situation would not create a favourable impression of the judiciary. He asked which rules and laws allow the IO to take the case record on a vacation with him.
In response, Judge Zulqarnain said the SP and DSP could be sent to jail if the case record was not produced and issued show-cause notices to both officers. He also summoned the Islamabad IGP for the next hearing.
The hearing was then adjourned until November 3.
Separately, the court ordered the discharge of workers arrested in connection with the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf long march from the cases registered against them.
It also granted bail to Jammu Kashmir Democratic Party Chairperson and Advocate Nabeela Irshad against surety bonds of Rs5,000.

title: Egypt s Sisi seeks parliament s backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked
description: Says Egypt ready to defend Saudi Arabia if asked  as Houthi attacks on kingdom escalate
content:
Says Egypt ready to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, as Houthi attacks on kingdom escalate
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, ​amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom, and parliament announced ‌an emergency session on Sunday.
"It is inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, its security or stability to be harmed," Sisi said at a graduation ceremony ​at the Egyptian Military Academy. He said Egypt was not seeking ​to attack anyone, but was prepared to act in ⁠defence.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the ​state oil giant Saudi Aramco , amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of ​the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce.
Read : Iran offers help to end Saudi-Houthi conflict through dialogue
Sisi said Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin ​Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited, ​to discuss issues including security and navigation in the Red Sea.
"I know this requires ‌the ⁠approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I ask that an emergency session be held so that it can give us that authorisation if we are asked," Sisi said.
Shortly after he spoke, parliament said it would ​hold a plenary ​session at 1pm (1000 GMT) on Sunday in response to the request, though it did not disclose the agenda.
Egypt and ​Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi ​Arabia and ⁠other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist president Mohamed ⁠Morsi ​in 2013.
Egypt also joined the Saudi-led coalition ​that intervened in 2015 to support the Yemeni government against the Houthis.

title: Billy Crystal reveals his honest reaction when Rob Reiner offered him  When Harry Met Sally  role
description: It was difficult in that I was not his first choice for Harry     Crystal said
content:
“It was difficult in that I was not his first choice for Harry,” Crystal said
Billy Crystal has opened up about how he landed his iconic role in When Harry Met Sally..., revealing that his close friend and director Rob Reiner initially considered several other actors before offering him the part.
In an exclusive interview with People, the 78-year-old actor reflected on the making of the beloved 1989 romantic comedy and his creative partnership with Reiner, who died alongside his wife, Michele Singer Reiner, in December 2025.
Crystal admitted that learning he was not Reiner's first choice to play Harry Burns opposite Meg Ryan's Sally Albright was difficult, although he understood why his friend wanted to explore other options.
“It was difficult in that I was not his first choice for Harry,” Crystal said.
The actor recalled accepting that Reiner needed to consider different performers for the role. Albert Brooks, Tom Hanks and Michael Keaton were among those reportedly considered for the part before Reiner ultimately approached Crystal.
“I said, ‘Listen, when he wants me, if he wants me, then he wants me. But I know he's seeing other people, which he should do,’” Crystal recalled.
When Reiner eventually called, he reportedly reassured his friend that he had always envisioned him playing Harry but wanted to see other actors first.
Crystal's response was characteristically humorous. After Reiner asked him to read the screenplay, the actor joked that someone had secretly given him the script and that he did not like it. The pair then burst into laughter before discussing how they could approach the film.
“I have a lot of ideas,” Crystal remembered telling Reiner. The director responded by suggesting they begin working the following day.
Crystal ultimately contributed significantly to the film's dialogue and character development, bringing his own ideas to Harry rather than simply following Reiner's interpretation.
“It was great to do them because Rob was Harry,” Crystal explained, referring to the director's personal connection to the character. Reiner was going through a divorce from actress and filmmaker Penny Marshall during the film's development, experiences that helped inform Harry's emotional journey.
Crystal said he eventually had to tell his friend to step back so he could develop his own interpretation of the character. Reiner understood the request, allowing the actor to bring his perspective to the role.
Some of the romantic comedy's most memorable moments also emerged from their conversations outside the screenplay. Crystal recalled regularly speaking to Reiner late at night, with their discussions inspiring scenes that became central to the film.
One example was the sequence in which Harry and Sally watch Casablanca together over the phone from their separate apartments. Crystal said the idea drew on his frequent late-night conversations with Reiner while the director was navigating his personal life.
The pair also developed the film's famous exchange about a headache and the possibility of having a tumour. Crystal recalled Reiner complaining about a headache during a phone call and dismissing the suggestion that he see a doctor because he expected the doctor would tell him it was nothing.
“And it's one of my favourite little exchanges,” Crystal said. “That was pure us.”
Released in 1989, When Harry Met Sally... became one of the most celebrated romantic comedies of its era. Written by Nora Ephron and directed by Reiner, the film explores whether men and women can maintain a friendship without romantic feelings eventually complicating their relationship.
Crystal's performance helped establish Harry Burns as one of the genre's most recognisable characters, while the film's dialogue and New York setting have kept it popular with audiences across generations.
Reflecting on the collaboration, Crystal's memories highlight how his friendship with Reiner shaped the film beyond the casting decision itself. What began with uncertainty over whether he would get the role ultimately developed into a creative partnership that helped produce one of Hollywood's most enduring romantic comedies.
